This study addresses high-dimensional Schrödinger eigenvalue problems using two-layer neural networks. We establish an upper bound for the expected generalization error of test functions, considering both bounded and unbounded data, derived from the neural network's parameters. Our findings indicate that the error bound relies on the training set size but remains independent of the input dimension, thereby confirming the absence of the curse of dimensionality for these problems. Additionally, we derive an upper bound for the generalization error of test functions regarding the run-time complexity of network evaluation. These results are supported by examples and numerical simulations. As a contribution to applied statistics, we offer new insights into the error analysis of machine learning methods applied to partial differential equations. Furthermore, our approach to estimating generalization error for test functions extends beyond standard linear regression and falls outside the scope of classical statistical learning bounds, which typically depend on sample size, hyperparameter selection, and network configuration. We also examine specific choices for kernel functions and activation maps, demonstrating their impact on generalization error estimates. Finally, our error bounds for both eigenvalues and eigenvectors are derived without relying on assumptions about the ground state. To our knowledge, this is the first application of neural networks to PDE-driven eigenvalue problems. Our methodology and error bounds are expected to be applicable to a broader class of PDEs. The entire codebase is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/akaramitsos/ML-Eigenvalue}. Understanding the link between a neuron's activity and its function is a primary objective in systems neuroscience. This study presents a data-driven approach to modeling neuronal dynamics, utilizing the *Caenorhabditis elegans* (*c. elegans*) as a model organism. We introduce techniques for analyzing and modeling neuronal activity, including the reconstruction of neuronal signals (Ca²⁺ traces) from spiking data (*C. elegans* neurons convert Ca²⁺ traces into spikes via an unknown process) through the application of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN). Furthermore, we developed a method to generate data from virtual neurons, enabling the investigation of the relationship between a neuron's connectivity and its activity. This work offers a modeling framework for neuroscience that complements traditional experimental approaches, leveraging data-driven methods to address complex biological questions. The *c. elegans* worm, being one of the simplest organisms, makes it feasible to reconstruct the complete neuronal connectome and reconstruct neuronal activity throughout the entire brain. We have also made our code and dataset publicly accessible. We demonstrate that the stable point forest exhibits an ergodic regionally independent limit. In this limit, marked points within any bounded region behave independently as if generated by a stable process with index $\alpha = 1$, while the marked points of regions outside the region under consideration remain invisible. This result provides a rigorous foundation for the intuitive expectation that the stable point forest is regionally limited. Additionally, we present several corollaries and examples derived from this finding. Notably, we establish the regularity of the Poisson stable process in the one-dimensional case and confirm that the stable point forest is also regionally limited in this dimension. Furthermore, we illustrate how the stable point forest can be approximated by stable processes applied to finite subsets of infinite sets of increasing size, where these sets become increasingly dense as size increases. We also show that applying the stable point forest map to the product of two Poisson point processes yields regionally independent factors, and that the stable point forest can be constructed as the limit of a sequence of functions, each mapping the product of specific processes to a regionally independent process. Finally, we derive the weak star convergence from the regional limit and utilize it to prove that every probability measure on the space of marked configurations that is regionally independent and invariant under marked graph isomorphisms must be the Poisson stable process. The proof also reveals that the stable point forest is the unique marked graph isomorphism invariant measure on marked configurations that is regionally independent and has finite expected degree. Additionally, we establish that the Poisson stable process is the only such measure with an infinite expected degree. These properties of the stable point forest follow directly from its construction. We also examine the marked configuration properties of the stable point forest, such as its clusterness, and derive properties of the Poisson stable process, including its clusterness, from them. Specifically, we show that the Poisson stable process possesses the largest possible cluster size among all regionally independent processes that are stable under marked graph isomorphisms and have finite expected degree, and it is the only such process with a cluster size exceeding one. We also note that while the Poisson stable process is regionally limited, it lacks the property of being rapidly decaying. We identify all robust Gelfand pairs (G,H) for SL(2,p), where G is an finite subgroup of SL(2,p) and H is a subgroup containing the center of G. We also demonstrate that if H lies within a Borel subgroup of a group G in SL(2,p), it cannot form a robust Gelfand pair with G. Furthermore, we determine the corresponding regular functions and their degrees, and derive a formula for the absolute value of the Casimir element of any irreducible representation restricted to SL(2,p) when limited to a subgroup. Finally, we calculate the relevant parameters for all groups and subgroups of SL(2,p) that appear as robust Gelfand pairs. This work serves as a precursor to extending these results to the classical groups SO(n,q), SU(n,q), and Sp(n,q).

This research investigates hidden-charm molecular pentaquarks possessing single strangeness. We examine their molecular structures, mass spectra, magnetic moments, and form factors. Our findings indicate that the magnetic moments and electromagnetic form factors for these single-strange molecular pentaquarks can be accurately derived from their magnetic content. Furthermore, these electromagnetic properties offer a pathway to explore the internal arrangements of their constituent quarks. Finally, we suggest that experimental initiatives, such as LHCb, LHCb-SQ, and PANDA, should prioritize the study of these hadrons with single strangeness. This effort will enhance our understanding of their molecular structures and challenge existing theoretical predictions regarding their mass spectra. Additionally, this work aims to stimulate further investigation into these dynamically generated exotic hadrons. **Keywords:** hidden-charm molecular pentaquarks; single strangeness; mass spectra; magnetic moments; magnetic content; electromagnetic form factors; QCD sum rules.**Keywords:** hidden-charm molecular pentaquarks; single strangeness; mass spectra; magnetic moments; magnetic content; electromagnetic form factors; QCD sum rules.

We demonstrate that any Zinbiel algebra $U$ over a field with characteristic not equal to 2, when equipped with the bracket operation $\left[x,y\right]=xy-yx$, satisfies the abelian Jordan identity and constitutes a nilpotent Jordan algebra of step 3. Furthermore, if the Zinbiel algebra is nilpotent of step 2, the resulting Jordan algebra is also nilpotent of step 2. Additionally, we establish that any Zinbiel algebra $V$ defined over a commutative ring is both commutative and associative. Finally, we provide an example of a Zinbiel algebra $W$ over a field of characteristic 2 that is not abelian, noting that its associated Jordan algebra is likewise non-abelian. This example is constructed as the tensor product of the Zinbiel algebra $K[2,1,1,1]$ and the commutative nilpotent algebra $K[0,1,1,0]$ for any commutative ring $K$. Consequently, the characteristic of the underlying field is a crucial factor in the nilpotency of both the Zinbiel algebra and its induced Jordan algebra. All definitions, theorems, and examples are supported by references. Notably, some of these results were previously presented without proof or as conjectures in the literature. Specifically, examples of non-abelian Zinbiel algebras were cited without justification, and it was conjectured that their associated Jordan algebras are nilpotent. We conclude by listing several open problems and areas for future research. We establish global-in-time scattering theory for nonlinear Schrödinger equations featuring an inverse square potential. These equations are homogeneous yet critically nonlinear, rendering standard scattering results inapplicable. To address this non-stability while maintaining homogeneity and invariance under spatial translation, we adopt a new variational framework based on the spectral properties of the Hamiltonian. This approach offers an alternative to current nonlinear dispersive techniques. Within this study, we construct a minimal model integrating our variational method with nonlinear resonance to present a comprehensive picture of scattering phenomena. Specifically, we examine a cubic heterogeneous equation where the Hamiltonian's spectrum exhibits an essential singularity at zero energy. This spectral characteristic complicates scattering theory by preventing the use of perturbation arguments, as heterogeneity cannot be treated as a small disturbance of the homogeneous case. The proposed model incorporates essential spectral effects through resonant nonlinearities and demonstrates scattering in all spatial dimensions. Furthermore, we investigate the role of critical nonlinearity by presenting an infinite family of scaling-invariant nonlinearities; within this family, we identify a critical exponent that separates three distinct regimes of scattering behavior. Finally, we analyze the relationship between Hamiltonian spectral properties and scattering, highlighting intriguing connections between scattering theory and spectral theory. These findings are anticipated to offer novel insights and significant perspectives for future research in this domain. Our work introduces a new paradigm for analyzing scattering in heterogeneous nonlinear Schrödinger equations and provides a robust framework for studying spectral geometry. This framework is expected to serve as a valuable tool for addressing complex spectral problems in theoretical physics. Additionally, we aim to contribute to the ongoing effort to understand how geometric and topological irregularities in heterogeneous media influence wave propagation. By demonstrating that this specific type of irregularity does not hinder scattering, we offer a significant contribution to this ongoing discussion. Our methodology is expected to provide a solid foundation for future investigations into how various forms of irregularity affect scattering phenomena. Overall, this work represents a significant advancement in our understanding of wave behavior in irregular environments and marks a crucial step toward achieving our long-term objective: developing a unified theory of wave propagation in heterogeneous media. Such a theory would not only deepen our fundamental comprehension of physical phenomena but also drive innovation in emerging technologies, including metamaterials and photonic crystals. Furthermore, it would provide a powerful tool for addressing complex real-world problems in fields such as seismology, acoustics, and medical imaging. This study integrates a SIR model with an ordinary differential equation system to track how an infection spreads within a community as a function of the cumulative migration volume from other regions. The research examines the stability of this system and determines the thresholds for in-breaking and out-breaking of infection processes. These findings are validated through two case studies: the migration and infection dynamics involving the SARS-CoV-2 virus and COVID-19. The methods employed are straightforward, utilizing systems of ordinary differential equations, while the theoretical outcomes are accessible to the general public. Consequently, this work establishes a foundation for forecasting the trajectory of migration-induced infections. Specifically, it identifies the critical points at which migration triggers an infection outbreak and the levels at which the infection curve begins to decline. Furthermore, the study explores the feasibility of using migration as an effective strategy to diminish the total number of infected individuals. The analysis concludes that if the cumulative infection rate in the source region is low, migration can significantly lower infections in the destination; however, if the infection rate is already high in the source, migration may exacerbate the situation and increase the number of infected individuals in the target area. Ultimately, this approach offers the potential to mitigate the adverse effects of migration on infection spread. Additionally, the model is applicable to various other migration and infection scenarios, such as the transmission of the flu. K2-138 serves as a prime example of an exoplanetary system hosting multiple transiting planets. Although previous studies identified a 3:2 mean motion resonance (MMR) between planets c and d, the dynamical stability of the full system has not been thoroughly examined. This work employs the PyDYN code to analyze the stability of K2-138 across various initial conditions, specifically investigating 3:2, 2:1, and first-order (k=1) MMR configurations. Our findings indicate that both the 3:2 and 2:1 resonance sequences remain stable for at least 1 Gyr, while the k=1 MMRs are unstable within 10 Myr. Additionally, we present new estimates for the initial orbital parameters of K2-138. We conclude that the initial configuration of K2-138 most likely involved planets b, c, and d trapped in a 3:2 resonance chain, with planet a occupying an eccentric orbit outside this chain. This setup is supported by the fact that the initial semi-major axes of planets b, c, and d differ by no more than 10%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a 2:1 resonance chain involving planets a, b, and c is unlikely, as it would require planet a to have an eccentricity exceeding 0.1. We also explore the formation history of K2-138, suggesting that its initial architecture may have included up to eight planets. Finally, we discuss the prospects for detecting MMRs in other exoplanetary systems using the PLATO mission. Specifically, we show that PLATO can identify 3:2, 2:1, and 4:1 MMRs for systems with radii larger than 0.7 R☉, provided the planets have masses greater than 2.5, 1.5, and 2.5 M⊕, respectively. This capability is illustrated using the exoplanetary system HD 106906.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.01.0

In the classical limit, these applications recover analogous results from Brundan and Kleshchev. Additionally, our combinatorial description is shown to correspond to Leclerc's description through the Leclerc-Schiffmann correspondence. The SiD detector design was originally proposed in the early 2000s as a readout system for an international 1 TeV e+e- collider. Since that time, significant advancements have occurred in SiPM technology, SiPM arrays, and SiPM-based detector concepts. These developments have motivated a review of SiPM readout as a potential external layer for the ATLAS and future e+e- collider detectors. This paper presents a conceptual design for a SiPM-based outer electromagnetic calorimeter (EMC) optimized for maximum granularity, superior spatial resolution, and precise photon conversion tracking. The design incorporates a pad readout structure, the dimensions and performance of which are evaluated based on simulation studies. Additionally, the feasibility of this concept is analyzed in the context of its implementation for the ATLAS upgrade and as a standalone outer detector for an e+e- collider. The study concludes that a SiPM-based SiPM-dimensional (SiD) EMC and conversion tracker pad plane could achieve energy resolution better than 1% and spatial resolution under 1 mm. Furthermore, such a SiD-style detector could be successfully deployed at an ATLAS-based e+e- collider operating at center-of-mass energies ranging from the $\Upsilon(4S)$ for B physics to multi-TeV scales for precision Higgs and new physics research. This work is prepared for publication in the special issue of JINST commemorating 20 years of the ATLAS collaboration. This document is also available on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.07002. In 2018, the observation of diffraction peaks from ice nanodroplets frozen within aluminum matrices suggested the existence of crystal-like regions within what was intended to be an amorphous ice sample. Inspired by the recent discovery of crystalline domains in hyperquenched water-ice at room temperature, the present study aims to identify the crystalline regions responsible for the earlier diffraction signal. To achieve this, we conducted annealing experiments on the ice nanodroplets and subsequently investigated the ice-aluminum interface using aberration-corrected transmission electron microscopy. Our findings indicate that the ice nanodroplets exhibit a high density of defects, which we attribute to the amorphous nature of the ice-aluminum interface. Furthermore, our results suggest that the ice nanodroplets are largely amorphous, lacking the crystal-like domains that the diffraction experiments had previously indicated. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the discovery of water ice in outer space. This research focuses on the visualization and analysis of the Local Density of States (LDOS) for the surface layers of silicon, gold, and graphite using Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM). While earlier studies have employed high-resolution STM to map the LDOS of silicon and gold, this study extends such analysis to graphite for the first time. Graphite is particularly significant because its electronic structure is primarily governed by the $\pi$ orbitals of carbon atoms. Scanning Tunneling Microscopy operates by scanning a conductive probe over a conductive sample surface; in this configuration, the tunneling current is influenced by the LDOS of both the tip and the sample. Although high-resolution imaging of gold and silicon surfaces has previously revealed features linked to their respective LDOSs, the connection between image characteristics and the sample's LDOS was not explicitly established. This work addresses that gap by correlating high-resolution STM images with the LDOSs of gold, silicon, and graphite. The findings demonstrate that STM images are directly associated with the LDOS of the sample, confirming that tunneling current is driven by the sample's LDOS. These results offer critical insights for interpreting scanning probe microscopy data, especially when analyzing data acquired at atomic resolution. Furthermore, the study confirms that Scanning Tunneling Spectroscopy (STS) can successfully measure the LDOS. STS involves positioning a sharp tip at an atomic site within an STM image and varying the bias voltage to measure the tunneling current. STS measurements on gold, silicon, and graphite successfully identified the symmetry of the LDOS and determined the band gap of silicon. Collectively, the evidence confirms that STM imaging and STS are capable of visualizing the LDOS of atomic-scale materials. This capability holds great promise for nanotechnology, as the LDOS influences the functional properties of nanomaterials. Understanding the LDOS is therefore essential for designing nanomaterials with tailored functions. Future applications of STM and STS in visualizing the LDOS will facilitate the development of nanomaterials with specific electronic and optical properties. Additionally, STM imaging of the LDOS will serve as a valuable tool for understanding the behavior of nanostructures during nanotechnological processes. Ultimately, scanning tunneling microscopy will play a pivotal role in nanotechnology by providing a direct visualization of the local electronic structure of materials. This ability will enable scientists to identify the optimal locations for attaching nanoparticles to functional components, such as nanoswitches and nanotransistors, thereby enhancing their performance. Human involvement remains essential in formally proving mathematical theorems, specifically within the proof verification stage. While computers handle the statement of lemmas and proofs using tools like Isabelle, human experts are needed to examine these proofs to ensure their authenticity, a task that demands significant effort. Our objective, supported by the Principles and Principles for Software Engineering for Science (P4S), is to identify strategies for enhancing the efficiency of formal theorem verification. To achieve this, we developed AI-driven frameworks for verifying theorem validity, with detailed findings presented in our prior research. We applied these frameworks to 14,221 declared theorems in the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs (AFP), analyzing 286 pairs of related theorems based on their similarity, dependency, redundancy, and complexity. Our analysis revealed that most theorems either lack counterparts or depend on other theories, yet most can still be verified effectively. We introduce two novel approaches: RetProv and ThmGen. RetProv ensures the authenticity of existing theorems by converting verification results into machine-readable proofs within AFP, addressing issues such as missing theories, unavailable definitions, outdated notations, and unsatisfied type constraints. Conversely, RetProv also generates new proofs for newly added theorems across all relevant theories. ThmGen, on the other hand, automatically generates proofs for new theorems by leveraging the provenance knowledge of theorems in AFP. We propose that our frameworks can substantially improve the efficiency of formal theorem verification, a critical component of formalization. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our frameworks can scale to larger AFPs, such as those anticipated in the next Isabelle 2024 release. Finally, we discuss the practical implications of our frameworks for the community engaged in formalization.

The interaction between the solar wind and Earth's magnetosphere generates kinetic energy that drives the formation of the Earth's magnetic field within the solar wind environment. Fluctuations in solar wind velocity and magnetic field strength create variable magnetic field disturbances, known as ultra-low frequency (ULF) waves. These waves, which manifest as oscillations in the intensity of the magnetic field, typically fall within the human hearing range of 20 Hz to 20 kHz. This study aims to determine the optimal method for audibly representing the amplitude of ULF waves. Various conversion techniques were examined, including those relying on magnetic field direction (phase), different ULF wave intensities, and multiple scenarios involving magnetic field direction and intensity. The results indicate that when visualizing ULF waves audibly, a single conversion method based on magnetic field intensity is generally preferred. However, if the objective is to highlight the significance of both magnetic field direction and intensity, then utilizing conversion based on either direction or intensity (or both) becomes preferable. Consequently, the auditory representation of ULF waves should ideally be adaptable to accommodate diverse purposes and user needs. Finally, the paper proposes a universal, objective, and customizable ULF auditory visualization framework to facilitate the seamless interconversion between the visual and auditory dimensions of magnetic field data. This framework is designed to be easily extensible and customizable to support a wide array of applications. To demonstrate its effectiveness, two case studies were conducted using one-dimensional and two-dimensional data. The findings suggest that the ULF auditory visualization framework can enhance the accessibility of magnetic field data, particularly benefiting individuals who are visually impaired. Furthermore, it offers the potential to significantly improve the efficiency of data visualization analysis for both scientists and the general public. The ULF auditory visualization framework is anticipated to become a standard tool in magnetic field visualization software, thereby facilitating the auditory exploration of magnetic field data. Keywords: Magnetic Field, Accessibility, Auralization, Sound, Ultrasound, Ultralow Frequency.

This study investigates the classical dilaton-coupled nonlinear electrodynamics framework, specifically focusing on the impact of logarithmic nonlinear terms and rotational dynamics within a black membrane system. The analysis yields a new class of ionized, rotating, dilaton-coupled nonlinear electrodynamics black membranes. We examine the equation of state and thermodynamic properties, revealing that these membranes behave similarly to three-dimensional charged diluted black holes in the high-temperature regime. Furthermore, we verify that the membranes obey the first law of thermodynamics and satisfy the second law, thereby confirming the stability of this specific system. Additionally, we explore how rotational speed, charge, and other relevant parameters influence the thermodynamic characteristics of the membranes. Our findings indicate that these parameters significantly affect the system, with the most pronounced effects observed at low temperatures. Finally, through numerical analysis, we validate that a nontrivial temperature ensures the existence of a black membrane, and we confirm that all thermodynamic quantities remain finite. The logarithmic nonlinear term proves highly significant, with its most dramatic impacts evident at low temperatures. Finally, we demonstrate that various thermodynamic properties are highly sensitive to rotational speed, with the most pronounced influences occurring at very low temperatures. These conclusions are supported by numerical analyses of relevant parameters. Overall, this work introduces a novel class of solutions to dilaton-coupled nonlinear electrodynamics, which may hold potential for astrophysical applications. Additionally, the study offers a comprehensive framework for investigating the thermodynamic properties of various black hole solutions. Our research paves the way for further investigations into the physical properties of these objects. Additionally, our numerical framework establishes a foundation for exploring the astrophysical implications of rotating dilaton-coupled nonlinear electrodiction black membranes. Our findings may contribute to the broader understanding of astrophysical phenomena, including gravitational waves, accretion disks, and black hole mergers. Moreover, our work may aid in the search for exotic matter and its potential applications in advanced propulsion systems. Finally, our research may provide valuable insights into the behavior of matter under extreme conditions, such as those found near black holes, thereby advancing our understanding of fundamental physical processes in the universe. This could potentially lead to new discoveries in quantum gravity, high-energy physics, and cosmology. Natural language is inherently multi-dimensional and complex, making it difficult for machines to process without a method to capture this complexity in its information structure. We argue that recall taxonomies address this challenge by defining the multi-dimensional spaces of text through word classes and their interrelationships. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a processing framework rooted in recall can support various text-based applications. Specifically, the format of declarative queries within this framework enables the development of tools that produce human-readable, interpretable, and explainable text processing. The paper presents a text processing framework based on the eCARE system, which utilizes an information retrieval approach that models both word co-occurrence and co-annotation to capture semantic relationships between lexical units. This approach allows for the representation of dynamic and complex text information structures. QRecare, a web application for queries in the QCare system, illustrates the recall-based framework using example queries. These queries can define processing tasks within eCare, such as identifying relevant documents from an information retrieval database or retrieving semantic information about specific word classes from a knowledge base. The examples provided cover instances of word co-occurrence, equivalence, and hierarchy. By combining eCare with the qRecare web application, users can query the retrieval and knowledge components of the system, demonstrating the versatility of the recall-based framework. Ultimately, eCare and qRecare illustrate the benefits of a recall-based framework for integrating semantic and lexical information, whether derived from linguistic analysis or human judgment. Furthermore, the framework offers a pathway to making machine processing more interpretable and understandable for humans. While eCare focuses on information retrieval, the described framework is also applicable to other text processing tasks, including those in question answering and machine learning. We anticipate that this framework will facilitate the creation of more human-centric text processing tools that are interpretable and aligned with human understanding. Additionally, we aim to extend the framework to handle queries involving distributed semantic information across multiple dimensions. Overall, eCare and qRecare provide a practical example of a real-world implementation of a recall-based framework for text processing. This example highlights the advantages of the framework and suggests future research directions to further advance human-centric text processing. To support these future initiatives, eCare and qRecare serve as a valuable resource. Given that eCare is an open-source system, researchers can leverage it to continue advancing human-centric text processing. For real numbers $r$ and $z$ lying on the unit circle, we present a novel functor that maps the CCR or CAR algebra $G_r(\Gamma)$ associated with a locally finite abelian group $\Gamma$ to a Cuntz-Toeplitz algebra. This algorithm generates a continuous path of $C^*$-isomorphisms connecting the CCR algebra at $z=r=e^{i0}$ with the Cuntz-Toeplitz algebra. Consequently, these algebras are specifically connected through a continuous deformation. Furthermore, this process offers a conceptual framework for understanding and implementing the one-parameter automorphism group known as Bratteli's shift. This group, previously noted for its ability to distinguish the QCR and CCR sectors of a spin system, arises naturally as a byproduct of our main result. Additionally, this automorphism group can be interpreted as the shift operator acting on the one-leg representation of the CCR algebra. We also demonstrate that the Bratteli shift commutes with the described $C^*$-isomorphisms and preserve the internal structure of $\Gamma$. Finally, our method provides a new perspective on the QCAR and CAR algebras, revealing that they are also linked via a Bratteli shift within the fermionic setting. In this context, the shift operator acts on the charged sector, thereby restoring symmetry. This finding aligns with the QCAR interpretation of Bratteli's shift, where the charged sector is the unique non-trivial sector. We conclude by outlining a future research direction aimed at explicitly constructing this continuous path. Specifically, this path can be formulated as a continuous interpolation between two extreme cases: either between QCR and CCR algebras, or between QCAR and CAR algebras. This approach offers a new insight into the relationship between these fundamental algebras. Additionally, we detail various interesting subalgebras situated between them. This phenomenon underscores the need for a deeper investigation into the subalgebraic structure of CCR and CAR algebras. For instance, it would be valuable to explicitly identify which subalgebras remain invariant under the action of the shift operator. Moreover, exploring the dynamics induced by the shift operator on these subalgebras constitutes a promising avenue for future research. In summary, our work paves the way for developing new methodologies to investigate and better understand the structural properties of CCR and CAR algebras. GP 2 is a small-step operational semantics for the lambda calculus extended with control operators. Although GP 2 is known to be equivalent to weak head normal form operational semantics (which mirrors call-by-name evaluation), it offers distinct advantages. Specifically, it directly models call-by-value evaluation and simplifies the understanding of bridge rules. This paper introduces a small-step operational semantics for the lambda calculus with both call-by-name and call-by-value abstractions, demonstrating its equivalence to a unique weak head normal form operational semantics. To establish this equivalence, we construct an operational correspondence between weak head normal form operational semantics and mini-step (call-by-name) semantics using rewriting logic. The primary technique involves composing the target semantics with a guard that limits evaluation to weak head normal form evaluation. For the equivalence proof, we construct eponymous contexts that mediate between GP 2 and unique normal form weak head operational semantics. This construction relies on the concept of "eponymous lambda," which enables the definition of eponymous contexts through a simple matrix of lambda expressions. By proving that these eponymous contexts accurately represent evaluation contexts, we deduce the desired equivalence. The paper concludes with a discussion of these equivalence results and their applications. Notably, these findings can assist in formally verifying programming language transformations, such as those required to justify compiler optimizations. Furthermore, they support the formal justification of language extensions, for instance, when adding syntactic sugar. Finally, the equivalence results provide a foundation for developing formal proof tools, allowing users to directly invoke GP 2 and verify that programs are evaluated correctly according to specific semantics. This approach avoids the need to manually construct and verify each reduction step, thereby mitigating potential errors. To demonstrate the utility of GP 2, we have developed a prototype implementation of weak head normal form operational semantics using the Coq proof assistant. This implementation employs the mini-step semantics to verify the correctness of various syntactic extensions. Additionally, GP 2 is well-suited for mechanized proof construction due to its straightforward reduction rules and eponymous contexts, which facilitate the formal verification of various transformations. To illustrate, we present examples of verified transformations using Coq, including the justification of compiler optimizations and the formal correctness of syntactic sugar. In both cases, we provide Coq versions of GP 2 that verify the equivalence of specific programs before and after the application of transformations. This study focuses on the two-core symmetrical phase-angle regulating transformer, a device designed for emergency voltage regulation within high-voltage transmission networks. Unlike regulating reactors, which cause significant voltage drops, this transformer offers negligible voltage drop in normal operation while providing a regulation range of ±10%. By employing star-point angle regulation, it facilitates symmetric phase shifts in both directions, ensuring no zero-point voltage drop. Additionally, angle regulators feature low no-load power consumption.

To support these advantages, researchers have developed specialized designs, including regulating transformers with separate cores, shared cores, and tower-type configurations. The symmetry of regulation and phase shifts makes these devices ideal for compensating asymmetric voltage drops across power lines. This symmetry also enables their use in other applications, such as achieving emergency voltage adjustments through single-phase angle regulation, although this requires accepting a voltage drop at the zero-point.

Furthermore, the paper addresses the transients generated by phase shifting, analyzing their characteristics, magnitude, and duration. It also explores various suppression and safeguarding techniques tailored to the specific circuit conditions and the required degree of regulating transformer isolation. Given that the phase-shifted transients can be significantly more intense than those found in conventional transformers, special categorization and safeguarding measures are essential. These include the application of specific insulation coordination principles, the use of modern semiconductor switches like IGCTs, and the implementation of suitable protection systems.

The paper concludes by examining the current state of design and modeling practices, with a focus on safeguarding transients. Finally, it outlines potential future research directions regarding the utilization of these transformers in power transmission systems. These directions emphasize the need for more detailed design guidelines, the application of insulation coordination principles, the development of optimized switching strategies, and the advancement of simulation and modeling tools. Such efforts aim to ensure the safe operation of the system and extend the lifespan of the regulating transformer. Optimizing efficient data delivery to mobile users remains a critical challenge in cellular networks. To address this, multi-group broadcasting (MGB) leverages mmWave technology's massive beamforming capabilities to enhance hybrid encoding (HE) performance. However, HE's optimal design relies on precise knowledge of individual user channel states, a requirement that conflicts with the HE objective of reducing signaling overhead. Consequently, this study proposes a new method that bypasses individual channel state information by utilizing only aggregate data. This approach employs semidefinite relaxation to determine a robust beamforming matrix capable of effectively serving multiple user groups. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this method achieves near-optimal HE performance with significantly less overhead compared to traditional strategies. Furthermore, the proposed scheme supports data transmission to all users within a group once a single beamforming matrix is generated. Ultimately, this enables the simultaneous delivery of multiple data streams to users in the same group, thereby maximizing spectral efficiency in mmWave systems. Additionally, the paper introduces a low-complexity algorithm based on the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions to achieve these data transmission rates. Results indicate a substantial reduction in computational complexity, making the proposed HE method practical for real-world implementation. Notably, increasing the number of users per group further improves HE performance. Overall, this work provides a robust framework for multi-group broadcasting in mmWave systems. Additionally, the paper explores MGB applications in non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) and millimeter wave non-orthogonal multiple access (mmW-NOMA) networks. It is demonstrated that the HE-based beamforming matrix can facilitate data transmission to multiple groups within a single cell, thereby enabling efficient multi-user data delivery to maximize spectral efficiency. Finally, the work investigates multi-group non-orthogonal multiple access (MNG-NO MA) delivery, offering an efficient solution for multi-user data transmission in mmWave networks. The results illustrate that MNG-NO MA achieves optimal spectral efficiency by fully exploiting the spatial multiplexing gains of mmWave communications. Furthermore, this approach significantly outperforms conventional MGB-based data delivery methods. Ultimately, this research offers a novel and promising perspective for multi-group data delivery in mmWave systems. Finally, the paper outlines potential future directions for multi-group broadcasting. Notably, it suggests that MGB could play a pivotal role in next-generation cellular networks, including massive machine-type communications (mMTC) and ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC). A finitely generated group $G$ exhibits exponential residual finiteness expansion if there is a sequence of finite quotients $\langle G_i \rangle$ arising from normal subgroups where the growth of $|G/G_i|$ with respect to $|N_i|$ (where $N_i$ is the largest normal subgroup contained in $G_i$ with quotient size $e^{ei}$) is bounded by a constant. While it is established that every finite group is a quotient of a finite group sharing this expansion property, the existence of an infinite finitely generated group with this trait remained an open question. This paper resolves the issue in the negative by introducing a group $G$ where $G'$ is both finitely generated and free, demonstrating that $G$ possesses exponential residual finiteness expansion. Furthermore, it is shown that any group $H$ satisfying these conditions must admit such expansion, implying that no group with exactly "one" level of normal subgroups can achieve this growth pattern. Additionally, for any $k \geq 1$, there exists a group $G$ where the series of subgroups $\Gamma_i$ required to generate $G/G_i$ has an index sum bounded by $e^{ei+k}$ rather than $e^{ei}$; however, the groups in these examples are not residually finite. Finally, it is proven that if $H$ is residually finite and its series of finite quotients $\langle G_i \rangle$ displays exponential residual finiteness expansion, then $H$ itself must exhibit this property. It is conjectured that no group with a derived subgroup of rank 1 can possess such expansion, a claim further supported by the observation that no group with rank 2 can have $k$ levels of normal subgroups while simultaneously demonstrating exponential growth in the size of their largest finite quotients. Finally, for any $k \geq 1$, there exists a group $G$ where the series $\Gamma_i$ has section rank at most $k$ and maximal section rank at most $k+1$, with the quotients $G/\Gamma_i$ showing exponential residual finiteness expansion. The groups constructed in this example are not residually finite. This study investigates the stability of an elongated system comprising a coupled elastic (non-dissipative) component, modeled as a three-dimensional beam, and a dissipative component, represented by an ordinary mass. The boundary between these beams features a star-shaped graph, which induces graph waveguides; consequently, the boundary is non simply connected and possesses a non-trivial first homology group. Focusing on the longitudinal motion of the beams and the mass under small perturbations, we demonstrate that the system is unstable due to positive eigenvalues arising from the real spectrum of its linearization operator. These eigenvalues result from the specific geometry of the boundary graph. Furthermore, we establish that the linearization operator generates unbounded trajectories in homogeneous Sobolev spaces, thereby confirming the instability of the full nonlinear system under small nonlinearities. Additionally, the analysis reveals that the real spectrum of the linearization operator, derived from a system of differential equations, is not merely a singleton set, highlighting a significant distinction from systems modeled by partial differential equations. Finally, the problem of small nonlinearities serves as a motivation for employing a singular perturbation approach to analyze the boundary graph, a method designed to address the inherent limitations of local coordinates near such structures. This approach enables the investigation of the linearization operator's spectrum, which exhibits fractal characteristics within the complex plane. Specifically, the operator possesses a real spectrum composed of a fractal set and countably many points, alongside a purely imaginary spectrum with countable accumulation points at the origin. The fractal nature of the spectrum is a consequence of the star-shaped geometry of the boundary graph. Moreover, the real eigenvalues stem from a singular Sturm-Liouville problem, while the fractal spectrum of the operator on the star-shaped graph is linked to the fractal spectrum of the same operator when modeled as a system of ordinary differential equations. In both scenarios, these spectral properties are inherited from the one-dimensional operator defined on each branch. We provide a spectral analysis of the single-branch problem and its associated eigenfunctions. Additionally, the methodology developed allows for the examination of spectral properties when the star-shaped graph is substituted with other topologically equivalent structures. The paper also offers a comprehensive description of the ill-posed Cauchy problem for the nonlinear system, detailing the asymptotic behavior of the nonlinear system's solutions in homogeneous Sobolev spaces. The model's accuracy was validated against both training and independent testing datasets, with results compared to those of other ML approaches. The rate of decoherence in quantum systems is frequently governed by dielectric losses within nearby microwave cavities. This study presents the first precise measurement of sapphire's dielectric attenuation ($Q_{CSR}$), a standard dielectric material extensively used in superconducting quantum computing. We measured $Q_{SR}$ using a high-performance dielectric cryogenic sapphire resonator, achieving a measurement accuracy of 0.005 ppm. This exceptional precision allows for the first direct comparison of microwave dielectric attenuation across different materials, including silicon and quartz. The results indicate that sapphire exhibits the lowest microwave dielectric attenuation among tested materials, with $Q_{SR}$ ranging from 50 to 100 ppm at 5 GHz. These findings provide critical insights into the development of superior microwave resonators and substrates for advanced quantum technologies. Furthermore, the measurement techniques employed here can be adapted to enable future investigations into dielectric losses within quantum devices. Such capabilities would allow researchers to directly correlate system losses with specific materials, thereby facilitating targeted efforts to mitigate dielectric losses in quantum devices. The developed methodology also holds potential for advancing the understanding of fundamental material properties. For instance, it could enable the first measurements of how microwave dielectric attenuation in sapphire varies with temperature in the gigahertz range, a factor that is not yet well understood. This is particularly relevant for quantum computing utilizing gapped systems, where temperatures as low as 10 mK are becoming increasingly common. The proposed measurements are feasible using a recently introduced, highly precise and sensitive method for measuring dielectric loss in microwave circuits. This novel approach enables the first measurement of sapphire's dielectric attenuation with 0.005 ppm accuracy and can measure the quality factor of microwave resonators with 0.01% precision. These advancements offer unprecedented control over dielectric sources of loss in quantum systems, paving the way for the creation of high-performance dielectrics essential for next-generation quantum technologies. Additionally, the work demonstrates the viability of employing the microwave Brillouin scattering technique for dielectric characterization. This method allows for the investigation of dielectric properties at the GHz frequency, representing the highest frequency at which such measurements have ever been conducted. The concept of optical pulling forces is examined within both classical and quantum frameworks. In the classical description, the pull arises from the transverse momentum component, which is both non-local and non-conservative. In the quantum description, a similar phenomenon occurs, but the momentum is derived from the photon wave function rather than the electromagnetic field. In both scenarios, the pull extends beyond the region where the optical field is present. This indicates that the force is not solely contingent on the field but also involves non-local quantum nonlocal interactions between the particle and the vacuum. Consequently, the existence of optical pulling forces in quantum regimes cannot be merely reduced to their classical equivalents. Furthermore, it becomes feasible to simultaneously generate, manipulate, and detect pulling forces on a particle's translational, rotational, and vibrational degrees of freedom by appropriately designing the vacuum field. Finally, specific experimental protocols are proposed for observing these quantum optical pulling forces. Notably, such forces are predicted to be present in experiments involving nanoparticles and in setups utilizing surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy. However, it is crucial to emphasize that these forces are typically extremely weak, often weaker than any dissipative drag forces, which may render them difficult to detect experimentally. To address this, a corresponding theoretical framework for the quantum friction phenomenon is also provided. Ultimately, this work aims to deepen the understanding of momentum conservation, momentum dissipation, and the interaction between light and matter. Additionally, it serves to advance the emerging field of quantum nanomechanics, which is closely linked to quantum information and quantum computing. The study offers a new perspective for the quantum control of mechanical systems, such as nano-antennas and molecular rotors, and may facilitate the development of quantum nanomechanical sensors. These advancements could lead to breakthroughs in quantum force microscopy, quantum surface chemistry, and quantum molecular machines. This paper introduces two methods for addressing three-way robust optimization problems where the uncertainty set is defined by sparsely populated, binary uncertain parameters. We demonstrate that the Lagrangian dual of such problems can be formulated as a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) of comparable scale and complexity to the original. While the problem is generally nonconvex and NP-hard, we propose a sufficient condition that simplifies the Lagrangian dual to a convex linear program, a strategy that is particularly effective for highly sparse uncertainty. Furthermore, we develop an exact algorithm for the Lagrangian dual and a convex relaxation for the original problem. Numerical experiments on representative case studies validate our theoretical findings. Finally, we examine two application areas to highlight the practical utility of our methodology. Specifically, we analyze a unit commitment scenario characterized by uncertain generation costs and network loads, alongside a power system operator scenario with binary ambiguities regarding transmission line outages and capacity constraints. In both instances, our numerical results indicate that the proposed methodology yields promising outcomes. Finally, both applications can be integrated into existing decision-making frameworks to support human operators. The availability of multi-source, multi-modal, multi-distributional, and multi-view data has significantly advanced the fields of multi-view learning and data fusion. However, the complexity of the modern data ecosystem has introduced new challenges, particularly in the domain of urban computing. Existing open-access datasets often suffer from limitations such as small sample sizes, single-source and single-modal characteristics, and a focus solely on the physical environment, thereby restricting their utility in broader urban computing applications. This paper introduces H4M, the first large-scale open-access dataset designed for macro-level socioeconomic analysis. Comprising 10 million entries, this dataset offers multi-source, multi-modal, multi-view, and multi-distributional information specifically for Beijing. Its development required the integration of 17 distinct sources across three categories: communication towers, the Beijing Municipal Government, and the H4M research team. These sources yield 10 views across six sources and three channels, covering three aspects: communication, administrative, and research data. This work details the collection methodology and explores its potential impact on urban computing. Additionally, the dataset is released under the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) license to facilitate future research. It can be accessed at https://github.com/huawei-ost/Beijing_Dataset. Utilizing the H4M dataset will facilitate multi-modal, multi-view, and multi-distributional macro-level urban analytics. Furthermore, the collection methodology established in this paper will serve as a foundation for subsequent multi-modal, multi-source, and multi-view macro-level datasets. We anticipate that H4M will contribute significantly to both the theory and practice of urban computing. The primary research challenge associated with the H4M dataset is how to effectively leverage its multi-source, multi-modal, multi-view, and multi-distributional information for macro-level urban computing. This includes developing efficient data fusion and feature engineering techniques to extract features from various sources, views, modalities, and distributions, as well as ensuring data quality through the mitigation of noise, missing values, and errors. These multi-faceted features must then be combined to generate accurate and actionable insights for macro-level urban governance. This research direction is expected to yield multi-level, multi-source, multi-modal, and multi-view data fusion and feature engineering methods, alongside improved data quality and accuracy for macro-level urban computing. Furthermore, this approach will foster interdisciplinary research at the intersection of data science, social science, and humanities. This paper introduces VSDI, a system designed for the visual inspection of extensive flat schemas. In contemporary data-driven enterprises, transitionning from traditional to data-driven models has created significant challenges due to the vast volume and variety of flat files required to support business operations. While existing solutions primarily address data ingestion, integration, and indexing, they often neglect effective navigation and investigation of the resulting schemas. We propose leveraging visual techniques to facilitate the interpretation and exploration of flat schema structures. Our approach employs visual methods to manage the inherent volume of schema information and enables visual exploration through the exploration of schema properties and constraints. The paper presents the VSDI framework, which offers both an abstract framework and a framework of visual techniques, alongside a functional prototype that demonstrates how to apply visual techniques to the investigation of flat schemas. We illustrate the benefits of this approach with several practical use cases. Ultimately, this work demonstrates that visual techniques are highly effective for investigating and interpreting data schemas, thereby supporting initial data investigation and data integration processes. These insights address an often-overlooked aspect of data management, aiming to assist data professionals in managing and interpreting data sources. The paper concludes by identifying promising directions for future research, particularly in the application of visual techniques to data management systems. Graph Neural Architectures (GNAs) have recently gained significant attention for their ability to handle problems involving network-structured data. While transfer learning has proven effective for CNNs and Transformer-based models, its application within GNAs remains largely unexplored. This study investigates transfer learning across three key dimensions: data, and demonstration goals. Our experiments reveal that GNA-based transfer learning is most effective when source and target datasets exhibit strong structural similarities and only moderate differences in feature distributions. Furthermore, GNA transfer learning yields the greatest benefits for models with greater depth and those utilizing graph convolutional or attention-based mechanisms. Finally, we observe that GNA-based transfer learning excels in preventing overfitting on small demonstration goals, thereby surpassing standard fine-tuning approaches. Overall, GNA-based transfer learning serves as a promising strategy for mitigating overfitting in limited data scenarios and difficult feature distributions within GNPs. Additionally, we introduce GraphArena, a new benchmark suite designed specifically for evaluating GNA transfer learning. This suite encompasses four regression and one classification graph prediction tasks, covering diverse data types, sizes, and feature distributions. We have made GraphArena publicly available to facilitate future research in this domain. The entire codebase is accessible at: https://github.com/DeepMind/graph_arena. We introduce a fundamentally novel approach to the Set Disjointness problem, defined over the uniform product probability space for two $n$-element sets. Specifically, given $n$ distinct elements from $\{0,1\}^d$, the task is to determine whether the intersection of two such sets is empty or contains at least one pair of elements differing in at least $t$ positions. When $d$ is constant, this problem can be viewed as identifying the intersection of two data streams, where the stream elements possess specific privacy characteristics. We provide a purely combinatorial lower bound on the communication required for data streams to solve this problem. Furthermore, by integrating this combinatorial bound with existing results on data stream intersections, we establish a new, non-trivial lower bound for the $\ell_0$-approximate $k$-distinctness problem. This new lower bound surpasses all previously achieved bounds in the literature. Additionally, we investigate data streams composed of pairs $(i, v_i) \in [T] \times [U]$, where $T$ and $U$ may differ, representing a more general framework than the standard data stream intersection model. We demonstrate that our combinatorial lower bound extends to this generalized context. Finally, we prove that the $\ell_0$-approximate $k$-distinctness problem, when applied to this more general data stream model, yields lower bounds that strictly exceed all prior results for the distinctness problem on that model. This advancement stems from a novel extension of the $\ell_p$-norm framework to the broader data stream model. Notably, this work introduces the first lower bounds for the $k$-distinctness problem on the general data stream model, a model that has recently attracted significant interest. Our findings establish that the $\Omega(kn)$ lower bound is optimal for this problem. Furthermore, our general framework enables the first lower bounds for the $k$-distinctness problem on the fully oblivious data stream model, achieving an $\Omega(kn)$ lower bound. This result also resolves an open question posed by Moshkovitz and Ronen [Proc. 2019 ITW] regarding the feasibility of lower bounds for $k$-distinctness on the fully oblivious model. Finally, our results yield the first lower bounds for the $k$-distinctness problem on the fully oblivious data stream model when $U$ is significantly larger than $T$. The simultaneous presence of interactions and disorder in two-dimensional (2D) topological insulators can alter single-particle band structures, induce charge density waves, and generate nontrivial, quantized, and robust electrical conductance even without an external magnetic field. This phenomenon is termed the linear Hall conductance. Furthermore, when a finite DC electric field is applied, a transverse voltage can emerge due to the non-linear Hall effect observed in noncentrosymmetric crystals. Unlike the linear Hall effect, this non-linear Hall conductance lacks the protection of topological invariants. However, in the specific context of a non-interacting system with weak disorder, both linear and non-linear Hall effects have been demonstrated to remain quantized and robust through the phenomenon of Berry curvature polarization. This review examines both effects within the framework of interacting and disordered non-centrosymmetric crystals. It begins by outlining the non-linear Hall effect in the free electron model and its extension to the non-interacting regime, emphasizing the quantization arising from disorder and the instability of this quantization under electron-electron interactions. Subsequently, the article explores the effects in the renormalized single-particle limit, where interactions renormalize the band structure but do not drive the system into a new phase characterized by broken translational symmetry. Finally, adopting a fully interacting perspective, both linear and non-linear Hall effects are analyzed in a two-dimensional lattice model featuring electron-phonon coupling and disorder, resulting in the spontaneous breaking of translational symmetry and the formation of a charge density wave. In this phase, both Hall effects exhibit quantization, robustness, and periodicity. Finally, potential experimental realizations and future research directions are briefly outlined. We achieve a constant phase estimate for solutions of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation under a minimal smoothness constraint. The initial data must belong to the Besov space $B^{1/2}_{2,1}$ without imposing any conditions on the mass. This result is formulated using the recently developed "nearly linear" framework by Ginibre and Velo, which aligns with the approach of Colliander et al. Our proof relies on uniform bounds derived from dispersion, conservation laws, and Induction Steps, alongside an innovative application of Strichartz estimates near the diagonal. Furthermore, we extend the uniform dispersion bound to weighted $L^2$ spaces with sublinear weights, a crucial element in establishing the constant phase estimate. While the initial exposition targets the cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation in three dimensions, the argument extends to broader dimensions and power-law ranges. We anticipate that the "nearly linear" formulation will prove valuable in other contexts, such as proving global well-posedness or constructing scattering transforms. Finally, we demonstrate global well-posedness and derive a scattering estimate for the five-dimensional nonlinear Schrödinger equation with logarithmic nonlinearity, provided the initial data resides in $B^{1/2}_{5/6,1}$. This represents the first instance where such results are achieved with smoothness strictly below $1$. Additionally, we generalize the analysis to the vector case under the assumption of a power-type nonlinearity. The objective is to efficiently identify key equilibrium solutions using an adaptive regularizing term within a regularized kinetic model that incorporates these adjustments. This updated kinetic framework is subsequently discretized using the $\theta$-Runge-Kutta-Chebyshev scheme, which is adapted to a time-lag structure for the collision operator. The detection of multiple gravitational wave events that share similar characteristics offers a valuable opportunity to investigate the underlying physics of their sources. Such distinct properties may reveal details about the early universe, the formation of binary systems, and the specific mechanisms driving these events. This study examines the potential for the Horizon-10T network to identify and group such events. The analysis involves the creation of realistic simulations of binary black hole mergers, the application of realistic noise models to these waveforms, and the subsequent detection of these events within the Horizon-10T network. Finally, the event data is processed using a clustering algorithm to identify the various groups. The results indicate that the Horizon-10T network can detect and categorize between 10 and 20 Gravitational Wave events, depending on the specific event type. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the relative abundance of identified event types remains consistent across different time intervals, regardless of the specific clustering algorithm employed. Beyond the standard binary black hole waveforms, this work also investigates the potential of the Horizon-10T network to detect exotic phenomena, specifically self-confining axion quark nuggets. The findings suggest that the network could detect between 1 and 5 such events, contingent upon the specific parameter choices. Finally, it is concluded that the temporal distribution of both binary black hole and axion quark nugget events differs significantly, which may facilitate their distinction. These results collectively highlight the promising potential of the Horizon-10T network for the future study of gravitational wave events. Additionally, the entire codebase used in this study is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmed-omar/MBHClustering. Future efforts will expand this analysis to include additional event types, such as binary neutron stars and mergers involving exotic matter. Specifically, the temporal distribution of events from these other sources will be examined to determine if they can be differentiated from binary black hole events. Distinguishing between these various event types is crucial for understanding the unique physical phenomena associated with each. Furthermore, the detection of binary neutron star events is expected to be significantly lower than that of binary black hole events, primarily due to the greater rarity of neutron star systems. Consequently, the focus of this study remains on binary black hole events. However, the proposed clustering method is highly adaptable and can be readily extended to analyze other event types in the future. This paves the way for further research into the origins of gravitational wave events, their binary system formation, and the physical characteristics of the events themselves

This paper addresses time-fluctuating matrix problems, which encompass time-varying matrix equations (TVEs) and time-varying matrix equations (TVMs). Such dynamics frequently emerge in time-varying systems characterized by time-periodic parameters. To accelerate the design of zeroing neural networks (ZNNs) for handling these issues, zeroing calculations (ZNCs) are proposed. These ZNCs enable the rapid derivation of appropriate neural dynamics for solving time-fluctuating matrix problems. By utilizing ZNCs to define the evolution of error matrices, the proposed ZNNs ensure the exponential decay of these errors to zero. To enhance the practicality of these ZNNs based on ZNCs, three noise-robust extensions are introduced: zeroing neural networks with finite-time convergence (ZNTFCNs), zeroing neural networks with time-varying convergence (ZNTVCNs), and zeroing neural networks with asymptotic convergence (ZNTVCNs). The study begins by defining the core concept of ZNCs. Subsequently, the paper presents four representative cases of time-fluctuating matrix problems alongside their corresponding ZNNs. Finally, the validity of these approaches is verified through numerical simulations. The results demonstrate that the proposed methods offer a powerful framework for efficiently resolving time-fluctuating matrix problems. Notably, the application of ZNCs represents an original contribution to zeroing neural network theory. Additionally, the work expands the scope of ZNNs from time-invariant to time-varying contexts and introduces a novel concept to control theory. These contributions significantly advance both computational intelligence and control theory. Furthermore, the methodology holds significant potential for application across diverse computational intelligence domains, including fuzzy systems, evolutionary algorithms, and support vector machines. The underlying principles of this paper are also highly relevant to other intelligent computing fields such as machine learning, deep learning, and pattern recognition. Ultimately, these contributions are expected to foster significant innovations within those respective fields. The authors anticipate that this work will serve as a valuable resource for researchers in the domain. Finally, the paper concludes with an outlook on future research directions. Specifically, the authors aim to extend these results to discrete-time systems and time-delay systems in forthcoming studies. Additionally, there is a strong intention to apply these findings to nonlinear time-varying systems and nonlinear parameter estimation problems. Ultimately, the goal is to apply these methods to real-world applications involving time-varying parameters. Keywords: Time-varying parameters, Time-varying systems, Time

Training artificial neural networks (ANNs) to perform classification on raw images without significant preprocessing poses a significant challenge. We introduce a method that incorporates a spatial derivative filter into the initial layers of a convolutional neural network (CNN) to facilitate precise localization and robust recognition. This approach utilizes an optimized version of the difference of Gaussians (DoG) filter as a center-surround receptive field. The DoG filter serves as a mathematical approximation of the difference of Gaussians (DofG), effectively functioning as a Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) operator. Its role as a band-pass filter in frequency-domain image processing makes it an ideal tool for achieving precise localization, while the algorithm itself is computationally efficient and well-suited for deployment on resource-constrained hardware. Experimental results indicate strong performance when classifying raw images of handwritten digits and CIFAR-10. Our models achieved an accuracy of 98.2% for CIFAR-10 and 99.2% for the MNIST dataset. Furthermore, these models demonstrate resilience against common image distortions, including noise, rotation, scaling, and cropping. Finally, we provide a Ruby/C++ implementation of the receptive field optimization code, which can be integrated into existing CNN architectures. This implementation is available on GitHub at: https://github.com/akshaykothari/CSRF-receptive-field-optimization. A demonstration video of the model classifying distorted CIFAR-10 images is also available at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=14424222220. Our findings suggest that the proposed center-surround receptive field and spatial derivative filter are applicable to a broad spectrum of image classification tasks. Additionally, we outline potential extensions to the model, such as color image classification and object detection. Our ultimate aim is to enable precise localization and robust recognition for raw images in real-time applications using highly optimized Ruby and C++ versions of the model. These versions are designed for deployment on embedded systems, leveraging Ruby's extensive AI and machine learning libraries alongside C++'s computational efficiency. We anticipate achieving approximately 30 frames per second (fps) on a Raspberry Pi 4. To support further development, we have made the codebase for both Ruby and C++ implementations public on GitHub: https://github.com/akshaykothari/CSRF-receptive-field-optimization. We hope the Ruby and C++ communities will find this implementation valuable for their respective AI and machine learning projects. Our next steps

Broad-field x-ray optical components are experiencing growing demand from both established and emerging applications. These elements are currently utilized in existing instruments, such as hard x-ray imaging and microscopy systems, and are being integrated into new devices, including those for medical diagnostics and therapeutic radiation dosimetry. Additionally, they are a core component of emerging technologies like x-ray endoscopes and flexible lenses. This review examines recent advancements in the materials science and engineering practices necessary to boost the performance of broad-field x-ray optics. It addresses material properties and production methods for beryllium, amorphous and polycrystrine boron, and amorphous and polycrystalline aluminum. The primary objective is to analyze how the material characteristics and manufacturing techniques of these substrates influence the final instrument's performance. By providing this in-depth material and production analysis, the review aims to guide readers in selecting the most appropriate substrates for their specific x-ray optical applications. Furthermore, we analyze the reasons behind the declining quality of current beryllium foils and offer potential solutions to this challenge. Finally, we explore the emerging concept of formable liquid metal alloys as a viable alternative to traditional beryllium foils. This approach leverages the unique properties of liquid metals to overcome existing limitations and has the potential to significantly enhance the performance of broad-field x-ray optics. By connecting substrate material properties to instrument performance, this review offers a framework for advancing the field of broad-field x-ray optics. Ultimately, we propose a path forward for the development of next-generation x-ray optical materials. This will enable the realization of superior performance, lower costs, and greater accessibility for broad-field x-ray optical components. Such advancements are essential to meet the growing demand for these elements across various applications. Furthermore, this work seeks to inspire further research into novel materials that can continue to push the boundaries of x-ray optics. This is particularly relevant as the field moves toward increasingly miniaturized, lightweight, and energy-efficient systems. These developments aim to expand the capabilities of x-ray optics beyond their current limits. (For more information, see http://www.bxlens.com). This work investigates the electronic structure of twisted bilayer graphene under a strong magnetic field using a continuum model. We demonstrate that bilayer graphene exhibits reentrant graphene-like behavior at sufficiently field strengths by identifying reentrant $2\pi$ gaps within graphene's Dirac points on the $k$-lattice. Furthermore, we establish that bilayer graphene possesses $2\pi$-periodic energy bands separated by $2\pi$-periodic flat energy levels. These $2\pi$ gaps correspond to reallocated reentrant zero energy states, a phenomenon termed magnetic Bloch states. The twisted bilayer system is modeled as a bilayer with moiré potential, resulting in a reentrant bilayer band structure at high magnetic fields. Additionally, we derive analytic expressions for the $2\pi$ gaps and propose a classification scheme for these reentrant gaps. Finally, we show that within each $2\pi$ gap, the number of reentrant zero modes equals the index of that $2\pi$ gap. These reentrant reentrant zero modes are described by magnetic Bloch states and are derived from analytic solutions of the twisted bilayer graphene model. This discovery of reentrant bilayer electronic structures at high magnetic fields is attributed to the reentrant nature of both bilayer and graphene electronic structures under such conditions. Our findings may be of interest to experimentalists studying twisted bilayer graphene at elevated magnetic field strengths. Additionally, we provide an algorithm to identify reentrant $2\pi$ gaps in the electronic structure of twisted bilayer systems with time-reversal symmetry breaking. Our results may also be relevant to other twisted bilayer electronic systems, such as transition metal dichalcogenides and transition metal dichalcogenide heterostructures. Steganography involves concealing secret messages by embedding them within other text. While steganographic images are frequently investigated, textual variants are less common. Traditionally, methods for hiding messages in text rely on frequency encoding, which is difficult to execute effectively on a character-by-character basis. This study explores a character-level recurrent neural network (RNN) that incorporates attention mechanisms to facilitate message concealment in plain text without requiring frequency constraints. We evaluate this approach on English Wikipedia dump data, and although the method is not perfectly stealthy, we demonstrate that it successfully conceals messages in text with low mutual information with the hidden content. Furthermore, we detail how the model can be adapted to recover the hidden message from the encoded text. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/ahmed-ayoub/stega-lstm}. This work appears in the Proceedings of the 2019 Workshop on Neural and Representation Methods for Security, Privacy, and Robustness of Machine Learning at ACL 2019.
