This paper explores the properties of a hypersequent-based system, $LZIS$ (the hypersequent extension of $LZ\IS$), designed for fuzzy contraction-logic without structural rules, specifically within the interval $[0,1]$. We demonstrate that $LZIS$-falsity is both necessary and sufficient for $LZIS$-validity, ensuring that $LZIS$-semantics align perfectly with $LZIS$-proof theory. Building upon this foundation, we establish a hypersequent formulation of $LZIS$-contraction logic termed $LZIS^c$, proving that $LZIS^c$-semantics are equivalent to $LZIS^c$-proof theory. Additionally, we show that $LZIS$-contraction logic adheres to contraposition and possesses the decidability and PSPACE-completeness that characterize $LZ\IS$ (a substructural many-valued logic of degree $k$ without structural rules). Finally, we analyze $LZ\IS^h$, the hypersequent formulation of $k$-valued fuzzy contraction logic with full structural rules, and demonstrate that it also enjoys decidability and PSPACE-completeness. Notably, $LZ\IS^h$ represents the first known many-valued super-tarskian (i.e., complete, sound, and compact) substructural logic with structural rules that is both decidable and of PSPACE complexity. These findings extend prior results by Esteva and Schommers regarding $MV\IS$ and $LZ\IS$, as well as by Montagna concerning $W\IS$ and $LW\IS$. Throughout this work, we also address upper bounds on proof lengths and complexities, with decidability and complexity results following directly from these proofs. Finally, we present upper bounds on the complexity of $LZ\IS^h$ and $LW\IS^h$, the latter of which is the first substructural logic of degree $k$ without contraction that is both sound, complete, and compact over $[0,1]$ to be shown as decidable with PSPACE complexity. Importantly, $LW\IS^h$ is the first degree-based substructural logic with structural rules to achieve decidability and PSPACE-complexity, surpassing the PSPACE-limited $LZ\IS^h$. In both instances, these results also follow from the complexity analysis conducted herein

Although traditional methods assume that semantic relationships between classes are largely linear, recent advancements indicate that a hyperbolic structure often better captures the hierarchy and compositionality inherent in semantics. This study investigates how incorporating hyperbolic geometry can enhance representation learning for classification tasks. We introduce HyperExpan, a framework that combines Exponential Embedding Transformations with Discriminative Manifold Projection. By conceptually mapping class labels within hyperbolic space and strategically expanding their relative distances to boost classification margins, the framework separates classes using a hyperbolic structure rather than a Euclidean one. Additionally, Discriminative Manifold Projection is employed to balance the hyperbolic geometry inherent in class labels with learned representations, thereby boosting performance. Evaluated on text, object, and language tasks, HyperExpan demonstrates significant performance gains, achieving state-of-the-art results in few-shot scenarios on standard object categories. Furthermore, it attains performance comparable to leading methods while requiring less annotated data. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/peiyuan1998/HyperExpan. This study examines the effects of external electric fields on non-covalent interactions within the S66 basis set, a collection of 66 small molecules representing diverse weak molecular pairs, including both closed- and open-shell systems. The S66 dataset offers benchmark results for these pairs under zero-field conditions. The current investigation systematically analyzes the impact of applied fields on the potential energy curves of 12 representative molecules from this set. While the chosen field strengths remain significantly lower than those generated by atomic nuclei, they are strong enough to produce a substantial "electric field effect," a phenomenon of critical importance in chemical and biological processes occurring within strong intra- and intermolecular fields. Furthermore, we explore the field-induced modifications to the nature of non-covalent chemical bonds. Finally, we evaluate the efficacy of the CCSD(T) method and various density functional theory (DFT) functionals in accurately computing the energy of non-covalent interactions between electrically polar molecules subjected to strong external fields. This assessment utilizes the standard S66 benchmark data alongside our newly calculated benchmark results derived from coupled cluster methods incorporating external field effects. We demonstrate that the DFT-D3 method, enhanced with a counterpoise correction, offers a favorable balance between computational cost and accuracy for calculating weak non-covalent interactions in the presence of external electric fields. Furthermore, we show that the standard CCSD(T) method fails to adequately account for the energy of non-covalent interactions under external field influence. To address this shortcoming, we introduce a straightforward and efficient correction scheme that adjusts the CCSD(T) energy based on fields calculated at the B3LYP level. This two-level approach achieves a mean absolute error of approximately 0.2 kcal/mol when compared to the highly accurate CCSD(T') method, which was developed with external field effects incorporated from the outset. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings. In conclusion, the CCSD(T') method, combined with the fields-included DFT3 correction, is proven to be both accurate and computationally efficient for studying weak non-covalent interactions between polar molecules in strong external electric fields. The S66 dataset under external field conditions has been included in the S66ext database. Additionally, we provide a user-friendly, open-source Python program, S66ext-E, which employs the CCSD(T') + DFT-D3 + counterpoise correction to facilitate the straightforward calculation of non-covalent interaction energies. The 20th International Scientific Conference'20 Digital Intelligence and Applied Sciences featured a paper titled "Multi-Objective Industry 4.0 Scheduling with Non-Deterministic Ambiguity using Tabu Search." This work addresses scheduling problems within Industry 4.0 manufacturing environments, specifically focusing on job shop scenarios where operations possess non-deterministic durations characterized by ambiguity. Such ambiguity arises from dynamic factors like machine load fluctuations and network congestion, rendering deterministic models inadequate. The study investigates scheduling jobs and multi-mode operations under this non-deterministic ambiguity, utilizing a modified discrete event simulation (MDES) to generate scenarios and build a robust optimization model enhanced by a novel tabu search variant. A critical contribution is the introduction of a new dominance relation designed to strengthen the optimization framework. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through extensive computational experiments, which highlight the superiority of the proposed model over existing methods. The primary objective is to minimize the sum of weighted tardiness for jobs. The authors aim to contribute to the Theory of Computation domain, as well as to Industry 4.0 and operations research by advancing ambiguity modeling and management through this enhanced optimization strategy. The resulting model is robust, versatile, and scalable, with broad applications in Industry 4.0 scheduling and project management. Furthermore, the proposed dominance relation is general and applicable to various ambiguity types. This research holds significant scientific value for advancing ambiguity modeling and management theories, offering new opportunities for developing novel optimization approaches. The authors intend to contribute to scientific progress in computational intelligence, operations research, and optimization, providing a foundation for future studies. This paper extends the work presented at the TSOC 2020 conference. The primary distinction lies in the inclusion of a new dominance relation to improve the model's robustness and optimization capabilities, alongside minor notational and structural adjustments. Consequently, this research expands the original presentation's scope and depth. Additionally, the work contributes to the multi-disciplinary fields of Multi-Criteria Decision Making (MCDM), Management Science, and Operations Management. Keywords: Multi-Objective Optimization, Non-Deterministic Ambiguity, Tabu Search, Discrete Event Simulation, Dominance Relation.

This paper presents an STL-based robustness framework for cyber-physical systems. Specification Temporal Logic (STL) is widely recognized for describing desired system behaviors, where the degree of satisfaction is determined by a signal representing system states over time. We propose a novel robustness formulation that extends the standard pointwise robustness definition by incorporating a cost function over a trajectory $\mathbf{x}(t)$. Pointwise robustness focuses exclusively on the sign of the predicate defining a STL formula, disregarding how much a signal violates constraints. In contrast, our approach integrates both the signed value of the predicate and a temporal cost function to measure the system's overall robustness against disturbances. Leveraging this definition, we develop dynamic programming algorithms to compute robustness for two fundamental classes of STL formulas. We demonstrate the practical utility of this framework and the associated algorithms through a case study on a cardiac pacemaker, which highlights advantages in robustness assessment and optimization capabilities. Simulation results confirm that the proposed method is efficient and scalable for typical STL formulas. The source code for computing robustness is publicly accessible. Furthermore, we introduce a new library for calculating robustness in hybrid systems, which is available for download. Our framework offers general robustness evaluation for CPSS, with a specific application to disturbance detection and attribution. Additionally, the framework supports reasoning about disturbance robustness in control tasks, such as motion planning, and enables optimization of robustness as a cost function, where the decision variables represent the system's control inputs. This capability facilitates disturbance tolerance and motion planning with robustness awareness. In this work, we provide a general definition of STL-driven robustness for CPSS, describe its applications, and establish a foundation for future research. Specifically, we demonstrate that computing robustness can be cast as a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP), and that the disturbance optimization problem resulting from robustness assessment can also be formulated as an MILP. These findings enable the use of robustness assessment and optimization within a broader framework for CPSS design and control, which is illustrated in this paper. For instance, we show how to design robust controllers for hybrid systems, and how to perform robust motion planning for cyber-physical systems. In both scenarios, the design optimization is formulated as an MILP, with the STL robustness computation embedded as a black box. Designers can subsequently optimize for robustness using various metrics, such as maximizing the robustness threshold, minimizing robustness violation costs, or maximizing the robustness time horizon. These MILPs can be efficiently solved using commercial software

We introduce a strategy for investigating "obscure matter" by utilizing a distributed system of acceleration sensors. This matter, characterized by high density and low pressure, is believed to exist within the cores of large galaxies that are heavily obscured by dust, gas, and stellar outflows. To effectively detect the gravitational influence of this substance, the sensor network must cover a vast area with a high node density. We illustrate how to deploy such a network using a satellite constellation around the Milky Way, alongside a system of small, affordable cubesats targeting a dwarf galaxy within the Local Group. Our approach outlines the necessary network design parameters, the data analysis techniques to extract signals from noisy backgrounds, and the constraints regarding target galaxies and achievable localization precision. Additionally, we examine how this design could facilitate the astrometric mapping of a galaxy like M32. Finally, we conclude by suggesting that a successful demonstration of this concept in a nearby dwarf galaxy might pave the way for an intergalactic sensor network, which would be instrumental in mapping gravitational fields across cosmological distances. This could advance our understanding of galactic dynamics and offer new evidence for or against the existence of Dark Matter subhalos. However, we note that achieving such a mapping would necessitate an exceptionally large number of additional galaxy satellites. We also provide a brief discussion of the financial costs required to develop a M32-based network. Overall, we argue that despite the challenges, the scientific value of this proposed design justifies the investment. We believe that advancing this intergalactic sensor network is essential for a comprehensive understanding of galactic cores and their gravitational fields. We also address the potential impact of such a network on our current understanding of galactic formation. Specifically, we discuss how detecting a Dark Matter subhalo in a dwarf galaxy would contradict standard cold dark matter theory and could influence our interpretation of galactic rotation curves. Finally, we outline the steps needed to advance this proposal, including the development of a detailed technical design document, the creation of a prototype network for one of the two target galaxies, and securing funding for the remaining network. We also identify the key decisions that must be made to move this proposal forward. We believe that pursuing this intergalactic sensor network offers a promising avenue for achieving a more complete understanding of galactic formation and for uncovering the true nature of galactic rotation curves. We also highlight the critical decisions that need to be made to advance this proposal, such as selecting the target galaxies and determining the optimal node density and coverage area. We also discuss the potential societal benefits

This work investigates a nonlinear diffusion equation featuring an integrodifferential operator with exponential kernels and establishes a nonlinear Liouville theorem regarding bounded solutions. By employing specially designed gradient representations, we demonstrate convergence to a classical Liouville theorem for solutions on specific geometric domains, such as Cartan-Hadamard manifolds or those satisfying Ricci curvature pinching conditions. These methods utilize techniques from potential theory, including an integral representation of solutions via a Green function, alongside recent findings on the asymptotic behavior of heat kernels and Brownian motion. Notably, the gradient representations derived here may extend beyond their current application to provide fresh perspectives on other partial differential equations. Furthermore, the gradient representations established in this paper were previously employed in our subsequent work \cite{CKS21} to prove isoperimetric inequalities and characterize optimal solutions. This article serves as a foundational step for that line of research. Specifically, it presents two distinct methods for estimating gradient estimates and proves several key lemmas that will be utilized to derive sharp constants in isoperimetric inequalities. Ultimately, these results enable a complete classification of manifolds where bounded solutions to the diffusion equation are constant, based on Ricci curvature pinching conditions. Additionally, as a byproduct of our analysis, we establish new Liouville theorems and heat kernel asymptotics pinching results for complete manifolds. These findings rely on the Laplacian comparison theorem, Hessian comparison theorem, and Laplacian estimates for heat kernels. Our approach is particularly effective in cases where a Liouville theorem cannot be directly derived from the Li-Yau Harnack inequality. This paper was submitted concurrently with~\cite{CKS21}, which provides a comprehensive overview of pinching conditions for Ricci curvature and utilizes the techniques introduced here to derive sharp isoperimetric inequalities. Both papers are intended to serve as a solid foundation for future research. Specifically, \cite{CKS21} will establish a sharp isoperimetric inequality for diffusion on a complete manifold with appropriate pinching conditions of Ricci curvature, thereby generating a new class of Ricci-pinched manifolds with constant Liouville theorems for diffusion. This achievement surpasses existing results concerning constant coefficients or polynomial kernels. Furthermore, the approach used in~\cite{CKS21} to derive sharp isoperimetric inequalities can be interpreted as a sharp criterion for the Liouville theorem for diffusion, which stems from the techniques presented in this work. The origin of compact radio sources remains a significant unresolved issue in radio astronomy. This study investigates the angular dimensions of these sources by stacking radio images with specific angular sizes and examining the distribution of their total flux density. We analyzed 1,090 sources from the 1415 MHz Steward Low Frequency Synthesis survey, covering a 1.5 square degree region with an angular resolution of 4.1 arcseconds. Using radio images at various angular scales, we calculated the average linear size of these sources and derived the ratio of total flux density to angular size. Results indicate that the mean linear size is approximately 1.5 arcseconds, and the total flux density is roughly 1.5 mJov/arcsec. We conclude that the total flux density and linear size of radio sources are roughly equal, suggesting a physical size of approximately 1.5 arcseconds. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the total flux density of radio sources is likely not a function of angular size. These characteristics may represent a combination of different source types, and the resulting properties may reflect the statistical average of a mixed population. The implications of these results for various astrophysical models are also discussed. Ultimately, the data support the hypothesis that starburst galaxies are the primary sources of compact dim radio emission. Additionally, we propose that the total flux density of radio sources is approximately 1.5 mJov/arcsec, and we estimate that the total flux density of unresolved radio sources is roughly 10% of the sky's total flux density. This estimate is consistent with the value of 8% reported by Condon et al. (1982). Finally, the total flux density of unresolved radio sources is estimated to be about 10% of the total flux density of all radio sources. This estimate is lower than the 20% value reported by Condon (1974), which may be attributed to the use of a more sensitive radio survey in this work. Specifically, we introduce abstract concealed Markov models (ACMMs), which employ a probabilistic concurrent transition system to model programs and their executions. executions can result in observations, some of which may remain unrecorded. We present a framework to model nonlinear coherent stirring in active fluids using stochastic partial differential equations that incorporate statistical nonlocal interactions. This approach addresses the challenge, inherent in activity, of defining a coherent pattern's influence on fluid dynamics without precise spatial knowledge. We demonstrate that this method captures key features of nonlinear stirring patterns and their correlation with nonlocal interactions. Furthermore, we find that mean-field approximations are valid when nonlocal interactions are sufficiently strong, regardless of the correlation decay of the underlying statistical distribution. Additionally, our analysis of the energy cascade reveals a distinct mechanism for inverse cascades, one that is independent of coherent vortices. Finally, we examine the convergence of the series expansion for nonlocal kernels and establish that our framework is effectively approximated by truncated models. These approximations are validated through active scalar simulations, which show that the spectral properties of coherent patterns in active fluids are well-reproduced. This method leverages the analytical solvability of multipoles within the massless limit, allowing mass-dependent radiative and soft gravitational corrections to be expanded and integrated term-by-term in a strictly even power series of the mass ratio. This algorithm facilitates a rapid and systematic exploration of the scatterscatter regime, where arbitrary multipole interaction can significantly alter dynamics compared to the massless regime, and where soft graviton exchange effects become substantial at two loops, scaling as $\alpha^3 (GM/m)^4$. Our findings align with previous analyses conducted in the four-dimensional, even-multipole, equal-mass massless limit. We demonstrate that this approach enables a systematic investigation of the relationship between dynamical observables in the scatterscatter regime and those in the standard gravitational wave community, which typically involves massive, non-cyclic, non-analytic, non-conservative, non-even-multipole interacting trajectories. This framework facilitates the identification of new observables and structures within the scatterscatter regime, thereby informing future scatterscatter research. This study addresses the 3D point cloud localization challenge within large-scale, high-precision environments. While transformer-based deep learning models have demonstrated significant success in Natural Language Processing (NLP) and computer vision NLP (CNLP) tasks like image captioning, they are less effective in traditional computer vision (CV) localization due to the difficulty of directly mapping 3D point clouds to transformers. To overcome this, we introduce NDT-Transformer, a new network designed for 3D point cloud localization. Our approach involves three key contributions: first, we depict Normal Distribution Transforms (NDTs) as a sequence of 3D Gaussian models to capture semantic information; second, we utilize n-dimensional vectors, which represent the mean shift direction of each Gaussian relative to others, to convey spatial context; third, we propose a multi-head self-attention mechanism that integrates semantic and spatial context, enhanced by a multi-kernel design for greater robustness. Experimental results on the ScanNet and Waymo datasets validate the effectiveness of our method and depiction. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/zhujingwei/NDT-Transformer. Furthermore, the multi-head self-attention mechanism supports parallel processing of Gaussian information, ensuring efficient computation. Finally, NDT-Transformer is lightweight, enabling its integration into autonomous driving systems. The abbreviation "NDT-Transformer" is preferred over alternatives like "Gaussian-Transformer" or "Gaussian-Attention" because it avoids confusion with 3D Gaussian Splatting (Gaussian-Splatting), a rapidly emerging computer vision technique. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) serves as a primary method for investigating brain connectivity. This study evaluates the precision of connectivity metrics derived from multisite experiments, specifically examining how signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), sample size, and the count of comparison pairs influence prediction accuracy. Using simulated data, we demonstrate that although the statistical strength of connectivity metrics can be significant, the precision of these metrics remains low, particularly for large sample sizes and an increasing number of comparison pairs. We identify the number of comparison pairs as a critical yet underappreciated factor that compromises the precision of connectivity metrics, thereby affecting the reproducibility of rs-fMRI findings. Furthermore, we propose the mean absolute error (MAE) as an effective tool for quantifying the precision of connectivity metrics. These findings may prove valuable for rs-fMRI researchers when designing and interpreting experimental results. The analysis code is accessible at: https://github.com/zhengyuan1992/MLRM.

Although single-node beeping networks are typically ignored, they are relevant in scenarios where only a few devices transmit simultaneously. This study investigates energy efficiency by addressing two specific cases: networks with a single transmitter, or "solo-beeping" networks, and networks with exactly two transmitters, termed "duo-beeping" networks. The authors propose new power-saving naming protocols for both scenarios and establish provable lower bounds on the necessary time and power resources. Specifically, for solo-beeping networks, an optimal $O(n\log n)$ time and $O(n)$ power scheme is presented. For duo-beeping networks, the method requires $O(n^2)$ time and $O(n)$ power. Furthermore, new lower bounds are established for each scenario. For solo-beeping networks, the findings demonstrate that any time scheme must consume at least $O(\log n)$ energy per node, meaning time schemes are not inherently more power-efficient than slot-based approaches. The inherent multilingual nature of these points makes them difficult to represent, particularly regarding the transitions where multiple languages merge. This study examines various codeswitching patterns and their impact on NLP tasks. To address this, we introduce PESTO, a transformer-based architecture featuring dynamic and relative positional embeddings, which achieves state-of-the-art results in both classification and token-level sequence tasks. PESTO demonstrates superior performance compared to baseline models, such as BERT, especially on tuning data with higher proportions of mixed languages. Additionally, we present an ablation study to analyze how different codeswitching patterns influence PESTO's classification accuracy. This study employs first-principles calculations to investigate the pressure-dependent isotope effect on the critical temperature of the H$_3$S hydride superconductor within the range of 150 to 250 GPa. By analyzing the nonhydrogenic isotope effect, we quantify the contributions of non-Superconducting Phonon Modes (SSPM) and anisotropy to the superconducting critical temperature. Our findings indicate that the isotope exponent $ \alpha_{CT} = \frac{\Delta T_{C,H_2S}}{\Delta T_{C_D_2S}} $ transitions from 1.0 to 0.93 as pressure increases from 150 to 250 GPa. Furthermore, we observe that the isotope effect on $T_{C}$ is suppressed at higher pressures. These results provide valuable insights into the mechanisms driving the ultrahigh $T_{C}$ in this material. Additionally, our analysis reveals that near 220 GPa, a nonmonotonic behavior occurs due to a van Hove singularity, causing a sharp drop in $T_{C}$ from 203 K to 150 K. This indicates that the ultrahigh $T_{C}$ is sensitive to slight variations in pressure within this vicinity. Ultimately, this analysis underscores the necessity of precise pressure control in experimental settings. Our research offers a comprehensive understanding of the physics governing the high $T_{C}$ in this system, which is essential for exploring new superconducting materials. We anticipate that these results will prove beneficial to the scientific community. The computational data supporting this work can be accessed at [1]. Furthermore, the H5 package utilized in this study is publicly available at [2].

Many motion planning problems in dynamic environments involve an agent moving among obstacles that shift over time. Since these obstacles can occupy specific phasing patterns, the problem of defining the most efficient phasing pattern that restricts the agent's movement is known as Spatial Limitation Creation (SPLOC). This paper introduces a novel motion planning scenario where an agent moves in a 2D grid containing charged and uncharged cells; the agent can only traverse uncharged cells. We propose a method to determine the most effective phasing pattern for placing a moving charge. Our research investigates phasing patterns on both cell and track levels. For the cell-level approach, we present a polynomial-time algorithm to find the optimal phasing pattern. Regarding the track-level approach, we develop a method that identifies a reasonable phasing pattern within a time frame independent of the cell count. Finally, we evaluate our methods through experiments comparing the generated phasing patterns. The results demonstrate that both proposed approaches are effective. Furthermore, our method yields better outcomes than the existing state-of-the-art phasing pattern generator. Additionally, the track-level approach surpasses the cell-level approach in terms of speed. However, the cell-level approach achieves more chaotic charging patterns on the obstacles, leading to more constrained motion plans for the agent. These findings are supported by the experimental results. Notably, the track-level method is the first to successfully generate charging patterns for the cells. Visual relocalization seeks to determine a camera's current pose by matching its input image against a pre-built 3D map. While visual place recognition (VPR) methods utilizing learnable features have demonstrated superior accuracy compared to hand-crafted descriptors, their reliance on trainable parameters restricts their application to domains with semantically similar locations. To address this, we introduce a hybrid relocalization framework that integrates global supervision from 3D surfel maps-assisted geometric recognition with representations from global learnable features. Our results show that this hybrid approach significantly outperforms existing VPR baselines when using 2D features or patches, as well as outperforms geometric recognition methods relying solely on 3D features when using 2D features or features on a 3D map. Furthermore, the enhanced representation from local features improves recognition performance in geodesic distances beyond 100 meters, while the improved alignment from 2D features reduces GSD errors at very close ranges. Across all datasets, the most effective strategy combines 2D features, 3D features, and 3D features embedded in a 3D map. Additionally, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Raikles benchmark and delivers promising results on IPLOP and VRDE. This study tackles the joint optimization of user selection and precoding in multiuser MIMO downlink scenarios. The objective function aims to maximize the sum-rate by simultaneously determining the precoder and user choice. To address the continuous variable of precoder design, the problem is formulated as a convex optimization task using semidefinite relaxation. To handle the discrete nature of user selection, a group $\ell_1$ norm is incorporated into the objective, transforming it into a group LASSO form. Viewed as a game, each group LASSO solution represents a Nash equilibrium. An algorithm is introduced to compute the group LASSO solution by iteratively designing precoders and choosing users until the first step of the algorithm converges. Furthermore, a new problem is defined to generate a sub-optimal solution that ensures at least the group LASSO result. This new formulation imposes a minimum sum-rate constraint, relaxes the group $\ell_1$ norm, and reduces the order of positive semidefinite matrices by one. The group LASSO solution is proven to be a special instance of this new problem, which is subsequently solved via an inner loop that design and choose users in each iteration until the outer loop converges. Finally, a numerical example demonstrates the proposed method's superiority over existing solutions in the literature. The results confirm the game's convergence and that the new approach significantly outperforms the SDR-based solution from the literature. Additionally, the sub-optimal problem is shown to be more efficient than the standard group LASSO. However, increasing the minimum sum-rate target in the sub-optimal problem causes the first step of group LASSO to converge in fewer iterations. Conversely, when the group LASSO problem is solved directly, the first step converges in very few iterations for high minimum sum-rate targets. This indicates that the sub-optimal problem can achieve higher sum-rates with fewer iterations, thereby reducing computational complexity. Ultimately, both the game and the sub-optimal problem prove to be more efficient than the literature's group LASSO-based solution. The first step of group LASSO converges in very few iterations for the sub-optimal problem, whereas it requires many iterations for the group LASSO problem itself. We demonstrate that the rational semifield consisting of piecewise linear functions defined on arcs within a finite-dimensional affine space over a tropical semifield $T$, and possessing coefficients in the rational closure $T^{\text{rat}}$ of $T$, is finitely generated as a semifield over $T$. Consequently, the rational semifield of piecewise linear functions on a finite-dimensional convex cone within a finite-dimensional real vector space is finitely generated over $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$. This result yields multiple applications, including a new proof of a specific facet theorem, the establishment of a generalized facet theorem, the characterization of piecewise linear functions on arcs as those whose restrictions to a particular subset of arcs are linear, and the identification of a subset of semialgebraic sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$ (for $n \geq 2$) whose indicators generate the piecewise linear semifield on $n$-tuples. Furthermore, our findings offer a positive resolution to a question posed by J. R. Stembridge.

Consider a continuous-time Markov process on a countable state space characterized by a strongly sub-Markovian Q-matrix. We demonstrate that if the associated Q-process exhibits local recurrence, the sequence of $n$-time joint distributions of a specific sequence of continuous-time Markov processes exhibits consistent weak convergence to the Q-process. A significant application of this finding is the derivation of various forms of consistent weak convergence to the Q-process of a random walk on a countable abelian group. Furthermore, we establish that the Q-process is the only strongly sub-Markovian process on the group that locally recurrently visits every state with probability one. Additional corollaries include: (i) the local transience of the Q-process implies that the Q-process is the unique strongly sub-Markovian process on the group with completely asymmetric local behavior; (ii) the local transience of the Q-process for a random walk on the free abelian group $\mathbb{Z}^d$ holds if and only if $d \geq 3$. The primary tool for proving the main result is a technique for constructing the Q-process via the time limit of a sequence of time-parameterized Markov processes. This method is also employed to demonstrate that the local transience of the Q-process of a random walk on a free group is equivalent to the local recurrence of the Q-process for a one-sided random walk on the free monoid. Additionally, we provide a characterization of the local recurrence of the Q-process for a random walk on a free product of finitely generated groups, which relies on the existence of a finite subset of the state space through which the process must pass. We also investigate the conditions under which the $t$-joint distribution of the Q-process for a one-sided random walk on a free group possesses an atom at the group identity for $t > 0$. In the case of a one-sided random walk on $\mathbb{Z}$, the existence of such an atom is equivalent to the local transience of the Q-process. However, this equivalence does not extend to one-sided random walks on the free group of rank 2 or higher, nor does it hold for a one-sided random walk on the free product of two finite cyclic groups of rank 1. This research investigates the relationship between the specific braid $B_{5,1}$ and its closure within the braid group modulo its commutator, denoted as $B_5^{ab}$. The terms "Fox-Hatcher" originate from William Fox's utilization of the fundamental group of the complement of a knot, followed by John Hatcher's demonstration that the abelianization of this group—referred to as the knot's "characteristic"—is equivalent to the knot's third Vassiliev invariant. Working in the abelianization of the braiding group of $B_{5,1}$ allows for the examination of the knot's characteristic. The study reveals that the word representing the closure of $B_{5,1}$ in $\pi_1(B_5\Lambda_{5})$ is not reduced; consequently, applying the abelianization map yields a non-trivial characteristic. This finding establishes a connection between the knot's characteristic and a braided version of the configuration space $CF_5$. Furthermore, the text explores the definition and implications of the "reduced form" of words within braided group complements, demonstrating how reduced words can elucidate the knot's characteristic. Finally, the work introduces the concept of "filling words," which are reduced words that become trivial upon abelianization, and investigates their presence within the fundamental group of the knot complement. These findings suggest that the existence of non-trivial filling words in the fundamental group of the knot complement is linked to the knot's characteristic. Overall, this study highlights the significance of words in understanding the characteristic of $B_{5,1}$ and explores the broader relevance of these concepts to knot theory. By bridging geometry, topology, and algebra, the paper advances our understanding of the complex relationships inherent in the field. This work addresses gaps in existing literature regarding the connection between a knot's characteristic and its third Vassiliev invariant, offering new insights and perspectives for future research in these areas. The results not only deepen our comprehension of $B_{5,1}$ but also open new avenues for investigation into knot group abelianizations and their relation to filling words. This approach opens fresh avenues for exploring the intricate relationships between knot group abelianizations, filling words, and their broader implications in knot theory. The structural transition from tetragonal to orthorhombic symmetry in LiFeAs, which occurs at approximately 175 K, exhibits characteristics of an nematic transition. To determine if this state results from spontaneous symmetry breaking, we analyzed the phonon dispersion relations along the a and b directions using density functional perturbation theory (DFPT). Our investigation revealed soft modes at the S point in the orthorhombic phase, though the differences between the a and b directions were minimal. Furthermore, we computed the coupling between nematic strain and these soft modes, finding no significant variation. These findings suggest that the low-temperature orthorhombic phase of LiFeAs does not arise from nematic instability, indicating that nematicity plays a limited role in this specific iron-based superconductor. Our results provide a quantitative framework for examining nematicity in LiFeAs and establish a robust DFPT methodology for evaluating nematic tendencies in other iron-based superconductors. Additionally, we compared our theoretical predictions with existing experimental phonon data for LiFeAs, finding strong agreement. This contrast between theory and experiment further underscores the complexity of the nematic phenomenon in LiFeAs. Our study offers valuable insights into the nature of nematicity in iron-based superconductors and sets a precedent for investigating nematic tendencies in other superconducting materials. Ultimately, our work advances our understanding of nematicity and its interplay with other physical mechanisms in iron-based superconductors. By demonstrating the utility of DFPT in predicting nematic strain couplings, we have created a foundation for future research into the fundamental nature of nematicity in these materials. This will contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the complex phenomena governing high-temperature superconductivity. Our findings have the potential to guide future experimental and theoretical studies, ultimately leading to a deeper understanding of the intricate physics underlying nematicity in iron-based superconductors. By providing a quantitative understanding of the phonon dispersion relations and the nature of the structural transition, our work advances the broader field of condensed matter physics and facilitates further research into the fundamental nature of nematicity in these materials. Ultimately, our findings contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the complex phenomena governing high-temperature superconductivity and provide a foundation for future research into the fundamental nature of nematicity in iron-based superconductors. Our findings have the potential to guide future experimental and theoretical studies, ultimately leading to a deeper understanding of the complex phenomena governing nematicity in iron-based superconductors

A significant hurdle in nanotechnology is the inability to regulate the formation of complex structures. Although numerical simulations can forecast the self-assembly of nanoparticles, current methods for designing materials that form desired structures remain limited. We introduce a computational strategy that iteratively trains artificial neural networks to produce target structures by controlling assembly parameters. Specifically, we investigate the formation of close-packed lattices using identical hard spheres and random structures via mixtures of colloidal particles with varying sizes. By mapping particle positions and momenta into input features for an artificial neural network (ANN), we train the ANN to control Monte Carlo simulations that generate structures matching the desired structure factor $Q$. Furthermore, we train a neural classifier to rapidly predict if a new set of assembly parameters will yield the target structure, facilitating a genetic algorithm (GA) to explore the parameter space for efficient formation of target structures. Our findings indicate that these design methods do not require fine-tuning of the features or architecture of the ANN, which significantly lowers barriers to applying machine learning to other particle assembly problems. Additionally, applying this methodology to multicomponent systems suggests that sophisticated structural designs can be achieved through simple materials. Overall, our results demonstrate that machine learning offers a straightforward approach to systematically engineer particle-based assembly, potentially advancing nanotechnology design. The accompanying open-source code enables rapid implementation of our methodology for various problems with minimal feature engineering. Specifically, users can employ our code to iteratively train particles and frameworks for self-assembly, thereby enabling the swift creation of complex structures from simple components. Our framework and code are accessible at https://github.com/ChenLabASU/particle-assembly-ANN. We investigate robust anomalies and chiral phases within chiral $SU(N)$ gauge theories augmented by massive fermions in the fundamental and $N$-dimensional representations. By employing a chiral effective action derived from four-fermion interactions, we construct an effective Lagrangian for the confining fermion-bosons. This formulation enables a systematic analysis of robust anomalies and the emergence of chiral phases, identified as pseudogaps where low-energy excitations persist despite strong interactions. These phases are characterized by massive dynamical fermion-bosons and emergent $O(4)$ chiral symmetry. Additionally, we identify a novel type of robust anomaly that persists even when the $O(4)$ symmetry is spontaneously broken. Finally, we offer insights into the phase structure of four-fermion models and the potential existence of chiral phases in QCD. Specifically, we argue that the ground state of QCD likely resides in a pseudogap phase rather than a confinement-plus-chiral-symmetry-breaking phase, which may help resolve the longstanding puzzle regarding the origin of eta' mass and the $U(A)$ problem. Furthermore, we propose that the pseudo-goldstone bosons within this chiral phase could serve as a new class of light particles detectable in current experimental searches. This framework also sheds light on the recent detection of a light particle in the SHiP experiment [R. Aaij et al., J. Phys. Conf. Ser. 146, 012011 (2009)], a result that challenges the conventional QCD vacuum structure. Finally, we suggest that the chiral phase might play a significant role in solving the baryon asymmetry problem. Specifically, we propose that a new type of robust anomaly could be responsible for baryogenesis, with the chiral phase emerging in the early universe after the electroweak phase transition. This proposal offers a fresh perspective on baryogenesis and the potential detection of light particles in upcoming experiments. Furthermore, it suggests that the future may hold the resolution to the eta' mass problem and the existence of a chiral symmetric vacuum. These findings open a promising avenue for future research into the phase structure of QCD. Finally, we anticipate that these findings will open a new window into the rich phase structure of QCD. Specifically, the chiral phase could be responsible for the origin of baryon asymmetry, and the future may hold the solution to the mass of the eta' meson

This study investigates the ill-posedness of the three-dimensional steady Navier-Stokes equations within critical Besov spaces. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any initial velocity field $u_0$ in the space $B^{2+\alpha}_{1/\alpha}$ where $0<\alpha\leq1$, there exists a corresponding initial pressure $p_0$ such that the Navier-Stokes system admits no solution, regardless how weak. Furthermore, any attempt to construct a solution via a weak limit of regular solutions—whether regular or bounded—necessarily yields a pressure term. Additionally, our findings indicate that the steady Navier-Stokes equations are infinitely many ill-posed in the critical Besov space $B^{2+\alpha}_{1/\alpha}$ with $0<\alpha\leq1$. Finally, the critical nature of this result is highlighted by the fact that for the range $1<\alpha\leq2$, the equations are well-posed in the critical space $B^{2+\alpha}_{1/\alpha}$. The overall criterion is expressed as $s<2$, with the critical threshold occurring at $s=2$. The paper concludes with several open questions regarding this critical threshold. Additionally, the results presented herein have been incorporated into our thesis, \cite{diss}. Specifically, Theorem 2.2 corresponds to Chapter 2, Theorem 3.1 to Chapter 3, Theorem 4.1 to Chapter 4, and Theorem 5.1 to Chapter 5. The proof techniques employed were also featured in my oral presentation at the 12th International Conference on Differential Equations, held in Xi'an, China, from June 21 to July 1, 2021. The presentation's title was: \textit{Ill-posedness for the steady Navier-Stokes equations in critical Besov spaces: $B^{2+\alpha}_{1/\alpha}$ with $0<\alpha\leq1$}. This work marks my first contribution to the field of fluid dynamics. I extend my sincere appreciation for his mentorship. Additionally, I offer my thanks to the members of my thesis committee for their time and consideration. I am also profoundly indebted to my family for their endless love, support, and encouragement, which have been indispensable to my journey.

We demonstrate that the magnonic dispersion relation in antiferromagnetic insulators becomes asymmetric as temperature rises, resulting in thermal compression. This phenomenon is analyzed within the framework of the two-sublattice Heisenberg model, where the symmetry in the Brillouin zone is broken by coupling magnons across opposite momenta via phonons. While this asymmetry is typically observed in magnonic spectra at finite temperatures, it is particularly pronounced for magnons with zero in-plane momentum. Furthermore, the nonlinearity induced by magnon-phonon interactions leads to spectral displacement, a critical factor in generating nonreciprocal magnonics. These findings are corroborated by recent experimental data from yttrium iron garnet. Additionally, our results are compared against time-dependent density-functional-theory-based calculations for the half-Heusler alloy $\beta$-PtBiSé, a promising candidate for nonreciprocal magnonics. We anticipate that this computational methodology will prove valuable for rapidly identifying new materials capable of supporting nonreciprocal magnonics, thereby accelerating the development of this field. Finally, we outline promising avenues for future experimental investigation, specifically regarding the finite-temperature behavior of magnonic dispersion relations, nonlinearity, and nonreciprocity. Specifically, we propose that comparing yttrium iron garnet with $\beta$-PtBiSé will advance the study of magnonics and its future technological applications. Furthermore, we recommend that simultaneously measuring the nonreciprocity of both group and phase velocities in yttrium iron garnet will significantly enhance our understanding of magnon nonlinearity. Finally, we recommend that the symmetry breaking in the magnonic dispersion relation of yttrium iron garnet be explored experimentally to better understand the role of magnon interactions in the physics of nonlinear nonreciprocal spin waves. \textit{Keywords:} antiferromagnetism, magnonics, nonlinearity, nonreciprocity. \textit{PACS:} 75.75.-l, 75.70.-a, 75.50.Lk, 75.70.Tq, 75.75.-l, 75.70.-a, 75.50.Lk, 75.70.Tq. \textit{DOI:} 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.3.013001. \textit{

The public key of Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem comprises two structured rank metric codes—a GRS code and a alternant code—which are relatively straightforward to decode. To enhance the system's security, we introduce two novel variants that utilize the same type of code in the public key but rely on less structured code bases, making them more difficult to attack. In one version, the public key includes a GRS code defined by a generic monomial; in the other, it features an oscillator code, also known as a Tukey code, which is even weaker. While the original system is secure against standard decoding attacks, its algebraic attacks are computationally infeasible. The first new version inherits this level of security from the original, whereas the second benefits from the inherently higher minimum distance of oscillator codes. Additionally, both versions support the generation of random public keys with larger parameters, making them promising candidates for future code-based protocols. Experimental results confirm that attacks on these new versions are no stronger than those on the original system. Finally, we propose a generic approach to analyze the security of these variants, which could serve as a foundation for studying other potential variants in the family. Finally, we implemented these new versions in the Python library `sagecrypthack`, which can be accessed at: https://github.com/sagecrypthack/codebasedcryptosystems. Their public keys are available there for testing purposes. In summary, oscillator codes represent a valuable resource for developing future code-based cryptosystems.

Although pre-training on extensive corpora has enhanced language models for numerous downstream tasks, their pre-training objectives remain largely unsupervised. We contend that incorporating high-quality, well-annotated auxiliary datasets can yield even greater improvements, particularly by aligning more closely with supervised learning through word alignments. This paper presents Dict-BERT, a BERT variant designed to leverage word alignments during pre-training. We utilize English Wikipedia word alignments ( Wu et al., 2019) as the primary source for Dict-BERT's pre-training data. Our experiments demonstrate that pre-training on the Dict-BERT model, rather than standard BERT, consistently boosts performance across eight downstream tasks, including eight translation scenarios, with particularly notable gains in translation. Additionally, we observe even more pronounced improvements on a few English NLP tasks when comparing Dict-BERT to BERT trained on English-specific data. These findings underscore the value of utilizing high-quality, well-annotated datasets for developing robust language models. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/zhuxin1997/Dict-BERT. This work is based on a long paper accepted to EMNLP 2021.

Topological data analysis (TDA) offers tools for detecting hidden topological structures within point cloud data. This paper explores the random occurrence of specific TDA features, including persistent homology groups, intervals, and their boundary pairs known as death-time pairs. It demonstrates that these phenomena arise randomly based on a geometric quantity called the mass of a space, which quantifies the minimum spatial extent required to connect scattered points. Mass serves as a fundamental quantity in probability theory, governing the random emergence of various TDA elements and defining the upper limits of several TDA methods. The paper highlights the variety of minimal spanning (co)cycles used to define these methods and illustrates their application in real-world data analysis. Furthermore, it examines the information content of different cocycles regarding the reconstruction of the underlying space from a point cloud. The discussion begins with an overview of key concepts, followed by an analysis of the random nature of topological features within data analysis methods. It proceeds to analyze the random occurrence of specific features like death-time pairs and assesses information content, before concluding with a summary, potential research directions, and a case study applying these insights to the classification of handwritten digits. The study includes Python code to demonstrate key ideas and results. Additionally, code is provided for the persistence diagrams of two datasets: the MNIST handwritten digit set and the Iris dataset. Finally, the paper investigates feature extraction using the persistence diagram of the Iris dataset. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) represents a privacy-centric framework where multiple parties collaborate to construct predictive models by contributing distinct feature sets for the same entities. It serves as a complementary approach to Horizontal Federated Learning, offering a robust defense against privacy breaches. This paper introduces two novel pragmatic privacy attacks against VFL: Access Control Assault (ACA) and Attribute Evasion Assault (AES). ACA aims to uncover features contributed by the attacker that were previously withheld, while AES targets the revelation of an attacker's attributes using fake data to mask their true data. We demonstrate that both attacks can successfully infer the attacker's data within existing VFL frameworks. Furthermore, we propose a novel VFL mechanism designed to mitigate these threats, utilizing a gradient-based feature value perturbation strategy to safeguard sensitive information from disclosure. Experimental evaluations confirm the efficacy of our proposed privacy protection method. To our knowledge, this study presents the first investigation into these specific pragmatic VFL attacks and their corresponding defenses. The exclusive production of dark antibaryons is investigated through the $B$-meson decay $B\to{P}+\bar{{\cal B}}_D$, where $P$ denotes a dark baryon. This study extends QCD light-cone synthesis rules to incorporate QCD moments and the nonperturbative wave function of the dark baryon. Numerical computations are performed for the $B\to{P}+\bar{{\cal B}}_D$ process within the non-derivative framework of the dark portal, with specific attention to the $B\to\eta'+\bar{p}$ channel. Results indicate that the primary contribution to the $B\to\eta'+\bar{p}$ form factor $f_0^{B\to\eta'}(q^2=0)$ arises from the second QCD moment of the dark proton, $\langle\lambda_6\rangle_p$. Additionally, the ratio of branching fractions ${\rm Br}(\bar{B}^0\to\eta'+\bar{p})/{\rm Br}(B^0\to\eta'+\bar{p})$ is estimated to be $0.49$. The derived predictions for the form factor $f_0^{B\to\eta'}(q^2=0)$ and this branching ratio ratio align with existing experimental data. Furthermore, the analysis yields the value $\langle\lambda_6\rangle_p=105\pm 15$ ${\rm MeV}$. These findings suggest that the production of dark antibaryons is feasible within this theoretical framework. The study also examines the $B\to K+\bar{p}$ and $B\to\eta'+\bar{s}$ processes, noting that the former is suppressed by the QCD moments of the dark proton, whereas the latter is enhanced by those of the dark strange quark. Finally, several recommendations are offered to enhance the production of dark antibaryons. The findings presented herein may assist in designing new experiments dedicated to antibaryon production. Intelligent cities are evolving into highly integrated systems that merge physical, computational, and human components. These systems are expected to become increasingly vulnerable to cyber attacks that disrupt their seamless operation. This paper introduces the Intelligent City Defense game, a computer-assisted simulation tool designed to investigate how defenders can safeguard intelligent cities against cyber assaults. The game facilitates the study of defensive strategies by enabling users to manage an intelligent city's security through a suite of countermeasures, including cyber, physical, and socio-technical counterattacks. Furthermore, the game allows participants to assess the effectiveness of various counterattack types and the optimal timing for their deployment. The paper details the design philosophy behind the City Defense game and illustrates its utility for both researchers and practitioners by showing three distinct applications. Ultimately, we argue that cyber-defense simulations are indispensable for formulating effective intelligent city defense policies. City Defense represents a crucial initial step toward a practical simulation environment that can be utilized by both city stakeholders and researchers in the field. Additionally, the game's open architecture allows for the easy incorporation of new features and countermeasures. This work details the design and implementation of City Defense and demonstrates its application in a cyber-defense research context. The computer code and the source code for City Defense are accessible at: https://github.com/irina-bargalova/CityDefense. Keywords: Cybersecurity, Cyber-Physical Systems, Cyber-Range, Cyber-Defense Research.

We examine the thermodynamic characteristics of both charged and uncharged asymptotically Anti-de Sitter (AdS) black holes confined within a confined space. Specifically, we analyze how the total charge ($Q_{total}$) and the total radius ($L_{total}$) influence the phase transitions of these black holes. Our findings indicate that, unlike the scenario without a cutoff, a phase transition is guaranteed to occur regardless of the specific values of charge or total charged radius when space is confined within a chamber. Furthermore, we observe that for any given charge, there exists a critical total radius ($L_{total})_{critical}$; when the total radius exceeds this threshold, the confined black hole's phase transition behavior is altered. Additionally, we explore how this phase transition influences the corresponding dual field theory. This research extends our earlier study on the holographic thermodynamics of black holes in a chamber. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that the holographic framework offers a more comprehensive and precise method for investigating the phase transitions of charged AdS black holes within a chamber compared to standard thermodynamic analysis. This conclusion is supported by the fact that the field theory within the cavity can be more accurately approximated by a black hole within the same cavity. Consequently, our findings may prove valuable for addressing various challenges in high-energy physics. Finally, we note that our conclusions align with those derived by other researchers. Other researchers have also examined the thermodynamic properties of AdS black holes with a cutoff, confirming that the existence of a horizon in the uncharged case and an event horizon in the charged case are both influenced by the total radius ($L_{total}$) and total charge ($Q_{total}$). Although deep neural networks excel at various information retrieval tasks, their performance degrades significantly in real-world scenarios involving noisy labeled data. While numerous approaches have addressed this issue within the broader context of machine learning, research specifically focused on text ranking remains limited. This study proposes a novel algorithm utilizing a graph model to detect clusters amidst noisy labels. By assigning weights to nodes and calculating shortest paths, the method identifies these clusters. Subsequently, the algorithm computes the cumulative distance between each sample and its cluster center to identify a data subset suitable for training a text ranker. Experimental results on the MLTOY label noise dataset demonstrate a 10% enhancement in label noise robustness compared to baseline models. Furthermore, in high-noise environments (exceeding 50%), the proposed approach outperforms baseline methods in both precision@10 and recall@10 metrics. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1992/label_noise. Ultimately, this paper aims to raise awareness of the challenges associated with label noise in text retrieval and offers a robust solution for the field. Although the current model was tested only on the MLTOY dataset, its underlying principles are broadly applicable to other datasets and domains. Future research will expand the evaluation to additional datasets, such as NoisyMNIST and NoisyMNIST-12. Additionally, while the current implementation was developed in Python for accessibility, a C++ version will be released to enhance execution speed. Finally, efforts will continue to refine the loss function, explore the use of Graph Neural Networks, and validate the solution's relevance in medical diagnosis and other medical fields. These steps are essential for advancing the field of deep learning under noisy labeled conditions. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated significant effectiveness across a broad spectrum of graph-related applications, such as Gene Regulatory Networks and Social Media Networks. However, acquiring labeled data for many of these scenarios is costly and time-intensive. To address this challenge, we introduce GNN-PLE, a novel pseudo-labeling framework designed to enhance graph classification tasks under limited annotated samples. Our approach begins by identifying outliers within the current training dataset to mitigate label noise. Subsequently, these initial pseudo-labels are utilized to guide the selection of hard examples, promoting diverse label distribution graphs. Finally, these secondary pseudo-labels facilitate graph sampling for model retraining. Extensive experiments on gene regulatory networks and benchmark graph classification datasets confirm the Challenging Performance of GNN-PLE. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/zhongyuan1991/PLE-GNN. The paper can be found at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.02201.

This study examines proton-driven laser wakefield acceleration (PWFA) as the second stage of the AWAKE experiment, which is currently operating at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Utilizing a multi-stage laser system, PWFA aims to generate intense photon bursts from relativistic protons, potentially offering on-demand, high-power sources for various applications. This non-thermal radiation distinguishes it from synchrotron or bending-magnet facilities that provide continuous radiation. To analyze PWFA radiation for AWAKE Run 2, we conducted a detailed simulation of the accelerator and detection setup. Our results indicate that current parameters are insufficient to observe the multi-keV spectrum predicted by PWFA. We identify three primary obstacles to achieving keV radiation: the laser's low power, excessive longitudinal compression of the proton bunch, and sub-optimal detector placement. Addressing these challenges could enable the realization of on-demand keV photon bursts. Specifically, we propose that a single order of magnitude increase in laser power would be adequate to reach the keV range. Additionally, we suggest that the detector should be repositioned 10–20 meters downstream from the current location. We conclude that further investigations into proton charge, bunch length, and other parameters may also yield positive outcomes. Ultimately, we argue that developing new detection techniques is essential to fully exploit the unique characteristics of PWFA radiation. This research provides a foundation for the next experimental phase at AWKE, where proton parameters will be optimized to reveal the non-thermal nature of wakefield-accelerated electron beams. Ultimately, this will validate multi-keV photon generation as a distinct feature of multi-beam accelerators. Additionally, we explore potential applications of PWFA radiation for free-electron lasers and coherent Compton scattering. These findings may also be relevant to other wakefield acceleration facilities, such as LAWAKE and the European XFEL. To facilitate this, we have released an open-source Python toolkit, `wakefield_radiation`, which models radiation from multi-beam accelerators and can be easily extended to study non-linear Compton scattering. The advent of distributed decision tree algorithms has opened new avenues for privacy-preserving machine learning, enabling secure collaboration between data owners and cloud servers while offering specific guarantees to third-party analyzers. However, current solutions often suffer from either high computational costs or the provision of no meaningful privacy assurances. This paper introduces SCAM-PDT, an algorithm designed to construct differentially private distributed decision trees in a three-party setting. By integrating a new sampling method with a pruning strategy, SCAM-PDT achieves a significant reduction in communication overhead compared to prior art. Furthermore, we present privacy analysis that offers provable privacy guarantees, ensuring all participants adhere to their differential privacy constraints. Extensive experiments involving real-world datasets and varying communication networks demonstrate that SCAM-PDT outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in both accuracy and efficiency. Additionally, the implementation successfully handles two distinct differential privacy definitions, supporting a diverse range of privacy policies. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first practical implementation capable of generating decision trees in the distributed setting with provable privacy guarantees. The source code is available at: https://github.com/SebastianSchulz/SCAM-PDT. This paper introduces a variant of Bregman proximal gradient algorithms utilizing constant R\'enyi divergences to address regularized optimization problems involving convex objective functions that are potentially nondifferentiable. We establish convergence to the global optimum for problems featuring both strongly convex and non-strongly convex objectives, analyzing both settings. Furthermore, we examine a specific instance of this algorithm employing Kullback-Leibler divergence to minimize the cross-entropy loss of a logistic regression classifier on a potentially nondifferentiable constraint set, demonstrating convergence to a constrained Bayes solution. Finally, we present a solution method for a convex relaxation of the rank-k approximation problem for nondifferentiable probability simplices, proving convergence to a low-rank approximation within a relaxed sense. These examples illustrate the algorithm's utility in machine learning contexts involving nonsmooth regularizers. Notably, the final example demonstrates superlinear convergence under certain conditions. All results herein are new. Additionally, we provide a bridge to a recently developed family of proximal point algorithms, highlighting current limitations. Numerical experiments compare the proposed algorithms against projected gradient methods across three cases, and we conclude with directions for future research. These results build upon and extend our prior work in [1]. The methods in [1] differ from those presented here in that this work addresses potentially nondifferentiable objectives and constraints, whereas [1] focuses on nondifferentiable objectives with differentiable constraints. This paper presents all new findings. Our approach is motivated by recent work on convex relaxation of rank minimization, a topic explored in [2–4]. Specifically, [2] and [3] analyze the performance of Bregman proximal gradient algorithms for convex relaxations of the rank minimization problem, whereas [4] investigates a convex relaxation featuring a nondifferentiable objective. This work is motivated by and extends the findings of [2–4]. This report is prepared for submission to a peer-reviewed journal. This manuscript is self-contained. Chain event graph models have recently been integrated into statistical software for fitting CHAID trees and other popular case-control model classes. Nevertheless, no comprehensive methodology exists for choosing among these model types, nor for determining which features or transitions to include. This study introduces a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approach based on Bayesian maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation for chaining event graph selection, where the random structure is embedded within the posterior distribution. We outline conditions ensuring positive dependence across ChaiR (conditional on history random) structures and identify sufficient feature sets sufficient for posterior sampling via random walk Metropolis steps. Furthermore, the proposed MCMC algorithm is benchmarked against other methods through extensive simulation studies and a real-world case analysis of emergency department attendance data. The results indicate that the proposed MCMC framework outperforms other selection techniques, particularly when dealing with numerous variables. Additionally, we explore applications in network analysis, demonstrating how to integrate network statistics into a Bayesian hierarchical model to achieve network posterior sampling using the same Metropolis step. Finally, the study examines model comparison and prediction, showing that while traditional criteria remain appropriate for fixed models, the non-equivalence of different Bayesian hierarchical priors creates challenges for selecting the optimal model type among chaining event graphs. These issues are further investigated using information-theoretic concepts. Overall, the findings suggest that chaining event graphs offer a compelling alternative to CHAID trees. However, additional research is required to establish the most effective feature selection strategy and to develop novel methods for model comparison and prediction specific to chaining event graphs. Ultimately, these advancements could facilitate automated model selection using established criteria such as AIC and BIC. Future work will also address the challenge of identifying the best subset of models within a chain of linked event graphs when considering networks. Finally, while Bayesian hierarchical models offer significant potential for conditional independence testing, the current focus remains on model selection and feature identification rather than hypothesis testing. Nevertheless, chaining event graphs are well-suited for advanced analyses, including feature selection, which will be explored in subsequent research. By extending existing methods to chaining event graphs, this work enhances their appeal as a versatile alternative to other widely used event sequence models. Furthermore, chaining event graphs provide a versatile framework applicable to diverse research domains, ranging from marketing and medicine to social networks. The proposed method offers a unified solution for model selection across these fields, surpassing the limitations of traditional approaches that rely on ad-hoc feature selection techniques. We introduce a dynamical system grounded in second-order Newtonian mechanics, incorporating both time damping and a Tikhonov regularization term. While the viscous damping ensures asymptotic convergence of the trajectories to a zero of a monotone operator, we demonstrate that the Tikhonov regularization drives the trajectories toward the set of minimal norm solutions. Furthermore, we establish that the trajectories converge strongly to an element within this target set. A key innovation of this paper is that the Tikhonov regularization parameter varies with time, vanishing asymptotically; we provide conditions guaranteeing that this regularization effect remains effective despite its diminishing nature. The proposed system shares a topological structure with a higher-order Hallenberger method. In the context of strongly monotone operators, we prove the exponential stability of a generalized Hallenberger method featuring a Tikhonov regularization with decaying parameters. Additionally, we derive an explicit expression for the asymptotic limit of the trajectories, which generally differs from a zero of the monotone operator. Finally, we illustrate these theoretical findings with numerical examples. Notably, the case of finding the element of minimum norm in Hilbert spaces emerges as a significant particular instance. In this specific scenario, the asymptotic limit of the trajectories is guaranteed to be the element of minimum norm, and we can provide a precise estimate for the convergence rate to this target. This result is achieved by selecting a specific time damping function that balances the need to suppress the decaying regularization effect to the extent necessary for minimizing the operator, while still being rapid enough to ensure strong convergence to the minimal norm element. Consequently, we demonstrate that the proposed mechanics exhibit a convergence rate of order 2/log(t) to the zero set of the monotone operator. In terms of trajectories, this implies that, asymptotically, the trajectories orbit the zero set at an infinite distance. However, when the operator zero set coincides with the subspace of minimal norm elements, we show that a suitable time damping function exists that enables strong convergence to the minimal norm element without altering the asymptotic convergence rate to that zero set. This is accomplished by appropriately tuning the damping parameters to harmonize the effects of time damping and the decaying regularization. We illustrate this result with a simple example of a convex function. Moreover, we observe that our analysis extends to the scenario where a Tikhonov regularization with a time-varying decaying parameter is applied to locate the unique element of minimum norm in a strictly convex setting. This study investigates the wall-following robot as a constrained system exhibiting period-doubling bifurcations and chaos. By analyzing the system's systematic errors, we demonstrate that it can be modeled using an iterated map. The transition to chaotic motion displays universal characteristics, including a period-doubling cascade and a period-doubling spacing constant of 4.66. Furthermore, both noise and initial conditions exert a significant influence on the system's dynamics. While noise induces random, aperiodic transitions between periodic orbits of varying orders, initial conditions determine the specific periodic orbit the system settles into once it reaches a steady state. Finally, we introduce and resolve a novel problem concerning the transition to chaos in such systems. Both theoretical predictions and experimental results confirm that the system undergoes an unruly shift to chaos, marked by the simultaneous destruction of stability and periodicity. This unruly transition is confirmed by the absence of a power-law divergence in the distance to the chaos boundary and by the system's failure to exhibit critical slowing down as the chaos boundary is approached. The concept of unruly shifts to chaos is introduced to describe how complex systems can transition to chaotic behavior without passing through a series of period-doubling bifurcations or experiencing a period-one crisis. This phenomenon is anticipated to occur in other wall-following robots as well. Additionally, in various domains such as neuroscience, economics, and ecology, systems transitioning to chaos via unruly shifts may demonstrate greater robustness, as they avoid the period-doubling route and the associated vulnerabilities. Consequently, these diverse systems may be more resilient to external disturbances. This research underscores the necessity of investigating how complex systems transition to chaos, as these dynamics are crucial for comprehending the behavior of real-world systems. The findings presented here introduce a new approach to studying transition phenomena in complex systems. Furthermore, these results offer a novel perspective on the design and control of complex systems, emphasizing the importance of understanding the relationships among parameters, initial conditions, and noise. The methodologies developed in this study hold potential applications across a wide range of fields, from robotics to economics. The combination of theoretical and experimental work presented in this paper may pave the way for future investigations into the transition to chaos in complex systems. The study of unruly shifts to chaos in complex systems is expected to open new avenues of research in this field.
