This work investigates quantum manipulation of information within the quantum channel sphere, defined as the projective Hilbert space $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}))$ for a finite-dimensional Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$. Employing the Gell-Mann-Lee two-sphere model, the quantum sphere is represented as the disjoint union of an $\lambda$-sphere and an $\mu$-sphere. By extending the $\mu$-sphere, we propose a $\lambda$-sphere, thereby creating a complete model for the quantum sphere. This $\lambda$-sphere extends the rotation group $SO(3)$ to the quantum rotation quaternions, known as the $\lambda$-sphere. These $\lambda$-sphere rotations are modeled using categorical structures, specifically symmetric monoidal closed categories and their functors. The paper demonstrates that the quantum sphere possesses an intrinsic categorical structure and highlights the utility of this structure for developing new methods to manipulate quantum information. Additionally, it is noted that the $\lambda$-sphere offers a convenient framework for converting between pure states and mixed states. Finally, a comprehensive comparison between the Gell-Mann-Lee and established quantum mechanics models is provided, with the resulting comparison table included. Keywords: Quantum sphere, $\lambda$-sphere, Quaternion, Categorical model, Manipulation of quantum information.

This study addresses a Stokes variational inequality within the context of glaciology, which is classified as semicoercive and non-coercive in the standard $H^1$ norm. While prior research has achieved only low-order convergence rates for the non-conforming Nitsche method in 2D, this work introduces a novel approach: the Stokes problem is reformulated as an optimization task utilizing a Tikhonov regularization term. This technique stabilizes the method without compromising its non-conformity. We demonstrate that, unlike other stabilization strategies, this convergence rate remains valid for general saddle-point problems featuring degenerate coefficients. Furthermore, this paper marks the first application of such a method to a variational inequality problem concerning ice sheet modeling. We develop a strategy to resolve the variational inequality by solving a sequence of regularized Stokes problems, utilizing non-conforming finite elements and a non-overlapping domain decomposition method to manage the large linear systems generated. The study presents new, optimal nonuniform $N$-th order convergence rates for the non-conforming non-closed Nitsche method in both 2D and 3D. Additionally, we examine the impact of the regularization parameter, revealing that it can be selected adaptively based on mesh size to achieve a specific error trade-off. Finally, a large-scale numerical experiment is conducted to validate the proposed approach. The code was developed in C++ using the deal.II and DUNE software packages. We introduce DUVET, a project investigating how galactic outflows regulate star formation, utilizing data from the VLT/UVES and MUSE instruments. Our target is the bursting disk galaxy 3C 313, which exhibits extended ionized gas structures and strong [O III] 5007 emission. By analyzing high-resolution spectra, we identified a high-velocity outflow (v ~ 1000 km/s) in the [O III] 5007 line. MUSE 3D spectroscopy enabled the mapping of ionized gas kinematics, revealing a large-scale outflow (v ~ 200 km/s) that curves at a distance of 10 kpc from the galaxy center. Spatially, UV imaging indicates that star formation is concentrated on the disk's upper surface, a region that coincides with the outflow's origin. Our findings suggest that galactic outflows are spatially linked to star formation and may serve as a mechanism to control its rate. Future observations will be necessary to confirm the nature of the outflow and determine its origin. The 3D velocity field of the ionized gas will be compared with molecular gas data from ALMA to further constrain the relationship between outflows and star formation. This study introduces the concept of a Simultaneous Robotic Structure (SRS), which encompasses multiple robots operating in close proximity to execute tasks that a single unit cannot accomplish alone. Structure formation involves simultaneously optimizing the robots' communication topology, control inputs, and configurations. We address the specific challenge of forming a 2-D polygonal SRS with nonholonomic agents subject to nonholonomic constraints. A model problem is defined, solved, and analyzed, revealing that the solution set is generally non-convex and disconnected. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the solution space is typically disconnected when the polygon has 5 or more vertices and requires disjoint interior angles of at least $\pi/2$ in the worst-case scenario. Finally, the proposed formation control law is shown to ensure practical stability. Numerical simulations are included to validate the theoretical findings. The main contributions of this work are the definition and initial characterization of 2-D SRS problems, an algorithm for solving the 2-D polygon case, and the subsequent theoretical analysis of the solution space, practical stability, and simulation results. The remaining problem of forming a general 2-D SRS, along with solution characterizations for higher dimensions, will be addressed in future research. The term SRS is selected to emphasize that these structures represent a novel class of systems within multi-robot and multi-agent frameworks. Additionally, the term underscores the simultaneous nature of the optimization, which contrasts with traditional approaches where the topological structure is often designed independently of the configuration. This distinction is significant because, in many classical problems, the resulting structures are typically stars or complete graphs, a limitation we aim to overcome. Topological formation design is also considered a distinct problem. Let $\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})$ represent the collection of analytic functions defined on the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$. A mapping $h$ is defined as a Bohr lifting on $\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})$ if, for every $f \in \mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})$ with $a_0=0$, the Bohr radius of $f$ is at least as great as that of $h$. This paper demonstrates that if $h$ is a lifting, then $h$ is also a starlike log-harmonic mapping. Furthermore, we determine the enhanced Bohr radius for the class of starlike log-harmonic mappings and show that this radius is optimal. Additionally, we establish a Landau class centered at the origin for starlike log-harmonic mappings and prove that its Bohr radius is sharp. Finally, we derive a Landau class for log-harmonic mappings based on their associated angular arguments; in this case, the derived Bohr radius is sharp only when the angular argument corresponds to the Koebe mapping. Throughout the study, we utilize the Jack lemma. Finally, we provide an infinite family of lifting examples and validate them through several finite examples. Notably, all examples in this paper have been verified using Wolfram Mathematica. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Landau class and Bohr radius for starlike log-harmonic mappings can be derived from functions with negative real parts. However, extending these results to the Landau class and Bohr radius for convex type $k$-univalent functions remains an open problem. The primary innovation of this work lies in its application to complex harmonic mappings. Additionally, the infinite number of examples presented herein may serve as a foundation for further research. Kendall's tau serves as a nonparametric metric for correlation. We establish efficient bounds for the variance of its estimator and propose a method to determine whether it reaches the boundaries of $\pm1$. For finite datasets, we derive exact moment estimations and prove that the variance of Kendall's tau is strictly positive, ensuring the existence of a non-degenerate distribution. Furthermore, we present novel lower and upper bounds for its moments and refine the variance upper bound previously suggested by Ma and Li (2011). These findings indicate that the effective sample size for Kendall's tau scales at $n^{\frac{1}{3}}$ rather than linearly with $n$. Additionally, we introduce a new class of transformations capable of increasing its magnitude toward $\pm1$ without compromising data integrity. Simulations demonstrate that our findings hold practical value and can enhance statistical power. Finally, we conduct an empirical analysis of the COVID-19 pandemic to examine the relationship between social mobility and the spread of the virus across European countries. To address this, we propose a novel approach that incorporates the ability to reason over visual content through vision transformers, marking a significant evolution in the detection of deep fake images and videos. In evaluating the efficacy of this evolved detection mechanism, we conducted a comprehensive experimental study focused on the most recent and sophisticated vision transformer-based deep fake generative models. To ensure reliable and meaningful quantitative assessments of the proposed solution's efficacy, we employed multiple objective metrics, including F1, ROC-AUC, and precision and recall at specific false alarm rates. Our results demonstrate that: (i) evolved detection mechanisms surpass traditional ones in terms of both accuracy and efficiency; and (ii) synthetic media generated by the latest vision transformer-based models are more challenging to detect than those produced by traditional convolutional neural network-based models. Finally, all our code and experimental results are publicly available to facilitate reproducibility and further research. asynchronous parallel (OP) algorithms (APEAs) offer the potential to substantially cut the computational time of standard sequential multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (SEAs) by employing a non-deterministic parallel execution model. However, without careful design, parallelization can introduce performance degradation. The primary issue in asynchronous algorithms stems from the risk of premature convergence, caused by the parent selector prematurely designating a subset of the population for replication. This selection must remain unbiased toward specific subregions of the objective space. A critical factor influencing this unbiased selection is the variance in asynchronous OP execution times. If performance degradation is avoided, the theoretical computational time of an APEA could be reduced by up to n times that of a SEEA, where n represents the number of parallel threads. This study addresses performance degradation by introducing a novel asynchronous algorithm that utilizes frequency-oriented selection. This approach constructs the mating pool based on the frequency of the multi-objective population individuals generated by each worker thread over a recent time interval. The primary contribution of this work is the analysis of how population variance variance evolves over time in asynchronous OP algorithms that use frequency-based selection, a property that can be tuned to prevent premature OP algorithm convergence. The effectiveness of this algorithm is evaluated using the asynchronous version of MO-DEAP (Multi-Objective DEAplication) on established benchmark suites. The results demonstrate that frequency-oriented selection successfully mitigates the impact of asynchronous OP execution time variations on evolutionary algorithms' performance. Additionally, the computational time of the MO-DEAP APEA is compared against the sequential version of MO-DEAP, along with other asynchronous OP algorithms derived from it. Finally, the computational time of the APEA is analyzed relative to the number of parallel threads. Overall, the findings indicate that population variance over time is effectively controlled by the proposed frequency-oriented selection, thereby preventing the expected performance degradation associated with asynchronous OP algorithms, and that increasing the number of workers can further reduce the algorithm's expected computational time. This study details the identification and validation of a new cold super-Earth within the system OGLE-2017-BLG-1434, with a planet-star mass ratio of $\mu \approx 2.8 \times 10^{-4}$. Leveraging near-infrared imaging from Keck Adaptive Optics, we have unequivocally confirmed the existence of this planet, which orbits at approximately 1.5 AU from a low-mass star at a equilibrium temperature of roughly 180 K. By incorporating this system into our dataset, we demonstrate that the observed low mass-ratio bias is statistically significant only at a confidence level exceeding 99%. Furthermore, we illustrate that the previously reported excess at low mass-ratios can be accurately modeled without necessitating multiple degenerate regimes. This system represents a robust instance of a planet falling in the $\mu \lesssim 10^{-3}$ regime, thereby confirming that microlensing is now capable of reliably detecting and confirming low mass-ratio planets. Additionally, this planet is among the closest to its host star among low mass-ratio microlensing planets and is the second most massive, highlighting its unique position. The verification of OGLE-2017-BLG-1434b marks a significant advancement in our understanding of small mass-ratio planet formation and the potential physical biases inherent to the microlensing technique. This work underscores the critical role of high-resolution imaging in advancing our comprehension of the low mass-ratio population. We report the detection of narrow-line self-absorptions in the neutral hydrogen (HI) 21 cm line toward the high-mass star-forming region G176.51+00.20, observed using the Nobeyama Radio Observatory 45 m telescope. This unique spectral signature indicates the presence of cold and dense HI clouds along the line of sight, which absorb the background emission originating from warmer and less dense HI regions situated between the absorbers and the observer. By applying the radiative transfer equation to the HI 21 cm line spectrum, we derived HI column densities and temperatures from the observed profiles. The spatial distribution of these HI structures was reconstructed from the deprojected line-of-sight geometry, revealing that the absorbing clouds are embedded within the neutral gas envelope surrounding the star-forming region. The temperature data indicate that these clouds are not heated by the forming massive cluster, suggesting they are distant from the cluster's center. Furthermore, the column densities of the absorbing clouds are approximately 100 times lower than those of the surrounding envelope, implying that these clouds will be assimilated into the main cloud as accretion proceeds. Finally, the spatial distribution of the narrow-line self-absorptions aligns with the infrared-emitting cloud core, indicating that these clouds are integral components of the cloud core. This evidence supports the theory that star formation occurs within a dense molecular core embedded within a more extended, less dense neutral hydrogen envelope. Additionally, we discuss the implications of these findings for understanding the relationship between HI and molecular clouds during star formation. Additionally, the average mixing frequency is measured as \phi s = -0.004 \pm 0.013 (stat) \pm 0.003 (syst) rad, consistent with Standard Model predictions. Deep learning has become a cornerstone in developing computer vision systems, yet most applications train models specifically for a single task. This approach is impractical when training data is scarce, scarce, or when data availability varies between tasks. Conversely, transferring pre-trained models offers a viable solution in such scenarios. This study evaluates the efficacy of transferring pre-trained deep neural networks for image recognition across different domains. We conducted experiments using three distinct architectures on three datasets with distinct domains: ImageNet, 2D-PALM, and 2D-H&E. Our findings indicate that simply utilizing a pre-trained model without modifications yields the best results. Additionally, we observed that data scarcity significantly impacts training, particularly for domains with complex structures. Finally, we explored the transferability of these models to a different domain, 2D-CT, which is more challenging. All source models performed well, though ImageNet exhibited a greater drop in accuracy compared to 2D-PALM and 2D-H&E. Furthermore, transferring between vastly different domains, such as cytology and radiology, is not recommended. We demonstrate that, provided $d \geq 2$, the maximum count of arc lengths $(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_d)$ for arcs in $\mathbb F_q^2$ with separation vectors $(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_{d-1})$ is $q$, and this count reaches $q$ if and only if all separations are distinct. Furthermore, we establish that the number of $d$-arc sets in $\mathbb F_q^2$ possessing the same distribution of separation vectors is maximized when variations along individual axes are independent, and it is exactly one if every separation distribution takes the value $q$. These extremal properties hold for $d$-arc sets that are invariant under variations in the second coordinate. Our findings extend to $d$-arc sets with initial vectors forming a subspace of dimension $k$. Additionally, we present an algorithm capable of generating the $q$ distinct maximal arcs in $\mathbb F_q^2$ in nondecreasing order of their slopes. Finally, a computational approach is proposed to verify our theorems for small finite fields. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have gained significant traction for analyzing complex graph structures across a wide range of applications. However, evaluating a GNN model involves multiple components, including the graph data, the specific algorithm, hyperparameters, and training procedures. These diverse factors complicate the standardized comparison and analysis of different GNN designs. To address this challenge, we introduce PIGNN, the first framework designed to generate parameterized representations of GNNs. By focusing on the algorithm itself rather than specific datasets or parameters, PIGNN enables direct and fair evaluation of the intrinsic expressiveness of graph algorithms. PIGNN operates by first translating a GNN algorithm into a generic neural network using the PyTorch module framework, and then automatically converting this module into a comprehensive set of neural networks through parameterization. Experimental results demonstrate that PIGNN successfully generates expressive parameterized graph algorithms and effectively captures the capacity variations within these parameterized graphs. The source code for PIGNN is publicly accessible at https://github.com/peiyangliu/PIGNN. Furthermore, PIGNN is integrated with PyTorch and PyTorch-Geometric, the leading frameworks in the graph machine learning community. Consequently, PIGNN offers a versatile tool for comparing, analyzing, and designing graph neural network algorithms. Additionally, PyG-DeepLearning, a well-known benchmark dataset collection, has been developed using PIGNN, featuring 1,000 distinct graph algorithms and 20,000 parameterized versions. This integration facilitates a more standardized and uniform approach to comparing and analyzing graph algorithms within the PyG-DeepLearning benchmark. The implementation can be accessed at https://github.com/peiyangliu/PyG-DeepLearning. Our paper and source code are also available at https://github.com/peiyangliu/PIGNN. Legendre Memory Module (LMM) is a newly introduced memory mechanism designed to enhance large language models (LLMs). Its core component, the Legendre Tensor (LLT), is an expanded tensor that relies on multi-dimensional tensor products of Legendre polynomials (PLP) and can be computed efficiently through parallel matrix multiplications. Although utilizing PLP increases memory capacity by two to three times compared to standard tensors and enables training of larger models on limited hardware, the LLT still grows rapidly with model size, creating significant memory bottlenecks. This paper addresses these challenges by first extending the LLT design to minimize memory usage during training. Subsequently, we implement a memory-efficient strategy for LLT computation by fully leveraging parallel matrix multiplications. Finally, we explore time-efficient training methods for LLMs utilizing LMMs by analyzing time complexities. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of LMMs in learning tasks. Furthermore, we successfully trained a 7-billion-parameter LLM on a single A100 GPU by adopting LMMs. Most significantly, our results indicate that LMMs can reduce training time by up to 50% while maintaining comparable loss values to standard LLM training. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are widely used to solve partial differential equations by embedding physical laws into neural network training. However, during optimization, these methods often prioritize frequencies earlier than desired, causing high-frequency components representing fine details to be neglected, which degrades solution accuracy. This study identifies the root cause as momentum, which inadvertently amplifies the optimizer's preference for large norms. Drawing an analogy to spectral regularization, we propose a spectral penalty term, the first of its kind applied to PINNs, to explicitly manage this spectral bias. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this penalty through a simple numerical test and evaluate its performance across various scenarios, including different learning rate and batch size configurations, a viscous shell problem, and the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. Our findings indicate that the spectral penalty significantly enhances accuracy, particularly when paired with a larger learning rate and sample batch size. Finally, we present additional results comparing our spectral penalty against other optimization techniques, including momentum optimization, quasi-Newton methods, and the Adam optimizer. Our results show that the spectral penalty consistently outperforms these alternatives, confirming its superiority in improving solution fidelity. While reinforcement learning (RL) has made significant strides in autonomous robotics, it struggles to generalize across different tasks and remains largely opaque, lacking both causal explanations and trust from users. Data compression is ubiquitous in computing, yet reversible compression schemes that allow decompressed data to be returned to its original state remain rare. In biological and physical systems, information is inherently linked to entropy and thermodynamics, implying that compression likely incurs an energetic cost. This study presents a physical system capable of compressing quantum information, where the compression error can be arbitrarily minimized by simply enlarging the quantum memory. When this quantum compression scheme is applied to an optical beam, it produces a distinctly nonclassical outcome: an output state where the beam's energy cannot increase through any passive, unitary evolution, representing both a quantum compression and dissipation process. We explore the potential applications of quantum compression devices within quantum thermal machines. Specifically, we demonstrate that such devices can function as switches for both energy and work, revealing nontrivial relationships between quantum compression and thermodynamics. These findings pertain to experimental achievements in quantum compression utilizing quantum engines. Furthermore, our model offers a platform for investigating the interplay between information and thermodynamics, with significant implications for quantum thermodynamics. Our findings underscore the promise of quantum technology in achieving energy efficiency. Furthermore, this research establishes a new field known as quantum thermodynamics of compressed data. Finally, this study underscores the necessity of quantum technology for achieving energy efficiency in a quantum world. Dark matter candidates possessing spin-dependent nucleon interactions could have masses below the current direct detection limits. To address this, we investigate the potential of direct detection experiments utilizing nucleon structure that matches these spin-dependent criteria. Specifically, we analyze the interactions of spin-dependent targets with the $\vec{S}$ state of $^6$Li, demonstrating that spin-dependent signals can exceed spin-independent ones by a factor of ten. We present a comprehensive framework for direct detection experiments that incorporate $^6$Li targets alongside standard targets such as xenon and zinc. This work establishes a basis for future experimental designs and data analysis strategies aimed at exploiting the advantages of spin-dependent interactions. Furthermore, we provide detailed numerical results for the required nuclear form factors. Our analysis indicates that next-generation experiments could achieve sensitivity to spin-dependent cross sections at the level of $10^{-39}$ cm$^2$ (corresponding to approximately $10^{-10}$ fb), with the ultimate limit for future experiments reaching $10^{-43}$ cm$^2$ (about $10^{-11}$ fb). These two sensitivity thresholds are necessary to fully explore the cross-section parameter space for spin-dependent interactions. We also examine the sensitivity of our proposed target combinations and compare these projections with existing and anticipated limits from other direct detection methods. Additionally, we address the role of xenon subcomponents in direct detection experiments and the necessity of including $^6$Li in theoretical constraints derived from such analyses. Finally, we show that the sensitivity of direct detection experiments is not significantly affected by uncertainties in the relative strength between spin-dependent and spin-independent interactions. This robustness ensures that direct detection results remain reliable even when only one of the two interaction types is assumed. Finally, we demonstrate that direct detection limits are not heavily dependent on the specific model used to connect cross-sections to the astrophysical parameter $J$, a factor that is otherwise crucial for constraining spin-dependent scenarios using indirect detection methods. Consequently, direct detection experiments can establish the first constraints on spin-dependent dark matter interactions in a model-independent manner. This serves as a strong motivation for developing direct detection techniques capable of measuring spin-dependent signals. To achieve this, we recommend that future direct detection experiments include $^6$Li targets to ensure sensitivity to spin-dependent interactions and to determine the fraction of subcomponents in other targets, such as natural xenon. Blind image restoration (BUR) addresses the challenge of recovering high-quality images from low-quality inputs by automatically estimating motion parameters without prior knowledge of scene details. This study introduces a novel approach that utilizes a nonparametric kernel mixture model to approximate the unknown motion parameters, thereby eliminating the need for discrete model selection. We derive a closed-form solution for the regression coefficients of the kernel mixture and apply the expectation-maximization algorithm to jointly infer motion parameters and scene details. Furthermore, we demonstrate a parametric approximation of the kernel mixture posterior to enhance computational efficiency. The proposed method was evaluated on synthetic data generated from public datasets, benchmarked against three competing algorithms on images with unknown motion parameters, and tested on real-world degraded images. Results indicate that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of image quality and parameter estimation accuracy, while delivering solutions approximately 1.5 times faster than other methods. The implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan2000/Kernel-Approximation. Additionally, we release a new dataset comprising 1,000 blurred images paired with ground-tripe motion parameters and latent images for performance evaluation. This dataset includes a wide range of parameters, including scale, rotation, and motion blur length, with the parameters used in this paper selected from a subset of 100 images. The full dataset will be made available to facilitate the development and comparison of new BUR methods. We anticipate that this resource will be valuable to the community for enhancing BUR techniques. The remaining 900 images from the dataset can be accessed here: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/11441444444444444444444444444444444444444444444444444444444444444. Formal validation of software relies on mathematical specifications, typically expressed in formal languages like first-order logic. While there is growing interest in value alignment—the alignment of human and artificial intelligence values—there is also increasing demand for communicating technical requirements to software engineers in a more intuitive and accessible manner. Consequently, there is a pressing need for new approaches to formal validation using specifications defined in natural languages. This paper presents such an approach, where natural language specifications are formally grounded in Hoare logic to enable software validation. We present a theory called Natural Hoare Logic (NHL), a variant of Hoare logic designed for first-order logic formulas in natural language. NHL serves as the foundation for our proposed method for formal validation using natural language specifications. Additionally, we explore several applications of NHL and report on progress toward implementing this logic within a formal verification tool. Our ultimate goal is to facilitate the formal validation of software through specifications expressed in natural language. To achieve this, we demonstrate how to model specific software requirements using NHL and how to automatically verify them against a specific C program. Our work advances towards automatically validating software from naturally specified requirements and establishes a bridge between natural language and formal methods. We demonstrate the applicability of NHL by showing that its sound program validation can be derived from sound Hoare triple validation. Furthermore, we highlight NHL's advantages over existing approaches, such as its ability to handle complex requirements involving subformulas and its soundness regarding the specification of C programs. The paper includes examples of software validation using both NHL and standard Hoare logic. Ultimately, our contributions include a theory of natural language specification, a method for validating software using these specifications, and a tool that supports this capability. The implementation is available at https://github.com/taiki-w/NaturalHoare. The soundness of NHL is proven in our previous study (https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.02005). The soundness of NHL is soundly extendable to C programs. Canopus is a new type of practical Byzantine Fault Tolerant (BFT) replica state machine (RSM) designed for large-scale cloud deployments. Its core innovation lies in a novel communication primitive called the Group Exchange (GX), which is implemented using large, multi-round message exchanges. Canopus achieves high scalability by assigning specific participants to GX rounds based on their required quorums, thereby overcoming the traditional $O(N^2)$ messaging complexity. However, this efficiency comes at the cost of resilience, as GX failures can stall Canopus operations.

To address this weakness, we introduce RCanopus, a family of RSM protocols that render Canopus robust against both failures and Byzantine behavior. RCanopus achieves this resilience by converting GX failures into the more manageable $O(N)$ point-exchange (PX) primitive. We present four distinct RCanopus variants, each offering different performance trade-offs. Evaluations demonstrate that the most resilient variant, dRCanopus, delivers Canopus-level scalability while maintaining up to 10x higher resilience, with only a 2x reduction in throughput. Furthermore, cross-comparison with other prominent protocols reveals that dRCanopus outperforms all competitors in both scalability and resilience. To our knowledge, this represents the first protocol to combine the benefits of large multi-round exchanges with Canopus-style quorum-based participants, an insight that enhances the overall practicality of Canopus. The RCanopus family is available as open-source software at https://github.com/utias-robotics/Canopus. Our repository also includes additional experiments and supplementary code to support these findings. Recent experiments have begun to measure the bending modulus of lipid membranes doped with varying amounts of cholesterol. Our analysis indicates that the observed trend in cholesterol's effect on this modulus aligns with coarse-grained density functional theory predictions for partial electron density. These findings suggest that cholesterol's influence extends beyond the monolayer, affecting regions farther from the interface. Furthermore, the bending modulus may be affected by an effective headgroup thickness, which increases as water penetrates deeper into the headgroup region. To account for this, we incorporate a term into the functional that depends on local variations in electron population. We demonstrate that this proposed model, utilizing density functional theory, can accurately describe experimental data across a wide range of conditions. The proposed model offers potential for extending the current application of density functional theory. Additionally, we examine how membrane tension impacts the bending modulus and report on the sensitivity of this quantity to the selection of lipid models. Finally, we outline several avenues for future research. This work was conducted in collaboration with experimentalists A. P. Makarov and A. V. Makarov. A. P. This study examines the loop quantum astrophysical model derived from the ADM Hamiltonian. By applying the loop quantum gravity method to ADM gravity within a symmetric sector, we develop this astrophysical framework. The loop quantum astrophysical parameter is calculated by substituting appropriate configuration space functions for the ADM system into the loop quantum gravity expressions. The resulting formula for the loop quantum astrophysical parameter indicates a cosmological constant term and a critical value beyond which a quantum gravitational phase transition occurs. Specifically, a cosmological constant term is derived from the area gap, while the critical value results from the cancellation of higher-order terms in the loop quantum astrophysical parameter. This critical value is independent of the cosmological constant, suggesting that a phase transition from a classical ADM gravity system to a loop quantum gravity system can occur even in the absence of a cosmological constant. Furthermore, the ratio between the ADM Hamiltonian and the loop quantum astrophysical parameter is determined by the loop correction factor. This factor is a polynomial function of the loop quantum gravity parameters, including the loop area, flux, and asymptotic angular velocity. These parameters rely on the loop area and are influenced by the ADM gravity system. Consequently, the loop correction factor demonstrates the compatibility between the ADM gravity system and loop quantum gravity. Finally, the criteria for the loop correction factor show that the ADM gravity system is more effective than the loop quantum gravity system when the loop area is small, and this conclusion is supported by numerical analysis. Additionally, the numerical values for the loop correction factor and its corresponding efficiency range are provided. These findings suggest that the loop correction factor is essential for the loop quantum astrophysical parameter. Therefore, the evolution of the loop quantum astrophysical parameter is governed by the change in the loop correction factor, which is determined by the loop area. This relationship is further confirmed by the consistency between the loop quantum astrophysical parameter and the loop area. Ultimately, the loop correction factor is more significant than the loop area. The theoretical conclusion regarding the ADM Hamiltonian's effectiveness is also applicable to the Ashtekar variable Hamiltonian. This conclusion is based on the fact that both the ADM Hamiltonian and the Ashtekar variable Hamiltonian share the same loop correction factor within the loop quantum astrophysical parameter. Furthermore, the theoretical conclusion regarding the loop correction factor is also applicable to a chiral loop quantum gravity system, as this system utilizes the same loop correction factor found in the ADM Hamiltonian. Integrating deep neural networks into safety-critical domains like autonomous driving demands a robust uncertainty quantification framework. While the benefits of uncertain inference are well-documented in classification tasks, the specific nature of errors in deep object detectors remains under-researched. This study introduces a novel Bayesian approach that propagates dropout masks through a detector test batch to sample weight values from a detector network. By employing Monte Carlo (MC) dropout, the method generates an uncertainty map for each input, where uncertainty is defined as the standard deviation across these maps. The proposed technique is validated on a deep object detector trained on over 100,000 traffic signs, comparing three architectures: DeepSORT, YOLOv3, and a custom detector. Results demonstrate that BayesOD can reliably flag out-of-distribution samples, such as occluded traffic signs. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/SebastianKoch/objdet_uncertainty. The methodology is also applicable to other deep detectors, including Mask R-CNN and Faster R-CNN. Furthermore, uncertainty maps can be utilized for downstream tasks in computer vision and autonomous driving. This work offers a new pathway for uncertainty assessment in deep object detectors and establishes a foundation for developing safer automated driving systems. The study underscores the necessity of rigorous uncertainty evaluation in object detection and provides a promising solution for the automotive industry. Additionally, the method represents a significant step toward the safe deployment of deep learning in safety-critical applications. The methodology was validated on a deep object detector trained on a dataset of traffic signs containing more than 100,000 samples across 100 classes. BayesOD was tested on DeepSORT, YOLOv3, and a custom detector trained on the GTSDB Traffic Sign Dataset. The validation process involved testing all three detectors on 100 images not present in the training set, including object occlusions and objects absent from the dataset. The results indicate that BayesOD can flag out-of-distribution samples, such as occluded traffic signs. The uncertainty maps generated by BayesOD can be utilized for downstream tasks in computer vision and autonomous driving. This work validates a new pathway for deep object detector uncertainty assessment and offers a solution for the automotive industry. The results demonstrate that BayesOD can reliably flag out-of-distribution samples, such as occluded traffic signs. The uncertainty maps generated by BayesOD can be utilized for downstream tasks in computer vision and autonomous driving. This work validates a new approach for deep object detector uncertainty assessment

This study tackles short-term traffic prediction for traffic streams by initially detecting and tracking segments within moving traffic to model its dynamic patterns. A recursive Bayesian predictor is employed to forecast these segments, featuring a streamlined design that focuses on predicting speed without requiring shape estimation. The proposed system is assessed using both synthesized and real-world data, comparing its performance against existing methods. Experimental results indicate that the approach achieves state-of-the-art accuracy in predicting speed for shape-dynamic traffic streams. Furthermore, the method's computational complexity is analyzed, and a benchmarking suite is made available for future research in traffic prediction. This suite comprises real data, established baseline predictors, detailed complexity metrics, and comprehensive evaluation protocols. Additionally, the suite is extensible, allowing new predictors to be easily added by implementing their classifiers. The entire suite, excluding the latest synthesized datasets, can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/SebastianSchaefer/traffic-prediction}. These newly released synthesized datasets are also available on the same platform under the path Synthesis/data_2020/. The core components, including the traffic stream analyzer, segment detection and tracking method, and the segmentation results used as input for the predictor, are also hosted at \url{https://github.com/SebastianSchaefer/segmentation}. Finally, the segmentation repository will be updated periodically with newer versions of the synthesized datasets. Specifically, one dataset will be drawn from these updated synthesis results for predictor evaluation, while another dataset, prepared via earlier synthesis versions, is included in the analysis repository for testing and benchmarking purposes. The segmentation repository will continue to evolve to support further research. The predictor itself is also open-source and hosted at \url{https://github.com/SebastianSchaefer/predictor}, where it will undergo evaluation in the future. Additionally, the suite includes various predictors developed by other researchers, which are cited in their respective original papers. While the segment tracking algorithm is not included in the predictor implementation, it is available in a separate repository. This separation ensures that changes to the segmentation algorithm do not impact the predictor code. The predictor implementation will also be utilized in a mobility simulation to generate synthetic traffic streams for evaluation purposes. The simulation code is hosted at \url{https://github.com/SebastianSchaefer/ mobility_simulation}. This tool allows researchers to create traffic streams with varying levels of dynamic shape, controlling parameters such as the amplitude and frequency of shape fluctuations. It also supports various motion patterns, including acceleration, by adjusting the amplitude of acceleration against distance.

A fundamental concept in proof theory is the provably total functions of a theory, which encompasses the collection of all functions that every functionally closed extension of the theory must also totally define. This paper offers a novel perspective on this class by utilizing the notion of $S$-rewriting, where $S$ represents a $\Sigma_n$ pointclass. Specifically, if $f$ is a totally defined function that every model of a theory $T$ believes to compute via some code $c$, then $f$ is explicitly $S$-rewritable from the pair $\langle c, x\rangle$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the provably total functions of $\Pi_{n+1}-AFA$ constitute precisely those functions $f$ for which the joint $\Sigma_{n+2}$ type of $\langle c, x\rangle$ holds. Furthermore, for any theory $T$ and set $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, the functions explicitly $S$-rewritable in $T$ are all provably total in $T$. Leveraging this result, we prove the consistency of $\Pi_{n+1}-AFA$ provided $\bigcirc^{\sharp}_{n+3}$ does not include 0. This proof mirrors the structure of Sharp's original demonstration that $Con(A-\mathsf{CA}_0)$ equals $\bigcirc^{\sharp}_{3}$. Additionally, we establish the consistency of $\Pi_{n+1}-A-\mathsf{S}^1_{n+2}$ under the same condition. The primary tool for our primary result is the $S$-rewriting class, the properties of which are derived from the inductive definition of $\Pi_{n+1}-A-\mathsf{S}^1_{n+2}$. We contend that this research represents the initial link between an abstract combinatorial property and the consistency strength of an arithmetical theory. Finally, the paper concludes with several open questions. This study leverages the unique capabilities of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to partition the hippocampus for assessing disease severity in both Alzheimer's and Epilepsy. We assess the effectiveness of various CNN architectures, including ResNet, VGG, and LeNet, in classifying Hippocampus Longitudinal Segmentation (HLS) images into four distinct zones: the dentate gyrus (DG), hippocampal head (HH), hippocampal body (HB), and hippocampal tail (HT). To enhance classification precision, we employed data augmentation techniques, such as horizontal and vertical flips, rotations, and translations. The high performance of the proposed model demonstrates its potential utility in supporting the clinical management of these neurological conditions. We introduce and analyze the pigeonhole phenomenon within the framework of quantum key distribution (QKD), offering a quantum information-theoretic interpretation of this concept. Our analysis begins with a straightforward entanglement-based QKD protocol where pigeonhole effects are readily observable in both preparation and post-selection. Subsequently, we examine the BB84-based entanglement-based protocol, for which we derive an expression describing pigeonhole phenomena as a function of source preparation rates, the frequency of measurement comparison, and the number of comparison cycles. This expression serves to highlight the importance of the comparison cycle frequency in pigeonhole-based security proofs. Furthermore, we apply this formula to analyze the security of the GG22 device-independent quantum key distribution protocol, demonstrating that the derived key rate aligns with findings from other studies. Ultimately, we establish that pigeonhole phenomena are intrinsically linked to the study of quantum correlations. Additionally, we explore protocols that mitigate pigeonhole effects by utilizing transversal modes. In these scenarios, even though measurements are conducted on single photons, the non-orthogonality of quantum states is leveraged to eliminate pigeonhole issues during the error correction phase of key rate distillation. This approach enables the achievement of a higher key rate than methods relying on error rate distillation. Notably, the transversal mode itself functions as a valuable quantum resource capable of facilitating high-quality quantum communication. Finally, we outline potential extensions of this research in upcoming studies. This study utilizes a Monte Carlo simulation to model the propagation of cosmic ray secondary particles, aiming to calculate the average absorbed dose rate for a 70 kg human in low Earth orbit (LEO). The simulation tracks annihilation products of cosmic ray primary particles up to 10 GeV, which are deflected by Earth's magnetic field before interacting with the atmosphere to generate secondary particles. Dose absorption is computed using a tissue-equivalent phantom. Results indicate that the average absorbed dose for a 70 kg person varies with orbital altitude, and this average is analyzed in relation to the whole-body organ equivalent dose. Furthermore, the radiation environment in LEO is examined in the context of long-term space missions, such as those planned for the International Space Station. Additionally, the simulation was employed to assess crew exposure during the SpaceX-7 Starlink satellite launch on June 27, 2020, and an analysis of space weather data from that date revealed a correlation between radiation environment fluctuations and solar wind conditions. These findings are presented as recommendations for the safe operation of launch vehicles and spacecraft in LEO. The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) and their subsequent evolution into Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have driven significant advancements in both language and vision processing. To further advance artificial intelligence, it is essential to integrate audio modalities into this existing language-vision paradigm, which has led to the emergence of the multi-modal LLM (LLMs). To effectively merge disparate graph structures and heterogeneous data from languages, visions, and sounds, we propose a modular framework that connects various Deep Graph Neural Networks (DGNNs) through a hierarchical pyramid-like architecture. This approach facilitates cross-modal alignment and joint learning, enabling cross-modal transfer and generalization. Specifically, we address two primary challenges: first, we design a global shrinkage framework to merge diverse graph structures into a unified topology; second, we implement local reconfiguration to align heterogeneous graphs during the learning process. Experimental results across multiple modalities demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this proposed framework. Extending the $\varepsilon$-differential privacy framework to database queries has a significant impact on publishing tables, which is crucial for maintaining privacy in contemporary society. This work focuses on a specific query family to demonstrate that revealing the full database poses a distinct risk compared to disclosing answers to low-rank matrix completion queries. To address this, we propose a differentially private algorithm for low-rank matrix completion that leverages the Huber function. Our method for estimating the rank of the underlying matrix draws on the Restricted Isometry Property, while bounds on reconstruction error are derived from Singular Value Decomposition properties. Finally, numerical experiments are presented to validate the proposed reconstruction error bounds and to compare our algorithm's performance against a baseline. These results confirm the effectiveness of our approach for low-rank matrix completion within a differentially private framework. Furthermore, our method for determining the matrix rank is more accurate than existing techniques. Overall, this work offers a promising alternative for releasing tabular data through low-rank matrix completion. Specifically, it advances the goal of providing sufficient privacy protection for table releases, thereby mitigating the differentially private noise required for such disclosures. Additionally, the proposed algorithm is designed to be computationally efficient. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first application of differential privacy to matrix completion problems. Finally, the efficiency of our approach may prove valuable for other emerging applications involving tabular data. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/fernandoalvarado/dp-matrix-completion}. The "crisis of Galactic parameters" stems from the discrepancy between Galactic models and observations of individual sources, such as stars and star clusters. To address this, we introduce a unified, physically motivated model that describes how dust in the interstellar medium affects the polarization and photometry of background sources at both ultraviolet-optical and infrared wavelengths. This framework incorporates the emission of Astroparticulaire Interstellaire (Astrodust) and is designed to be readily applied to source populations in observations where foreground dust contributions are negligible. The model is validated against the Gaia Data Release 2 (DR2) color-magnitude diagram of unreddened main sequence stars, which shows a reasonable fit. Furthermore, applying the model to reddened main sequence stars in Gaia DR2 successfully recovers solar neighborhood dust properties consistent with those derived from unreddened stars. The Astrodust+PAH model serves as a valuable tool for quantifying dust properties in the local Galactic environment and may be integrated with other modeling approaches to address the interstellar medium (ISM) dust crisis. We report on a significant kinematic shift in the gas within the circumstellar disk of CIDA 1, a massive, young, low-mass star. The inner disk region rotates as a solid body, but at a radius of 100 au, the gas exhibits super-Keplerian velocities comparable to those seen in protoplanetary disks around more massive stars. This finding suggests the presence of a massive planet, the strongest evidence yet for such an object around a brown dwarf. Additionally, we identify a large, dense gap in the millimeter dust, which aligns with the kinematic break. The gap is best explained by a giant planet with a mass between 4 and 10 MJup located at approximately 100 au. The millimeter gas surface density profile also shows a distinct break at this radius, consistent with the gap's position and size. These results indicate that disks around very low-mass stars can host massive planets, and that these planets are effective at opening gaps in both dust and gas. Furthermore, the system's young age implies rapid planet formation, underscoring the efficiency of the process. Finally, the observed features in the disk of CIDA 1 are consistent with predictions from hydrodynamical simulations of planet-disk interactions. We conclude that the shift in disk rotation and the gap in millimeter dust are best explained by a massive planet (4–10 MJup) at roughly 100 au, providing compelling evidence for a giant planet forming within a few million years in a disk around a low-mass star. This system is likely in the early stages of planetary formation, and the system's youth suggests that giant planets can form quickly around low-mass stars. The characteristics of CIDA 1 also match simulations of planet-disk interactions. This study examines the game of reducing a graph $G$ to a state with no self-looves by removing self-looves at specific vertices, where the act of removing a loop from vertex $v$ generates new loops connecting $v$ to its original neighbors. The process concludes when all self-looves are eliminated. We investigate two strategies: (i) a local strategy that maximizes the count of self-looves removed from a single vertex, and (ii) a global strategy designed to minimize the total number of moves required to fully reduce the graph. Our work focuses on determining the worst-case outcomes for both approaches across all graphs with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges. Furthermore, we present an algorithm to determine the maximum number of clicks needed to reduce a given graph $G$ in no more than $k$ moves, and we explore various properties and open questions related to this problem. Specifically, we examine the challenge of reducing any graph $G$ to a single vertex using the minimum number of moves. We demonstrate that this problem is NP-complete when $k=2$ and parameterized fixed-parameter complete (FPT-complete) in a more general form. Additionally, we establish upper and lower bounds for both local and global strategies and investigate the existence of optimal strategies for arbitrary graphs. Finally, we introduce the concept of "clickable loops" to illustrate the behavior of the game and establish lower bounds for the (i) and (ii) problems based on the count of clickable loops. Our primary findings are as follows:

(i) For any graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, the maximum number of self-looves that can be removed from a single vertex using a local strategy is bounded by $2^{m/n}$. This bound is sharp, as there exists a family of graphs where every local strategy results in the complete removal of all $m$ self-looves from a single vertex.

Compressed sensing (CS) is a recently developed technology utilized for reconstructing images from highly undersampled measurements within the sensing domain. Driven by the rapid advancement of CS, numerous algorithms have been proposed; for instance, various approaches have been developed to simultaneously solve image reconstruction and segmentation challenges. These methods typically employ a variational model that integrates CS constraints with image reconstruction and binarization components, utilizing the $L_1$-norm as the primary measure for segmentation and reconstruction. However, this prior art often suffers from suboptimal segmentation, resulting in inaccurate boundaries. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a novel variational model for high-quality image recovery. The proposed framework incorporates a segmentation term utilizing a modified total variation norm alongside a data fidelity term rooted in compressed sensing. The study demonstrates the theoretical solvability of the proposed model and presents an efficient numerical strategy based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). Numerical experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the validity and superiority of the proposed model. The results indicate that the proposed framework effectively recovers images from undersampled data, overcoming the segmentation drawbacks present in existing methods. Furthermore, the model exhibits superior performance in handling strong impulsive noise. Ultimately, the proposed framework holds significant potential for future applications in high-quality image recovery. Abstract interpretation operates in two distinct phases: a rising stage utilizing over-approximation to generate an invariant that ensures soundness, followed by a falling phase employing invariance checks with goal-oriented refinement to restore precision. This paper introduces two novel algorithms for the falling phase within the framework of Abstract Interpretation. Unlike traditional approaches, these algorithms eliminate the need to retain intermediate results from the rising phase, initiating the process directly from the concrete (sound) over-approximation. By decoupling the rising and falling phases, we enable the use of highly efficient, non-exact data structures for the rising phase and exact, precise data structures for the falling phase, thereby overcoming limitations inherent in existing techniques. Experimental findings indicate that these new algorithms can surpass current state-of-the-art methods. To our knowledge, this represents the first introduction of falling-phase algorithms that are independent of the rising phase. The computational model for these algorithms is straightforward, facilitating straightforward implementation. Furthermore, we propose a generic strategy for selecting the most appropriate data structure for a given problem, ensuring that the resulting programs are both simple and straightforward. Our evaluation demonstrates that the proposed algorithms are straightforward to implement and that the selection strategy yields optimal outcomes. Finally, we show that these approaches can significantly improve the precision of actual implementations. The code is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/afgarcia22/decoupling-ai}. While the evaluation in this paper is limited to specific instances, it provides a promising foundation for future research. The evaluation includes experiments on various programs, ranging from straightforward to complex, with a primary focus on C-bugs. Topological phononics represents a rapidly developing field focused on engineering novel states of sound propagation through the manipulation of phonon band topology. Although oxide ceramics possess complex non-linear properties, they are typically unsuitable for observing topological phonons due to the high quality factors required to resolve these states. In this study, we report the experimental realization of topological phonons in yttrium aluminum cobaltate (YAC) oxide ceramics through quantum engineering via quantum flux pumping. This pumping mechanism effectively regulates the phonon band structure by modulating the effective mass of acoustic phonons. We successfully achieve and detect a pair of non-dissipative, chiral surface phonons that traverse the entire Brillouin zone without scattering. Furthermore, we have designed a phononic circuit that supports a closed-loop signal path free of backscattering. The success of this experiment establishes a promising pathway for developing novel topological phononic devices in ceramics and enhances our understanding of the electronic-phonon coupling inherent in oxide ceramics.

Outlier detection within high-dimensional data, particularly under metric distances like Euclidean, remains a significant challenge in data mining and machine learning. This paper introduces a novel outlier score calculation method that utilizes a proximity graph built via the R-tree. The R-tree's efficient metric proximity search enables fast neighbor queries, serving as the foundation for the tree-search-based outlier score. By integrating local density variations with high-dimensional data metrics, this mechanism enhances both speed and precision. Experimental evaluations on various datasets, including image, text, and natural sciences data, demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed algorithm, with results showing superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the study highlights that high-dimensional data mining remains a persistent challenge, especially concerning outcome accuracy. Consequently, we propose that ensemble learning combined with metric distances offers a more effective solution for high-dimensional outlier detection than relying solely on individual classifiers or distance functions. Finally, the paper concludes by identifying key open issues and future research directions regarding high-dimensional data mining. Specifically, it addresses challenges such as high dimensionality curse, dimension reduction, and feature selection, while offering insights into high-dimensional ensemble learning, the comparison between instance-based and vector space representations, and the application of metric distances in this domain. Additionally, the effectiveness of metric distances for outlier detection is analyzed, and the advantages of using a distance-based R-tree for metric proximity searches are explored. Finally, the tree-search approach for metric density, along with ensemble learning, is presented as a viable solution for enhancing the accuracy of high-dimensional outlier detection. These topics collectively form the basis for future research. Keywords: Outlier detection, High-dimensional data, Metric distance, R-tree, Ensemble learning.

This study examines primary quantum optical characteristics of an excited atom in vacuum adjacent to a slender, perfectly conducting wire. The atom's excitation and associated optical optical self-energy are computed using formal Dyson equations. The time evolution of the primary atomic dipole moment and the system's emittance are numerically analyzed. Results indicate that the slender geometry of the mirror significantly alters atomic dynamics, causing a substantial suppression of both the decay rate and dephasing compared to those of a free atom or an atom near a flat mirror. Furthermore, the decay rate exhibits weak dependence on the atom-wire transverse separation but strong variation with the angle between the atomic dipole moment and the wire. Additionally, total emissivity shows an abrupt transition from the flat-mirror regime to the slender-regime as the wire's thickness decreases. Finally, we explore the potential stability of a quasi-bound state supported by the wire. These findings provide a foundation for future investigations into atomic systems near ultrathin materials and for developing thin-wire-based atomic devices. Such devices could be controlled by manipulating atomic parameters (such as position and orientation) via nearby structures and by reading out atomic states through their coupling with quantum electromagnetic field modes near slender wires. This approach offers superior control over atomic decay rates and dipole moments compared to using conventional flat mirrors. Moreover, the proposed system is applicable to a broad range of atoms. Specifically, atoms possessing a dipole moment parallel to the wire can be utilized as optical switches, while those with a moment perpendicular to the wire can function as attenuators for optical signals passing near the atom. Additionally, weakly excited atoms with a moment aligned to the wire may serve as a new class of matter-based slow light sources. These devices offer tunable group velocities and wide operational bandwidths, addressing limitations found in existing slow light devices that rely on narrow atomic transitions or narrow resonance lineshapes to achieve slow group velocities. Furthermore, the absolute scale of these effects can be adjusted using wires of varying thicknesses. To facilitate experimental detection, we also address challenges in measuring atomic positions and orientational angles, which are essential parameters for confirming the observed phenomena. Finally, we outline specific experimental configurations to test the predicted effects, including configurations involving atomic pairs and nonlinear effects. These are expected to advance fundamental research on light-matter interactions in the slender regime and offer promising prospects for future device applications. The theoretical framework developed in this work also holds potential for broader applications. With the widespread adoption of social network analysis, ensuring fairness in social graphs has become increasingly critical. Existing approaches typically adapt tabular fairness methods to tabulated graphs, where node features are used to determine sensitive attributes and roles. However, this assumption of node feature availability often fails in complex graph structures. This paper introduces the concept of fairness within localized communities. It presents the definition and characterization of various localized community fairness notions, along with their interrelationships. Furthermore, it examines the hardness of testing these conditions and both directly and indirectly addresses their learnability. Finally, the work validates these theoretical findings empirically. To our knowledge, the fairness of localized communities represents a novel perspective on graph fairness. Our direct and indirect characterizations and learning results appear to be the first of their kind in addressing graph fairness. We demonstrate that directly learning community fairness can surpass solutions derived from tabulated graphs, thereby circumventing potential biases inherent in those representations. Our empirical results highlight that tabulated graph fairness can be discriminatory toward certain groups and offer guidance on the conditions under which such fairness is learnable. Beyond advancing the field of algorithmic fairness, our work elucidates the trade-offs between accuracy and fairness, revealing that the most unfair classifier can be both the most accurate and the most fair. Furthermore, our proposed algorithms are highly scalable, capable of handling graphs with millions of nodes and edges. The associated code is publicly available at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar1999/Local-Community-Fairness. Our algorithms are also the first to support the specification of arbitrary localized community conditions, such as degree, clustering coefficient, and betweenness, enabling fairness assessments based on nodes' positions within the graph. Additionally, our algorithms accommodate node and/or edge-sensitive fairness. The paper covers both theoretical and computational aspects of graph fairness, with our computational experiments demonstrating that community fairness can be learned from samples. This finding is particularly significant as it underscores the necessity of graph learning for community fairness, even when the graph is fully observed. Our work extends the algorithmic fairness literature by developing methods to measure and ensure fairness in localized communities, a domain previously unexplored. We demonstrate that tabulated graphs are insufficient for representing localized community fairness and that tabular-based solutions can be discriminatory. We also establish that learning community fairness is possible even in the absence of ground truth for community ground-set labels. Finally, our methodology allows for the specification of graph position-based fairness and sensitive attributes on both nodes and edges. We construct a series of iterated approximate solutions for kinetic models governing reversible enzyme reactions, defined by the equation $\dot{y} = K \mu / (e_0 - \sum_{j=1}^n y_j)$, where $e_0$ denotes the total enzyme concentration. For each variable $y_j$ representing the quantity of product $A_j$, the value is constrained by the initial conditions such that $0 \leq y_j \leq a_{0j}$. The vector $a_0 = (0, \dots, 0)$ represents the case where no substrates are present at the start. We establish the kinetic reversibility principle, which asserts that the sum of the upper bounds for $y_j$ and the lower bounds for the corresponding substrates $x_j$ remains constant and equal to the initial substrate amount $a_{0j}$ throughout the reaction: $y_j(t) + x_j(t) = a_{0j}$. This principle facilitates a method for approximating solutions to the kinetic equations by transforming the original system into a new system of differential equations with globally defined solutions. We derive sufficient conditions ensuring that the solution to the approximate system converges to the exact solution of the original system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the reaction reaches completion in finite time if and only if the enzyme concentration $e_0$ exceeds the sum of the initial amounts of all products $\sum_{j=1}^n a_{0j}$. In this scenario, the reaction completes when the enzyme is fully saturated with substrates, causing the reaction rate to drop to zero. Additionally, we establish sufficient conditions for the convergence of the iterative scheme. These findings are applied to a model of a reversible single-enzyme reaction involving one substrate and one product. Finally, to address the issue of finite-time completion, we extend both the original and approximate solution systems into complex space and prove that all solutions are now defined over the entire real line. We further show that all solutions of the extended system are real-valued within a region bounded by a specific algebraic surface. Through computer simulations, we validate these theoretical results. The methodology developed in this study is also applicable to analyzing the kinetic equation for irreversible enzyme processes with $n$ products. However, since no reversibility principle exists in that context, we must rely on the theorem regarding the extension of analytic functions to prove the validity of the approximate solution. We also examine whether a similar extension to complex space can be constructed for the irreversible case

This study proposes a new stochastic logic framework for modeling asset price dynamics, incorporating a random expected time until the price-relevant event (RTE) occurs, such as a bubble's termination. By applying this random expected RTE approach to a basic constant-parameter Fokker-Planck process, we derive a new family of functions characterized by dynamic size and a decay rate aligning with the random mean lifetime. Additionally, we apply this methodology to systems with nonlinear diffusion, where the effective diffusion coefficient adaptively shifts between subdiffusive and superdiffusive regimes, and the termination probability is defined by the cumulative distribution function of first-passage times. We also address how to generalize the random mean lifetime and related statistical properties when the termination time's distribution is known only for large times. Furthermore, we explore the creation of new dimensionless variables and dimensionless logic to assess the dynamic state of financial bubbles. Finally, we test the proposed random mean lifetime and related statistical tools by analyzing the dynamics of the S\&P 500 index over the period from January 1990 to December 2020. This analysis covers the three most prominent historical bubbles: the 1990s bubble, the 2007–2009 financial crisis, and the 2009–2020 COVID-19 pandemic bubble. The resulting 25 years of data provide a comprehensive view of bubble dynamics, including a comparison of pre- and post-pandemic states. Additionally, we show that the S\&P 500 index can be described by a system of coupled first-order Fokker-Planck equations, with the random mean lifetime of a bubble determined by the sum of the two associated theoretical solutions. These findings offer a new perspective on bubble dynamics, providing a more complete statistical picture that includes both successful and failed bubble predictions. Ultimately, our results suggest that the dynamic bubble diagram based on the random mean lifetime offers a more accurate and complete picture of financial bubble dynamics than the traditional diagram relying on constant prediction parameters. Consequently, the "new" dynamic diagram derived from the random mean lifetime is shown to be superior for predicting bubble states. Finally, the paper concludes with several recommendations for future research. (This study was conducted prior to the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic bubble.) We demonstrate that the path integral formulation of a quantum harmonic oscillator, subjected to both damping and an in-coherent driving force, can be evaluated via time-discretization and simulated using Monte Carlo methods. These methods are applied to compute individual paths, which are subsequently averaged to determine the system's mean position and mean square displacement. Furthermore, we show that the chosen Monte Carlo algorithms—Metropolis and Hybrid Monte Carlo—are capable of sampling the corresponding Euclidean probability distribution without bias, even when short-time propagators are approximated using the second-order Trotter formula. The efficiency and effectiveness of these Monte Carlo techniques are assessed by comparing their outputs against the known exact analytical solution for the harmonic oscillator. Our findings indicate that the path integral method yields results consistent with exact analytical derivations, even when utilizing a limited number of Monte Carlo samples. This confirms that both analytical and numerical approaches are effective in characterizing the quantum harmonic oscillator under damping and in-coherent driving. Additionally, we illustrate that Monte Carlo methods are highly effective at depicting the oscillations of individual paths around their average trajectory. Finally, we highlight that paths generated by the Metropolis algorithm exhibit more pronounced quantum characteristics, such as larger displacements, compared to those produced by the Hybrid Monte Carlo algorithm. Recent research indicates that textual data holds potential value for enhancing recommendation systems. However, existing approaches often fail to fully leverage rich textual insights, typically treating all review sentences uniformly. This study introduces the Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN), a text-based model designed to improve Product Recommendation Systems (PRS) by assigning greater importance to informative sentences and minimizing the impact of unhelpful ones. Evaluations on the Textual Product Review (TPR) dataset demonstrate that our baseline model achieves a 10% to 20% increase in Next Item Prediction (NIP) accuracy compared to current state-of-the-art methods. The source code is accessible at the following link: https://github.com/chenchen1993/SIFN. Furthermore, this NLP-driven enhancement for PRS is anticipated to be transformative for the Tech4Good initiative. Ultimately, the primary research contribution lies in successfully integrating NLP into the PRS for Next Item Prediction. Additionally, we anticipate that the proposed model will serve as a strong baseline for future NLP-enhanced PRS applications. Finally, we hope this pioneering work inspires the research community to further explore the synergies between Natural Language Processing and Product Recommendation Systems.
