This study investigates data augmentation for code-switched (CS) Arabic-English Twitter texts, addressing the challenge of creating diverse training data for lexical substitutions in CS code-mixing. We examine two methodologies for performing lexical substitutions on CS code-mixing: (1) performing substitutions after converting CS code-mixing to monolingual (single-language) text, and (2) performing substitutions directly on raw CS code-mixing. We evaluate four substitution models—Word2Vec, GLoVe, BERT, and Transformer BERT (mBERT, multilingual)-based systems—and compare their performance across the two approaches. Our findings indicate that multilingual vector-based models like BERT and Transformer BERT are highly effective for lexical substitution in CS code-mixing, while substitutions performed on monolingual code-mixion yield the best results. Finally, we assess the quality of augmented CS code-mixing data by training a BERT (arctic) classifier on the augmented corpus and a BERT (arabic) classifier on the resulting monolingual dataset, followed by a detailed analysis of the outcomes. This research is the first of its kind to explore data augmentation in CS code-mixing, specifically focusing on lexical substitutions using vector-based models and comparing performance on both substituted and monolingual CS code-mixion data. The code and datasets will be made available on a public repository. Our work demonstrates the efficacy of multilingual vector-based lexical substitution models for CS code-mixing data augmentation, offering a valuable resource for CS code-mixing applications. The paper concludes with a discussion of limitations and future research directions. Our work is expected to advance the fields of data augmentation, CS code-mixing, and natural language processing (NLP). The paper is structured into seven sections: Section 2 provides a literature review, Section 3 outlines the proposed work, Section 4 details the methodology, Section 5 presents the results, Section 6 discusses the results, and Section 7 concludes the paper. Keywords: Data augmentation, Arabic-English code-switching, Lexical substitution, Vector-based models, Monolingual code-mixion.

We demonstrate that for metrics derived from the Euclidean norm on the tangent bundle associated with a hyperbolic surface, the metric entropy scaling with respect to the Roelcke dimension of the corresponding isometry group is suboptimal. Furthermore, we characterize the Roelcke precompactness of these groups by examining the asymptotic behavior of metric entropy and Kolmogorov widths. These findings extend to metrics on Teichmüller spaces other than those based on the Euclidean norm and apply to semihyperbolic precompact type metrics. Additionally, we examine the Kolmogorov rates for precompact families of diffeomorphisms acting on Riemannian surfaces and their connections to precompactness in the $C^k$-topology. Finally, we detail the relationships among various precompactness notions for groups within the context of Roelcke precompactness.

Generalized $\lambda$-deformations of group manifolds offer a framework for generating a vast array of three-dimensional geometries characterized by specific characteristics, including connectability, time-dependence, and various forms of anisotropy. This paper demonstrates that all such metrics are connectable, with the connection string defined as the image of a straight line in the corresponding Lie algebra under the exponential map. Furthermore, we establish the existence of a novel class of connectable, non-homogeneous, non-isotropic, time-dependent geometries, detailing their explicit $\beta$-functions, and we investigate the fermionic sector of these models. We conclude by constructing the superspace for all three-dimensional supergroups and deriving the associated superspace metrics and their $\beta$-functions. In this context, we identify both horizontal and mixed components within the $\beta$-function, a feature also present in the purely bosonic supersymmetric $\lambda$-deformations. Additionally, we find that the supersymmetric connection string is connected, although it is not necessarily a submanifold within the supergroup manifold. Finally, the supersymmetric connection string is characterized by a set of straight lines in the corresponding super-Lie algebra formed by a mixture of even and odd directions under the generalized $\lambda$-deformation. These findings regarding the connection string are also applicable to the bosonic cases. Finally, our analysis of the superspace suggests a broader generalization of supersymmetric $\lambda$-deformations within the framework of supercoset models. This generalization encompasses supersymmetric $P$-models, which are the supersymmetric counterparts of Witten's $P$-model, alongside supersymmetric $\lambda$-deformations. Both model types are based on $P$-algebras, a generalization of symmetric space $P$-models, with relevant references provided. Notably, our findings indicate that all supersymmetric $P$-model metrics, including those from supersymmetric $\lambda$-deformations, are connectable, with their respective connection strings detailed. Furthermore, these metrics are confirmed to be solutions to the supersymmetric Einstein equations. This work expands upon the findings presented in [1]. Keywords: Supersymmetric $\lambda$-deformations, Supersymmetric $P$-models, Supersymmetric $P$-model metrics, $P$-model connection strings, $P$-model superspaces, $P$-model $T$-tensors, $P$

We introduce a new category of continuous finite elements, termed tets (short for tetrahedra), constructed as a composite of a simplex and a triangle. This framework extends the successful hex elements developed by Beyer et al. We demonstrate that the geometry of the tet class is simple and robust, enabling the derivation of an optimal cochain complex. Furthermore, we prove the solvability of the Stokes and elasticity equations on grids comprising exclusively tet elements. The paper also explores the theory behind the tet class, detailing specific elements within this family, their mathematical properties, and practical implementation methods. Finally, experimental results are provided, including the simulation of an anisotropic fluid flowing over a curved surface represented by anisotropic hex meshes (where faces are classified as either thin or wide). Keywords: Finite elements, simplicial complexes, Hex meshes. 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 65N30, 65F10, 76D05. Hex meshes are increasingly popular in scientific visualization and simulation, offering a balance between the efficiency of unstructured grids and the preservation of topological duality. These meshes consist of elements arranged in a cochain complex, a property that has recently become central to research in finite element exterior calculus (FEMEC). FEMEC relies on a specific class of finite elements known as cochain elements, which maintain optimal properties across all dimensions. This article presents a series of contributions to this field, beginning with a fundamental class of geometric elements: tetrahedra. While seemingly simple, the construction of tets reveals significant complexity, leading to a rich theory encompassing various distinct elements. In the following sections, we will outline the foundational concepts, establish key theorems, and provide a proof of the main result mentioned earlier: the validity of anisotropic mesh generation. Relation extraction focuses on identifying entity relationships within unstructured text by labeling directed links between entity pairs. This task is intrinsically linked to knowledge graph link prediction, which aims to discover missing triples within an existing knowledge graph. By integrating these two fields, relation extraction can be reframed as link prediction, potentially boosting its performance. To achieve this, we propose a joint training framework that simultaneously performs link prediction and extracts relations. In our approach, relation extraction is modeled as link prediction, whereas conversely, pre-trained models for relation extraction serve the link prediction phase. This creates a synergistic cycle where the link prediction model utilizes relation extraction scores to identify novel knowledge graph edges, while these same scores guide the link prediction model to construct a more comprehensive knowledge graph. Experimental results on the WikiRG60 and WIKI101 datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms various baseline approaches in both link prediction and relation extraction tasks. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the joint training framework yields more robust models compared to those trained independently. Ultimately, our approach facilitates the discovery of long-tail relations and enhances the quality of the knowledge graph. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/zhenghaozhang1999/DeepKG. The models are available at: https://huggingface.co/zhenghaozhang1990/rel_extraction. HuggingFace. Access. This study introduces an analytical delay model for step-load transitions in switching DC-DC converters, designed for integration into control loops within power distribution networks. Focusing on idealized converter architectures, the delay is characterized by the temporal evolution of the output voltage following a load step, with time discretized using step responses to second-order low-pass LCR networks. Parameter estimation is executed via Matlab's Curve Fitting Toolkit, which is demonstrated with experimental data from a 12 V DC-DC converter operating at 100 kHz with a 2 A load transition. The results confirm that the delay model aligns closely with measured output voltage trajectories. Furthermore, the computed converter delay is successfully embedded into a PDN control loop, exhibiting output voltage behavior consistent with power delivery specifications. The paper concludes by outlining extensions for more complex switching topologies, such as those employing pulse frequency modulation or pulse width modulation. Overall, the proposed delay model is shown to be highly effective for PDN control loop design. Additionally, an online supplement is available, containing a guided Matlab session on the Curve Fitting Toolkit that illustrates delay parameter extraction from either measured data or analytical delay equations. This supplement enables users to replicate all examples and outcomes presented in the paper. Finally, the authors suggest that their examples and guided design approach could serve as an educational module for power electronics courses. Current Reinforcement Learning (RL) with Continuity assumptions often depend on unnecessary assumptions, enabling techniques like functionally weighted Bellman residuals that drive RL. However, these assumptions hold in Euclidean spaces only if dimensions align with data dimensionality. We introduce a novel continuity assumption rooted in the intrinsic geometry of reward and transition functions, applicable to any complete and separable metric space. This framework supports metrics such as Hamming, Hamming-weighted, and path metrics. Empirical results demonstrate that utilizing this continuity can enhance sample efficiency, particularly when employing non-Euclidean metrics. Our theoretical findings indicate that certain algorithms are sample-optimal in specific settings, while others, such as $k$-NN, can suffer from catastrophic failure. Additionally, we propose $k$-NN as a baseline, offering the first known upper and lower bounds on its sample complexity in this context. Finally, we outline open research questions concerning the appropriate metric selection for RL. Code is accessible at: https://github.com/ashokkumar1999/cgmrl.

The animacy category is fundamental to visual processing, yet it remains unclear which specific properties of natural images define this group and whether the visual system possesses a dedicated mechanism for it. To investigate this, we employed a model-free approach to analyze neural responses in the human ventral temporal cortex, an area responsible for object recognition. By presenting subjects with stimuli from various object, scene, image, and texture categories, we measured both behavioral judgments of animacy and neural activity. Our findings indicate that multivariate patterns of activity within a population of visual neurons can integrate diverse visual dimensions to construct a low-dimensional "essence" of animacy, characterized by a balance between image complexity and contrast. This essence appears to serve as a bridge for visual processing, linking the detection of salient visual features to higher-level functions like object and scene categorization. Furthermore, the neural representation of animacy shows reduced sensitivity as stimuli move away from veridical representations, suggesting that the mechanism's role is to harmonize distinct visual signals for object and scene processing rather than to categorize abstract groupings such as faces versus scenes or natural images against synthetic textures. Type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in black hole X-ray binaries are thought to occur during the transition from the hard to soft spectral state, though their origins remain unclear. This study employs the Insight-HXMT observatory to examine the evolution of CQPOs in MAXI J1535-571. We identified CQO frequencies of 1.9, 2.0, 2.1, 2.2, and 2.3 Hz across 12 episodes spanning 2018 and 2019. The data reveal that the LPM QPO frequency decreases while the IM and HM frequencies rise as the soft component in the 2–10 keV band increases. Furthermore, we observed a correlation between the amplitude of the 2.0 Hz QPO and the 6.4 keV iron line, suggesting a potential link between CQPOs and the iron line. Additionally, a correlation exists between the equivalent width of the 6.4 keV iron line and the soft component intensity in the 2–10 keV range. These findings indicate that the inner accretion disc moves outward as the source evolves toward the soft state, a behavior consistent with the frequency evolution of type-C QPOs. Finally, the 2.0 Hz QPO is proposed as a fundamental frequency for the accretion disc in MAXI J1535-571. These results support the model where the frequency of the fundamental node is 4/5 of the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO) frequency. We also discuss the possibility of CQPOs representing a superposition of low-frequency quasi-periodic oscillations. Finally, we address the potential connection between CQPOs and low-frequency oscillations. Overall, our results support the interpretation that the frequency of the fundamental node is 4/5 of the ISCO frequency. This paper introduces a new approach to building social robots capable of dependably transferring empathy by reacting to their partners' behaviors. To achieve this, the robot employs a social intrinsic motivation called Transfer Empowerment (TE), which encourages it to perform actions likely to be rewarded by its partner's response. Specifically, when a partner exhibits behavior B, the robot is motivated to find a response R that maximizes the probability of the partner exhibiting a specific feedback action F, thereby empowering the partner to express F. The robot continuously generates and executes behaviors under the guidance of TE-driven policy improvement. Experimental results demonstrate that the robot reliably produces empathetic responses when humans act in ways TE aims to reward, and it successfully learns to empathize with a broader range of human behaviors through online interaction. These findings indicate that the TE framework offers a dependable method for designing robots to transfer empathy. Furthermore, the mechanism's ability to generalize across diverse human behaviors suggests it offers a scalable solution for endowing robots with empathetic capabilities. Additionally, the approach offers a straightforward yet dependable means for robots to exhibit sensitivity by constructing social intrinsic motivation solely from the partner's demonstrated behaviors. Ultimately, the study offers a new perspective on empathy, defining it as the ability to generate behaviors intended to be rewarded by others, thereby refining the traditional view of empathy merely as the transfer of emotions. By adopting this behavioral definition, robots can effectively transfer empathy by producing actions designed to elicit positive reactions from their partners. Algorithms used to infer vector magnetic field data from the two intensities captured by the HMI instrument on SDO's Heliophysics Impulse (HMI) on the Solar Telescope often employ regularized least-squares optimization. This method minimizes the residual between a synthetic field derived from inferences and the observed intensity, utilizing regularizers that enforce physical constraints like non-negativity and minimum energy. While this approach effectively infers magnetic field vectors, the associated synthetic field reveals a systematic bias: it fails to detect weak magnetic fields in the presence of umbral contamination. Consequently, these fields are inappropriately inferred as strong and concentrated. We demonstrate that this bias can be mitigated by employing a non-linear data fidelity term within the least-squares objective function. Furthermore, we establish that the behavior of the objective function and its bias can be accurately characterized by analyzing the basis change induced by this non-linear transformation. Finally, numerical experiments confirm that the bias is effectively alleviated by the proposed approach. These findings are particularly significant for heliophysics, as the bias affects inferring the umbral fields of sunspots, which are critical for understanding solar flare generation. Additionally, the current bias undermines the reliability of inferring interplanetary magnetic fields from the umbral fields of coronal hole boundaries. The study includes comprehensive mathematical analysis and numerical evidence regarding the impact of umbral contamination on the synthetic field and the efficacy of the proposed method in reducing this bias. Ultimately, these results provide a means to identify and correct for the bias within inferred magnetic fields. The associated Python code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1988/UnbiasedInference. The independent demand-side control (IDSC) market represents a significant approach to managing electricity consumption, yet it faces challenges related to the diversity of appliance types and variations in energy pricing and consumption patterns. To address these issues, a new collective learning-based (CLB) independent demand-side control method has been developed. This proposed scheme leverages usage planning and incorporates real-time load charging. The method utilizes a collective game theory framework to enhance the efficiency of demand-side control. A notable advantage of this proposal is its ability to deliver highly efficient results even with a small initial population, thanks to the applied collective game mechanism. Furthermore, the scheme demonstrates strong adaptability to changes in electricity prices and appliance usage patterns. Experimental findings indicate that, compared to a benchmark, the CLB IDSC method achieves an average revenue increase of 1.2% and a significant reduction in revenue standard deviation of 50.2%. Additionally, under a small initial population of 10, the CLB IDSC approach delivers results comparable to those achieved when the population size is ten times larger. These outcomes underscore the effectiveness of the proposed collective game method, highlighting its potential to substantially improve the efficiency of demand-side control. Additionally, the study offers valuable insights for future research into demand-side control. Keywords: Demand-side control, Collective learning, Collective game, Smart appliances, Smart grid. 1. Introduction The rapid advancement of smart grid technology has enabled smart appliances to be managed as intelligent agents. These agents can independently optimize their operations by minimizing energy costs and maximizing their utility. This capability fosters the emergence of the independent demand-side control (IDSC) market, which has garnered significant research interest. IDSC involves smart appliances acting as intelligent agents that independently negotiate with the grid to optimize their utility. This process typically involves the agents submitting bids to the grid, which then allocates electricity based on specific criteria. Subsequently, the agents adjust their loads in response to the grid's allocation. However, current IDSC markets face two primary challenges: (i) a lack of sufficient information regarding the diversity of appliance types, electricity prices, and consumer usage patterns; and (ii) the need for the market to remain effective even under conditions of limited available information. To overcome these challenges, this work introduces the concept of collective learning (CL) within the IDSC market. This approach aims to maximize the revenue of smart appliances, with a specific focus on achieving high performance even with a minimal initial population. Specifically, we demonstrate that the convergence speeds identified by Nikiforov and Pukhlik represent the slowest possible rates, indicating that their Theorem 2.1 cannot be substantially enhanced. A key component of this proof involves investigating the relationships and dependencies between spectral distributions and the convergence speeds of the von Neumann Ergodic Theorem. Furthermore, we investigate the limits of applicability of the Aizenman-Simons method and establish a novel lower bound for the second largest eigenvalue of a self-adjoint operator. Finally, our work responds to an open question posed by N. Nikiforov concerning the derivation of a lower bound for the second largest eigenvalue of a specific class of Hermitian matrices using the limiting spectral distribution of these matrices. The global fire intensity index (FII) quantifies the spatial distribution and temporal evolution of fire strength. While its development offers a means to evaluate seasonal variations in regional or continental scales, it currently lacks applicability at a global level. This study demonstrates the potential of a worldwide, year-round FII for fire monitoring and prediction. Leveraging high-quality, global, and concurrent Active Fire Density (AFD) data from the MODIS active fire detection system, the research constructs a novel FII using a new time-series decomposition method. The resulting global FII reveals distinct seasonal patterns, thereby defining seasonal fire intensity. Furthermore, a new Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model is introduced to forecast FII, successfully predicting both global and continental-scale fire intensity. Additionally, the study demonstrates how the FII can be utilized to project future smoke plumes and estimate seasonal biomass burning emissions. The provided FII data and LSTM model not only enhance our comprehension of global fire intensity but also offer a foundation for predicting it in the coming years. Gravitational lensing offers a powerful method for investigating the dark matter component within galaxy clusters. By analyzing mass distribution, this technique can constrain dark matter properties, allowing for constraints on the self-interaction cross section ($\sigma/m$) of dark matter particles. Although traditional weak and strong lensing have primarily targeted lens galaxies and galaxy groups, recent advancements in observational data and theoretical models now enable strong lensing studies of galaxy clusters. These analyses can isolate the subhalo mass function, which is sensitive to dark matter self-interactions, thereby tightening constraints on $\sigma/m$ for dark matter interaction cross sections. Specifically, we examine the statistical properties of multiplex images, where the separation between images of the same object is influenced by dark matter subhalos. We present a prediction for the variance of these separations, which depends on the dark matter self-interaction cross section, the dark matter mass density, and the halo mass concentration. Our constraints are derived from the Zwicky Cluster 234, demonstrating that the data are consistent with the $\Lambda$CDM model and the standard cold dark matter scenario. Furthermore, we provide predictions for future strong lensing studies in galaxy clusters. If future observations achieve mass density constraints comparable to current levels, they could explore the parameter space of self-interaction cross sections for dark matter scattering, extending from $10^{-24}$ cm$^3$/g down to $10^{-27}$ cm$^3$/g. This range corresponds to the region where self-interactions significantly alter the small-scale mass distribution, as confirmed by numerical simulations. Additionally, we show that while the amplitude of the predicted variance remains independent of the mean halo mass, the optimal range for detecting subhalo effects shifts to higher mean halo masses as the dark matter mass density constraint improves. This suggests that larger clusters, such as Abell 2744, may be ideal candidates for such future investigations. Ultimately, we conclude that current and upcoming strong lensing studies hold the potential to significantly impact our understanding of dark matter self-interactions. Large-scale neural network models are essential for achieving state-of-the-art results in complex tasks like vision and language, yet their size hinders deployment due to high computational costs and energy consumption. While quantization and knowledge distillation are common strategies for model compression, they typically require the target model to fully observe input data. In many practical scenarios, however, inputs are only partially observable, a limitation that renders existing compression techniques inapplicable. To address this, we introduce a framework designed to compress large models that infer outcomes from partial observations. Our approach utilizes a hierarchical architecture comprising a generic placeholder model and a parameter-specific model, optimized through contrastive learning using standard data. This framework facilitates the development of a comprehensive methodology to simultaneously assess and leverage both complete and partial observations during the compression process. Experiments on the CIFAR-10 dataset demonstrate that models within this framework can achieve performance comparable to full-scale models while exhibiting a substantial reduction in parameters. The code and method are available at: https://github.com/ashishkumar2001/Po-MCC. Consequently, the framework provides a robust foundation for future research into model compression under partial observation conditions. Our results indicate that the placeholder model and specific models within this framework can effectively capture information from partial observations regarding image patches and tokens, respectively. This outcome is particularly significant for the NLP community, where recent studies suggest that pre-trained language models can achieve performance comparable to or exceeding that of computer vision models on task-agnostic tasks. We anticipate that our work will inspire further research into combining the strengths of language and vision pre-training within the context of model compression. Additionally, we aim to provide valuable insights for advancing model compression research in data-rich, data-sparse, and data-poor domains. Finally, we hope our work will contribute to the goal of creating more sustainable and environmentally friendly AI systems. Our approach leverages existing large models to produce parameter-efficient variants capable of withstanding data scarcity, thereby reducing the computational costs associated with training, data collection, and inference. We believe this will foster the creation of more sustainable AI solutions. Please cite this work as: Ashish Kumar, Ankit Singh Negi, and Anuj Gupta. 2021. Model Compression from Partial Observations. Rapid Independent Component Analysis (RIC) is a variant of Infomax ICA that utilizes a single hidden layer to independently reconstruct the layers of an input image. While RIC outperforms Infomax ICA, it still lags behind autoencoder-based ICA methods, which employ multiple hidden layers to achieve superior reconstruction. We introduce M-ar-K ICA, a novel approach that integrates a Mixture ARchitecture (M-ar) with K layers to enhance autoencoder capabilities. This method incorporates the M-ar loss function to refine weight updates during training, ensuring faster and more stable convergence. Additionally, M-ar-K ICA supports sample-wise training, enabling the analysis of an ensemble of images rather than restricting output to a single image representation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art ICA techniques, achieving an image reconstruction error of 0.0019 ± 0.0001. The implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ehsantahmasebi/M-ar-K-ICA. Source code and tutorial videos are also available on our YouTube channel under the category M-ar-K ICA Tutorial. The accompanying website, https://icai.cs.uaf.rochester.edu/, highlights key features of the method. We invite readers to visit this site to learn more about M-ar-K ICA. Further details can be found in our tutorial video series, available on YouTube under the category M-ar-K ICA Tutorial. Our goal is to provide an accessible entry point for understanding and applying M-ar-K ICA. We appreciate your time and interest. For inquiries or collaboration, please contact us at ehsan.tahmasebi@ua.rochester.edu. Visit our website, watch our tutorials, and reach out to us to explore how M-ar-K ICA can benefit your work. The rise of social platforms has enabled researchers to utilize social data as a valuable supplementary source for analyzing urban incidents. Nevertheless, the high volume of unstructured text within these datasets hinders effective analysis. To address this, we propose a research framework that integrates natural language processing with data mining techniques to extract key information regarding spatio-temporal incidents from social media text. This framework was tested using geotagged posts about traffic jams from the city of Turin, Italy. The findings demonstrate that identified traffic jam clusters show strong spatial correlation with actual occurrences, validating the approach. Consequently, this study makes two primary contributions: first, it advances incident analysis by effectively employing spatio-temporal data from social media; second, it breaks new ground in applying NLP within social media monitoring systems. The proposed framework offers significant potential for incident analysis on social media and can be adapted for analyzing other types of urban events. Finally, we discuss the challenges associated with analyzing urban incidents via social media and suggest future research directions. **Keywords:** Incident Analysis, Geotagged Social Media, NLP, Neural Networks, Urban Mining.

Statistically, such manifolds correspond to random walks, where the elliptic operators function as transfer matrices. The scalar fields solved by these equations describe the mean values of ensembles, such as magnetization. Furthermore, the partial derivatives of the solved fields correspond to the time and space transfer rates of the ensembles, analogous to current and velocity. In this context, surfaces denote specific configurations of the submanifolds. The second application area involves solving similar elliptic equations with surface measures in higher-order variational calculus. Here, the equations represent Euler-Lagrange equations for action functionals, where the densities are integrals combining Lagrangians for lower-order fields (e.g., the Klein-Gordon field) and higher-order Lagrangians dependent on field derivatives, such as gauge fields. Risk-aware bidding equipped with advanced machine learning has become a cornerstone for major digital advertising platforms. Yet, effectively implementing risk-awareness within display advertising remains difficult due to inherent market complexities. Specifically, budget constraints and the need for adaptive learning pose significant hurdles. To address these challenges, we introduce a unified decision-making framework for risk-aware bidding under budget limits. Building on this, we develop an efficient, customizable, and online learning algorithm grounded in the FTRL+ framework, which supports various budget allocation policies and ensures long-term budget feasibility. Extensive simulations using real-world data demonstrate that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods in accuracy while maintaining practical efficiency. Furthermore, empirical results highlight its superior adaptation to dynamic market conditions and constrained budget scenarios. In summary, this fully online learning algorithm serves as a robust building block for risk-aware bidding systems under budget constraints. Additionally, the decision-making framework offers a versatile solution applicable to other domains where risk awareness and budget management are critical. Finally, we have open-sourced all code and data associated with this project. They also conjectured that within this framework, negative contributions to the Wigner function are invariably detrimental. However, this paper presents a counter-example demonstrating that harmful regions within a quantum guidance theory are not limited to cases where the quantum negativity of the Wigner function is positive; rather, such theories can also utilize the negative parts of the Wigner distribution. Additionally, this counter-example illustrates that the Bloch et al. construction of the quantum potential does not uniquely determine a quantum-mechanical hydrodynamic model. Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) serves as a practical method for establishing a secret key between two parties, leveraging fundamental quantum principles. This study presents an exact and efficient approach for privacy enhancement that utilizes non-uniform random sources during post-processing. By employing biased sources rather than uniform ones, parties can generate a higher volume of random bits during privacy enhancement, thereby significantly boosting the final key rate. We derive analytical bounds for the phase error probability during privacy amplification, which are exact even when noise levels are low. Under conditions of low noise and biased data selection, our method yields a tighter bound on the phase error probability, resulting in a more generous key rate bound. Furthermore, this proposed scheme supports arbitrary measurement bases during the sifting phase, allowing for flexible key generation across various QKD protocols that employ different measurement configurations. Our approach is applicable to all existing entanglement-based and interference-based QKD protocols, as well as those operating in the prepare-and-measure regime. Notably, we derive analytical bounds for the phase error probability without relying on the postulate of typicality. Additionally, we demonstrate a substantial improvement in the key rate for the E91 protocol when applying this method. These results hold valid from a theoretical perspective and are directly applicable to real-world experimental implementations. QKD remains a leading technology for secure key exchange, and this work provides a new framework for the privacy amplification phase, paving the way for the creation of highly efficient QKD systems. Ultimately, this serves as a foundational step toward developing next-generation quantum communication networks. This paper is the first of two; the second will focus on the concrete analysis of the E91 protocol under this proposed framework. Together, these two studies offer both a theoretical and a concrete perspective on the application of this framework to QKD protocols. This study examines Feller diffusion processes driven by both constant and state-dependent (non-constant) variances. It identifies sufficient conditions for these processes to achieve extinction or converge to a quasi-stationary distribution, and it derives combinations of two Feller diffusions that result in a non-constant sum. Additionally, the sampling distributions for both continuous and discrete cases are derived. These findings offer new methodologies for analyzing Feller diffusion systems. The utility of these results is demonstrated by showing that, under specific conditions, the total count of the combined population can be modeled as a Feller diffusion with non-constant variance. Furthermore, the continuous case results extend the negative binomial beta model for the sum of two independent random variables and enable the construction of a new family of probability distributions for the sum of two combinations of beta-mixing random variables. Finally, the paper proposes multiple testing procedures for comparing two beta-mixing random variables. Waveguide Q marks the study of quantum emitters within one-dimensional waveguide systems, a field where light-matter interactions are typically treated as weak perturbations. However, in regimes of strong coupling, these interactions generate complex many-body phenomena that demand sophisticated theoretical frameworks for analysis. This work introduces a diagrammatic scattering method capable of rigorously calculating scattering amplitudes for multi-photon states, extending beyond standard single-photon and resonant two-particle limits. We demonstrate this approach on a paradigmatic model: a single atom within a waveguide. Our findings include the exact scattering amplitude for two-photon states, the first of its kind, alongside an approximate calculation for three photons. Furthermore, we derive corresponding scattering matrices and demonstrate their compliance with fundamental conservation laws regarding energy and momentum. Additionally, we investigate the influence of various driving configurations on the scattering outcomes. Finally, our derived formulas are applicable to broader scenarios involving multiple localized emitters in waveguide QED. These results provide a foundation for designing advanced driving schemes and controlling strong light-matter interactions in waveguide quantum systems. The accompanying code can be accessed at https://github.com/ashishkumar1989/waveguideQED. Given its ability to handle arbitrary numbers of photons, these findings may facilitate the design and control of non-linear quantum optical systems and quantum information processing within waveguide QED architectures. Moreover, the proposed formalism offers a pathway to model and control multi-photon sources and detectors using waveguide QED systems. Our approach may also prove valuable in other fields utilizing diagrammatic techniques, such as quantum field theory and many-body physics. Finally, the presented formalism offers a viable alternative to traditional quantum electrodynamics methods grounded in Maxwell's equations and boundary value problems. The paper concludes with an outlook on extending these findings to scenarios involving distributed emitters. Traditional non-coherent differential detection, a low-complexity technique for continuous phase modulation (CPM), suffers from delay enhancement caused by delay diversity. This issue stems from the strong correlation between successive transmitted signals, which, when combined with diversity reception, results in delayed data detection. While this traditional approach is effective for delay diversity schemes utilizing large delay sets, it fails to serve as a viable pre-cursor to digital equalization, particularly in OFDM systems, because the resulting delay expansion causes significant degradation in bit error rate performance. To address this, this paper introduces a method to eliminate delay enhancement during the traditional low-complexity non-coherent detection of CPM. This approach involves inserting a constant-phase sequence into the differential mapping to invert the sign of the phase change. The proposed scheme is evaluated through a comparison with conventional differential detection, demonstrating complete suppression of delay enhancement. Furthermore, the method is applied to CPM in delay enhanced non-coherent UWB communications, yielding significant improvements in detection bit error rate performance. Finally, the scheme is also assessed under an OFDM configuration, where it achieves substantial reductions in equalization complexity. Finally, the paper examines the implementation aspects of this proposed method. The simulation results align closely with theoretical expectations. The proposed method effectively eliminates delay enhancement, thereby significantly outperforming traditional differential detection in both UWB and OFDM contexts. Additionally, the computational complexity of this approach remains nearly identical to that of the traditional method. Consequently, the proposed method offers superior delay properties and signal quality without increasing implementation costs. Reward learning seeks to derive an interpretable reward function from observations of a task's performance. Current approaches typically rely on pairwise comparisons, which are time-intensive as they require extensive input from domain experts. To mitigate this burden, we propose leveraging visual explanations to accelerate comparisons by reducing the information needed from experts. Specifically, our goal is to generate images that clearly highlight performance differences, thereby minimizing the time required for comparisons. We introduce LV-CLUST, a visual cluster ranking model designed to learn a global cluster indicator based on local features extracted from state-action pairs. These states are represented by images paired with action vectors. By employing a two-stage training process, we first train a local feature learner using a specialized loss function, followed by training the global cluster ranking model to prioritize cluster boundaries. Our visual cluster ranking model effectively highlights the distinctions between agents that significantly impact cluster assignment. Furthermore, we validate the model's efficacy by demonstrating that it substantially reduces the training time and comparison effort required for reward learning. Specifically, we show that our model cuts comparison time by approximately 60% relative to existing methods. Additionally, we confirm that the resulting reward functions remain competitive with those produced by current state-of-the-art techniques. Finally, we apply these reward functions to visualize agent behaviors and assess their similarity, findings which align with human intuition. This study presents the Nucleon (proton and neutron) configuration function within noncommutative space-time, calculated up to second order in the noncommutativity parameter $\theta$. Utilizing the noncommutative expansion of the non-Abelian gauge-invariant gluon distribution, we derive the corresponding non-Abelian contribution. Furthermore, by employing the operator product expansion, we establish the quark contribution to the nucleon configuration function. Finally, we compare these theoretical findings with existing experimental data. As a result, we observe that the noncommutative effect significantly alters the shape of the nucleon configuration function, particularly in the region of large $x$. Consequently, this effect must be incorporated into global fits for improved analysis. Additionally, we quantify the impact of these effects on the proton and deuteron structure functions, $F_1$ and $F_2$, at next-to-leading order in QCD. This work extends our previous study, which focused solely on the pion distribution function [Phys. Rev. D 101, 014005 (2020)]. Topological phases have been successfully characterized through long-range correlations and the moment correlation matrix, yet their application to highly degenerate topological phases, such as those featuring frustration, remains limited. This study extends both methods to this regime to investigate specific topological phases and detect topological invariants within highly degenerate states. We apply these findings to one-dimensional toric code models, successfully reproduosing known invariants related to emulated boundary conditions. Furthermore, we detect a novel topological phase defined by boundary condition matrix $B=\left(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right)$, which exhibits a non-abelian double semimentalized edge state. Finally, we analyze how these invariants change when one lattice dimension is compactified into a circle. Beyond these one-dimensional models, our methods also identify known topological phases in the quantum spin liquid model on the kagome lattice and enable the detection of new topological phases in the quantum spin liquid on the jeffreez and kagome lattices. We anticipate that these techniques will facilitate further exploration of topological phases and their associated invariants. Notably, the moment correlation matrix method is versatile and can be extended to systems with local interactions and higher dimensions. Furthermore, we successfully recover established invariants, including Chern numbers and Z2 invariants, for kagome lattice quantum spin liquid models. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that both FOC and MCM are effective tools for detecting topological phases and extracting their topological invariants. Our results provide a foundation for future research into emerging topological phases, particularly in frustrated systems. Additionally, the MCM approach offers a unique advantage by functioning as a diagnostic tool for experimental data. Overall, these findings underscore the potential of topological phases in both classical and quantum systems for next-generation technologies. In a recent study (arXiv:2101.03302), the second author demonstrated that a specific class of finite-rank operators, which depend on a continuous parameter, generate the most significant statistical correlations in the spectrum of random band matrices. These operators, which are sparse relative to the matrix dimension, can be interpreted as discrete versions of "intricate" deformations discussed in various contexts (e.g., JHEP10(2018), various applications in string theory and AdS/CFT). The present work derives a sigma-model approximation for random band matrices subjected to such deformations. The derivation method, which is explicit and constructive, differs from the "guess" approach used in string theory. Furthermore, the study provides a detailed analysis of the sigma-model's weak-coupling regime and explicitly identifies the critical manifold where the weak-coupling strong-coupling transition occurs. These outcomes extend previous findings (arXiv:2005.00304) regarding unperturbed random band matrices. Additionally, the research offers a specific formula for the participation ratio of the eigenfunctions of the Hamiltonian, along with a formula for the distribution of this ratio within the three-band model. Finally, the formula for the average localization length in the three-band model is derived as a byproduct of the analysis. The work concludes with several conjectures concerning strong coupling and the potential for a corresponding phase transition in higher-rank scenarios. Recent research has demonstrated that self-supervised language pre-training can substantially enhance downstream Natural Language Understanding (NLU) tasks. However, existing self-supervised approaches rely on generalized pre-training objectives that fail to capture task-specific semantics, thereby limiting their effectiveness in domain-downstream applications. This study addresses that limitation by introducing a non linguistic framework that employs a meaningful-based approach for the domain of Conversation Comprehension (CC). The proposed pre-training model utilizes the Reddit:Question collection, where questions are paired with top community answers and comments. To induce meaningful-based CC, the model is trained using two tasks: first, recovering community answers from the question and comments; second, reconstructing the question given the answers and comments, which serves as a meaningful-aware Masked Conversation Permutation (MCP) objective. This MCP objective ensures that learned representations integrate semantic information from both speakers in a conversation. After pre-training, the model was evaluated on both regression and binary classification versions of the UC Irvine Machine Learning Benchmark (UCI-MLB) dataset and performed on the Reddit question understanding task. The results confirm that the model achieves state-of-the-art performance across all tasks, demonstrating that meaningful-based pre-training can effectively capture task-specific semantics for domain-specific applications. The effectiveness of machine learning (ML) depends heavily on interpretability, which refers to humans' capacity to comprehend the algorithms they employ. Since humans possess distinct cognitive characteristics, the human-combined ML approach leverages these strengths, outperforming both standalone human and algorithmic solutions. This paper introduces a human-centric interpretability framework grounded in the principles of human learning. It demonstrates that these learning-oriented principles can guide human-combined algorithms to enhance performance, particularly in high-dimensional contexts. Furthermore, the study develops a cognitive intricacy score to quantify the difficulty of interpreting ML models from a human learning perspective. Empirical results indicate that models with lower cognitive intricacy achieve higher accuracy when evaluated by human experts. The research concludes by outlining potential applications and necessary future investigations regarding algorithmic interpretability through this human learning-based framework and its associated cognitive intricacy metric. Overall, this work advances the understanding of human-computer collaboration in ML by providing practical guidelines for creating principled, interpretable models that facilitate effective human-combiner algorithms. Additionally, it offers a potential pathway for formalizing human interpretation by incorporating a rigorous definition of algorithmic interpretability. Finally, the proposed cognitive intricacy score may serve as a foundation for a formal theory of human interpretation, addressing the significant challenge of quantifying interpretability. Ultimately, this study represents a pioneering effort in establishing a formal theory of algorithmic interpretability. Keywords: machine learning, interpretability, human learning, human-combiner, cognitive intricacy. Citation: Wang, Z., & Li, C. (2021). Deep learning models are typically trained by minimizing empirical risk, often using cross-entropy for classification or mean squared error for regression. However, these approaches fail to address anomaly detection, a critical challenge in machine learning where anomalies are rare and often distinct from normal data. While Isolation Forest (iF) is a widely used, efficient, and scalable unsupervised method leveraging the "anomaly is rare" principle, it lacks the ability to function as a local, node-level predictor within decision trees—the core component of modern neural networks like Decision Tree Networks (DTN) and Wide Networks (WTN). Our objective is to create an iTree variant that serves as a local predictor, enabling its integration into neural networks to enhance performance. We introduce TiWS-iForest, a novel model that combines TiWS-DTN and iF, demonstrating that TiWS-iForest achieves state-of-the-art results across various anomaly detection benchmarks. Our research demonstrates that TiWS-iForest effectively integrates TiWS-DTN features with iF's anomaly scoring and classification capabilities, significantly outperforming competitive baselines. Additionally, TiWS-iForest surpasses existing iTree-based local predictors in both training speed and accuracy, marking the first step toward embedding TiWS-DTN into neural networks. This research highlights the effectiveness of combining TiWS-DTN with iF, establishing TiWS-iForest as a new benchmark for anomaly detection. Poisson processes serve as the foundational model for analyzing extreme values across disciplines like hydrology, finance, and physics. This paper proposes a reparameterization of the classical spectral measure within the Poisson process framework, which becomes particularly advantageous when spectral measure estimation is the primary objective. We demonstrate that this reparameterization yields significantly smoother point estimates and more accurate confidence bands, specifically in scenarios involving a large number of high quantiles. These improvements are demonstrated through a simulation study and a case study examining record-breaking heatwaves in the Northern Hemisphere. Additionally, a R package implementing this approach, known as \texttt{epois}, has been developed and made publicly available. A comprehensive tutorial on the methodology, featuring simulation results, the Northern Hemisphere heatwave case study, and an extensive simulation experiment, is also provided. The associated R packages, \texttt{epois} and \texttt{epoisTutorial}, are available on CRAN. Furthermore, the package \texttt{epoisTutorial} includes step-by-step code that replicates all figures and analyses presented in the tutorial. This research examines the electronic cross sections for the $H(e,H)e$ and $e(H,e)H$ processes at high energies, showing that the dependence on incident electron energy remains nearly linear. The slopes of these quasi-linear regions are determined through three methods: numerical solutions of the integral-differential equations, analytical evaluation based on these equations, and estimates derived from the one-gluon exchange approximation. Within the energy range studied, the reliance on renormalization scale is minimal. Comparisons with existing data and other authors indicate agreement. The study concludes that both numeric and analytic approaches yield consistent results. Notably, the reliability of using the target rest frame for high-energy processes is confirmed. Furthermore, the similarity between the energy dependencies of the $H(e,H)e$ and $e(H,e)H$ processes suggests they share underlying mechanisms. The incidence of intervals with stationary values of the average cross sections is also estimated. Additionally, an analysis of the soft target effect for the $H(e,H)e$ and $e(H,e)H$ processes is provided. This work represents a contribution to the field of high-energy electronic hadro- and nucleophysics. Keywords: electronic hadronization; high energy; cross section; soft target effect. To enhance AI capabilities, such as natural language understanding, it is essential to integrate common sense knowledge, which includes general facts, causal relationships, and everyday experiences. This study evaluates methods for constructing common sense knowledge graphs, comparing the performance of using only textual data against a hybrid approach that combines textual data with diverse sources like Wikipedia, encyclopedic texts, encyclopedic knowledge graphs, and bibtex metadata. The research investigates how varying training data affects the capabilities of the resulting graphs and identifies the specific advantages contributed by non-textual sources. By analyzing the differences between the ATOMIC graph and a new, hybrid common sense graph called COMET, we aim to clarify the impact of using only textual information versus incorporating a rich variety of sources. The findings indicate that textual data alone is insufficient for learning all common sense knowledge; specifically, non-textual data enhances the graph's ability to represent everyday experiences. Furthermore, the symbolic representation in COMET enables the acquisition of experiences absent from the textual corpus, thereby improving the graph's experience completion score. Ultimately, this research underscores the necessity of diverse data sources for building a comprehensive common sense graph like COMET, which supports large-scale natural language understanding applications, including machine translation. Finally, the study proposes using the zero-shot translation task within Machine Translation as a metric to assess the common sense knowledge embedded in both ATOMIC and COMET. The code for COMET and the evaluation code are available at https://github.com/robertorosa/comet-atomic. Our analysis of the impact of non-textual data on the symbolic graph offers valuable insights for future common sense knowledge engineering efforts. The comprehensive evaluation of COMET supports its use as a free alternative to Wikidata for enhancing large-scale neural language models. Additionally, the experiment regarding everyday experiences highlights the unique value of non-textual data for commons, which has significant applications for encyclopedic knowledge graphs. The evaluation also demonstrates the utility of BibTex metadata as a knowledge source, offering a solution to the challenge of labeling causal relationships. Finally, enhancing common sense graphs with experience knowledge through non-textual means has opened new avenues for symbolic AI research. The machine translation experiment further highlights the value of experience knowledge and the effectiveness of symbolic knowledge graphs in enhancing transformer models for zero-shot learning. Overall, this research provides significant insights for advancing common sense knowledge engineering. The experiment with semantic parsing offers new perspectives on the composition of common sense graphs, while the analysis of hallucination in common sense classification underscores the need for careful consideration of knowledge graph quality

This study details the data reduction pipeline developed for the Hi-GAL survey, a project utilizing the HARP+ and BOCA heterodyne instruments on the JCMT to map the high-mass star-forming regions TMC-1 and OMC-2/3 in CO and CN within the 160–220 GHz range. The initial reduction process, executed in GILDAS, addresses data calibration and flagging, alongside the creation of observation and spectral libraries. Subsequently, a custom Python pipeline is employed to perform data extraction and modeling. A primary objective of Hi-GAL is to conduct statistical analyses across numerous regions; therefore, the pipeline is optimized to batch process data from multiple files. Finally, the pipeline's output is illustrated using the TMC-1 observation as a case study. This work establishes a standardized reduction protocol for the Hi-GAL survey, ensuring that data processing remains consistent and reproducible. Furthermore, the methods presented are designed to be adaptable for individual user requirements. The GILDAT script for data reduction is provided in the online supplementary material. Additionally, the Python code can be accessed via a public GitHub repository, with GILDAT scripts also available there for the benefit of individual users. The Hi-GAL data libraries referenced in this paper will be made accessible through the public archive CDS via a dedicated entry point. The analysis of the TMC-1 region will be published in a forthcoming paper. The globular cluster NGC 2808 is renowned for its multiple stellar populations and a significant spread in helium and metal abundances. This study presents the first comprehensive analysis of high-quality spectra obtained using the UVES spectrograph on the VLT. We identified 110 stars within the cluster, spanning a broad range of abundances, and derived precise radial velocities. By employing the MILES library for stellar atmospheres, we calculated surface gravity, radial velocity, [Fe/H], [Na/Fe], and [Mg/Fe] for 90 giant stars. Our findings reveal a clear correlation between the [Na/Fe] and [Mg/Fe] ratios, alongside a previously noted metallicity gradient. Additionally, we confirmed the existence of a turn-off star in NGC 2808. The radial velocity distribution of these giant stars aligns with the cluster's center, while their radial distribution exhibits a slight deviation from the cluster's center. Our results indicate that the spread in [Na/Fe] and [Mg/Fe] ratios is comparable to that observed in [Fe/H]. These conclusions are consistent with recent studies utilizing globular cluster data for asteroseismology. Our paper includes the first-ever radial velocity and abundance maps for NGC 2808. We conclude that NGC 2808 serves as a valuable target for future investigations into globular cluster formation. We investigate single-file 1D self-interacting diffusion using the Jaynes formalism for single inference models. The dynamics involve self-interacting Brownian particles with fixed density moving in a solvation field derived from a Kac-Hughes-Holstein type entropy. The dynamics of single-file diffusion are governed by single-file entropy, which consists of configurational and correlation components. The former arises from combinatorial entropy of non-adjacent particle arrangements, while the latter stems from correlated particle configurations. We demonstrate that single-file self-interacting diffusion can be mapped to single-file entropy-generating diffusion by applying the maximum entropy principle to the 1D self-interacting Fokker-Planck equation. This results in a Fokker-Planck equation featuring a drift term and a position-dependent diffusivity. By employing the mapping and the martingale method, we derive an exact solution for the first passage time distribution of an exiting particle from a slit. Furthermore, we show that the duration an exiting particle leaves the slit is influenced by the correlation between the file length and the position of the particle at the moment of exit. Finally, we map the single-file diffusion problem to a queueing theory model known as the M/M/1 system. This model, which describes a single-server queue with Poisson arrivals and service times, is well-established in both physics and queuing theory. The mapping between single-file diffusion and queueing theory provides a new perspective for future research. Additionally, we explore the non-Gaussian nature of the single-file entropy-generating problem through an analogy to a gas in a box. We demonstrate that while the central limit theorem applies to the position of the last particle in a one-dimensional self-interacting file, it does not extend to the position of the leading particle. This is because the position of the leading particle is highly sensitive to the specific configuration of particles in the file, whereas the position of the last particle is less affected by the file's configuration. Consequently, we show that the exit time distribution lacks the symmetry characteristic of the continuous time random walk model. These results are supported by numerical simulations. Our findings may offer a new perspective for future research into self-interacting diffusion and interacting Brownian motion. In Bayesian learning, the posterior distribution of a hypothesis's probability serves as an updated belief derived from updating prior probability beliefs through the evaluation of new evidence. When applying Bayesian learning to the quantum domain, it is essential to derive quantum Bayes' theorem to maintain consistency with quantum physics. Consequently, numerous applications of quantum Bayesian learning have been proposed across various quantum fields, including quantum mechanics foundations, quantum information, and quantum machine learning. However, these applications often implicitly assume the direct application of classical Bayes' theorem to quantum mechanics, which lacks a rigorous justification. This paper addresses this critical issue by rigorously deriving quantum Bayes' theorem from fundamental assumptions about quantum physics, which are naturally satisfied by operation-based quantum mechanics. Furthermore, based on this derived theorem, we demonstrate the implicit assumption used in existing quantum Bayesian learning applications and clarify how quantum Bayes' theorem enables these applications to construct quantum prior and posterior beliefs consistent with quantum physics. Our findings provide a comprehensive and clear overview of quantum Bayesian learning, which is highly relevant to the quantum information community. Additionally, we illustrate the utility of quantum Bayes' theorem in quantum machine learning by deriving a quantum Evidential Distance metric from it, which effectively measures the similarity between quantum states representing quantum priors and quantum posteriors. Through numerical experiments, we show that this quantum prior and Evidential Distance-based method surpasses the classical Bayesian method in both accuracy and stability. This study examines the QCD thermodynamic equation of state for tiny systems, typically consisting of one or two strongly interacting hadrons, within a canonical ensemble framework. Unlike the grand canonical ensemble, particle number fluctuations are suppressed in tiny systems because their specific fluctuation-to-mean ratio ($\delta N/\langle N\rangle$) is significant only at high temperatures or very low temperatures, where the influence of the ideal gas limit becomes apparent. Consequently, the compressibility of tiny systems is reduced compared to the ideal gas, though the effect of hadron-hadron interactions is negligible in the low-temperature regime. We derive the equation of state for all tiny systems and specifically address the proton within the context of tiny QCD matter. Our findings indicate that the interacting proton behaves similarly to a paramagnetic system, a model that has proven essential in various contexts, including the low-temperature production of real pseudoscalar photons in heavy-ion collisions. We also investigate the equation of state for the antiproton, which is relevant to predictions of antiproton accumulation near the critical point. Furthermore, we explore a potential link between the magnetic system of the tiny proton and the Higgs mass, a factor crucial to the viability of new physics beyond the Standard Model. Finally, we note that the equation of state for the tiny neutron is nearly identical to that of the proton. These results may contribute to the theoretical analysis of the sPHENIX experiment's anticipated excess of pseudoscalar real photons in ultra-peripheral heavy-ion collisions. Additionally, the experimental search for a tiny Higgs-induced antiproton accumulation near the critical point could serve as a valuable independent probe of the critical region. These theoretical predictions regarding the equation of state for tiny QCD matter provide a foundation for future investigations into the interaction between hadronic systems and quantum fields. To this end, we propose a theoretical framework for the equation of state in tiny QCD matter. Our proposed framework is compatible with the production of real photons in ultra-peripheral heavy-ion collisions and the search for antiproton accumulation in the critical region. These theoretical predictions can be tested in the near future, as the anticipated start of the sPHENIX experiment in 2021 marks the beginning of the exploration of the critical region. We also highlight that the prediction of an antiproton accumulation in the critical region is compatible with the concept of a locally restored discrete symmetry. Cooper, Harris, and May previously established that certain special elements in the Steenrod algebra $\mathcal{A}$ are defined by specific criteria. This paper presents a mathematical note exploring the cohomology groups of $\mathcal{A}$ with coefficients in a Desnanjou module, with a focus on understanding how these special elements interact with the cohomology of other $\mathcal{A}$-modules. We demonstrate that the cohomology of a Desnanjou module is a finitely generated module over $\mathcal{A}$. Furthermore, we investigate the mechanism by which special elements annihilate the cohomology of these modules. This analysis yields new, non-trivial special elements within $\mathcal{A}$, which are derived from the combinatorial structures of the $Q_I$ basis elements of the cohomology itself. Additionally, we examine the relationship between $Q_I$ and special elements, noting that certain $Q_I$ basis elements appear to satisfy the definition of a special element. The paper concludes with an outline of potential future research directions, of which this work is but a preliminary step. Our goal is to identify a finite set of elements within the cohomology of a Desnanjou module that can be utilized to generate the cohomology of modules for other algebraic structures. This work serves as a foundational step toward achieving that objective. Specifically, we aim to locate finite elements in the cohomology of a Desnanjou module whose restrictions to the subalgebra $R$ generate the cohomology of the group $G$, where $R$ is the subalgebra associated with the finite group $G \leq C_{p-1} \subset GL_k(\mathbb{F}_p)$. To achieve this, we must first understand the characteristics of elements in the cohomology of a Desnanjou module, their algebraic relations, and their actions on the cohomology of modules for algebraic structures. This note initiates that investigation. Our approach involves selecting an arbitrary element from the cohomology of a Desnanjou module, examining its properties, and deriving its characteristic polynomial. We anticipate that analyzing the cohomology of this module will yield characteristic polynomials of degrees greater than $p$. We demonstrate that our analysis produces a characteristic polynomial of degree $p+1$. Consequently, we observe that the $Q_I$ basis elements of the cohomology of a Desnanjou module exhibit properties analogous to those of $Q_I$

Quantum filters are compact and affordable devices capable of blocking Lyman-alpha radiation while transmitting most visible light. By shielding detectors from this dominant Lyman-alpha source, these filters enable astronomers to conduct photometry in the visible spectrum in the future, even within the dense interstellar medium of relativistic relativistic jets. This proposed filter costs approximately $100 and weighs only 10 grams. The study introduces a model for the spectral transmission of such quantum filters, demonstrating how they can be integrated into existing filter systems to block Lyman-alpha. Results indicate that a model filter could suppress Lyman-alpha radiation by a factor of 1,000 across a 380 nm wide passband centered at 400 nm. A simple method is provided to determine the transmission curves for the Lyman-ultraviolet range, and a database of transmission curves is available at http://www.nrao.edu/~jgull/FilterModel/ for researchers. This model has been applied to simulate observations from the transition region between the wind-shock and jet in SS 433. The analysis reveals that the current gap between wavelength ranges covered by optical and X-ray instruments can be bridged using quantum filters. Additionally, a set of filters is proposed to enable observations from 300 nm to 750 nm, extending the range currently accessible only with visible light cameras. A set of 11 filters with transmission curves generated using this model is available for consideration by commercial filter manufacturers. Furthermore, a simulation of a camera utilizing these 11 filters and quantum filters is included, which could serve as a proof-of-concept instrument for agencies such as the National Science Foundation or NASA. A simulation of such an instrument is available at https://github.com/jgull/QuantumFilterTestInstrument. The paper concludes that Lyman-ultraviolet photometry should be considered for upcoming space missions, and a case for including quantum filters as an instrument option is presented. Ultimately, quantum filters offer an innovative solution for ultraviolet astronomy, potentially enabling observations at wavelengths that have been previously inaccessible. Missions that incorporate Lyman-ultraviolet capabilities are expected to yield unique scientific results. For instance, a mission with 11 quantum filters and 11 standard filters could achieve a factor of 10 return on investment compared to a mission with only 11 standard filters. This is because quantum filters are inexpensive, lightweight, and consume negligible power, allowing for larger apertures and longer exposures, thereby generating significantly more data

This study investigates the distributed ideal control problem within a zero-order hold networked system featuring a graph-filter coefficient matrix that varies daily, a framework applicable to noise cancellation, voting mechanisms, and frequency filtering. Initially, we demonstrate ideal controllability under a connectivity assumption for any graph-filter coefficient matrix. Subsequently, we derive a scalar-controlled and multi-sensor-controlled implementation using first- and zero-order protocols, respectively. Finally, we validate the proposed schemes through simulation studies. Notably, this work represents the initial effort to address distributed ideal control problems via graph filters in noise cancellation and voting scenarios over networked systems. Additionally, the system's graph filter coefficient matrix is permitted to be singular, distinguishing it from previous literature and enabling broader applicability. Crucially, the designed control inputs rely exclusively on locally available data, eliminating the need for additional network resources. Furthermore, our results indicate that the convergence speed of the first-order protocol is directly proportional to the graph filter's pass-band. Most significantly, the proposed second-order protocol achieves faster convergence than the corresponding first-order approach, thereby enhancing the efficiency of noise cancellation, voting, and frequency filtering. These findings also hold for time-varying networks under an agreement assumption. Notably, this study marks the first instance of addressing distributed ideal control problems via graph filters in noise cancellation and voting scenarios. Search engines currently serve as the primary method for discovering images on the World Wide Web. We introduce a new algorithm called Dynamic Picture Indexing (DPI) to improve image discovery through searchable dynamic visual index tracks. This approach enables users to input visual queries, allowing the system to identify images with similar or evolving appearances. Our implementation relies on an existing open-source computer vision library for visual feature extraction and custom code for conducting a personalized picture index search. This framework facilitates dynamic visual indexing and facilitates when-to-wear suggestions by analyzing how an image's appearance changes over time. The proposed solution offers an efficient alternative for dynamic visual search and allows for personalized style recommendations based on current weather conditions and the day of the week. Furthermore, we have developed an automatic image descriptor based on the solution's functionality to support dynamic visual search. In a preliminary evaluation, our results indicate that the tracks achieve mean average precision scores ranging from 0.75 to 0.85. Additionally, we demonstrate that the open-source solution outperforms existing solutions in dynamically searching for picture index tracks. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1999/Dynamic-Picture-Indexing. Future work will focus on enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of the search algorithm and refining the automatic image descriptor by integrating additional features for dynamic visual index tracking. We also aim to improve and expand the co-occurrence matrix and time-based index search to better identify images with changing or similar appearances. Ultimately, we intend to implement and evaluate a personalized picture index search using an existing fashion dataset. The keyless communication framework eliminates the necessity for security keys by leveraging channel noise as inherent noiseless randomness for secret generation. This approach has been extensively studied in broadcast channels with noisy receivers and feedback-enabled point-to-point channels. Recently, the keyless verification problem, which addresses authentication in point-to-point channels, was formulated without a solution. This paper revisits that problem, proposes a new achievable rate, and resolves it for the additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel, where the achievable rate equals the solution to the dual optimization problem. Additionally, we compare the keyless verification rates of the AWGN channel against the point-to-point problems defined in previous works. Finally, we illustrate an example that demonstrates how keyless verification can double the achievable secret-key agreement rate in a broadcast channel. Our results indicate that for certain noise distributions, the keyless verification rate is unlimited. Furthermore, we observe that keyless verification can be interpreted as achieving the capacity of a synthetic channel with a noisy broadcast link, utilizing a Bernoulli(0.5) noise distribution for encoding. Ultimately, we demonstrate that keyless verification can significantly enhance both secret-key agreement and communication reliability over noisy channels. To our knowledge, this is the first work to explore reliability improvements in a keyless setting, and these findings lay the groundwork for future research in this area. Numerical examples are provided to validate the optimality of the keyless verification solution for the AWGN channel. Additionally, numerical examples are included to illustrate how keyless verification can enhance secret-key agreement rates in broadcast channels. Finally, we examine the impact of noise distribution on achievable keyless verification rates. Specifically, we show that keyless verification can yield unbounded improvements in achievable reliability, and that broadcast channels with highly non-Gaussian noise distributions can achieve higher reliability through keyless verification.
