Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are set to play pivotal roles in future time-constrained services, including emergency medical transport, last-mile delivery, and disaster relief. However, the three-dimensional nature of UAV flight introduces significant complexity to trajectory planning, making it impossible for closed-form solutions to solve these problems effectively. Consequently, this study addresses time-critical routing by proposing two approaches: one based on Graph Theory and another leveraging the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm. The graph-based method addresses both holonomic and non-holonomic challenges, whereas the non-holonomic solution is further optimized using the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm. These methods were tested using a Python library that simulates various scenarios with multiple pickup and drop-off points. Results demonstrate that the graph-based approach yields superior outcomes, enhancing delivery efficiency by 15% and improving delivery to specific locations by 10%. Ultimately, the research indicates that the graph-based methodology is the more effective strategy. The code is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/Ankit-12345/Unmanned-Aerial-Vehicles. The stability of bilayer graphene is investigated through RG analysis of a model incorporating multiple-body Coulomb interactions between electrons in the same (intra-layer) and adjacent (inter-layer) layers. In the absence of any other interactions, all RG equations demonstrate that every relevant coupling constant decreases under RG transformations, indicating that all multi-body Coulomb interactions are renormalization-group irrelevant and that bilayer graphene remains stable without invoking additional interactions. However, when at least one additional interaction is present, the outcome depends on the specific combination: if the additional interaction is nematic scattering, all electrons become unstable; if electron-phonon interaction is present, holes become unstable; and if both are present, all electrons and holes are unstable. The instability of all electrons and holes, driven by at least one additional interaction, implies that bilayer graphene is unstable without the requirement of symmetry-enhancing interactions. The instability of all electrons is observed with only the phonon interaction, which is irrelevant, whereas the instability of all electrons and holes requires the quantum critical point where all coupling constants vanish. Furthermore, if any interaction beyond multi-body Coulomb interactions exists, all coupling constants are relevant, meaning they grow under RG transformations away from the quantum critical point. Consequently, all electrons and holes are unstable regardless of the specific additional interaction, provided it is not symmetry-enhancing. In the scenario where only a single additional interaction is present, it must be symmetry-enhancing to prevent any coupling constant from increasing under RG transformations. This confirms that all electrons and holes are instability in the presence of: (i) multiple-body Coulomb interactions; (ii) a single additional interaction; and (iii) either interlayer hopping or interlayer exchange interaction. This conclusion aligns with findings from the Luttinger liquid approach. Notably, the RG analysis of multiple-body Coulomb interactions in bilayer graphene reveals that this additional interaction is irrelevant, whereas the Luttinger liquid analysis suggests it is relevant. This discrepancy arises because the Luttinger liquid approach is limited to single-body interactions and cannot account for multiple-body Coulomb interactions. In contrast, the RG method employed here is applicable to multiple-body interactions and yields a more accurate result. The RG analysis also indicates that the Fermi surface nesting vector is irrelevant, consistent with previous studies on single-layer graphene. Overall, the RG analysis of multiple-body Coulomb interactions in bilayer graphene demonstrates that this interaction alone is sufficient to induce all-electron and all-hole instability, thereby eliminating the need for any other additional interaction. The stability of the $P_{6}/mm$ and $I_{h5/m}$ isomers of C80 in the presence of an $h$-BN/Ni(111) substrate was investigated using density functional theory. Findings indicate that the $P_{6}/mm$ isomer, when covalently bonded to the substrate, forms a highly stable compound with Sc2TbN@C80, yielding a binding energy of 2.3 eV. Notably, the interlayer distance between C80 and the substrate shifts from 3.28 Å in the stable configuration to 3.02 Å within the metastable configuration. Additionally, the vibrational spectrum of the molecule is sensitive to the substrate interaction, a factor critical for identifying these C80 derivatives via scanning tunneling microscopy. Finally, the study demonstrates that the rotation of the Sc2TbN@C80 molecule on the substrate is influenced by temperature. These results offer valuable insights for future experimental studies utilizing C80 derivatives as building blocks in nanotechnology. Keywords: Fullerene, C80, Sc2TbN@C80, P6/mm, Ih5/m, DFT, STM. The development of Internet of Things (IoT) technology has driven the creation of energy-efficient devices capable of performing complex computations even with minimal power supply. However, energy constraints are a primary hurdle for widespread IoT adoption. Lightweight cryptography aims to address the need for secure, low-power solutions in the near future. This survey examines the latest advancements in the fields of lightweight cryptography and cryptography for IoT. Furthermore, it presents three open research challenges in this area, specifically focusing on the selection of appropriate cryptographic algorithms, hardware implementations, and standardization issues. Finally, the survey outlines four potential future research directions for lightweight cryptography within the context of IoT devices. Expected outcomes include a current state-of-the-art overview, resolved challenges, and future research trends. Given the dynamic nature of the field, new advancements are anticipated. Finally, a bibliography of 95 references related to the topic is provided. Radiofrequency pulse sequences designed to measure physical parameters with high precision are typically formulated through an iterative process that leverages classical trial functions to explore the vast sequence space. This empirical method relies on a human expert to assess the significance of perturbations and sample new functions. We introduce a Bayesian algorithm that adapively executes the trial function step by step, autonomously and efficiently generating sequences. Specifically, we apply a sequential Monte Carlo algorithm featuring a thermodynamic integration step, which enables accurate exploration of highly non-linear sequence spaces. Additionally, a belief propagation step facilitates the analysis of local features to guide the refinement of the best sample set into a superior trial function. Through examples involving the determination of a static magnetic field, we demonstrate that adaptive measurement optimization can occur in real-time, eliminating the need for external human input. This approach facilitates automated design, allowing researchers to concentrate on essential experimental details. Furthermore, we discuss the algorithm's capacity to handle experiments utilizing multiple sequential trial function measurements. Finally, we illustrate its effectiveness in designing pulse sequences for two complex experiments: the dynamical decoupling of a single spin against two types of noise, and the measurement of a time-dependent driving signal for a quantum bit. These examples highlight how adaptive optimization discovers global minima that are inaccessible through local search methods. Notably, in both cases, the adaptive algorithm identifies multiple local minima that are significantly deeper than any minimum found by the external expert. We contend that this superior trial function should be incorporated into the global search for highly precise quantum measurements. To facilitate reproducibility, we have developed an open-source Python package that implements the sequential Monte Carlo and thermodynamic integration steps, which can be accessed at https://github.com/QuantumBayesLab/seqMC. The examples discussed in this work are available at https://github.com/QuantumBayesLab/adaptive_design. This package is designed to be easily extensible for other applications, including the use of thermodynamic integration with step sizes adjustable based on sequence space dimensionality. Additionally, the package includes an open-source implementation of the expert model described in this paper. We anticipate that these tools will empower researchers to design, test, and optimize pulse sequences for precise quantum measurements. We propose that this design workflow will become an integral component of the experimental process in quantum information laboratories. Supplementary materials are provided in Appendix A, detailing the expert model, Figure 1, Figure 2, and Figure 3. Numerous centrality metrics have been proposed to evaluate the significance of nodes within networks. Many of these metrics, either directly or derivatively, prioritize nodes connected to others via shortest paths. However, networks often possess structural heterogeneity beyond simple node degrees, including short-range correlations that generate semi-local clustering. This phenomenon typically manifests as a negative triangle inequality surplus. The surplus, defined as the difference between the length of the two shorter sides of a triangle and the length of the longest, serves as an indicator of the local clustering of a node's neighbors. Building on this concept, we introduce the Gromov centrality metric, which leverages the surplus to assess node importance. This metric quantifies the average surplus relative to all triangles formed by a node's connections across various scales, thereby capturing the semi-local nature of network topology. We analyzed the degree distribution and triangle surplus probability distribution of synthetic networks designed to model the scale-dependent clustering characteristic of many real-world networks. Furthermore, we compared Gromov centrality against established centrality measures on both synthetic networks and several real-world networks. Our results demonstrate that Gromov centrality outperforms other metrics in identifying a small subset of nodes that are highly clustered relative to their degree, with cluster levels comparable to the most densely clustered nodes in the network. Additionally, we propose random node sampling as a strategy to accelerate computations for graphs where memory constraints prevent loading the entire structure. This sampling approach enables the calculation of Gromov centrality on networks that exceed available memory capacity. Finally, we highlight the versatility of Gromov centrality as a scale-dependent tool for characterizing the network structures to which a node is most connected. To ensure reproducibility, the code required to generate the networks and results presented in this study is accessible at https://github.com/alexei-gromov/gromov-centrality. The associated GitHub repository also includes the package for Gromov centrality calculations. Gromov centrality can be computed on networks larger than can fit in memory by employing random node sampling, a technique implemented in the package. We introduce a new gravitational theory featuring complete linearity and azimuthal symmetry, characterized by two non-negative linear functions: one for the local speed of light and another for the local time dilation factor, with the latter approaching unity at large distances from a source. These local quantities are treated as established physical entities, analogous to the local acceleration of gravity. These choices significantly constrain the theory, necessitating a single additional fundamental variable: the generalized distance, which generalizes Euclidean distance. The core equation of the theory expresses the gradient of the gravitational potential, $\Phi$, as the difference between the local speed of light, $c(r,\theta)$, and a universal constant speed, $c_0$, both tending to infinity as one approaches spatial and temporal limits. This difference is scaled by the azimuthal angle $\theta$ and divided by the universal constant time dilation factor. This equation is the azimuthal counterpart to the well-known Eddington linearity condition for the gradient of the Newtonian potential. Utilizing the generalized distance, we construct a universal vector potential for this new theory. Subsequently, we derive the field vector potential, which remains finite at large generalized distances when generalized time is held constant, and verify that the azimuthal component aligns with experimental data on solar system planetary orbits. Finally, we demonstrate that the field vector potential represents a generalized monopole, and we prove that the field vector potential remains finite everywhere except at the origin. Furthermore, we show that the field vector potential constitutes a generalized dipole. Additionally, we prove that the field vector potential is composed of two components: a dipole term that diminishes with increasing generalized distance, and a quadrupole term that grows with generalized distance. The quadrupole component arises due to generalized time dilation. In the Euclidean limit, we observe that our potential reduces to the standard monopole and dipole potentials. However, in the Lorentz limit, it differs from both the monopole and dipole potentials of special relativity. The monopole component of our potential corresponds to the monopole of the Lorentz-Newton system, whereas the dipole component corresponds to the dipole of the Lorentz-Newton system. Consequently, the monopole and dipole components of our potential are proportional to those of the Lorentz-Newton system, with the proportionality factors being the universal constants $\kappa$ and $\tau$, respectively. We demonstrate that a rigorous equivalence exists between linear systems under similarity transformations and matrix pencils under equivalence with respect to both their realizations and associated graded structures. Furthermore, we provide complete classifications for both matrix pencils under equivalence and linear systems under similarity based on this graded structure, derived from their complete invariants. In the process, we also establish a classification for matrices under strict equivalence. Finally, these findings are extended to cases involving pairs of matrix pencils under simultaneous similarities. Specifically, we link pairs of matrix pencils under simultaneous equivalence to linear systems under pairs of simultaneous transformations, and we provide complete classifications under strong equivalence, similarity, and graded equivalence for the resulting pairs of linear systems. These relationships are further explored through the analysis of pairs of linear systems subject to graded equivalence. Finally, we explicitly detail the complete invariants required to characterize pairs of matrix pencils under simultaneous equivalence, pairs of linear systems under similarity, and pairs of matrix pencils under simultaneous strong equivalence. Our formulation of T-duality relies on Morita equivalence and employs a generalized torus constructed from a locally compact abelian group, twisted by a topological central extension involving the circles, a discrete abelian group, and a component of a Lie group with a discrete quotient isomorphic to the circle. Furthermore, our construction encompasses T-duality for higher tori found in higher geometry, utilizing the concept of weakly groupoidal n-groupoids developed by Schommer-Prieß. Additionally, we extend the dualization process to twisted toroidal n-torsors within Schommer-Prieß's framework of fully extended T-duality. The dual of an extended T-duality functor is anticipated to offer a conceptual understanding of the dualization of Boardman's board games and part of Freed-Hopkins' board categories. We conclude with an explicit description of the dual of a twisted toroidal 2-torsor, which corresponds to the dual of a parallelizable surface algebraic bundle with structure group U(1). Its dual resembles a flat U(1)-bundle over a noncommutative torus with a twisted trace. In 2001, Klein and Marx demonstrated that every $n$-vertex metric graph featuring an integer edge length function possesses a subgraph with treewidth at most 12 whose distance-preservation ratio does not exceed 3. This paper establishes an $O(1)$-time algorithm for the metric subgraph deletion problem specifically for graphs with sublinear treewidth, thereby extending prior findings by Demaine et al. and Marx and Sankowski. Leveraging this result, we prove that every $n$-vertex metric graph with a sublinear edge count, an integer weight function, and no cycles of length at most $k$ can have $O(k^{2})$ vertices removed in $O(n)$ time to embeddability into a subgraph with treewidth at most 25, while maintaining a distance-preservation ratio of at most 3. Furthermore, the $k$-clique deletion problem can be resolved in $O(n)$ time to achieve a subgraph with treewidth at most $f(k)$ and a distortion no greater than 3. Finally, the $k$-clique deletion problem admits an $f(k)$-deletion algorithm under a logarithmic-factor distortion, which we anticipate can be improved to a constant factor given sufficient time. These findings provide the first sublinear algorithms with polynomial runtimes for low treewidth embeddings of non-planar graphs under metric constraints. Additionally, we present a nearly linear-time algorithm that removes $O(\log k)$ vertices to enable an embedding into a graph with treewidth at most 35, maintaining the same distortion bound. Our methodology also yields a novel $f(k)$-deletion algorithm for the planar embedding deletion problem, surpassing the previous $f(c(k))$-deletion approach. Finally, we address an open question raised by Demaine et al. regarding the existence of an embedding algorithm with sublinear additive distortion; we confirm that such an algorithm does exist. Our results are derived by integrating techniques from Demaine et al., Klein and Marx, and Demaine et al. with an $O(1)$-deletion solution we developed for the low treewidth deletion problem. Our findings also establish a metric variant of the $d$-gon embedding problem, which is resolved in $O(n)$ time. Finally, the $d$-gon embedding problem is shown to be fixed-parameter tractable, and the $k$-clique deletion problem is proven to be fixed-parameter tractable.

The study of mathematical models, particularly in the natural sciences, has gained significant traction due to the recent emergence of highly effective personal computing devices, such as smartphones and tablets. Consequently, there is a surging demand for software tools capable of analyzing complex systems and predicting their future behavior. Among these tools, discrete-time dynamical systems stand out as a fundamental concept for predicting outcomes, widely recognized for their simplicity and effectiveness. This paper explores the behavior of smooth, strongly monotonic discrete-time systems, demonstrating that such systems exhibit the same core dynamics as those identified by S. Ulam and J. von Neumann. Specifically, we show that these systems possess a unique globally attracting fixed point, generate unbounded orbits, and possess saddle fixed points that support period-two orbits. These findings establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for modeling real-world phenomena using smooth, strongly monotonic discrete-time systems. Furthermore, we illustrate that this important class of systems is ubiquitous across various scientific disciplines by presenting examples drawn from multiple fields. Finally, we conclude by proposing several directions for future research. Our hope is that the insights and perspectives offered in this work will inspire scientists to investigate the rich and extensive theory of discrete-time dynamical systems further. Additionally, we aim to encourage them to develop new models based on these systems and to encourage students to explore the ubiquitous behaviors we have highlighted. Ultimately, we believe this will contribute to a more technologically advanced future. Notation. The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) serves as a key method for determining molecular ground states on near-term noisy quantum hardware. This study introduces a qubit-excitation-driven adaptive strategy for constructing adaptive variational ansätze within the VQE framework. Utilizing qubit-excitations as a physical indicator of entanglement generation, this approach automatically selects multi-parameter squeezed gate sequences to build a depth-optimal circuit for ground-state simulation. Molecular excitations act as control signals to identify which qubits become entangled during algorithm execution, enabling the sequence selection process. We demonstrate that adaptive gates facilitate ground-state simulation with lower circuit depths compared to non-adaptive ones. Our findings indicate that excitation-based adaptive VQE successfully determines both ground and excited states. Additionally, we illustrate a method for reducing circuit depth in excited state simulations by leveraging multi-parameter phase gates to model qubit unitary evolution. These results establish a framework for adaptively and excitation-efficiently determining qubit excitations, with potential applications for excited-state algorithms in future quantum chemistry simulations. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of excitation-adaptive VQE for ground-state simulations using the adaptive UCCSD (UAVCCSD) algorithm, which requires a circuit depth 2.5 times smaller than UCCSD. This achievement is realized without relying on prior knowledge of qubit excitations. The findings presented herein significantly expand the algorithmic landscape for adaptive variational quantum algorithms. All code is publicly accessible on GitHub. We introduce a straightforward yet highly effective technique for training variational autoencoders (VAEs) to dramatically improve the quality of the reconstructed data. The core concept involves applying mean-field variational inference (MFVI) to estimate the representation $z$ and the posterior $q(z|x)$, but instead of minimizing the standard MFVI loss, we optimize the standard ELBO plus the mean-field VAE loss. This new loss function can be interpreted as the VAE loss constrained by the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimates of the representation $z$. We refer to this approach as the MFVI+MAP VAE. Our method is straightforward to implement and can be integrated into any existing VAE. We also demonstrate how to incorporate this new loss into both autoencoding and generative variational inference frameworks. Experimental results on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets show that our method can enhance VAE performance by approximately 1.0 to 1.5 bits, resulting in the highest reported VAE test log-likelihoods for these datasets. Furthermore, we observe that the posterior bound gap (PBG) of a trained VAE using our method is significantly lower than that of a standard VAE. Additionally, we find that the PGB of a trained VAE serves as an effective indicator for determining when the training has converged. Finally, we note that the PGB can function as a reliable training metric to replace traditional metrics like loss. The PGB exhibits clear and consistent gradients relative to test-log-likelihood across various datasets, architectures, and hyperparameters, making it a robust metric for assessing VAE performance. We have made the PGB available as a standalone module for users to employ in their training and evaluation processes. The PGB is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/profound_generative_decoder. The source code for the MFVI+MAP VAE can be found at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/profound_generative_decoder/tree/master/profound_generative_decoder. The paper itself is available at https://github.com/ChenYi2020/profound_generative_decoder/tree/master/paper. Recent high-precision measurements of fundamental cosmological parameters, including the Hubble constant and the primordial gravitational-wave background, are essential for a comprehensive understanding of the universe's origin and subsequent evolution. This study investigates the effects of post-inflationary physics on the primordial gravitational-wave spectrum, specifically examining whether a phase transition in dark energy can resolve the Hubble tension. We demonstrate that, provided the equation-of-state parameter $w$ of the post-inflationary vacuum fluctuation field is greater than $-1$, the resulting scenario produces the same dimensionless spectrum and the nearly scale-invariant curvature power spectrum observed today. This mechanism generates an accuracy cosmology, yielding a Hubble constant value of $H_0 = 73.04 \pm 0.42$ km/s/Mpc, which aligns closely with the value derived from the gravitational-wave method. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the post-inflationary dynamics can suppress the amplitude of the primordial gravitational-wave background by approximately three orders of magnitude, thereby explaining the recent NANOGrav data and the recent constraints from Advanced LIGO-Virgo. The post-inflationary universe described herein consists of $b$aryonic matter, dark matter, and dark energy, with the latter modeled as $q$-essence. Our results suggest that the post-inflationary dynamics can significantly alter the post-recombination expansion history of the universe, potentially offering a solution to the Hubble tension. Our proposed solution is consistent with the recent NANOGrav results, as the residual gravitational-wave background is sufficiently suppressed to be compatible with current Advanced LIGO-Virgo constraints. Our findings provide a viable solution to the Hubble tension and offer a new perspective on the nature of the vacuum energy driving the late-time accelerated expansion of the universe. Additionally, this research offers a novel perspective on the gravitational-wave background, with the post-inflationary dynamics capable of suppressing the spectrum's amplitude by up to six orders of magnitude. The Atacama Compact Array (ACA) serves as the most expansive interferometric configuration of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), covering a field of view from the center of the Atacama Desert up to approximately 375 meters. This study details the deployment of the ACA to investigate the spatial distribution of H2CS in Comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS). The survey was conducted on 2019 June 10, when the comet was roughly 1.5 AU from the Sun and 2.3 AU from Earth. The ACA was tasked with detecting H2CS emissions in the coma, with a primary focus on identifying any spatial asymmetries in the molecular distribution. The observations were executed in Band 6 (183–275 GHz) using the K-band H2CS J/K doublet at 122.902 GHz and 122.903 GHz. Data were analyzed using GILDAS, and imaging was performed with ALMA's standard imaging tools Common Subarray Imaging (CSI) and Common Subarray Clean (CSC). The resulting image revealed a diffuse, circular emission pattern centered on the comet, with a peak intensity of 0.07 mK. This emission was found to be consistent with a model featuring a point source at the comet's nucleus, suggesting that the H22CH2CS signal originates from the nucleus itself. The study concludes that the ACA is highly effective for this type of investigation, demonstrating that cometary emissions can be observed with spatial resolution capable of distinguishing between cometary and interstellar sources. Furthermore, the detection of H22CH2CS in a diffuse, circular emission indicates that certain cometary molecules are characterized by a high degree of isotropy. This finding contradicts the prevailing hypothesis that these molecules are produced in localized regions of the coma, such as the sunlit side, and points toward the necessity of a distributed source. The research also addresses the challenges associated with imaging a diffuse, circular source using an ACA with a single beam size. Finally, the study explores the implications of this finding for future research on other comets and their comae. The presented data will be utilized to examine the characteristics of cometary emissions and to evaluate the suitability of the ACA for similar studies in the past and future. This study addresses the challenge of generating diverse, natural speech for any input text without requiring supervised annotations. To enhance the variety and expressiveness of the generated speech, we utilize a conditional generative adversarial network (CGAN) focused on providing monophonic utterance-level conditioning. Our results demonstrate that the GAN produces speech with significantly greater variability than models based on a non-conditioned Generative Adversarial Network (GAN). Furthermore, our evaluation indicates that the synthetic speech is intelligible and expressively natural, particularly when compared to previous unsupervised generation methods. Additionally, we introduce a comprehensive dataset of neural TTS benchmarks to facilitate the assessment of unsupervised speech generation. The Tsallis-Holographic Dark Livelihood (ThO) model represents a new framework for exploring dark livelihood (DL) and cosmic expansion. Its foundational basis rests on the principle that the total DL represents the difference between the total energy and the energy of the reference model. This study employs a complex form of the Hubble parameter within a Tsallis-Holographic Dark Livelihood (ThO) model, where the reference model consists of the pressureless matter and a free parameter. The analysis reveals that the imaginary component of the generated ThO model functions as a perfect dark vitality (Dl) candidate. Furthermore, the graphical behavior of the coeval Hubble parameter indicates that the cosmic expansion transitions from an accelerating phase to a decelerating one. Additionally, the results demonstrate that the cosmic contraction rate remains constant throughout the coeval period. Finally, the critical state of the DL and cosmic expansion is corroborated by the free energy and pressure of the DL model, which are derived using the first law of thermodynamics. Finally, the validity of the model is confirmed through the examination of the cosmic equation of state. The code used for the analysis is available at: https://github.com/AbdulBari2020/TsallisHolographicDarkLivelihood. This study introduces a variation of the NSGA-II algorithm enhanced with Branch and Bound (B&B) techniques to address Multi-Objective Mixed Integer Non Linear Programming problems. The primary challenge lies in the computational intractability of these problems, which often necessitates the development of approximate solutions. The proposed hybrid approach utilizes Branch and Bound to filter non-feasible candidates and employs NSGA-II as a non-dominated sorting method that maintains solution diversity. Numerical testing was conducted on two datasets: the MOMINLP benchmark and a real-world air cargo revenue management case study. Results indicate that the hybrid B&B-NSGAII method demonstrates effectiveness in solving these challenges. Furthermore, comparison tests reveal that this approach outperforms the standard NSGA-II algorithm in terms of both convergence speed and diversity. Finally, within the context of air cargo revenue management, the study illustrates how the proposed method generates multiple high-quality, diverse schedules for end-users. In healthcare and biomedical research, exchanging clinical, medical, and biological data is a common activity. However, initiating a data exchange often requires substantial manual effort and coordination between trusted data custodians and users. These custodians must ensure compliance with strict legal and regulatory standards, such as HIPAA and GDPR, while managing sensitive challenges related to data de-identification and security. To address these hurdles, we have created CyberRange Data Exchange Gateways (DEGs), which enable exchanges between custodians and users while maintaining data integrity, confidentiality, and legal adherence. DEG operations are managed by trusted custodians, and users submit requests that are then matched with appropriate custodians based on eligibility criteria defined by each custodian. Once a match is found, a handshake protocol is initiated between the custodian and the participating DEG to execute the transfer. This paper outlines the design and implementation of DEGs within the CyberRange platform and details how users and custodians interact with them. Furthermore, we present preliminary evaluation results from a prototype implementation. These results indicate that DEG operations are highly efficient, with user activities such as data upload, search, and download completing in approximately 1.5 seconds. Additionally, network traffic analysis demonstrates the security of the DEG implementation, highlighting the robustness of the handshake protocol against potential attacks. Biomedical Research Custodians are then shown to manage and monitor exchanges, as well as control the publication of research findings utilizing their biobank resources. Overall, this work demonstrates that DEGs significantly streamline the data exchange process for both users and custodians in the biomedical domain. By reducing exchange times from several days to just a few seconds, DEGs facilitate access to samples, sequences, and clinical data for users and enable biobank custodians to support diverse users and initiatives. Ultimately, DEGs provide users with a seamless experience and assist biobank custodians in supporting biomedical research. Furthermore, this approach is highly general and can be adapted to other domains, such as healthcare, where multiple custodians manage samples, medical images, or clinical data. Such exchanges are essential for clinical trials, disease monitoring, and biomedical research. We anticipate that this work will be valuable to users and biobank administrators seeking to simplify and enhance the efficiency of data exchange processes. This study investigates a multi-user secure communication system enhanced by Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS). The RIS reflects a single information carrier toward multiple legitimate users (Information Decoding Users - IDUs) and a dedicated security user (Security Decoding User - SDU) from a single base station (BS). The BS transmits a composite signal comprising four elements: the primary information message, a confidential key for IDUs, a confidential key for the SDU, and a countermeasure signal aimed at the SDU to safeguard IDUs. The SDU deciphers the information by nullifying its impact, while the IDUs extract data by decoupling the key from the countermeasure. To ensure robust operation, the system accounts for hardware imperfections affecting RIS reflection, analog-to-digital conversion, and power amplification. Using Maximum Likelihood (ML) estimation, the system optimizes RIS configuration to maximize the SDU's information rate and minimize the worst-case rates for both IDUs and an eavesdropper. This joint design addresses a convex optimization problem, solved via an Interior Point Method (IPM). Numerical results confirm that the proposed system outperforms conventional approaches in terms of security and reliability. Furthermore, sensitivity analysis demonstrates that the ML approach remains stable under realistic hardware imperfections, meeting reliability requirements. Finally, the analysis reveals that while minor increases in the countermeasure signal boost IDU rates, a significant surge degrades their performance. Consequently, the ML-based RIS optimization is essential for ensuring a balanced trade-off between security and reliability. Overall, this system offers a promising solution for secure, reliable wireless communications, with potential applications in military, healthcare, and financial sectors. Future work will explore extensions to mobile IDU/SDU scenarios and energy harvesting capabilities. Specifically, when users move, the ML approach must be adapted to account for dynamic channel conditions and update RIS configurations in real-time to maintain optimal RIS configuration. Additionally, the ML method must be computationally efficient to meet practical deployment constraints. These extensions will further improve the system's performance and usability, making it a viable solution for next-generation wireless communication networks. We present the ability-contrastive value function, which serves as a piecewise approximation of a value function by sequentially summarizing and relabeling trajectories. This approach is motivated by hindsight summarization, which enables agents to learn from previously failed attempts. By utilizing a memory bank of historical data, the ability value function approximates a target reward by counting transitions between specific states and actions. To facilitate convergence, we introduce the evidence-contrastive value function, a Markovian approximation of the ability value function designed to balance exploration and exploitation. Furthermore, we develop an off-policy variant of this value function to enhance sample efficiency. Our theoretical analysis and experiments across various Atari games demonstrate that the off-policy ability value function outperforms both standard reinforcement learning methods and their contrastive value function counterparts. Additionally, the off-policy ability value function converges to an optimal policy that outperforms the policies derived from other contrastive value functions. Finally, we show that the off-policy ability value function converges to a piecewise approximation of the optimal value function. These findings underscore the sample efficiency and near-optimal performance of the ability value function, with our code available at https://github.com/akshaykumar1999/Ability-Contrastive-Value-Function.

The solar breeze is a low-speed, high-density wind that covers a vast range of velocities and flows continuously from the Sun, extending at least to the termination shock. Although the term "solar wind" is often used indiscriminately to describe all such flows, it would be more accurate to reserve "coronal wind" for material leaving the corona and reserving "solar breeze" for that of low speed. This paper examines the characteristics of the solar breeze, specifically focusing on low-speed streams, wind acceleration, and coronal mass ejections (CMEs), by analyzing data from the Parker Solar Probe (PSP) and its predecessors, the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO) and the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOLAR). The study addresses how low and intermediate speed streams are defined, their spatial and temporal distribution, and their evolution as they propagate outward. Additionally, it explores their relationship with heliolongitude, solar activity, and the solar cycle. A significant portion is dedicated to characterizing low-speed streams and their fine structure, including whether they are composed of multiple components and their average width. The paper also examines the velocity distribution of all solar breeze events, their temperature and entropy, and the energy flux they transport. Finally, the occurrence and energy flux of CMEs are discussed. The findings are primarily based on in-situ observations from the Parker Solar Probe, which has provided the first detailed analysis of solar breeze energy flux at the closest distances ever recorded. These results are compared with earlier data from SOHO and STEREO, which served as the primary sources for low and intermediate speed streams prior to the launch of PSP. The overall conclusion is that the solar breeze is a complex phenomenon that cannot be fully understood without direct, close-up observations of its source. The energy flux carried by the Parker Solar Probe's low-speed streams is approximately one order of magnitude lower than previously thought. However, when considering both low and intermediate speed streams, the energy flux approaches the critical value required for the "turbulent heating" mechanism, which is thought to be the primary driver of solar wind acceleration. The energy flux from CMEs is also discussed, with the Parker Solar Probe providing the first detailed analysis of their characteristics. The probe has observed several CMEs, including one that was not detected by the coronagraphs on the PSP's WISPR instrument. This work investigates free actions of discrete groups $\Gamma$ on commutative C*-algebras $A$, interpreting these actions as noncommutative countable principal bundles. For such a bundle, we define its structure group as the C*-algebra generated by $\Gamma$'s action on $A$ and identify the fibers as the abelian C*-algebras $A_g$ corresponding to individual group elements $g \in \Gamma$. We develop a noncommutative version of the local triviality principle: any continuous section of a freely grouped, locally trivial principal bundle with a continuously acting structure group possesses a uniquely determined covariant lift. Furthermore, we establish conditions ensuring that all continuous sections arise via this localization process. Finally, we identify sufficient conditions under which the fibers exhibit the Approximation Property and the weak nuclear dimension. Specifically, when $\Gamma$ acts freely and minimally on a compact Hausdorff space $X$, and $X$ admits a finite cover by a torus of significantly lower dimension, the fibers are guaranteed to possess the Approximation Property and weak nuclear dimension. Additionally, assuming $\Gamma$ acts freely and minimally on $X$, we demonstrate that the fibers are simple. As an application, we construct a novel family of one-parameter groups of endomorphisms on these fibers. Finally, we illustrate that the properties of the acting group $\Gamma$—namely amenability, property (T), property ($\tau$), and property $(\tau)$—directly influence whether the resulting fibers have the Approximation Property or weak nuclear dimension. Notably, there exist amenable groups $\Gamma$ acting freely on $X$ for which the fibers lack the Approximation Property. However, if $\Gamma$ acts freely on $X$ with a free semigroup of stabilizers of codimension at least 2, the fibers do possess the Approximation Property. Group examples supporting both scenarios are provided in \cite{KKP21}. Similar findings regarding weak nuclear dimension apply. The Unruh effect predicts that uniformly accelerated observers perceive the vacuum as a thermal bath, a phenomenon entangled with past light cones that generates unphysical effects, such as entanglement harvesting between accelerated modes. By utilizing entanglement from early and future light cones, we demonstrate that these unphysical consequences can be eliminated, offering a consistent framework to understand how accelerated observers interact with a bath. Leveraging the Berry phase, we derive an expression for the phase associated with the previous light cone unruh effect, revealing that this phase is fundamentally tied to entanglement from the previous light cone. We propose a measurement protocol for the Berry phase based on position measurements, which can be interpreted as detecting the timelike unruh effect. Furthermore, we illustrate a protocol for measuring entanglement using the symmetric dual Kraus representation of unextendible product states, demonstrating that this approach can also detect the timelike unruh effect. Our findings indicate that entanglement derived from future and previous light cones cancels the entanglement from the previous light cone alone, confirming that only future light cone entanglement provides a consistent description of the unruh effect. Additionally, we show that future light cone entanglement is sufficient to explain unphysical phenomena, including entanglement harvesting and Berry phases. This outcome suggests that concepts such as entanglement, the unruh effect, and Berry phases should be redefined in terms of future light cone states to ensure a consistent formulation of quantum field theory. To achieve this, we examine the implications of these findings for the structure of quantum field theory. Finally, our proposed method for measuring entanglement offers a new tool for studying quantum gravity, with potential applications in analyzing black hole evaporation. Evaporation is typically modeled as a timelike unruh effect, where entanglement from both past and future light cones contributes to the increase in black hole entropy. In contrast, past light cone entanglement alone yields an inconsistent description, necessitating the inclusion of future light cone entanglement to properly account for entropy production. This future light cone entanglement also explains the non-monotonic behavior of entanglement entropy observed in Hawking radiation. To fully comprehend these results, we examine the implications of entanglement from both future and previous light cones on black hole entropy and the information paradox. Our findings suggest that the past light cone unruh effect is not merely a theoretical construct but a significant component in describing black hole entropy and the information paradox. This has profound consequences for understanding black hole evaporation

To address this limitation, we introduce a novel dataset named MEE (Multilingual Event Extraction) specifically for Indonesian and English. This dataset comprises 10,000 instances collected from news articles, featuring annotations for Event Mentions, Argument Roles, and Modifier-Marker pairs. We provide a comprehensive analysis of annotation guidelines and statistical properties of the data. Additionally, we evaluate several state-of-the-art models to demonstrate their performance on our new dataset. Ultimately, MEE aims to foster event modeling research and is anticipated to facilitate event discovery across the two languages through mass application. This work examines the positivity of characteristic forms linked to the curvature of hermitian vector bundles on global compactifications. Under a separation assumption, we demonstrate that the characteristic forms associated with the direct sum of vector bundles, whose sections exist globally, remain global when pulled back via certain canonical morphisms. As a consequence, we establish that the characteristic forms derived from the curvature of ample hermitian vector bundles on global compactifications are strictly positive. Furthermore, we present an application to the adjunction mapping problem.

This study investigates how the spectral-temporal evolution of matter ejected from the donor star varies with the accretor's X-ray spectral state. We analyzed the most recent XMM-Newton observation of Cyg X-1, which was conducted during its hard-state phase. Spectral-timing methods revealed that in this hard state, the black hole accretor was surrounded by a thermally dominated atmosphere, with the soft component arising from reflection off the surrounding intercloud medium. By applying the spectral-timing formalism, we determined the spectral-timing evolution of the hard X-ray component in the 2–10 keV band. This evolution was decomposed into fast and slow components, with the slow component attributed to the superwind driven by the stellar breeze from the companion. By comparing the mass transfer rate derived from this spectral-timing analysis with that from CO(1-0) observations, we confirmed that the superwind is the primary matter-ejection channel in the hard state. Furthermore, the spatial distribution of the intercloud medium, as inferred from the spectral-timing evolution, aligns with the results of the CO(2-0) observation taken in the transition state. These findings demonstrate that the thermally dominated intercloud medium is a key factor in shaping the spectral-timing evolution of HMXBs in their hard states. Additionally, our results indicate that the X-ray irradiation-driven superwind is the dominant matter-ejection channel from the donor star in the hard state, showing no significant difference between the hard and transition states. This suggests that the wind-driven superwind, driven by the stellar breeze, is not the primary matter-ejection channel in either state. Overall, this research reveals the spectral-timing evolution of matter ejected from the donor star in the hard state of Cyg X-1, highlighting the distinct characteristics of matter-ejection channels in HMXBs during different X-ray states. The study also underscores the critical role of spectral and temporal evolution in understanding the characteristics of intercloud matter. Future work should focus on analyzing more XMM-Newton observations from various states of Cyg X-1 to further explore the spectral-timing evolution of matter ejected from the donor star. This paper introduces the Collaborative Universal Syntactic and Semantic Analysis (CUSSEA) Framework, which employs a common, language-independent formalism to describe syntax and relations between words and constituents. Relations are denoted using two-dimensional tables that align with natural language structures, where rows represent constituents and columns represent words. The CUSSEA framework unifies existing linguistic formalisms, including Relational Syntax Diagrams, Pure Relational Grammar, Relational Grammar, Relational Algebra, and Relational Tables. Additionally, it addresses challenges related to cross-lingual transfer and data sharing by providing a shared representation of syntactic and semantic structures across all human languages. The framework also aligns with information systems designed to manage natural language structures through two-dimensional data representations. Document-level representations consist of two-dimensional tables containing complete texts, while sentence-level representations involve smaller tables for individual sentences. Two representative implementations are the Collaborative Universal Syntax and Semantic Analysis Database (CUSSEA-DB) and the Collaborative Universal Syntax and Semantic Analysis Framework (CUSSEA-FW). Document processing utilizes table algebra to perform operations on database table representations, whereas neural networks operate on the CUSSEA Framework representation. Cross-lingual transfer is facilitated through shared representations derived from CUSSEA-DB and enhanced by CUSSEA-FW. To demonstrate practical utility, the paper presents experimental results on part-of-speech tagging, coreference resolution, and semantic role labeling. A web interface for CUSSEA-DB and a web interface for CUSSEA-FW are accessible at http://cussea.org. The CUSSEA-DB interface can be reached at http://cussea-DB.org, and the CUSSEA-FW interface is available at http://cussea-fw.org. This framework has also been applied to language acquisition, creating experiments on the web interface at http://cussea-interface.org. Furthermore, the CUSSEA Framework has been utilized to develop a new language model, the Collaborative Universal Syntax and Semantic Language Model (CUSSEM), accessible at http://cussem.org. This paper details the representations, data processing, and theoretical underpinnings of CUSSEA, with the associated web interfaces offering opportunities to explore representations across diverse languages. The document concludes with proposed future research applications of CUSSEA. This work is based on the book Common Representation of Syntax and Semantics: The Collaborative Universal Syntax and Semantic Analysis (CUSSEA) Framework, published by Springer in 2019, with the corresponding manuscript available at http://cussea.org/cussea

We examine the post-merger dynamics of a nonrotating, magnetized binary neutron star system using three-dimensional general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamics simulations. Within the first few seconds following the merger, the central dynamical disk expels approximately $0.005\,M_{\odot}$ of material. This ejecta is composed of roughly half alpha particles and includes a significant neutrino heating component. Utilizing a newly developed neutrino-matter interaction model, we demonstrate that the disordered magnetic field within the central disk amplifies in strength during the ejection, reaching about $10^{15}$ G. This field growth is attributed to the rapid stretching of magnetic field lines by hydrodynamic turbulence, a process that appears more pronounced in neutrino-heated flows than in hydrodynamic ones. The disordered magnetic field within the ejecta is expected to drive a magnetized shock, launching a pair-plasma jet powered by neutrino heating. This mechanism represents a distinct alternative to the successful common-envelope dynamical ejection observed in magnetized, rapidly rotating binary neutron star mergers. The total ejected mass is comparable to that from rapidly rotating systems, whereas the ejection timescale is roughly two orders of magnitude longer. The kinetic energy of the ejections is approximately $10^{52}$ erg, while the heating flux is around $10^{53}$ erg s$^{-1}$. These values align with the requirements for an extended, high-flux neutrino burst and a late-time kilonova powered by the ejecta's kinetic energy. Consequently, we propose that binary neutron star mergers may exhibit both a pair-plasma jet driven by neutrino heating and a common-envelope dynamical jet. Furthermore, we explore the potential for observing these phenomena in both gravitational-wave and electromagnetic data. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the kilonova associated with GW170817. Given that the observed kilonova was primarily powered by a dynamical jet, we conclude that the pair-plasma jet must be either significantly weaker or absent in the physical system corresponding to GW170817. Nevertheless, our findings suggest that such pair-plasma jets, driven by neutrino heating in neutrino-cooled accretion disks, could be a frequent occurrence in binary neutron star mergers. This hypothesis is supported by the fact that no extended neutrino signal or bright infrared/optical emission were observed during the LIGO/Virgo O1 observing run

We analyze the HSC-SSP catalog to investigate tidal features linked to large early-type galaxies (LETGs), which are defined as systems with effective radii exceeding 10 kpc. Our analysis reveals that 1.5% of all LETGs and 10% of those possessing prominent tidal features exhibit fluorescence in the H$\alpha$ filter, suggesting the latter group contains young stellar populations and potentially higher merger rates. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between the large-ETG population and the flux fraction of tidal features, utilizing this correlation to estimate large-ETG flux contributions and merger rates. We also identify fluorescent, H$\alpha$-positive LETGs with tidal features, finding that 17% of these objects possess substructure. Additionally, we observe that substructure is more prevalent in H$\alpha$-positive systems compared to H$\alpha$-negative ones, a trend that is significantly more pronounced among galaxies displaying prominent tidal features. These findings collectively indicate that the majority of prominent tidal features in large early-type galaxies arise from systems with young stellar populations and elevated merger rates. Finally, we demonstrate that the ratio of H$\alpha$-positive to H$\alpha$-negative galaxies, as well as the ratio of galaxies with prominent tidal features to those without, is higher among substructured systems than among structured ones, implying that substructure does not necessarily indicate a high flux proportion of tidal features. Overall, this study provides the first quantitative characterization of the physical properties of the population of large early-type galaxies possessing tidal features. This study presents a new gravitational framework grounded in the principles of relativity and azimuthal symmetry. It proposes that mass shells, rather than point particles, serve as the fundamental building blocks of matter. Utilizing the azimuthally symmetric metric and associated relativistic field equations, the paper derives the field equations and boundary conditions specifically for a bipolar ejection scenario involving the Bessel function. This approach yields a novel solution characterized by a negative gravitational constant. The azimuthally symmetric gravity law is defined as a repellent gravitational law, mathematically expressed as $U(r) = -(-Gm/r)$. This law generates a repulsive force that diminishes with the square of the distance, creating a negative gravitational potential well. The study demonstrates that negative potential wells can be generated when a bipolar ejection velocity exceeds a newly defined bipolar escape velocity. Additionally, azimuthally symmetric gravity predicts that light will bend away from massive bodies. To validate the underlying azimuthally symmetric solution, the paper applies it to model the bipolar ejection observed in the Herbig-Haro object HH47-1. The resulting model accurately reproduces the object's morphology, including its two opposing lobes, bulbous knots, and filamentary structures. The findings confirm that bipolar ejections can be interpreted as a repellent gravitational phenomenon. The authors anticipate that the concepts introduced in this work will prove valuable for modeling other bipolar outflows, such as those originating from young stellar objects and black holes. The Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (II) represents a significant advancement over the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (I), which failed to account for bipolar ejections. Together, these two studies establish a new paradigm for understanding repellent gravitational phenomena. The Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (II) offers a solution to the repellent gravitational problem that is grounded in relativistic principles, utilizing a self-consistent metric and boundary conditions to calculate ejection velocities. This provides a more robust theoretical foundation compared to ad hoc bipolar ejection velocity formulas found in existing literature. Furthermore, the (II) theory resolves the issue of negative mass that plagued the (I) theory. Ultimately, the (II) theory serves as a valuable tool for modeling repellent gravitational phenomena, offering a more accurate and comprehensive framework than the (I) theory. Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) are intense extragalactic radio bursts characterized by their repeatability, although most FRBs typically do not exhibit optical emission. This study investigates the feasibility of multi-messenger observations involving both concurrent and delayed optical signals from repeating FRBs, utilizing Poisson statistics. We demonstrate that high-rate optical monitoring of the sky during radio burst events could enable the detection of a small, highly luminous population of concurrent optical photons emitted by these bursts. Furthermore, we propose that wide-field optical telescopes might detect a distinct population of FRBs that release lower luminosity photons with a time delay of approximately 100 seconds relative to the radio signal. These findings suggest that future optical surveys will significantly expand the FRB multi-messenger sample, thereby enhancing our understanding of their progenitor mechanisms. Additionally, we have developed an open-source Python package, FRBOptical, available at https://github.com/alexei-gelfgat/frboptical, which calculates the expected number of concurrent or deferred optical photons based on the duration, duration uncertainty, and sky coverage of an optical survey. Additionally, we present a novel method for estimating the optical photon production rate of FRBs, derived from the cumulative number of radio bursts and the sensitivity of radio surveys. This approach differs from traditional methods that rely on photometric light curves of individual events. By comparing our results with those from recent studies, we illustrate that this technique can recover the well-constrained luminosity function of optical counterparts to gamma-ray bursts. Ultimately, this simple and efficient approach can be applied to investigate the optical emission properties of any class of high-energy transient sources. The FRBOptical package is also available on the PyPI repository at https://pypi.org/project/frboptical/. High-energy lasers serve diverse applications, including laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS), directed energy, directed propulsion, directed decontamination, and directed synthesis. This work presents the development of laser-driven LIBS, directional energy, propulsion, purification, and synthesis technologies capable of field deployment. Additionally, we demonstrate methods for characterizing and reverse-engineering laser-produced plasmas from both solid and gaseous targets. Specifically, we analyze plasma plumes generated by high-power CO$_2$ and frequency-doubled YAG lasers to reconstruct laser parameters and determine plasma properties. Additionally, we examine LIBS spectra to reverse-engineer material characteristics. Finally, we design new laser systems to achieve specific plumes for defined applications. We demonstrate that utilizing gas jets to generate thinner plasma plumes enhances spatial resolution in spatially resolved LIBS, while multi-pulse LIBS improves temporal resolution, thereby increasing LIBS sensitivity and enabling a broader range of applications. Furthermore, we show that multi-pulse LIBS can reverse-engineer laser parameters, including pulse energy, pulse duration, and repetition rate. Finally, we illustrate the use of multi-pulse LIBS for reverse-engineering LIBS plasmas, providing insights into plasma characteristics such as electron temperature, electron density, and elemental composition. Collectively, these advancements in LIBS offer a comprehensive approach to characterizing laser-produced plasmas, facilitating accurate reverse-engineering and enabling the design of new LIBS-based material characterization and analysis methods. Ultimately, this research establishes a robust framework for developing novel laser-driven technologies for field use. Ultimately, these achievements represent a significant step toward achieving a sustainable future through globally deployable, high-power laser systems. This paper introduces Delegated RingCT, a ring currency protocol incorporating zero-knowledge proofs. It functions as a streamlined alternative to the full RingCT protocol, primarily omitting the encryption of ring signatures and instead securing them through a generic efficient signature scheme. The proposal also details a simplified version of RingCT featuring "weak ring members," which reduce computational demands at the expense of anonymity set size. Furthermore, the paper outlines two methods for generating zero-knowledge proofs. The first, while simpler, necessitates interaction between the prover and verifier. The second, however, provides non-interactive anonymous transactions by leveraging the Common Reference Frame containing pre-generated proofs, mirroring the approach in the full RingCT protocol. Finally, the paper compares the various proposed ring currency variants with the complete RingCT protocol regarding anonymity, scalability, and resource consumption. Additionally, benchmark tests are presented to validate these resource efficiency claims. Ultimately, the new ring currency protocols outperform the full RingCT protocol in terms of both time and memory efficiency. Specifically, they offer significant time improvements over full RingCT: Delegated RingCT achieves nearly a 50% time reduction, while the two weak ring member variants show decreases of 25% and 33% respectively. In terms of memory usage, the time complexities associated with generating ring signature signatures and zero-knowledge proofs dictate that Delegated RingCT and weak ring member schemes require 25% and 50% less time, respectively, than full RingCT. Furthermore, the number of weak ring members in weak ring member schemes is significantly lower than the total coin count in standard ring currencies. Finally, we successfully deployed a test network utilizing Delegated RingCT and made it publicly accessible. (Code available at https://github.com/BitEconomy/Delegated-RingCT) In conclusion, Delegated RingCT and weak ring members represent efficient and practical solutions for achieving anonymous transactions. Specifically, Delegated RingCT offers non-interactive anonymous transactions, while weak ring members provide these at a reduced computational cost. Additionally, weak ring members can be easily integrated into any cryptocurrency by simply hardcoding the common reference frame into its source code. Furthermore, the weak ring member scheme can be adapted for use with interactive zero-knowledge proofs, thereby eliminating the need for a common reference frame. Overall, this paper successfully fulfills its objective. (See [1] for more information) Keywords: Cryptography, Anonymity, Ring Currency, Zero-Knowledge Proofs. The back-propagation technique is employed to reconstruct the phase space portrait of electron bunches by analyzing their propagation through a "brightness scanner" that modifies the beam envelope. The system's linearity and tunability can be enhanced during the design phase by constructing it from cascaded quadruplets, each featuring a specific relative phase shift. The reverse engineering algorithm operates without requiring prior knowledge of the system's design parameters. Its effectiveness is demonstrated on bunches with various initial conditions and in scenarios with partial access to experimental data. Additionally, the implications of this technique for diagnosing non-linear beam dynamics are explored. The proposed approach shares many attributes with tomographic reconstruction methods found in other fields. The forward model is formulated as a system of linear equations, while the reconstruction itself is solved using a non-linear functional minimization. The linearity of this functional ensures a stable reconstruction, while its tunability allows for the incorporation of physical constraints regarding the beam's brightness profile. In tomography, incomplete data acquisition is addressed by employing iterative algorithms; similarly, this study utilizes the same iterative method, which proves effective in partial reconstruction scenarios. Furthermore, these algorithms facilitate the inversion of highly ill-conditioned equation systems. Finally, numerical examples are provided to illustrate the proposed methodology. The study concludes with a discussion on the technique's prospects and the challenges it faces. The development of brightness scanners and the application of machine learning in their analysis represent a promising avenue for future research. Data-informed modeling (DIM) represents a new method for merging data analysis and modeling to enhance inference and decision-making. This approach leverages data to refine models, which are frequently complex and difficult to manage alone, while utilizing models to interpret data, reducing reliance on potentially biased assumptions. This article reviews the theory, algorithms, and applications of various existing and emerging DIM techniques. Furthermore, it proposes a collaborative DIM (CDIM) framework to address challenges posed by heterogeneous data sources, non-trivial model structures, and complex decision-making processes. The goal is to leverage the strengths of both data and models in a unified framework. Theoretical foundations and proofs for a unified and extended DIM framework are provided, followed by the design and analysis of scalable algorithms. Finally, applications are explored to demonstrate the effectiveness and utility of the proposed framework. Experimental results indicate the feasibility of the CDIM framework, with significant improvements observed in both computational efficiency and statistical accuracy. Additionally, the CDIM framework is designed to be extensible for handling other types of models and data. Finally, open challenges and future research directions regarding the practical implementation of the CDIM framework are discussed. Although neural networks are typically computationally intensive, leveraging the massive parallelism of modern hardware makes inference practical even in resource-constrained environments. Quantized neural networks represent a significant advancement in deploying neural architectures over the coming years. However, quantization is difficult to manage because neural networks are generally non-convex, resulting in numerous local minima during optimization. This difficulty is exacerbated when dealing with non-standard quantization schemes, such as asymmetric quantization or unbalanced histograms. This study addresses these challenges by extending asymmetric, interval-limited SGD (AskewSGD) for safe annealing, offering a straightforward method to avoid catastrophic collapse. Additionally, we examine the impact of annealing on non-convex optimization and its specific relevance to AskewSGD. Finally, we introduce a straightforward histogram equalization technique that works seamlessly with AskewSGD, providing a safe and direct approach to training. To our knowledge, existing literature does not adequately address the combination of non-standard quantization methods, histogram unbalance, annealing, and asymmetric, interval-limited quantization. Our work fills this gap by demonstrating that a straightforward application of AskewSGD, utilizing standard symmetric hardware-friendly quantization, results in a model with significantly lower hardware requirements and comparable accuracy to a quantized version trained with Adam and non-asymmetric, infinite-range soft-quantization. Furthermore, we show that our approach successfully addresses catastrophic collapse in non-convex optimization. The code is available at: https://github.com/alexeagley/AskewSGD. While recent studies indicate that decomposing table interactions into a sequence of steps with intermediate states can enhance performance in these domains, it remains unclear whether such decomposition is effective for Table-oriented Fact Confirmation (TOFC), a more advanced task involving fact confirmation across multiple tables with restricted interaction access. This work evaluates multiple decomposition strategies across different models to determine their impact on TOFC. Our experiments demonstrate that model performance improves with decomposition, and we identify a gradual attention shift across intermediate states as the primary mechanism driving this gain. Furthermore, the example-based learning approach combined with decomposition yields superior results compared to fine-tuning, even within a unified pre-trained language model framework. Given the promising outcomes, we anticipate that decomposition will establish a new benchmark for future TableQA and TableVac-inspired tasks. The dataset and code are accessible at https://github.com/brandon-wang2000/decomposition_tableVac.

We introduce a novel extension of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) capable of producing conditional samples. We refer to our approach as Hidden Space Conditioning on GANs, or HC-GAN for short. Unlike previous methods that condition sample generation on explicit features or attributes, our technique relies on latent vectors containing implicitly conditioned information. By utilizing conditional training, the generated data becomes sensitive to both the supplied conditions and the embedded data within the latent space. Furthermore, we propose a unified framework for extending both Unet-based and NILEGAN architectures to support conditional generation. Empirical results on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets highlight the versatility of the HC-GAN method, demonstrating capabilities such as standard and conditional image generation, continuous interpolation within the sample space, and the creation of statistically accurate sample sequences through Markov Chain sampling. Additionally, the ability to embed data into generated samples opens new possibilities, including the development of new datasets and model interpretability. Our contributions include: (a) a unified framework for implementing conditional GANs, (b) an extended HC-GAN model for CIFAR-10 achieving higher likelihood scores, and (c) advancements in implicit model conditioning, interpreted data, and inter-modal generation. Our source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ehudk/HC-GAN. The resulting model offers a unified, interpretable, and extensible framework for conditional generation, significantly advancing the field of GANs. Our findings provide new avenues for creating conditional data, improving model interpretability, and enabling cross-modal generation. We believe these contributions will offer diverse avenues for future research and development in generative models. Our work addresses the need for more interpretable and controllable generative models by introducing a unified framework for conditional GANs, achieving state-of-the-art likelihood scores on CIFAR-10, and offering new perspectives on implicit conditioning, data visualization, and cross-modal generation. Lithologic sampling in geotechnical rock mechanics involves layer-by-layer data collection from core drill holes. Because of this, the sampled rock mass is partitioned into distinct layers, each possessing a unique mean value. Traditional statistical analyses of such data often depend on the assumption of independent and identically distributed (iid) random variables, which can result in significant underestimation of uncertainty. To address the non-iid nature of these samples, we examine two Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms designed to perform statistical analysis on rock masses with dependent lithologic structures. These methods include iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) and adaptive MCMC. IRLS operates as an orbit sampler, generating an infinite-length Markov chain with a specific target distribution. Adaptive MCMC functions as a rank sampler, producing a Markov chain that adapts over time to a distribution dependent on a sequence of tuning parameters. Simulation studies were conducted to compare the performance of these two samplers. Finally, an existing real-world dataset was analyzed using both methods to evaluate their effectiveness. The comparison results indicate that for layered data, adaptive MCMC may offer superior performance compared to IRLS. Furthermore, both iterative reweighted and adaptive samplers exhibit faster convergence to their respective targets than standard Markov chains derived from naive thinning. Additionally, they provide a unified analytical framework for handling various data types, including continuous, binary, and mixed continuous-binary variables. Finally, we explore extensions of these methods to other common sampling schemes in geotechnical rock mechanics. Overall, these approaches facilitate the development of a more comprehensive statistical theory for rock mass characterization. Additionally, the open-source R packages litho and lithoR are available to support these methods. The litho package includes the adaptive and IRLS samplers, while lithoR offers a unified analysis framework for continuous, binary, and mixed data. Furthermore, lithoR incorporates a new homogeneity test for rock masses, originally proposed by the first author, which is now integrated into the open-source homogeneity test library homtestr. This paper also introduces a new homogeneity test for rock masses generated by adaptive sampling, extending prior findings to adaptive scenarios. All supporting code and data for the analyses presented in this study are available at https://github.com/rglath/AdaptiveSamplingLayeredData. These resources include the litho and lithoR packages, the newly developed test for homogeneity in adaptive sampling, and the datasets used in the analysis. The objective of distance labeling in graphs is to assign $n$ labels to the vertices of an $n$-vertex graph such that the pairwise distances between these labels in an appropriate metric remain consistent with the distances between the vertices in the graph. Initially proposed by Diestel and Lehner in 2017 for general graphs and subsequently extended to planar graphs by Diestel, J\'{a}n\v{a}k, and Volec in 2020, this concept has been further explored with a focus on label size and fault resilience. While recent work by J\'{a}n\v{a}k and Volec (2022) achieved the first constant-sized labels for outerplanar graphs and a nearly optimal size of $O(\sqrt{n})$ for planar graphs, a new label family is presented here specifically for planar graphs that demonstrates a significantly shorter length, reaching $O(\sqrt{n}/\log n)$. Additionally, the study addresses the fault-resilience of distance labeling, proving that a similar label family can correctly represent distances even when up to $k$ vertices are faulty. For the general case where $k=O(n)$, the label size is $O(k^{2/3})$, whereas for planar graphs with $k=O(k/\log k)$, the size is $O(k^{2/3})$. This result improves upon previous findings regarding fault-resilient distance labeling in both general graphs and planar graphs. Finally, it is demonstrated that the newly presented label for planar graphs cannot be extended to Wagner graphs. However, by combining existing label families for planar graphs and universal graphs containing many $K_{r}$-minors, fault-resilient distance labels are constructed for universal graphs with $k=O(k/\log k)$ such that they remain valid even if $k$ vertices are faulty. The label size for these universal graphs is $O(k^{2/3})$. Similar to the scenario with planar graphs, the length for universal graphs is $O(k^{2/3})$ when $k=o(n)$. Furthermore, the previous best result for universal graphs is generalized to include fault tolerance. Finally, it is noted that this new result also surpasses the previous best result regarding fault tolerance in universal graphs.
