This study examines the existence, uniqueness, and regularity of weak solutions for second-order elliptic equations expressed in divergence form, featuring drifts in $L^2$ and measurable coefficients defined on a divergence metric measure space $(M,d,\mu)$. Our findings rely on a $C^{0}$ estimate established in our previous work (to appear in \emph{J. Geom. Anal.}). We further explore applications within divergence-type metric measure spaces, including Riemannian manifolds and Euclidean spaces, and highlight potential applications involving singular drifts, such as those arising in sub-Riemannian geometry, and in SDEs on smooth manifolds where the connection Laplacian and Olami-Federbush Hamiltonian act on $L^2$ sections of vector bundles. These applications benefit from the fact that our solutions possess additional regularity. Additionally, the methods employed can be adapted to establish $C^{0}$ estimates for parabolic equations. As an illustration, we apply our main result to analyze sub-Riemannian manifolds, specifically the Heisenberg group, a contact sub-Riemannian manifold on a Lie group featuring singular drift, and a sub-Riemannian manifold on a hyperbolic group with divergence-type measures. We also revisit a well-known counter-example by demonstrating that a key hypothesis is satisfied. Finally, the parabolic applications extend to solutions of sub-Riemannian manifolds and a parabolic equation on a hyperbolic group with a specific divergence measure. Furthermore, we address a long-standing question regarding the regularity of weak solutions, showing that, contrary to common belief, these solutions are indeed Hölder continuous. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of such a result in the literature. Our conclusions also provide a positive answer to a conjecture regarding the solvability of sub-Riemannian manifolds, where elliptic equations with singular drifts in $L^2$ were previously considered to lack regularity. Finally, the parabolic equations analyzed here exhibit regularity and uniqueness properties that stand in sharp contrast to those of parabolic equations with singular drifts in $L^p$ for $p<2$. These outcomes underscore the necessity of the Poincaré inequality and other assumptions, as their removal can lead to counter-examples. The techniques utilized also have relevance to SDEs on divergence-type manifolds, offering insights into whether the uniqueness of SDEs with singular drifts in $L^2$ can be proven

Deep neural networks frequently struggle to reliably flag out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs, a critical capability for safety-sensitive tasks. This paper introduces DNPL, a novel out-of-distribution detection framework. Our approach leverages a recent deep learning technique that assigns a probability to each distribution normal process layer (DNPL) in a deep network, indicating the likelihood that the data originates from the corresponding distribution. We evaluate DNPL on OOD detection benchmarks, including OutlierEx, SWEAT, and 800+ NNDatasets. Our results demonstrate that DNPL achieves state-of-the-art performance on the OOD Accuracy metric for OutlierEx and SWEAT datasets and attains the best average score across all NNDatasets. The code for this work is publicly available at https://github.com/ehsan-rahimian/DNPL-OOD-Detection. Periodically driven quantum systems typically experience heating, a phenomenon that is generally intensified by open boundaries. While prior research has identified special initial states in closed systems—known as many-body scars—that evade this heating, it remains uncertain whether such states exist in open systems. This study investigates the dynamics within a two-dimensional optical-lattice model featuring many-body scars, where a single atom is introduced into an excited mode at the boundary. We demonstrate that this system avoids heating by exploiting a unique self-purification mechanism; the injected excitation repeatedly traverses the boundary, enabling it to purge open boundary conditions. Consequently, the system stabilizes into a Bose-condensed state within a scar-like configuration. Furthermore, we show that this self-purification can be externally controlled by adjusting the Floquet driving frequency. These findings suggest that many-body condensation, normally unstable, is achievable in open systems through the interplay between Floquet driving and open boundaries. Additionally, our work identifies a new class of open scalar-protected many-body scars that bypass thermalization. Finally, our results indicate that this system can function as a single-atom sensor with high sensitivity to variations in the driving frequency. This model holds significant potential for both experimental verification and technological applications. In terms of applicability, our framework extends to various optical lattice models, including those hosting spin-orbit coupling, as well as other driven many-body systems such as Bose-Hubbard and Fermi-Hubbard models, provided they possess a single-particle ground state with zero momentum. Furthermore, our approach is relevant to other systems that support a momentum state with zero momentum, including those found in nuclear and high-energy physics. The key requirement for our system is the presence of a momentum state at zero. Our findings may contribute to the creation of novel quantum devices and have broader implications for understanding fundamental aspects of nature. For instance, our work sheds light on the relationship between symmetry and many-body physics, offering insights into the behavior of complex systems. Our findings may also have relevance to fundamental questions in philosophy, such as the nature of reality and the role of consciousness. Our research has broad relevance, as it has the potential to impact various fields, including economics, political science, and sociology. Our findings may also have relevance to the environment, as they could contribute to the development of sustainable technologies and solutions to environmental challenges. Our study may also have relevance to the future, as it could pave the way for the development of advanced quantum technologies with the potential to transform society. Our findings may also have relevance to international relations

This work establishes the uniform Hölder continuity of affine invariant derivatives for almost all viscosity solutions to a class of constrained Monge–Ampère equations defined on a convex open subset $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ where $n \geq 2$. The established Hölder exponent equals $\frac{2}{n+2}$, which represents the optimal rate. This solution to a longstanding open problem posed by J. J. Chang, X. J. Liu, and Z. P. Wang extends their enhanced Alexandrov maximum principle—derived from an optimal continuity result by A. Figalli, C. A. Lohkamp, and L. R. Mahnke—almost entirely to the category of viscosity solutions. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that viscosity solutions to the relevant class of constrained Monge–Ampère equations possess twice differentiable densities on every compact subset of $\Omega$. These advancements yield several applications, most notably a streamlined derivation of the Brunn–Minkowski inequality. Additional insights into the asymptotic behavior of a solution near the boundary of $\Omega$ are also presented. Finally, the asymptotic behavior of viscosity solutions to the corresponding double-obstacle problem is examined. To achieve these results, we employ a variational approach grounded in the theory of functions of bounded variation and bounded convex integrands. Specifically, we demonstrate that a suitably regularized functional, defined as the convex hull integral of the integrand, remains uniformly Lipschitz continuous with respect to the $W^{2,p}$-norm for any $p > 2$. This methodology offers a novel perspective on the classical problem of uniform Hölder continuity for viscosity solutions of the standard unconstrained Monge–Ampère equation, thereby providing a concise proof of C. A. Lohkamp's result and a proof of X. J. Yans's theorem under the more restrictive condition $n < 8$. Additionally, this approach may prove more effective than traditional techniques for deriving further regularity results. Finally, the proof of uniform Hölder continuity is completed by adapting the technique developed by A. Figalli, C. A. Lohkamp, and L. R. Mahnke. A significant portion of this paper consists of an appendix that formalizes the theory of convex functionals on spaces of functions of bounded variation. Non-repetitive optical clocks represent the next generation of optical time-frequency standards, expected to achieve superior short-term stability compared to current non-repetitive microwave clocks. This study presents the first statistical time-domain analysis of a non-repetitive optical clock, based on 20 hours of data from a prototype device. The proposed statistical model characterizes the data using two key parameters: an allan deviation of 1.2×10⁻¹⁸ at 1 second and a noise whitening time of 100 seconds. We demonstrate that a time-domain description incorporating these two parameters surpasses both the conventional allan deviation model and stochastic processes in capturing the data's statistical properties. Furthermore, applying this two-parameter model to real data enables the prediction of future clock data, allowing for the simulation of hypothetical superior clocks and providing a method to estimate clock performance based on current prototype results. This work offers valuable insights for evaluating non-repetitive optical clock performance and establishes a new framework for characterizing these devices. The code used for all calculations is available at https://github.com/AdamKrasowski2000/Non-repetitive-optical-clock-characterization. The dataset can be requested from the corresponding author. Additionally, we introduce a new Python package, NonRepetitiveOpticalClockCharacterization, to assist researchers in predicting and simulating non-repetitive optical clocks. This package includes two modules: NRocPredictor for simulating clock data and NRocPerformanceCalculator for calculating performance metrics. Both modules utilize the proposed two-parameter model for simulation and characterization. The package is freely accessible via PyPI at https://pypi.org/project/NonRepetitiveOpticalClockCharacterization/ and GitHub at https://github.com/AdamKrasowski2000/NonRepetitiveOpticalClockCharacterization. We invite researchers to utilize the package for their own clock characterization and simulation tasks. We welcome feedback and contributions, such as bug fixes and new features, and invite collaboration to expand the package's capabilities. For more information, visit https://adamkrasowski2000.github.io/NonRepetitiveOpticalClockCharacterization/. To contribute, please contact krasowskiadam@icfpoland.pl. For joint projects, also reach out to krasowskiadam@icfpoland.pl. If you encounter any issues or have suggestions for improvement, please report them at https://adamkrasowski2000.github.io/NonRepetitiveOptical

The dynamic and unpredictable failure scenarios in SDN-driven Software-Defined Networks (SDN), alongside the demands of Service Function Chains (SFC) for next-generation services, necessitate intelligent and efficient management strategies. To address this, we propose a fog-supported SDN framework designed for real-time SFL management, fault mitigation, and resource optimization. This system utilizes a fog node-based architecture to achieve low-latency processing of real-time failure events and cross-layer coordination for efficient execution. Furthermore, the proposed approach employs a multi-objective optimization technique to enhance the efficiency of fault mitigation and resource allocation under failure conditions. Simulation results indicate that, compared to baseline methods, our proposed approach reduces the end-to-end delay increase by 10% to 20% and improves the network failure recovery ratio by 10% to 20%. Additionally, the overall source-destination end-to-end delay improves by 10% to 20%, achieving a 50% reduction in total resource consumption. Consequently, the proposed solution offers superior performance regarding failure recovery, delay, and resource usage, demonstrating its potential to serve as a foundational framework for future intelligent networks. Keywords: Fog Computing, Service Function Chains (SFC), Service Function Placement (SFP), Service Function Chain (SFC) Restoration, Fault Tolerance, Fault Mitigation, Energy Efficiency, Resource Management.

In supervised machine learning, the choice of loss function significantly impacts model performance. While researchers have explored numerous alternatives to standard cross-entropy, selecting an optimal loss remains challenging due to the difficulty of predicting outcomes on unseen data. Consequently, evaluating losses often relies solely on empirical results from simple tasks. This study investigates how different losses affect gradient surgery optimization—a recent method that automatically modifies gradients during training—to better understand their individual contributions. Our work makes two key advancements: first, we extend gradient surgery beyond neural networks to polyhedral non-convex energy landscapes, introducing a new "frustrated landscape" that hinders standard gradient descent by reaching local minima that enclose global solutions; second, we develop a systematic framework for systematically altering gradients to dissect the specific influence of various loss functions on these landscapes. We demonstrate that these two innovations mutually reinforce each other, offering profound insights into how loss functions shape optimization environments and enabling more rigorous experimentation. Ultimately, our work provides deep understanding of loss function impacts, facilitates discovery of promising new candidates, and fosters research focused on fundamental principles rather than merely empirical performance. By promoting a deeper grasp of loss function properties, we aim to accelerate progress toward the development of robust machine learning systems. To support the reproducibility of our findings, we have released all code and materials at https://github.com/Chen2020Xuanli/Dissecting-Loss-Functions-with-Gradient-Surgery. Supporting materials are available at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/14141111111111111111111111111111?usp=sharing. Chen2020Xuanli/Dissecting-Loss-Functions-with-Gradient-Surgery.

We introduce and examine a new class of holographic quantum error correction codes termed Hyper-INvariant MERA (HIMERA). Starting with a linear spin chain and applying a power-law dispersion relation $\omega(\lambda) \sim \lambda^{\alpha}$, we systematically construct a bulk-spacetime characterized by a power-law metric. HIMERA exhibits a tensor network structure that mirrors the topological arrangement of standard MERA, though its bonding tensors are uniquely shaped by the $\alpha$-power dispersion. When $\alpha=1/2$, the network converges to the INvariant MERA (INMERA) code. By analyzing the renormalization process, we demonstrate that HIMERA maintains a local bulk-spacetime isometry for any $\alpha$. Furthermore, the network supports a dual reconstruction mechanism via minimal geodesics defined by the bulk spatial coordinate, $\lambda$, and the boundary site index, $i$. Utilizing the "bulk-holography dictionary," we show that HIMERA accommodates a broader spectrum of operators, including those with non-local support. Additionally, we investigate the performance of HIMERA as a quantum error correction code, revealing that increasing the distance enhances correction capabilities while reducing fidelity. Finally, we explore the potential to derive a gravitational action from HIMERA and outline future research directions. This study not only uncovers a family of holographic codes linked to power-law dispersions but also expands the known landscape of quantum error correction codes and their corresponding dual gravitational theories. These findings hold significant promise for advancing our understanding of quantum gravity. (arXiv ID 2202.01007)

The Galactic core hosts a dense assembly of magnetized gas structures, notably including filamentary formations. While these filaments are hypothesized to play roles in the Galactic magnetic field's architecture and energy generation, their precise nature remains uncertain. Consequently, we conducted a statistical analysis of filamentary features within the Galactic center to better comprehend their characteristics and potential functions. This study examines the radial and azimuthal distributions of filaments, as well as the distribution of distances separating them. Our findings indicate that filaments are not randomly dispersed in the galactic plane but follow a Gaussian distribution centered on the plane, with a standard deviation of approximately 0.2 pc. Additionally, the azimuthal distribution reveals a slight preference for the Northern direction. Regarding spatial separation, the mean distance between filaments is roughly 1.5 pc, though a significant number of filaments were observed to be much closer together. Furthermore, the distance distribution is notably asymmetric, with a standard deviation of about 2.5 pc. Finally, we explored various hypotheses to explain the observed distance distribution, with the Gaussian distribution emerging as the most plausible model. This study introduces a decentralized control strategy to address voltage reduction and loss savings in systems combining primary and secondary distribution networks that feature distributed storage. By utilizing decentralized "preservation" voltage reduction, utilities can lower losses and enhance voltage profiles without incurring the substantial costs associated with primary-side infrastructure upgrades. The proposed method involves secondary networks autonomously adjusting their voltages to preserve their aggregate, long-term average quadratic voltage deviation, which is synchronized with the primary network through periodic exchanges of specific average voltage data. Consequently, decentralized decisions drive most voltage control operations, thereby eliminating the need for expensive automated controllers on primary feeders. Results from a 38-bus system demonstrate that, relative to centralized potential-based voltage control, preservation-based control achieves comparable loss reductions while requiring only minimal and low-bandwidth communication. Furthermore, preservation voltage reduction attains these outcomes using only 2.5% of the secondary automated controllers that centralized methods demand. Finally, this preservation-based approach secures identical loss reductions as a specific model predictive control formulation while restricting primary-side computations to occur only periodically. Overall, preservation voltage reduction offers primary distribution networks a pathway to achieve substantial loss reductions without the high expenses linked to large-scale automated controllers. Additionally, by enabling secondary networks to autonomously manage their own voltage profiles, the approach mitigates the need for extensive automation in those sectors. This makes preservation voltage reduction a vital step toward fully automated voltage control across both primary and secondary distribution networks. The paper includes proofs demonstrating the stability and convergence properties of preservation voltage control and provides implementation guidelines for storage operators. Furthermore, it explores the connection between preservation voltage control and model predictive control, facilitating the development of advanced preservation-based control strategies. Finally, the study addresses storage dispatch and preservation-based voltage control under conditions of incomplete network topological information. This facilitates the deployment of preservation-based voltage control in networks with incomplete data by restricting primary storage operators to knowledge of their local sub-networks and secondary storage operators to their individual islands. Simulations on a 124-bus system indicate that preservation-based voltage control can still deliver significant loss reductions even when networks are partitioned into isolated subnetworks. Additionally, the analysis examines how preservation-based voltage control influences system reliability. Reliability assessments were conducted using both preservation-based and potential-based voltage control schemes, comparing their loss reductions against those achieved under no-load conditions. Finally, the paper evaluates the cost-effectiveness of preservation-based voltage control as a means to achieve loss savings. This study examines a data collection framework where arms operate under non-i.i.d. delays, rendering the standard "pull-the-best" strategy from Thompson sampling inapplicable. However, we demonstrate that this approach remains effective when delays are arm-specific rather than shared. We introduce and analyze a variant of Thompson sampling tailored for this scenario, alongside developing a specialized variant that leverages domain knowledge by prioritizing high-reward arms based on current parameter estimates. For the specialized algorithm, we establish a policy-agnostic, almost sure convergence guarantee. Regarding the standard variant, we prove an optimal convergence rate under reasonable delay assumptions. Finally, through carefully constructed counterexamples, we illustrate that the advantages of both methods are exclusive to settings with arm-dependent delays. Finally, numerical experiments confirm the practical superiority of these algorithms over existing baselines. Our work introduces novel technical tools and concepts relevant to non-i.i.d. bandits. Notably, the concept of "specialists"—arms whose high rewards depend on specific subspaces of the parameter space—provides insight into identifying top arms even when their statistics do not globally dominate. This motivates specialized algorithms that may prioritize certain arms based on parameter estimates without necessarily sampling them first. Additionally, we develop techniques to handle potentially infinite delay queues in theoretical convergence proofs, which may have broader applications. These special methodological contributions establish almost-sure delay constraints, represent upper bounds on delay distributions, and ensure finite delay with probability one. Furthermore, we propose a new framework for analyzing delay distributions that is both practically useful and theoretically rigorous. Collectively, these contributions significantly advance the understanding of non-i.i.d. bandits. Specifically, we offer a systematic method for characterizing delay distributions and their associated worst-case behaviors. The paper concludes with an outline of potential future research directions in this field. Finally, to address the inherent difficulties of non-i.i.d. bandits, we introduce novel methodologies that set a new benchmark for the field and pave the way for future advancements. The capability of generating text that closely mimics human expression is highly valued, as it facilitates the creation of engaging dialogue agents that users find appealing. This paper introduces a new open-source system for the Machine Translation/Dialogue Summarization (MTDS) task at the 49th Annual International Conference on Computational Linguistics. How do text producers generate text? How do they acquire the ability to do so? The LEATHER project was initiated to address these questions. The name LEATHER is an acronym for Learning to Emit Authentic Human Response, a text producer. The objective of this work is to develop LEATHER to understand the characteristics of text producers. This objective is aligned with the goals of the Dialogue Summarization (DLS) task, which requires a model to generate a plausible continuation of a provided dialogue. We argue that a text producer is defined by the ability to generate a text continuation in response to a dialogue, and that a text producer's output should be interpretable by a human listener. Consequently, we posit that the DLS task embodies the study of text producers. In this work, we demonstrate that LEATHER can successfully model a text producer who can emit a statistically plausible response to a given dialogue input, as measured by the Automatic Plausibility Measure (APM). This study evaluates the uncertainty quantification capabilities of the chained Gaussian process (GPP) surrogate model, which represents a novel statistical approach. By analyzing 10-minute data from the complete set of 64 sensor locations on the NREL's 5 MW X100 offshore wind turbine under 10 J/s and 15 J/s joint wave and wind conditions, the research quantifies the uncertainty in key structural responses, including base overturning moments, tower bending moments at the transition piece and the 50th and 80th nodes, and the tip overturning moment. The study also examines the uncertainty in the ultimate limit state (ULS) and limit state (LS) of the offshore foundation. Results indicate that for these response variables, the uncertainty in the 95th percentile is approximately 10% of the response magnitude. The chained GP model, utilizing piecewise linear regression to locally approximate the joint probability density function of input variables, offers a computationally efficient method for modeling nonlinear relationships between inputs and responses. Furthermore, it generates quantile uncertainty estimates for both individual and combined response variables. Quantile correlation analysis reveals a strong dependence between these responses, suggesting that simultaneous extreme events are likely to occur. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that the chained GP model can accurately quantify uncertainty in structural responses and extreme events for offshore wind-turbine systems. These findings are anticipated to enhance the reliability of reliability-based design optimization and support data-driven decision-making for the offshore wind industry. Additionally, the proposed modeling framework is applicable to other engineering systems, such as civil structures and aerospace vehicles. Finally, the approach facilitates the identification of the most probable future extreme events (MPEE) by minimizing the number of required Gaussian process model evaluations. This is achieved by solving a constrained optimization problem that determines the most probable future state based on historical data, thereby reducing computational costs. The MPEE concept is expected to be valuable for risk assessment and other applications. The proposed methodology is designed to be generalizable for any quantile regression-based modeling approach. Additionally, the code used to develop the chained GP model is publicly available for the quantile uncertainty estimation framework. This framework is currently being applied to a new machine learning model utilizing Gaussian process regression with Gaussian mixture models. The chain GP model was also applied to a subset of the 64 sensor locations from a wave-tower joint time series, and the results are expected to be published in an upcoming paper. The findings are also relevant to other applications involving offshore and onshore structural response

Social media platforms have evolved into essential tools for information dissemination, a capability demonstrated by research on the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, the 2010 Haiti earthquake, and Izmir's 2005 earthquake. This study aims to analyze Twitter data from the Izmir earthquake to determine user distribution patterns, the most discussed topics, and the languages employed during the event. To achieve this, researchers employed a web crawler to gather Twitter data for a specified duration. By applying a text mining algorithm to the collected data, the investigation extracted user distribution and language distribution using Twitter account classification algorithms. Subsequently, Twitter account classification (TAC) algorithms were utilized to identify the most discussed topics. The findings revealed that during the first 24 hours of the Izmir earthquake, 50% of the Twitter accounts were from Izmir, 20% from Turkey, and 10% from the rest of the world. Additionally, 90% of the accounts used the Turkish language, 9% used English, and 1% used Russian. The study also identified three primary discussion themes: (1) the earthquake itself, (2) aftershocks, and (3) damage assessments. These results align with previous research on information distribution during natural disasters. The paper concludes by discussing the limitations of the study and proposing future directions. This work demonstrates the efficacy of Twitter data collection and mining in disaster management, offering a foundation for similar applications in future research. The proposed methodology is also applicable to other natural disasters. This research was conducted at the Izmir University of Economics, Izmir, Turkey. For further details, contact Dr. Selim Zehabi at selim.zehabi@iu.edu.tr. Keywords: Twitter data examination, Natural disaster management, Information distribution, Text mining, Twitter account classification (TAC), Twitter topic classification (TTC), Twitter crawler.

Time-resolved spectroscopy is a powerful method for probing the dynamics of chemical and physical systems, yet extracting system information from the inverse problem typically demands multiple simulations. This paper introduces a forward-optimization method grounded in forward dynamics to resolve the inverse problem in time-resolved spectroscopy. This approach enables the simultaneous inversion of time-resolved data for both linear and nonlinear ultrafast spectroscopy, even under experimental constraints such as finite measurement time, data averaging, and noise. The forward-optimization method is applied to determine the relaxation times of a damped harmonic oscillator and a two-level system, as well as the dephasing times of a vibrating three-level system. Numerical experiments reveal that this technique is highly robust against experimental noise and constraints. Furthermore, the study demonstrates successful reconstruction of the system's potential function from time-resolved infrared spectra of an anharmonic oscillator, even in the presence of noise. These findings indicate that forward-optimization is a general algorithm for ultrafast time-resolved spectroscopy, particularly for modeling the time-dependent behavior of molecular vibrations. We introduce SceNDD, a situation-based naturalistic driving dataset designed to facilitate research into advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) and autonomous vehicles (AVs). Driving scenario databases are essential for algorithmic research, planning, and learning, yet they are difficult to generate, necessitating the collection of real-world driving data. While most existing datasets rely on professional drivers following scripted instructions, our approach utilizes everyday drivers traveling on public roads. We employed the Driving Recorder System (DRS) developed at TU Delft to automatically capture vehicle trajectories and surrounding environmental information. Additionally, on-board sensors recorded driver biometrics, including steering torque, acceleration, and steering angle. The resulting data comprises 20 hours of driving from 15 drivers, annotated with 1,100 driving scenarios, 35 event types, and 15 biometric modalities. This work demonstrates how to construct a driving scenario database from naturalistic driving data and underscores the value of such resources for advancing ADAS and AV technologies. We examine the reflected entropy $S_R$ across the ground state of Border/Interface Conformal Field Theory (BCFT), which characterizes a conformal system influenced by conformally invariant boundaries. This analysis covers both D-D and D-N BCFT scenarios, where D-D refers to a system with identical reflection relations on either side of the boundary, and D-N denotes a system with opposite reflection relations. The calculation employs Cardy's reflection equation alongside conformal weights. Our results for D-D BCFT align perfectly with those of D-D spin chains derived via the tensor renormalization group (TRG). Furthermore, the D-N BCFT results successfully recover the N-N results previously obtained through TRG. Notably, the differences between our analytical findings and the TRG numerical estimates diminish as the system size increases. Consequently, we establish a direct connection between reflection relation BCFT and BCFT spin chain systems, demonstrating that the tensor renormalization group can effectively capture the reflection entropy of the ground state. Additionally, our findings reveal that the reflection entropy of the ground state is independent of the reflection relation, depending solely on the central charge and the boundary Cardinal quantum dimensions. Finally, we illustrate how the entanglement entropy of a subsystem within a BCFT ground state can be derived from the reflected entropy using an entanglement decomposition theorem. In this framework, the entanglement entropy of a bulk subsystem in BCFT is equivalent to that of a corresponding subsystem in a 1D system described by a ground state modified by a Wilson line. The results for the latter subsystem are consistently recovered through the Wilson line method. Ultimately, these findings provide a new perspective on BCFT and highlight its intrinsic link to the entanglement structure of spin chains. The proposed method offers a viable alternative approach for calculating entropy in BCFT. Furthermore, our work suggests that the "holographic" nature of BCFT may extend to the entanglement structure of spin chains, potentially enabling the construction of boundary AdS/CFT models from boundary spin chain systems. This represents a significant advancement in the study of the holographic entanglement entropy of BCFT. Ultimately, this research holds significant value for advancing our understanding of the holographic principle. This line of inquiry is expected to open new avenues for exploring the relationship between spin chains and gravity. Spin chains can serve as the foundation for constructing models that explore the principles of the holographic entanglement entropy paradigm. We present findings from our enhanced channel estimation approach designed for OFDM systems featuring Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS), operating under conditions of a flawed hardware architecture and non-ideal cyclic prefix (CP). In this flawed configuration, the RIS's complex reflection coefficients are set to 0.5 instead of i, and random phase shifts are applied during time discretization. Furthermore, we relax the standard CP assumption of $K \geq L$, where $K$ represents CP length and $L$ denotes the maximum delay spread. To address these challenges, we developed channel estimators based on Extreme Learning Machines (ELM) that achieve superior performance compared to conventional estimators. This is realized by training the ELM network with synthetic data generated from flow graphs, which accurately model the challenges posed by the RIS and reduced CP. Consequently, the proposed method achieves a 2.5-fold improvement in normalized Mean Squared Error (MSE) relative to conventional techniques. Additionally, the network demonstrates robustness to parameter variations, maintaining stability even when the number of RIS elements changes. Finally, the network's weights are observed to remain invariant regardless of the RIS's reflection coefficient. These findings were validated through simulations using MATLAB. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhaleem/OFDM-ChEst-Elm. Keywords: RIS, Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces, Extremal Learning Machines, Extreme Learning Machines, Flawed Hardware, Non-ideal CP.

The Integral Fluctuation Theorem (IFt) serves as a robust validation method for calculating free energy differences via Umbrella Sampling (US) simulations. While prior research has demonstrated that applying the IFt to standard Boltzmann-weighted US simulations requires specific preprocessing to ensure the IFt's validity regarding the system's total entropy production, we show that similar preprocessing is unnecessary when using "single energy assessment" (SEA) simulations. In SEA simulations, the energy of the sampling ensemble is fixed to match that of the system under study, allowing for direct comparison of the two distributions without additional preprocessing. We validate the IFt for both canonical and NPT ensemble settings. Furthermore, we utilize the logarithmic ratio of the two distributions to test the validity of energy barometric equations. This validity confirms the existence of a quasi-potential and enables its estimation; additionally, the associated flux distribution provides insights into the system's dynamics. We show that the mean curvature of the quasi-potential correlates with the ratio of the logarithmic ratio's mean to its standard deviation. This relationship allows for the curvature's estimation without the need for time-series data, offering a non-invasive approach to characterize system properties. Finally, we apply these methods to interpret Umbrella Sampling data regarding the conformational states of the $\alpha$-helical peptide Trp-Cage. Specifically, we observe that the cross-correlation between x and y coordinates in the $\alpha$-helical state is positive, whereas it is negative in the random coil state. These findings align with the interpretation that the Trp-Cage peptide maintains its $\alpha$-helical structure through hydrophobic interactions. Additionally, the analysis of the logarithmic ratio indicates that the center of the sampling distribution is located near the boundary between the helical and random coil states. This positioning explains the limited success of the standard US approach in Trp-Cage simulations, as it suggests that a single umbrella function cannot adequately capture the system's free energy. Consequently, the study underscores the critical importance of selecting an appropriate umbrella function. Finally, we illustrate that the proposed methods can be applied to analyze the transition state of a chemical reaction. The analysis reveals that the transition state is not merely a point on the reaction path but possesses a finite width and depth. These findings highlight the significance of the system's dynamics in determining the shape of the transition state. This work examines the stability of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons within nearly parallel $\mathrm{G}_2$ geometries. By employing deformation theory, we demonstrate that instantons associated with cohomogeneity-one spaces admit a unique deformation class for each deformation parameter. Furthermore, we investigate large deformations and outline the conditions under which the resulting deformed instantons define new geometric structures. Finally, we apply this general theory to analyze the deformation classes of all known $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons in $\mathrm{G}_2$ cohomogeneity-one spaces. Specifically, we identify eight deformation families and determine that none of these instantons remain parallel after deformation. In the context of cohomogeneity-one spaces arising from Lie algebras, we find seven deformation families, comprising abelian and non-abelian cases; however, only the abelian instance possesses a deformation class representing exactly seven distinct parameters. For the $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton derived from an exceptional real-form of $E_6$, we observe that it admits deformation families of both cohomogeneity-one and cohomogeneity-two. Additionally, this instanton exhibits a deformation class containing precisely seven members when the underlying space is nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$. This class is parameterized by nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$-deformations of the Lie algebra and specific non-abelian bi-invariant 3-forms on compact simple Lie groups. We explicitly construct these geometries and corresponding instantons, demonstrating that they induce $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons on various $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifolds. In the final section, we present numerical computations regarding the deformations of the $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton on the $G_2$-Hopf manifold $S^1 \times \mathbb{CP}^3$. Our findings indicate that this manifold's instanton is rigid. However, the numerical data suggests that the $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton on $S^1 \times \mathbb{CP}^2$ deforms into the bi-invariant case on $SU(3)$ across a continuous family of nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ deformations. This implies the existence of deformation families with at least cohomogeneity-one, though computational constraints prevent us from identifying additional cohomogeneity-two families. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic necessitates the use of contact tracing applications to curb the virus's spread. These apps function by establishing a secure channel between users and the app developers, enabling the collection of data that allows users to detect potential infections. However, national implementations often deviate from standard models by having authorities directly access user data, a practice that compromises user privacy and confidentiality. This study evaluates the security of such national apps by modeling the entire system, including the network, as a game-theoretic framework. We introduce an information-theoretic metric to quantify user confidentiality. Our approach relies on two main assumptions: (1) the presence of eavesdroppers who can observe data transmission between users and authorities, and (2) that both user and authority agents act rationally within the system. Our findings indicate that the specific design of the application significantly impacts confidentiality, with certain configurations offering superior protection against eavesdropping. By utilizing mutual information, we can identify the optimal system configuration that maximizes user confidentiality. Ultimately, this research provides a novel method for designing secure national contact tracing applications and establishes a theoretical foundation for assessing their security. Additionally, the game-theoretic model developed here can be extended to other domains, such as blockchain security assessments. This study introduces a quantum-enhanced neural network designed to accelerate data processing for large datasets. The research utilizes quantum circuits characterized by exponential parameter and gate counts regarding data size, employing a quantum model where data is represented as quantum states within variational deep circuits. As an initial exploration of quantum machine learning, these models are intended for comparison against classical neural networks. We outline initial findings from a simulation of quantum data processing, demonstrating that quantum neural networks can accelerate data processing for large datasets. Although these models function as quantum-enhanced systems, they are susceptible to quantum measurement errors. Consequently, while they offer advantages over classical neural networks, further investigation is required to determine their relationship with existing models. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive discussion of the model's characteristics, including an analysis of its complexity and classical simulation costs. This paper introduces a code creator designed to generate proofs alongside code using a shallow embedding of C into ACL2, based on a prior implementation by the authors. Although effective, this approach has notable drawbacks: the C language representation in ACL2 is not fully faithful, proving too permissive for precise type and control-flow analysis, and all function calls are modeled as inlining, resulting in an unmanageably large embedded program. To address these issues, we propose a two-phase architecture for code creation: a writing phase utilizing the embedded C with the described shallow embedding, followed by a refining phase where code is lifted into a domain-specific language that accurately and precisely models the embedded C program using first-class functions and a language that is ACL2-faithful. This domain-specific language effectively balances the requirements for being practically useful for large programs and precise enough to enable meaningful analysis within ACL2. We demonstrate the architecture's feasibility by extending it with two proof generators: one that translates shallow embedding code with control flow annotations into deep embedding code and another that translates well-typed deep embedding code into provably correct C code. These generators facilitate the generation of type and loop invariant proofs for embedded C programs. We illustrate this with various examples, including integer and floating-point arithmetic, bit manipulation, and embedded systems. Ultimately, this approach offers users practical code and rigorous users provably correct implementations, effectively merging practicality with soundness. Finally, we provide an ACL2 specification and proofs validating the correctness of code creators and type and control flow analysis. Our work is supported by two ACL2 libraries available at https://github.com/rggomes/cacl2. We aim to provide users with practical tools and enable readers to independently construct type and loop invariant proofs. We believe this methodology establishes a promising foundation for tool-supported programming and analysis with provably correct extensions. We anticipate these approaches will serve as a viable basis for tool-supported programming and effectively bridge the gap between practicality and soundness. This study investigates the orbital dynamics of the Iochroma group, a collection of asteroids located in the 3:1 mean motion resonance with Jupiter. The group's formation is attributed to IAU object (39911) Iochroma, which is itself trapped in the $\nu_6$ secular resonance. Using the direct variational method, we analyzed the orbital elements of 12 asteroids within the group. Our results demonstrate that all members share common values for perihelion ($\varpi$), node longitude ($\varOmega$), and apsidal angle, with the Iochroma-asteroid correlation being the most statistically significant. These findings confirm that the group's orbital characteristics are a direct consequence of Iochroma's control. Additionally, we observed that the groups' eccentricity and inclination evolutions are primarily governed by Iochroma, though minor contributions from other group members cannot be ruled out. Finally, we examined the stability of the orbital elements, noting that the group's stability is primarily determined by Iochrama's high mass. These results align with previous studies, and the Iochrama group is expected to be the first asteroid group studied using the direct variational method. All calculations were performed using the numerical direct variational method within the n-body framework. The study concludes that the properties of the Iochrama group are not a natural outcome of chaotic dynamics. The authors demonstrate that combining Ramanujan's findings on zeta values at negative even integers with Hurwitz's evaluation of Bernoulli polynomials—which serve as the foundation for Hurwitz zeta values—yields new formulas for the odd zeta values. Furthermore, this approach enables a straightforward derivation of several of Ramanujan's results concerning the odd zeta values. Additionally, the paper examines implications of these findings within octonion algebra. Ramanujan's well-known conjecture regarding the non-rationality of odd zeta values remains unresolved to this day. However, specific progress has been made; for instance, Zudilin recently proved that at least one of the values $\zeta(5), \ldots, \zeta(11)$ is irrational, while Yasaki established the irrationality of $\zeta(13)$ and $\zeta(17)$. Some formulas presented in this work could potentially aid in addressing Ramanujan's problem, although the paper does not claim to solve it. The content is structured as follows: Section 1 introduces foundational concepts and introduces a novel concept of "causal functions" to derive a new series expansion for the Riemann zeta function. Section 2 begins by deriving a new series expansion for the $\gamma$ constant, followed by formulas for Bernoulli polynomials, and concludes by deriving new formulas for the Riemann zeta function. Section 3 explores formulas for octonions, focusing specifically on their causal components. Finally, the authors outline their ongoing research and future directions. Given that this work draws from diverse fields, the paper is intended for readers with a broad interest in mathematics. We provide an explicit, heavily computational determination of the $CP(V)$-based homology within the category of smooth, circle-equivariant spectra. Our approach begins with a heavily virtual construction that becomes genuinely non-virtual following extensive calculations. Representing a significant initial step in our broader project, this work demonstrates that rigorous computations are feasible within the realm of equivariant topological quantum field theories. Furthermore, we achieve this while maintaining a degree of "arithmetic" by adhering to an elliptic cohomology theory. Although our primary focus is on complex projective spaces $CP(V)$, the methods extend naturally to $CP_q(V)$, a extension involving extra $q$-twists in the circle action. By incorporating both circle and $q$-symmetries, we derive $K$-theoretic results for projective spaces and their $q$-extensions. Furthermore, our methodology applies to $GW$-based theories where $GW$ is a circle-equivariant generalized cohomology theory. This broad generalization enables our extensive calculations to remain "bottom line simple," effectively serving as $q$-deformations of standard homology. This strategy is particularly well-suited for elliptic cohomology theories, as their $K$-theoretic homology formulas are inherently simple. Ultimately, this work functions as a $q$-twisted Atiyah-Hirzebruch Spectral Sequence, where the $q$-twist manifests through circle and $K$-theory symmetries. Our findings are presented in a "strong sense" (as actual spectra) and in a "weak sense" (as spectra up to equivalence). In the weak sense, we employ spectral sequences to organize the computations, finding that the elliptic cobordism-based spectral sequence converges to the desired result with remarkable efficiency. In the strong sense, we utilize an explicit model for elliptic cobordism based on elliptic cohomology of classifying spaces. While this approach is less efficient, our computations remain entirely explicit, facilitating a top-down analysis. Additionally, we have recently employed our results to calculate the equivariant elliptic cohomology of projective spaces; this explicitness allows our work to serve as a fully explicit example within equivellarant theory. Our work also offers a novel example of equivariant cobordism theory, with our examples being fully explicit. A brief overview of emerging fields within Algebraic Topology and Machine Learning, along with their applications in Statistical Physics. These topics are explored through three survey articles in this volume, which are arranged here according to a thematic structure rather than the author's original proposal. A time schedule for the symposium is also provided. The first paper presents a general introduction to Machine Learning and its relevance to Topology, including a review of recent advancements in learning topological data analysis. The second paper focuses on learning the fundamental structures of Topology, such as Open Sets, Closed Sets, and Continuity, using Real numbers equipped with standard inequalities as the target task. The third paper examines learning properties inherent to Set Theory, specifically the size of finite sets and whether one set is a subset of another, utilizing data generated by random sets. The fourth paper investigates finite group theory as a learning target, demonstrating how group elements can be represented as neural networks. The final paper offers an in-depth analysis of metric learning applied to random point clouds in Euclidean space, where the underlying metric is unknown. The symposium's scientific program is detailed in the introduction, and the remaining two papers address combinatorial aspects of Topology and explore the connections between Algebraic Topology and Logic. The author extends sincere gratitude to Prof. D. D. Krioukov for his insightful discussions and valuable contributions to the volume. Special thanks are also due to Dr. A. V. Pimenov for his enthusiasm regarding the volume's subject matter. Finally, the author acknowledges the support of the Higher School of Economics' Laboratory for the Development of the Science of Data.

This study numerically investigates the ratios of vector (L=1) and pseudoscalar (L=0) charmonium production in $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \eta_c, \chi_{cJ}$ at $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.6$ GeV, comparing $J/\psi/\chi_{c1, c2, c3}$ production cross sections both individually and in combination with $J/\psi$ angular distributions. Utilizing the effective Hamiltonian for $e^{+}e^{-} \to c\bar{c} + c\bar{c}$, the analysis includes the order $v^2$ (where $v$ represents the $c\bar{c}$ pair velocity in the $\Psi, \chi_{cJ}$ state) alongside the leading order, both at the current order in the nonrelativistic QCD (NRQCD) perturbative expansion. Theoretical predictions for the energy dependence of production cross sections, the $L=1/L=0$ ratio, and the $\sigma(J/\psi, \chi_{c1})/\sigma(J/\psi, \chi_{c2})$ ratio in the $P$-wave $c\bar{c} + \chi_{cJ}$ sector are provided. Additionally, the $P$-wave $J/\psi$ longitudinal ($\sigma_L$) and transverse ($\sigma_T$) cross sections are examined, with the $L=1/L=0$ ratio defined as $\sigma_T/(3\sigma_L + 2\sigma_S)$, where $\sigma_S$ denotes the $J/\psi$ scalar component. The $3\sigma_L/2\sigma_T$ ratio in the $P$-wave $P$-spin $c\bar{c} + \chi_{c2}$ sector is also computed, corresponding to the $3\sigma_S/2\sigma_T$ ratio in the $P$-wave $P$-spin $c\bar{c} + \chi_{c1}$ sector. These newly calculated distributions are evaluated using the $P$-wave $P$-spin $c\bar{c} + \chi_{c1}$ ratio as a benchmark. Finally, the study compares the theoretical $P$-wave $3\sigma_L/(3\sigma_L + 2\sigma_S)$ ratio with experimental angular distribution data

Although the secure messaging application Signal mandates the creation of a personal identification number (PIN) during registration, there is a lack of research into how typical users perceive and understand this requirement. This study investigates ordinary Signal users' perceptions and comprehension of these PINs through a survey administered via the app. The findings reveal that users are generally unenthusiastic about their PINs; they are unaware of the specific security functions it performs and why it matters, frequently misinterpreting its purpose as merely establishing a direct connection with the server. Furthermore, users tend to treat their PINs as ordinary passwords, overlooking that the PIN serves a distinct role in the Signal architecture. These results highlight that users lack both the knowledge and the inclination to grasp the significance of their Signal PINs. To bolster users' understanding of their PINs' security functions, the paper offers several design and research recommendations for Signal's developers. Additionally, it outlines future directions for researchers to explore both the effectiveness of the Signal PIN and the relationship between users' comprehension of their PINs and their knowledge of digital security. This work represents the first of its kind to examine how users perceive Signal PINs. The survey is accessible at https://osf.io/75492/, and the dataset can be found at https://osf.io/55653/. The authors extend their gratitude to the participants who completed the survey and to the Signal team for their assistance in distributing the survey within the app. The paper also offers valuable insights for Signal developers, suggesting that the current design may be overly burdensome for users and that the developers should reconsider the approach to PIN management. The authors hope that, given these valuable results, Signal will take steps to improve its PIN design. The authors also aim to foster a culture of user involvement in security research, encouraging other researchers to engage with users to better understand their perspectives on and attitudes toward their messaging apps. This research underscores the critical need for users to grasp the purpose of their PINs and the consequences of their absence. Ultimately, this study demonstrates the value of understanding the users behind the technology. We look forward to seeing Signal implement changes to its PIN design based on these insights. We also hope this work inspires other researchers to investigate the purpose of their PINs and the impact of not having one. Precise solar energy integration is essential for deriving reliable times of sunrise and sunset, which are numerous (occurring twice daily) and thus require high precision. We introduce an algorithm grounded in Gaussian quadrature, enhanced with adaptive step sizing and polynomial coefficient calculation. This approach, termed Solar-EPG, is applied to the elliptic integrals defining sun elevation. The method's accuracy is validated by comparing its sunset times against the formula provided in the textbook *Astronomy Formulas for Computers*. Our results demonstrate that the precision of solar energy integration is governed by the degree of the Gaussian quadrature employed. Furthermore, we show that increasing the quadrature degree yields earlier sunrise and later sunset, with these effects being most pronounced during the extended periods of daylight near the solstices. Ultimately, our findings indicate that the symmetries and mathematical simplicity of Gaussian quadrature make it ideally suited for computing sunrise and sunset times. These conclusions are supported by plots of sun elevation as a function of time. Ultimately, our method is precise, adaptable, and efficient. Its formulation relies on standard functions and operations, and our implementation is written in portable, well-documented, and easily vectorizable code. Consequently, our approach is robust and can be integrated into programs for scientific computation, navigation, or ephemerides. Finally, our results may prove valuable for astrophysical or cosmological simulations that necessitate accurate tracking of diurnal solar cycles. This paper serves as a supplement to the study by Gonzalez et al. (2019). Our treatment of the problem is more precise, our program executes faster, and our algorithm is more general. Additionally, our conclusions are more comprehensive. Our program is publicly accessible and may be beneficial for those interested in the precise calculation of sunrise and sunset times. We have made our code available on GitHub. (A version of the original abstract was published in arXiv:1903.03020 [astro-ph.SR].) The primary objective of this study is to introduce the structure of the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix, commonly referred to as the D-shur, within the domain of computer graphics and visual effects. This approach is integrated into our broader initiative, ViViT (Vi-sualization through Tensor calculus), which aims to bridge theoretical and applied research. The primary challenge addressed by ViViT is the significant computational expense associated with directly computing and applying the Hessian in large-scale visual effects. By leveraging a variant of the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix, ViViT reduces the complexity of both matrix construction and linear system resolution. This efficiency gain is achieved by utilizing only a subset of second-order derivatives, the specific subset being determined by the size of the random sample used. Consequently, this enables the solution of highly non-linear problems with greater accuracy within a specified time budget. Furthermore, the use of the D-shur structure in ViViT enhances the statistical characterization of the solution, thereby improving the visual quality of 2D and 3D 计算机 graphics. The practical utility of the D-shur structure is demonstrated through its application to the general problem of non-linear least squares, with a specific application to the difficult problem of denoising 3D point clouds. This application was selected to illustrate the impact of curvature access on both solution quality and the visual appearance of rendered 3D models. Ultimately, point cloud denoising serves as an excellent example of how curvature information is essential for visual effects. Ultimately, point cloud denoising exemplifies how crucial curvature data is for achieving high-quality visual effects. To address highly non-linear problems, we propose the generalized D-shur structure, which we demonstrate provides a more accurate and reliable solution within the allocated time budget. To achieve this, we utilize the diminished structure of the generalized D-shur, a method known in theoretical computer science and statistics as "Stochastic Gradient Descent with mini-batches." This technique, which has proven highly effective in machine learning, is now applied to classical computer graphics problems. Our findings indicate that mini-batching yields superior results compared to both standard Gauss-Newton and standard stochastic gradient descent methods. Finally, we show how the variance of the solution can be estimated using the D-shur structure, a capability that directly influences the visual fidelity of the final result. Given these results, point cloud denoising provides a compelling example of why curvature information is vital for visual effects.

Grammatical gender influences how nouns are mentally represented in languages where this categorization is expressed through inflectional endings, such as Spanish, French, and German. Research indicates that gender affects both the categorization of nouns and the development of mental representations, often leading to semantic categorization based on gender despite the lack of inherent meaning in these categories. This study investigates how gender systematically alters neural representations of words in such languages by analyzing embeddings derived from annotated corpora across three specific languages: French, Spanish, and German. The study examines various inflectional annotations, including articles, adjective endings, and suppletive forms like "der Mond" (the moon) versus "die Sonne" (the sun). Results demonstrate a consistent pattern: gender-related neural representations align closely with the inflectional data across all three languages, confirming that gender-related effects are robust and consistent within the same language family. Furthermore, these gender representations demonstrate "zero-shot" transfer to tasks involving animacy and personhood. Finally, the analysis explores the relationship between gender representations and diachronic language change, specifically examining how gender has shifted over time in these languages. The paper concludes by discussing the broader implications of these findings for theories regarding the origins of grammatical gender. (Code and data available at: https://github.com/josh-lee-11/gender-reps)

We provide a novel characterization of locally finite charmers among arithmetic groups, where a group is defined as a charmer if it admits a non-trivial homomorphism to a finite jar. Specifically, we demonstrate that for a group $G$ resulting from a split quasi-split isotropic Kac-Moody overfield $\mathbb{Q}$, the following conditions are equivalent: (i) $G$ is a charmer; (ii) $G$ is locally finite; and (iii) $G$ possesses a finite charm. Furthermore, we establish that any two finite jars of a group within this class share a common multiple. We also examine the case where the base field is a number field $K$ containing a cubic subfield. These findings culminate in a proven conjecture asserting that every finite charmer among such groups possesses a bounded charm; consequently, this class comprises all known finite charmers with order $>1$. Additionally, we present a novel characterization of infinitely finite groups in this context—those groups whose all finite jars are jarred by a bounded multiple—by demonstrating that for the given field constraints, a group is infinitely finite if and only if it is both a charmer and rigidity 1. Finally, we outline several open questions and conjectures regarding the properties of charmers and their applications to the structure of arithmetic groups. Notably, we show that within the class of split quasi-split isotropic Kac-Moody groups over $\mathbb{Q}$, being a charmer, being rigidity 1, and being infinitely finite are mutually equivalent. These results extend to fields containing a number field with a cubic subfield, thereby providing affirmative answers to Conjecture 1.1 and Question 2.2 from our prior work. Our findings rely on newly established lemmas concerning the stability of charmers and their jars under field extensions, which we believe hold independent significance. We anticipate that these results will facilitate progress on several conjectures within this domain. Specifically, our work contributes to advancing the aforementioned conjectures, which are pivotal to resolving the validity of the Langlands program over fields with cubic subfields. Additionally, we provide a counterexample to a conjecture by Linton and Wilson regarding charmers in the class of all finite charmers. Monocular 3D object pose estimation is a difficult computer vision challenge that remains unsolved for class-level zero-shot inference. To address this, we introduce an analytical method capable of deriving zero-shot zero-degree inference for multiple object classes. Our approach leverages an analytical zero-shot solution to map object instances to their zero-degree zero moments, enabling pose inference by detecting these moments. We utilize the on-the-fly training of a moment detector, known as MomentNet, which learns a moment operator zero mapping. This operator facilitates zero-shot class-level inference by using solely a class name and image resolution, while the model can subsequently perform instance-level inference in a few shots by adding a small number of annotated images. Furthermore, we introduce a novel loss function, Zero-shot Object Pose Estimation (ZOP) loss, designed to enable zero-shot class-level inference, allowing the model to learn the zero mapping without annotated poses. Experiments on the CLEVR-Real, COCO-3D, and CoCoCap datasets demonstrate that our method achieves zero-shot class-level inference, surpassing previous zero-shot degree-level approaches and outperforming few-shot object pose inference in both performance and efficiency. The source code and additional details are available at https://github.com/1000x1000/ZeroShotPose. Consequently, this method is free to utilize for zero-shot zero-level inference. The model can also perform zero-shot class-level inference with a single annotated image, and a few-shot instance-level inference with a few annotated images. Notably, zero-shot class-level inference does not require pose annotations, only object locations. By leveraging zero-shot class-level inference, the model can achieve zero-shot object pose estimation without requiring pose annotations. Furthermore, the model can perform class-level inference with a few-shot pose estimation, achieving state-of-the-art few-shot class-level pose inference. Additionally, our method supports pose estimation for multiple object classes simultaneously without requiring class-specific training. The model can also perform pose inference for unseen classes zero-shot, partially seen classes few-shot, and seen classes few-shot. Finally, zero-shot class-level inference can perform zero-degree inference, few-shot class-level few-degree inference, and zero-degree inference. Accurate short-term traffic forecasting is essential for traffic management, planning, and control systems. Current state-of-the-art deep learning models achieve high precision on public datasets like PeMS-BAY by focusing on predicting speeds at a single target link. However, for broader sparse traffic forecasting across multiple links, two significant challenges emerge: (1) the need for cost-effective models with strong generalization capabilities, and (2) the difficulty of simultaneously addressing multiple correlated forecasting tasks. To address these issues, this paper introduces a novel deep learning approach for multi-link short-term traffic forecasting. The method begins by extracting latent traffic features from historical data using a similarity-driven autoencoder, leveraging traffic flow patterns to represent both spatial and temporal dimensions. Subsequently, a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network is employed to predict speeds for all links simultaneously based on these extracted features. Experimental results on the PeMS datasets demonstrate that this proposed method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, an extensive ablation study confirms that the method's effectiveness stems from its ability to jointly predict speed trends for multiple correlated traffic flows. Finally, extensive computational complexity analysis reveals that the proposed approach offers substantial advantages over competitors regarding training and inference times. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhengyaf/SDFE. The findings from this study have been utilized to address a real-world transportation problem in Beijing. We introduce VACA, a new class of variational graph autoencoders designed for learning the effects of graph-scale interventions. While previous graph autoencoders prioritize latent representations for tasks like node classification or graph generation, VACA focuses on capturing the dynamics of inter-node dependencies. Given a directed graph and an observed intervention, such as removing a specific edge, VACA can deduce the unobserved removal of a complementary edge added by a hidden mechanism. We evaluate VACA on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its robust performance across various interventions, including those that contradict the original learning dynamics. Our results indicate that VACA generalizes well to novel mechanisms, achieving comparable performance on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution queries. Furthermore, we provide evidence of the model's efficacy in discovering the latent dynamics of synthetic data generation tasks. We have made VACA accessible on GitHub. The associated results can be replicated using the provided code, which includes additional experiments. Real-time analysis of the sky is essential for monitoring rapid temporal variations in celestial sources. The Irish LOFAR station, operating at a sampling rate of 256 Msamples/s, utilizes the REAL-time Transient Collection (RTC) backend (REALTA) to monitor both the sky and the ionosphere. This system processes data in real time, detecting and flagging events as they occur. It identifies continuous point sources and continuous extended sources by measuring their positions and flux densities at a 2 Hz cadence. Additionally, it detects pulsed sources and variable continuous sources with integration times ranging from 1 to 10 seconds. By examining REALTA results from the Irish LOFAR station, we aim to determine the sensitivity of point source detection relative to RTC configuration parameters and explore potential enhancements to existing detection algorithms. This system offers a valuable method for studying active galactic nuclei (AGN) and other variable sources at low frequencies. Furthermore, monitoring the ionosphere is crucial for understanding its behavior and impacts on radio propagation. We discuss REALTA's capabilities in detecting ionospheric irregularities and how monitoring these features can inform research into their effects on communication systems. Our findings regarding POINT source detection and ionospheric monitoring are presented at the 54th International Astronomical Union General Assembly. (AIP Conference Proceedings, 2021) (Conference Date: 2021-08-01). The presentation lasts 20 minutes. Additional details are available at: https://doi.org/10.1017/S1743921221008837. The RTC system is open-source, and its code is accessible via GitHub at: https://github.com/realta-system. (2021-08-02)

Recent developments in machine learning and artificial intelligence have driven new insights into intricate systems. Concurrently, recent breakthroughs in metaphotonics—a discipline merging the fundamental principles of metaphysics with optics and photonics—have yielded novel findings. This review offers a comprehensive analysis of recent progress in metaphotonic research, detailing the methodology behind defining and designing this emerging field. We outline the foundational concepts, theories, and optical phenomena that enable the creation of metaphotonic structures, exploring the physical origins of these effects and the theoretical basis for their potential future applications. Furthermore, we highlight recent achievements in modeling, designing, fabricating, and experimentally investigating metaphotonics, specifically examining the interplay between topology and defects in two-dimensional systems. We also examine how topological optics has been reinterpreted through a metaphotonic lens, uncovering previously unobserved phenomena. Additionally, we discuss recent efforts to develop intelligent metaphotonic systems for hardware acceleration in machine learning. The review concludes by identifying current challenges and proposing pathways for metaphotonics to reach its full potential. We advocate for a paradigm shift that deeply integrates metaphotonic theory and experimentation with advanced machine learning algorithms to generate new research insights and enable the real-time adaptation of metaphotonic systems to their operational environments. Finally, we suggest that this convergence of metaphotonics and artificial intelligence holds the promise of revolutionizing modern optical research and technology. Topological optics and synthetic physics are expected to remain deeply intertwined with metaphotonics, which serves as its philosophical foundation. To conclude, we outline an agenda for the future development of metaphotonics. The metaphotonics review covers pages 1-14 (14 pages total). Although numerous studies have examined how various factors influence a film's box office success, they often overlook critical pre-release attributes such as genre, director, cast, reviews, and word-of-mouth. This research aims to analyze the impact of these specific pre-release characteristics on a film's gross revenue. To achieve this, the study introduces the Movie Data Collection (MDC) dataset, a newly compiled, comprehensive, and diverse collection of global film information spanning 1997 to 2019. The analysis reveals that movies with positive reviews and starring actors tend to generate higher revenues, whereas negative reviews and special effects films with long runtimes tend to see reduced earnings. Additionally, the study quantifies the significance of these features and ranks them according to their influence on box office performance. The findings indicate that while starring actors positively affect revenue, the presence of other elements like good reviews or special effects does not necessarily guarantee success. Ultimately, this paper offers valuable insights for stakeholders—including producers, distributors, theaters, and investors—enabling more informed investment decisions. Furthermore, the MDC dataset proves highly valuable for researchers studying diverse global film markets. Finally, the study addresses limitations inherent in this type of analysis and suggests avenues for future research. The MDC dataset is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abdullahkaya/Movie-Data-Collection. This study introduces and analyzes a frequency-regulation strategy designed to stabilize voltage dynamics, addressing concerns related to voltage regulation. The methodology is initially demonstrated on simple two-bus models linked by either lossless or lossy transmission lines, with extensions outlined for broader systems. The frequency-regulation technique involves adjusting the phase angle difference between buses, achieved through power flow modifications in the interconnecting line. These alterations are implemented via auxiliary frequency-regulation devices, which function as either constant or constant-frequency sources and sinks of power. The paper derives the frequency-deviation equations, establishes the necessary conditions for stabilizing voltage deviations, and defines optimal power-allocation rules. Finally, applicable conditions are generalized to networks of any size, utilizing lamplighters to metaphorically represent the auxiliary devices.
