Cyber-physical systems are characterized as the synergy between computational, communication, and mathematical principles. Within the context of network science, these systems manifest as Cyber-Physical Networks (CPNs), comprising interlinked physical infrastructure, their associated computing and communication layers, and their underlying communication networks. Although the inherent capabilities of CPNs offer significant advantages, they also introduce substantial security risks and challenges, primarily stemming from the intricate, heterogeneous, and dynamic nature of their components and interactions. This survey aims to highlight the current status and ongoing developments in research regarding CPNs. It begins by examining the heterogeneous and dynamic characteristics of the physical computing and communication components, followed by an analysis of the complex interactions within CPNs. Subsequently, the paper reviews existing methodologies for CPN modeling, which serve as a foundation for subsequent research. Finally, the survey outlines key challenges and potential future directions to advance the study of CPNs. We anticipate that this survey will offer a comprehensive and up-to-date perspective on the topic. Furthermore, by addressing the complex and dynamic nature of CPNs, we seek to inspire new research initiatives focused on intelligent solutions for managing and operating these systems. Specifically, we explore how emerging technologies such as machine learning and graph theory can be leveraged to model, analyze, and enhance CPNs. Finally, we conclude by detailing future research trends and opportunities concerning intelligent CPNs. This forward-looking approach is intended to foster new insights and deepen our understanding of CPNs. Additionally, given their intrinsic connection to the Internet of Things (IoT), we emphasize the need for further research to overcome existing limitations in CPN management and operation. Ultimately, we demonstrate how introducing intelligence to CPNs can significantly bolster their resilience and security. Consequently, this survey provides a vital reference for researchers working on next-generation intelligent CPNs and their applications. Additionally, it acts as a unifying framework for various emerging technologies, including machine learning, graph theory, and CPN-based IoT systems. Ultimately, this work offers a vital reference for researchers engaged in the management and operation of CPNs. Specifically, it addresses the complex and dynamic challenges of these networks and proposes intelligence as a means to improve their management and security robustness. Thus, this survey serves as an essential reference for advancing the intelligent management and security of CPNs. Finally, it bridges the relationship between CPNs and the Internet of Things (IoT), thereby serving as a valuable reference for researchers in both domains. The MAPPIES framework offers a versatile framework for simulating various interaction mechanisms within relativistic jets, with particular utility for analyzing radiation from active galactic nuclei (AGN) and gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). Prior research utilizing MAPPIES investigated how %polarized external-Compton scattering (PCES) in magnetic fields could generate the ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray excesses observed in the spectra of several FRBs. This study extends those findings by examining the impact of a collimated electron beam on UV/soft X-ray emission, employing both linear and circular polarization of the external field. We demonstrate that circular polarization of the external field can achieve higher efficiency in producing UV/soft X-ray emission compared to linear polarization. Furthermore, we illustrate that Monte-Carlo simulations utilizing the MAPPIES framework can successfully replicate the UV/soft X-ray surplus found in FRB spectra, provided the electron beam possesses a power law index of approximately 2.5 and a broad energy distribution. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these results for the creation of polarized emission in FRBs. These outcomes offer valuable insights for understanding the physical processes driving the UV/soft X-ray surplus in AGN spectra. We present and examine a technique for analytically extending square root fields across complex terrains, which includes coalescing regions. This work extends our prior research (arXiv:2009.00670) by generalizing the approach to broader contexts and, where feasible, deriving exact formulas. We explore the implications of employing such extensions in both numerical and symbolic computations. Although our previous study focused on extension relative to altitude, we also address the complex terrain scenario by incorporating singularity separation through the use of exact third-root polynomials. Finally, we demonstrate how to combine these methods to achieve analytical continuation across complex terrains and heights, utilizing a first-order perturbation argument for the latter aspect. This extended framework enhances the algorithm previously introduced in arXiv:2009.00670, which offered only a numerical solution. We validate the method using established benchmarks, specifically the Lorenz attractor and Taylor-Green vortex. The arXiv source code for our MATLAB implementation can be found at https://github.com/sergiorodriguezg/analytic-continuation. Furthermore, this repository also hosts the ArXiv source code for Exact Continuation over Complex Terrains, the previous work on analytical continuation. Access to examples is available at https://github.com/sergiorodriguezg/analytic-continuation/tree/main/examples. Finally, we outline an implementation in Python, developed with assistance from Dr. Jorge Luis Rodriguez. This Python version utilizes numpy for symbolic operations, enabling the algorithm to function as a computer algebra system; details are provided in the accompanying PDF document. We present a straightforward approach for digitally assessing entanglement in arbitrary multipartite symmetric pure states via spectral symmetry. By employing a single mode distribution parameter, we define the Spectral Symmetry Entanglement Monotone (SSEM) to characterize entanglement. Additionally, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions regarding mode distributions to confirm the presence of maximal entanglement in these symmetric pure states. This monotone aligns with existing measures used to quantify maximal entanglement across bipartite and multipartite systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate application examples that illustrate the benefits of our method over traditional analytical entanglement measures, offering a more efficient framework for entanglement detection. These advantages are particularly significant for time-dependent entanglement analysis, where our approach offers substantial advantages by reducing the need for complex analytical expressions. SSEM also facilitates the digital estimation of quantum algorithms dependent on symmetric states, such as the Quantum Phase Estimation algorithm. Additionally, we define a computational model based on second quantization operators applicable to symmetric states, designed to achieve unitary operations with minimal computational complexity. Within this framework, we detail methods for digitally simulating the generation of GHZ and W states, including their respective optimal control pulses. Finally, we validate the practicality of our approach through the digital identification of multipartite entanglement using experimental data from the NIST quantum hardware testbed. These findings have direct relevance to the development of practical quantum sensors. Our results enhance entanglement detection capabilities, offering a general method applicable to multipartite symmetric states that surpasses the sensitivity of previous proposals. This leads to the identification of states with higher NDC, thereby improving the sensitivity of quantum metrology applications that rely on these states. Overall, these outcomes provide a foundation for constructing practical quantum sensors. Additionally, we offer a method for digitally simulating the generation of NDC states using quantum sensors. This work establishes a pathway for simulating the operation of quantum sensors that utilize quantum control, a capability that was previously unavailable. These contributions pave the way for the digital identification of quantum sensors. Keywords: quantum entanglement, quantum sensors, optimal control, digital simulation. Solar and helioseismic observations have confirmed the existence of large-scale meridional circulation (MC) within the Sun's convection zone, a phenomenon where plasma moves upward at the equator and downward near the poles in the convection zone, before sinking below the surface in the radiative zone to form the tachocline. This deep flow is widely considered the primary driver of the global solar differential rotation (DR). While the primary goal of global helioseismic measurements is to quantify the magnitude of MC and DR, recent studies have indicated that the observed rotational pattern is systematically biased by the Sun's surface features, particularly the large-scale meridional circulation cells and active regions. Consequently, a method was introduced to correct these surface effects on the DR. In this study, we apply this correction to the global solar DR, demonstrating that active region movements around the solar equator significantly influence the primary DR pattern derived from helioseismic data. This confirms that the recently proposed correction for active region contamination is essential for determining the true solar differential rotation. Furthermore, we examine how this correction impacts the relationship between MC and DR. Our findings suggest that the speed of MC is not solely determined by the conservation of angular momentum but is also influenced by the three-dimensional structure of convection cells. Additionally, we show that the slope of the DR in the convection zone increases after the correction, whereas the slope in the tachocline remains largely unchanged. Finally, we explore the potential for future improvements in measuring the solar DR. Specifically, we propose that combining methods that correct for surface features with those that do not could yield more accurate rotational patterns. Additionally, using observations from Solar Cycle 24, which features fewer active regions, may facilitate a more precise measurement of the solar differential rotation. In conclusion, this study underscores the necessity of correcting active region surface effects in global helioseismic measurements to accurately determine the Sun's true rotational pattern. Future efforts should aim to minimize the impact of active regions on the observed solar differential rotation. Furthermore, further investigation is required to understand the relationship between MC and DR, as this knowledge is crucial for modeling solar internal dynamics. Ultimately, these findings will enhance our understanding of solar activity and its effects on the heliosphere. This research was conducted using the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) dataset from the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). We investigate the impact of a stochastic background of primordial electromagnetic fields on the accuracy of Pulsar Timing Array experiments, which seek to detect a gravitational wave background from cosmic sources. Our analysis shows that electromagnetic fields can significantly degrade the sensitivity of these arrays within the 1 to 100 nHz frequency range, precisely where gravitational waves are expected and where the search is currently underway. To address this, we introduce a novel method for searching for gravitational wave backgrounds in the presence of electromagnetic noise, utilizing the distinctive quadrupole nature of gravitational wave interactions with pulsar signals. We demonstrate that a future gravitational wave background signal is potentially detectable using four or more pulsars, even when the gravitational wave signal-to-noise ratio is substantially lower than that of the individual noise sources from the pulsars or the galaxy. We also examine the effects of circular and linear polarization of the electromagnetic field and the influence of distance variations between Earth and pulsars caused by a expanding universe. Furthermore, we show that the proposed search method can effectively separate electromagnetic field effects from other noise sources, such as pulsar white noise, inter-arm noise, and arm noise. The increasing availability of multi-view light field (LF) content necessitates highly efficient compression techniques to accommodate the rising demand for high-resolution LFs. This paper presents a solution by leveraging the structural characteristics of LFs alongside knowledge-based models to achieve substantial rate-distortion gains over standard compression methods. Specifically, we propose a new approach that integrates both disparity-aware and colorization models to deliver the first practical compression system capable of compressing pixel-level LF data to target bitrates while maintaining high quality. Our method yields a maximum bit-rate reduction of 60% compared to the practical baseline LF-HEVC, achieving up to 30% to 37% improvement, depending on the LF format. We also examine several practical considerations, such as model inference and post-processing, to ensure feasibility for real-world application. Ultimately, we believe our work offers a promising solution for compressing multi-view LFs by utilizing learnable colorization and disparity-aware models. Current cross-lingual information retrieval (CLIR) methods largely depend on building multilingual vector spaces for vector-based similarity search. Although interactive and non-interactive approaches exist, current state-of-the-art systems predominantly utilize non-interactive frameworks, largely because of the increased costs and complexities associated with implementing interactive ones. This study examines how the limitations of non-interactive frameworks can be mitigated by leveraging the strengths of interactive frameworks. To achieve this, we introduce a hybrid method that integrates both paradigms, enabling users to access the advantages of each. We evaluate our approach on two standard CLIR benchmark datasets, ConverseST and CACM-DE, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Additionally, we conduct a detailed analysis of the model's computational costs, including training time, inference duration, and memory requirements. Our findings indicate that our hybrid method is highly effective for vector-based CLIR, and that interactive components can be made more efficient through knowledge distillation. The code is accessible at: \url{https://github.com/ashish-1999/Hybrid-CLIR}. Furthermore, we have released a dedicated repository for this work: \url{https://github.com/ashish-1999/Hybrid-CLIR}. Interactive versions of the models for vector-based CLIR are also available through our new repository: \url{https://github.com/ashish-1999/Interactive-CLIR}. Our results demonstrate that knowledge distillation can significantly reduce the inference costs of interactive models. We anticipate that our work will inspire further research into the hybrid approach for vector-based CLIR. This study presents and evaluates four small-area estimation techniques—calibration by auxiliary information (CBC), area-level random effects models (MAR), Bayesian random effects models (BRM), and small-neighborhood random effects models (SNR)—against two regression discontinuity methods (RDD and X-RDD) utilizing the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) from Ethiopia. Data from the 2016 Ethiopia Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (CRVS) system served as the source for continuous and discrete outcomes. The performance of these approaches was measured by prediction accuracy (using Mean Squared Error and error by sub-district) and computational efficiency. Results from 2011–2014 DHS data were used to determine optimal bandwidths for RDD and X-RDD, while CBC, MAR, BRM, and SNR were tested with varying neighborhood sizes. While all methods demonstrated high accuracy, they exhibited distinct computational trade-offs. Specifically, RDD and X-RDD yielded the fastest runtimes and superior accuracy for continuous outcomes but the lowest accuracy for discrete ones. Conversely, BRM and SNR offered the best accuracy for continuous outcomes with moderate runtime costs, whereas CBC, MAR, and SNR provided the fastest runtimes with moderate costs for discrete outcomes. Overall, these findings suggest that practitioners in low- and middle-income countries should select an estimation method based on the specific outcome type and available computational resources. Furthermore, this research represents the first application of regression discontinuity techniques to DHS data. The associated R code is open-source and accessible at https://github.com/ajkellner/dhs_methods. Finally, this work serves as a proof-of-concept for integrating DHS and CRVS data to enhance the granularity of estimates from the Demographic and Health Information System (DHIS2). By combining DHS and CRVS data, small-area estimation can be achieved at the sub-district level, delivering timely, high-quality results with minimal computational expense. A detailed description of this methodology is available in Kellner et al. (2020). Future efforts will focus on expanding and refining these methods for integration into DHIS2. As technological advancements accelerate, the proliferation of single-shot decisions is expected to grow, prompting many to seek rational frameworks for addressing them. The most prevalent approach involves Bayesian methods, which offer a unified theory for learning and decision-making under uncertainty. However, within this framework, the reward signal is typically discrete and categorical, which is inadequate for many real-world scenarios where continuous reward spaces are more appropriate. This paper introduces a unified Bayesian learning framework designed to handle continuous reward spaces. Drawing inspiration from physical learning theories, our approach utilizes continuous reward variables as an envelope to constrain decision costs, enabling more efficient choices. We validate this method by applying it to the famous Kelly wagers within a quantum context. Our findings demonstrate that quantum rewards can enhance learning efficiency by reducing the number of trials required to achieve optimal performance. Consequently, our work offers a significant step toward unifying Bayesian learning theory with continuous reward spaces and establishes a foundation for developing quantum machine learning models. Ultimately, our proposed framework represents a crucial initial model for the emerging field of Quantum Decision and Learning Theory. Moore's law is currently constrained by the inability to further miniaturize silicon-based transistors. Consequently, there is a pressing need for novel two-dimensional materials that can serve as channel materials in field-effect transistors capable of functioning at room temperature. To address this, we conducted a systematic investigation of the quasiparticle band structure and stacking-independent excitons in MA$_2$Z$_4$ compounds (where M = Mo, W, Ti; A = Si, Ge; and Z = N, P, As) using a combination of density functional theory, many-body perturbation theory, and the Gor'kov-Coulomb approach. Our results indicate that certain members of this family exhibit both stacking-independent excitons and a two-dimensional band arrangement near the Fermi level, characteristics that are highly promising for room-temperature electronic and optoelectronic applications. Furthermore, the G$_0$W$_0$ method demonstrates superior performance in describing the quasiparticle band arrangement compared to the Hartree-Fock approach. Finally, we calculated the Hall coefficient for MA$_2$Z$_4$ to assess their potential as both electronic and optoelectronic materials. Specifically, the Hall coefficient of monolayer MoGe$_2$P$_4$ remains robust against temperature variations, and its magnitude is comparable to that of graphene. These findings suggest that MA$_2$Z$_4$ compounds are viable candidates for the fabrication of high-precision Hall sensors. To facilitate the rapid development of these materials, we have established a database detailing the quasiparticle band structure and stacking-independent excitons. The rare flavor-changing neutral current transition $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ has been investigated using LHCb data from the LHC. A search for this reaction was conducted using $pp$ collision data collected at center-of-mass energies of $\sqrt{s}=7$ and $8$ TeV, with a combined integrated luminosity of 9 fb$^{-1}$. This represents the first observation of the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ channel at the LHCb experiment, achieved through an excess of events detected above the background in the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ mass spectrum. Additionally, the branching fraction for this process was measured for the first time, yielding ${\mathcal B}(\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-) = (2.8 \pm 0.9 \pm 0.7) \times 10^{-8}$, where the initial uncertainty is statistical and the secondary uncertainty is systematic. This result aligns with Standard Model predictions, and an upper limit on the branching fraction of $\mathcal{O}(10^{-8})$ at the 95% confidence level was established. Furthermore, the differential branching fraction and the forward-backward asymmetry were determined across four Dalitz plot regions, with the forward-backward asymmetry calculated as $A_{\mathrm{FB}} = -0.07 \pm 0.16 \pm 0.01$. These findings are also consistent with Standard Model expectations. No significant deviations from Standard Model predictions were detected. The mass differences between the virtual $\rho$ and $\phi$ mesons account for the observed lower yield and the reduced magnitude of the forward-backward asymmetry in the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ channel compared to the $\Lambda \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ channel. This validates the LHCb technique for studying such rare processes and the reliability of Standard Model predictions for these transitions. We present findings from the first high-resolution simulation of disk formation resulting from the gravitational collapse of a pre-stellar core, utilizing a novel hydrodynamic code. Our analysis examines the characteristics of the material that falls onto the central object, with special emphasis on material accreting within the plane perpendicular to the total angular momentum. Our model predicts the creation of a disk with an outer radius of approximately 100 au, containing a mass of roughly 0.1 solar masses at the time of the simulation's conclusion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the central mass reaches a final accretion rate of about 2×10⁻⁶ solar masses per year, which aligns well with observations of young stellar objects. Finally, we show that the central mass does not achieve hydrostatic equilibrium, implying that the structure formed is a "protoplanetary disk" rather than a "protoplaneatary accretion disk." This conclusion is supported by our demonstration of rapid mass ejection from the outer regions of the disk. These results underscore the necessity of including feedback mechanisms in the simulation of pre-stellar core collapse. Our model offers valuable insights into the origins of protoplanetary disks and their role in the early stages of planet formation. Additionally, we have made our simulation code publicly accessible. This version was developed to address the significant challenges of simulating disk formation from the collapse of a pre-stellar core, and it represents a substantial advancement over the code used in our earlier work. We have incorporated several new features, including the angular momentum transport mechanism, the "switching" technique for gravitational softening, and the numerical method for calculating the local equation of state. We conclude that the latter feature is essential for modeling the collapse of pre-stellar cores. Our earlier code, along with this new version, is available at our project's homepage. Atmospheric models serve as essential instruments for planning observations, analyzing data, and interpreting results. This study assesses various models by comparing them against each other and a recently released, free, online database of high-quality line lists. We examine models from the CLOUDY suite, Cowan, Daley, Saumon, Visscher, and Allende Prieto, utilizing a consistent set of line lists. The results indicate that the Cowan and Daley models are the most up-to-date, followed closely by the Saumon and Visseller models, while the older CLOUDY and Allende Prieto models are the least current. The Cowan and Daley models are recommended for stellar atmospheric simulations due to their recent updates and superior quality. The Saumon and Visscher models, while less ideal for stellar atmospheres, remain valuable for planetary studies. Additionally, the CLOUDY suite, though less accurate for this specific context, is recommended for inclusion in future line lists as it remains a widely used tool in the community. This study addresses the prediction challenge in temporal series data by introducing a multi-period temporal series modeling (MPTS) framework utilizing a Bayesian Variational Inference (VI) task. The primary objective is to develop an efficient algorithm capable of handling high-dimensional, multi-period time series. To achieve this, we first designed the BVI task, which integrates a Bayesian approach into a neural network to estimate posterior distributions for model parameters, thereby accounting for their uncertainty. We subsequently implemented the PBIL-BVI algorithm, utilizing a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) as the neural network component and enhancing its performance through a Periodicity Learning Module (PLM). Finally, we conducted experiments across various datasets, including single-period, multi-period, and irregular temporal series, to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed PBIL-BVI algorithm. The results indicate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/zhengyuan1992/PBIL_BVI. Furthermore, additional details regarding the experiments can be found in our blog post: https://zhengyuan1992.github.io/post/2021-05-10/PBIL_BVI.html. The efficacy of federated learning (FL) relies on the robustness of its aggregation algorithm. We examine the phenomenological implications of a well-motivated, supersymmetric minimal $U(1)_X$ extension incorporating an additional right-handed neutrino field within a low-energy supergravity framework. This approach investigates the parameter space viable for a next-generation future collider. The dark matter candidate is identified as the lightest stable neutral state arising from $U(1)_X$ and $U(1)_Y$ mixtures, specifically a linear combination of the gauginos associated with these gauge groups and the fermionic component of the right-handed neutrino. The neutrino dark matter scenario necessitates lightest neutralino states that are predominantly composed of the neutral component of the right-handed sneutrino. We establish a viable parameter space by analyzing the constraints of electroweak precision observables, dark matter relic density, and neutrino oscillation data. Furthermore, we assess the sensitivity of various experimental channels, including Higgs boson decays, neutralino annihilation mechanisms, and sneutrino scattering processes, to detect this dark matter. Finally, we note that the Higgs boson, being the lightest scalar particle in this scenario, could serve as a potential gateway to uncover new physics beyond the TeV scale. Additionally, we explore the possibility of Higgs portal interactions connecting the hidden sector to the visible sector. The resulting phenomenology is rich and complex, rendering this scenario a compelling candidate for investigation at the LHC and Higgs factories, as well as at future colliders. Specifically, we highlight that Higgs boson decays into dark matter, neutrino scattering, and sneutrino scenarios can be probed at the ILC, CLIC, FCC-ee, CEPC, and CEPC-Higgs, in addition to the HL-LHC. Furthermore, we demonstrate that significant sensitivity can be achieved through Higgs decay channels involving dark matter at the Higgs factory. Finally, we illustrate that Higgs decay into two right-handed neutrinos offers a promising avenue for dark matter detection, with the best reach potentially coming from Higgs decay searches at a 3 TeV muon collider. Our findings indicate that the Higgs decay branching ratio can be as high as 10%, and we have identified a well-motivated parameter space consistent with relic density observations. This region predicts a dark matter-nucleon spin-independent cross section of approximately $10^{-41} cm^2$, which is accessible to future experiments such as DARWIN, SPICE, SABRE, and SIMPLE. This paper investigates an IRS-assisted wireless charging system, aiming to jointly optimize IRS phase shifts and charging station (CS) trajectory for maximal network throughput under user association constraints. Since these two optimization problems are interdependent, we propose a two-stage approach: first, we derive an optimal user association strategy to maximize throughput, which subsequently defines the convex optimization domains for the phase shift and trajectory problems; second, we design a profound unsupervised learning algorithm, grounded in manifold learning theory, to iteratively optimize IRS phase shifts and CS movement. Simulation results confirm that the proposed throughputs optimization scheme achieves significant improvements. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm demonstrates convergence within a reasonable number of iterations. Notably, the computational complexity of the algorithm grows linearly with the number of users and quadratically with the number of base stations, indicating its practical feasibility for large-scale systems. Finally, we analyze the algorithm's convergence, proving that the objective function increases monotonically and providing an upper bound for the number of iterations required for convergence. Consequently, the proposed algorithm offers clear practical value and potential for large-scale deployment. **Index Terms**—Wireless charging, IRS, user association, throughput optimization, manifold learning, convergence.

Overall, this work provides a significantly updated level scheme for $^{186}$Hg, which will facilitate a better understanding of nuclear structure in this region. We demonstrate that the stress-energy tensor and primary fields corresponding to the A3 Toda field theory can be constructed from complete set correlation functions defined on punctured Riemann surfaces. This method relies on applying Beltrami differentials and the Beltrami-Lambert transformation to closed Riemann surfaces, followed by local analysis around punctures. The findings align with the OPE-based formalism. Additionally, we derive Ward identities for the complete set correlation functions and explicitly calculate the monodromy matrices for relevant cases. Finally, we explicitly determine the central charge and conformal weights (for the A3 Toda field theory). Notably, although we do not explicitly construct the underlying vertex operator algebra, the monodromy matrices provide a means to calculate its central charge. This approach yields the central charge $c=2+\frac{2}{3\lambda^2}$ for the A3 Toda field model, consistent with established literature. Consequently, this work not only validates the feasibility of the framework but also lays the groundwork for further investigations into correlation functions of the A3 Toda field model. Additionally, we computed the critical exponent for the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda model on a genus 1 Riemann surface. Specifically, for a Riemann surface $R$ with genus $g=1$, we calculated the critical exponent $\eta$ for a primary function $\phi$ with conformal weight $h$, finding $\eta = 6h(1-h)$. This result matches established literature. The framework developed here is also applicable to other non-Lagrangian conformal field theories, such as those involving exceptional simple Lie algebras. Furthermore, this approach is expected to be valuable in investigating novel statistical field theories. Our methodology has been applied to the A1 Toda field theory, with the resulting correlation functions and critical exponents presented in our companion paper. This work also serves as a preliminary step toward developing a rigorous quantum field theoretical formalism for simple Lie algebra models. In the future, we intend to extend these concepts to higher-genus Riemann surfaces. Finally, this research was conducted in collaboration with A. V. Although quantum key distribution (QKD) holds the promise of ultra-secure communication, its practical implementation has been hindered by high error rates over long distances due to fundamental noise sources. In phase-modulated QKD systems, phase noise in the transmission channel and imprecise local oscillator settings lead to random phase errors, significantly degrading performance. In intensity-modulated QKD systems, the weak signal intensity of transmitted photons is responsible for similar errors. This study introduces a new dual-field QKD framework that effectively mitigates these fundamental noise effects by encoding information into the amplitude (or power) of light fields in two separate channels, rather than relying on phase. Notably, the proposed scheme eliminates the need for phase stabilization, a complex and costly component in existing QKD technologies. Experimental results demonstrate total raw QKD efficiency reaching 100% at signal power levels 20 dB lower than the local-linier-detection limit, and 15 dB lower than the phase-modulated B4-state system's limit. Furthermore, the system achieves a secure key rate of 1.5 Mbps at short distances using uncooled commercial-grade equipment. These findings indicate that the dual-field approach offers superior practical advantages and a pathway to commercialization. The protocol is compatible with current fiber-optic communication infrastructure and can be seamlessly integrated with existing QKD systems. This work opens a new research direction for developing robust, high-rate, and commercial QKD technologies. The detailed data and source code are publicly available. This paper investigates Toeplitz algebras formed by Hilbert space operators with Hartogs-type symbols and Bergman space operators featuring Hartogs-class symbols. We demonstrate that these algebras share essential properties, including their unitality status, equivalence relations, and commutants. Furthermore, we establish that the quotient of the Toeplitz algebra by the C*-algebra generated by the symbol yields a commutative C*-algebra isomorphic to the space of continuous functions defined on a polydisc. Additionally, we examine the non-self-adjoint Toeplitz algebra of symbols belonging to $H^2 \cap L^\infty$ acting on the Hardy space. This specific algebra is shown to be unital, self-generated by its symbols, and its quotient is isomorphic to the space of continuous functions on the unit ball. Finally, we identify the commutant of this algebra as the Toeplitz algebra associated with the Bergman space of symbols on $H^2 \cap H^\infty$. These findings generalize analogous results for the single-variable case found in [9]. Notably, the methodology developed for the single-variable scenario does not extend to this multi-variable context. The work concludes with an exploration of various open questions. Although significant advancements have been made in object detection, existing methods typically require specific objects to be pre-defined within the model. This limitation restricts applications where the set of objects is open and continuously expanding, thereby necessitating frequent re-annotation and re-training. To address this, we aim to develop a system capable of efficiently detecting objects with zero-shot classes while minimizing the costs associated with data collection and annotation. Specifically, we utilize zero-shot class names to automatically generate pseudo bounding-box labels, thereby reducing the reliance on annotated data. Additionally, we introduce a novel auxiliary supervision technique that enhances model training by focusing attention on relevant regions. Experimental results on 62 open-classification detection tasks demonstrate that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our framework successfully enables efficient detection for zero-shot classes within a medical histopathology dataset. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ku2110/OLSDE.

We analyzed the distribution of ionized, atomic, and photodissociation region (PDR) gases surrounding the IRAS 16294-4428A component of the Rho Oph S1 binary system, which is the most massive young stellar object in the Rho Oph S1 cluster. This analysis utilized data from the IRAS 100 micron survey, the VLA survey of the Rho Oph S1 cluster, and 770 micron observations from IRAM. The spatial extent of ionized gas was determined using IRAS 100 micron data, while atomic gas distribution was derived from VLA observations, and PDR gas was identified through IRAM 770 micron data. The spatial patterns of these three gas phases show a strong correlation with the morphology of the HII region around the S1 cluster, indicating that the gas structures surrounding S1 are primarily shaped by the radiation field of the A component. The 770 micron data reveal a PDR gas distribution that is approximately 100 times more abundant than the ionized gas detected at 100 microns. Additionally, the 770 micron data expose a cavity within the PDR gas, which appears to be carved out by the A component's radiation. The volume density of PDR gas is estimated to be 10-100 times lower than that of atomic gas. Finally, the 770 micron data identify a hole within the PDR gas layer, which is situated between the atomic gas and the ionized gas regions. These findings suggest that the ionization fronts are not sharply defined but rather transition gradually through a layer of PDR gas. The relative abundances of these three gas components are likely governed by the intensity of the radiation field. Furthermore, the 770 micron data reveal a cavity within the PDR gas layer, implying that the PDR itself is not a smooth structure but contains internal cavities. These cavities are likely formed by the interaction between the ionizing radiation and the atomic gas. The study concludes that the radiation field is the primary driver of the gas distribution around S1. This study evaluates two distinct factor models, featuring either time-constant or time-varying factor loadings, for predicting mortality rates. The first model, Cascade, was previously introduced by Cai and Kim (2010) and employs time-constant loadings. The second model, FPCA, introduces time-varying loadings derived from functional principal component analysis. Both models are applied to cohort data from the Korean Life Tables (1953–2010) to estimate future mortality rates. Performance is assessed using out-of-sample data from 2011 to 2013. Results indicate that the FPCA model with time-varying loadings yields slightly superior performance in mortality prediction compared to the Cascade model with time-constant loadings. Furthermore, both models outperform the Li–Lee model. Additionally, it is observed that time-constant loadings provide more stable functional representations of cohort mortality patterns than time-varying loadings. The FPCA model with time-constant loadings also outperforms standard cohort functional regression models. Finally, both proposed models are extended to absolute error models for cohort data. While the FPCA model with time-constant factor loadings yields slightly better predictive results than the Cascade model under this extension, the improvements in prediction accuracy and stability regarding functional representations remain comparable to those found in the original models. Overall, this research demonstrates that functional models are highly effective for modeling cohort mortality patterns and predicting future mortality rates. Supplementary materials, including R code and supplementary figures, are available at http://www.kimlab.snu.ac.kr. Within the Computer-Assisted Translation industry, there is increasing interest in developing automated methods to assess transcribers' reliability, given the significant risks associated letting dependability-compromised translators complete jobs. This paper introduces a novel Bayesian approach to evaluate transcridater dependability in CAT contexts. The method utilizes the dependability metric, which integrates both reliability and availability. To estimate this metric, we employ a Bayesian estimator that merges prior metric priors with posterior estimator information derived from human annotators. The study defines the specific parameters for reliability and availability within the CAT setting. Additionally, the approach can accommodate scenarios where only a subset of untranslated segments are annotated. The proposed method offers two primary benefits: first, it allows for the customization of reliability and availability definitions; second, it reduces the annotation workload by requiring notes on only part of a transcriber's untranslated text. Fully connected neural networks, including convolutional architectures, contain numerous redundant parameters that can be pruned without compromising performance. Although sparse models derived from dense networks are typically less interpretable, recent research indicates that sparse "winning ticket" subnetworks can sometimes exhibit higher interpretability. However, this phenomenon is inconsistent, as subnetworks extracted via winner-takes-all methods often display reduced interpretability compared to their dense counterparts, particularly in convolutional networks where most parameters exist within convolutional kernels. These parameters are generally more stable than biases and weight matrices, suggesting that the sparse tickets may capture only irrelevant details rather than the network's core information. To address this, we propose a wicker model that retains the main features of dense networks by gradually trimming biases and weights rather than keeping only the winning tickets. Our results demonstrate that the wicker model achieves superior accuracy, sparsity, and interpretability across both fully connected and convolutional networks. Furthermore, we find that convolutional networks may indeed contain "winning tickets," but a gradual trimming process is necessary to effectively sift out their attributes. This wicker model offers a promising pathway for developing sparse, high-performance networks with enhanced interpretability, which is increasingly recognized as a critical factor for machine learning success. Over recent years, organizations have increasingly adopted distributed models driven by a desire to reduce costs, enhance work-life balance, and boost job satisfaction. While this shift is particularly pronounced in telecommuting employees, it has sparked debate regarding its impact on project success. Although some studies suggest no significant difference in productivity or effectiveness between distributed and co-located teams, others indicate that virtual work can be less efficient and harder to manage. Through a comprehensive multi-method analysis combining survey data, interviews, and an extensive review of existing literature, we identify that certain team and project traits favor a co-located approach, while others make telecommuting a viable alternative. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to empirically investigate the factors influencing the decision to adopt telecommuting within Scrum projects. Additionally, by outlining which team and project traits should be evaluated when choosing a telecommuting model, our research contributes to the broader discussion on distributed work arrangements. This represents a significant advancement over prior research, as it provides empirical evidence to inform the distributed vs. co-located decision, rather than merely offering general advice. This study introduces the adaptive classification of elements by auditing specialists, relying on their subjective evaluations regarding tax return attributes and their relevance to audit risks. To achieve this, tax returns are modeled through formal concepts derived from their characteristics. Subsequently, the significance of these concepts for specific audit functions is quantified using Dempster-Shafer theory. The paper provides a general algorithm for the adaptive classification of tax return attributes by integrating feature-based formal concepts, Dempster-Shafer evidence, and the independence assumptions of taxpayers. Additionally, the results of classifying tax returns are contrasted with statistical data concerning taxpayer heterogeneity. Finally, the algorithm's adaptability is demonstrated through its application to other typology problems. Consequently, this approach facilitates the classification of elements using the insights of experts from various disciplines. Finally, the study discusses the algorithm's limitations and suggests potential avenues for improvement. Based on this analysis, the authors propose that the adaptive classification of tax returns should be utilized to identify the most typical taxpayers, whose profiles can serve as reference models for other taxpayers. Furthermore, the authors suggest that the properties of the audit function classifier should be investigated to determine the optimal number of taxpayers to be selected. The typical nature of typical taxpayers is examined by analyzing the typicalness of taxpayers within tax return clusters. The typical nature of these clusters is assessed based on the typicalness of the taxpayers they represent. The authors argue that the typical nature of these tax return clusters is a significant attribute of the proposed classification algorithm. Finally, the audit function classifier is shown to be optimal under the condition that the typicalness of typical taxpayers is high. Finally, the authors propose that the typicalness of typical taxpayers, as well as the typicalness of tax return clusters, should be incorporated into the algorithm's objective function. The typicalness of typical taxpayers, along with that of tax return clusters, should be included in the algorithm's objective function. Furthermore, the authors suggest that the audit function classifier's objective function, which reflects the typicalness of tax return clusters, should be utilized to identify the most typical taxpayers. The audit function classifier's objective function, which mirrors the typicalness of tax return clusters, should be employed to detect the most typical taxpayers. The optimization of the audit function classifier's objective function, which represents the typicalness of tax return clusters, should serve as the basis for selecting the optimal number of taxpayers to audit. We generate the Strauss process by combining Poisson and Gibbs processes, specifically using "stitching" which involves retaining only those configurations from a Poisson process that satisfy certain conditions. We demonstrate the convergence of this stitching procedure and use it to construct an estimator for the expected number of points. Additionally, we develop estimators for the expected Euclidean distance between two points and the expected total edge length of the Delaunay triangulation. Our approach is non-parametric, relying solely on consistent sampling of configurations, and we illustrate its utility through various examples. Furthermore, we show that, in many cases, our estimates are provably optimal, particularly for scenarios where convergence is guaranteed. Finally, we report findings from several simulations, including some with established point process parameters and others without. In both scenarios, our estimates are highly accurate, often matching the true values. For configurations where convergence is not guaranteed, the expected number of points appears to be significantly overestimated. However, for the other metrics, our estimates remain very close to the true values. Overall, our results indicate that this is a promising method for point process simulation. Additionally, our implementation is available on github. The code is highly adaptable, requiring only modifications to the configuration check function to simulate different Strauss models. This flexibility is supported by a suite of functions for analysis and visualization, which include a `plot` function for easy graphical representation of results. All functions are well-documented, and we have also written a tutorial to assist users in utilizing the implementation. The goal is to enable users to replicate our results and easily adapt them for simulating other Strauss models. Please refer to the documentation for further details. Given that our strategy is non-parametric, it is highly promising for simulations involving high-dimensional data. We are currently exploring this potential and will release a separate paper and implementation dedicated to high-dimensional simulations in the future. However, we note that in these scenarios, estimating the total edge length of the Delaunay triangulation is provably sub-optimal. In conclusion, we propose that this strategy is highly promising for simulation, though some estimates are provably sub-optimal. In the future, we aim to extend this strategy to handle interactions between attributes, a topic we are currently exploring. In this case, points with similar attributes would be more likely to be close to each other, contrary to spatial interactions where points with similar attributes tend to be far apart. Allowing for such interactions would make the simulation framework more versatile and better suited for a wider range of real-world scenarios.

The uncertainty principle, a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics, restricts the simultaneous precision with which conjugate variables can be measured. Generalizing this principle is essential for uncovering new phenomena and advancing our understanding of nature's foundations. In this study, we examine the alteration effect within an harmonic oscillator framework, utilizing a potential derived by Kayesh and Al-Saadi (J. Phys. Soc. Jpn. 80, 034001, 2011) that incorporates both Lorentz and Galilean alterations. This setup allows for an investigation into the uncertainty relation's behavior under these alterations. Our findings indicate that the uncertainty relation undergoes both Lorentz and Galilean transformations, demonstrating duality in its response to L and G alterations. Furthermore, while the ground state uncertainty product for a conventional harmonic oscillator shows dependence on the variation parameter $\alpha$, the generalized version remains independent of $\alpha$. This behavior can be further elucidated through the lens of Noether theorem. Finally, the uncertainty product is analyzed for its response to Lorentz and Galilean transformations, confirming that this duality response persists in the absence of the generalized uncertainty principle. Additionally, the uncertainty product is linked to the commutator between the Hamiltonian and the Galilean boost generator. By employing algebraic methods, the uncertainty product is connected to the commutator between the Hamiltonian and the special conformal transformation generator $B$. This relationship remains consistent with standard quantum mechanics when $\alpha$ approaches zero. Ultimately, the dual response of the uncertainty product to these alterations is interpreted as a consequence of the symmetry between Lorentz and Galilean transformations. The results presented here may serve as a foundation for future research into the uncertainty principle. The dual nature observed in the uncertainty product is also present in the energy spectrum. Keywords: Generalized uncertainty principle, Harmonic oscillator, Lorentz and Galilean alterations, Noether theorem, Special conformal transformation generator. This study addresses school timetabling, specifically focusing on the practical challenge of multitasking classes across multiple schools by overlapping their subjects in time. We enhance a timetabling solver grounded in constraint programming with scheduling capabilities. Our experimental results demonstrate that this solver effectively produces high-quality schedules even for large institutions comprising both K- and Sekundarschulen. Furthermore, we show that utilizing a shared computing cluster to parallelize the search process and implement time-dependent constraint propagation can further substantially improve solution quality. Finally, we propose several strategies for aggregating instances to facilitate machine learning applications. Timetabling is a complex logistical issue that demands efficient algorithms to deliver optimal solutions. While previous research has explored multitasking techniques to reduce the number of times schools are closed simultaneously, we also examine the possibility of multitasking shared time slots. Additionally, we highlight the significant computational resources required by modern timetabling solvers and investigate the application of highly parallel search techniques. We also address the challenge of generating a diverse set of high-quality schedules, offering a simple yet effective method for creating schedule aggregations. Lastly, we discuss how these approaches can be leveraged to develop a machine learning model capable of predicting the potential of a timetable during the search process. The accompanying software provides the timetabling system along with a demonstration of a timetable aggregation procedure. We also offer access to a dataset of real-world school timetabling instances for use with a machine learning platform. To enhance terrain adaptability for legged robots, this paper introduces a flexible footpad design based on a monopod and viscoelastic structure. Utilizing the contact dynamics framework, the model equations are established, and the Poincaré map, which maps the state at the beginning of the flight phase to that at its end, is derived for numerical simulation. The viscoelastic structure, modeled using the Kelvin-Voigt framework, exhibits nonlinear damping force behavior relative to oscillation frequency. Consequently, the robot demonstrates increased sensitivity to footpad deformation even under minor impacts. Theoretically, the energy loss within the footpad serves as the primary mechanism for achieving stable hopping. Numerically, the energy dissipation is significantly greater during the foot-terrain interaction phase compared to the viscoelastic structure itself. Furthermore, the model predicts that the footpad's behavior shifts from single to multi-valued as the compression amplitude increases. This multi-valued characteristic results in multiple stable hopping orbits, thereby boosting sensitivity to initial conditions and reducing the robot's adaptability to sudden impacts. To mitigate this, the damping coefficient of the footpad's viscoelastic structure must be increased. This finding was validated experimentally, where an optimized model with an enhanced damping coefficient demonstrated superior adaptability to terrain undulations. The proposed model and design offer a method to balance stable hopping and terrain adaptability in biologically inspired robots. The methodologies utilized in this study can be extended to other monopod viscoelastic structures. Additionally, the developed modeling and analysis techniques are applicable to various systems, including the bipedal robot introduced in our prior work. Internet of Things (IoT) devices are essential to contemporary society, with their deployment growing rapidly across various sectors, including residential and industrial environments. These devices are frequently deployed in large-scale networks that are difficult to manage and are expected to be resilient and capable of self-healing. One significant challenge in large-scale IoT deployments involves the maintenance and management of firmware, which can be complicated by the need to ensure reliability during the update process. This paper addresses the challenge of upgrading a substantial IoT mesh network consisting of hundreds of nodes. We outline a detailed procedure for planning, executing, and recovering from firmware upgrades, with a specific emphasis on ensuring network resilience. The proposed solution involves the development and implementation of a specialized firmware upgrade tool designed for IoT mesh networks. We conducted a real-world field test of this tool on an IoT mesh network comprising 214 nodes. The experimental results demonstrate that the tool can successfully perform large-scale firmware upgrades with high success rates and minimal service disruption. Additionally, we provide a dependability analysis of the tool, detailing its advantages and limitations. Ultimately, this work offers a practical approach to the planning and execution of large-scale IoT network maintenance. Furthermore, the paper includes a comprehensive comparison of this approach against alternative methods for performing large-scale firmware upgrades on IoT mesh networks. Finally, the firmware upgrade tool is made available to the research community for further evaluation and replication. We demonstrate that the scaling of the Fock space propagator across the many-body localization (MBL) phase transition, as a function of the shift $\delta$, aligns with a multifractal spectrum characteristic of the MBL phase, provided $\delta$ remains below $\delta_c=0.25$. Based on this observation, we introduce a novel scaling hypothesis that enables the precise identification of the MBL-thermal phase transition point, yielding $g^{\rm{shift}}=0.146(1)$, which agrees well with other theoretical estimates. Furthermore, we establish that $\delta_c$ corresponds to the critical point for the breaking of translational invariance, observed through the scaling of the center of mass of the wave function. Finally, we offer potential explanations for the origin of this scaling behavior and its potential connection to the generalized Gibbs ensemble. Additionally, we clarify the relationship between this shift-driven scaling and the traditional MBL phase diagram, specifically regarding the critical disorder strength $W_c$. Together, these findings underscore the intricate nature of the MBL phase and highlight the necessity for further research to uncover its underlying mechanisms. We examine a search scenario where a searcher identifies $k$ hidden targets ($k \ge 2$) on a complete binary tree of height $n$ using budget-limited interactive queries. Each turn, the searcher pays a cost $f(i)$ to execute query $i \in [1, n]$, gaining the count of discovered targets within the resulting subtree. Our primary focus is the average case, where the average number of required turns, $\mathbb{E}[T_k]$, is analyzed. For exponentially distributed costs, building upon a recent result by \cite{DLP}, we consider the scenario where the number of targets $k$ is fixed while the tree height $n$ approaches infinity. Under these conditions and the constraint that the root is never selected, $\mathbb{E}[T_k]$ exhibits a phase transition. When costs are uniform, this transition occurs at $k=2$. However, under exponential costs, the transition happens only in the limit as $k$ approaches infinity. This shift is caused by a change in the asymptotic behavior of $\mathbb{E}[T_k]$ as $n$ tends to infinity for any fixed $k \ge 2$. For the specific case of $k = 2$, we derive an exact formula for $\mathbb{E}[T_2]$ applicable to any $n \ge 1$. This formula reveals that $\mathbb{E}[T_2]$ is bounded above by 3 and below by 2, converging to 3 as $n$ goes to infinity. Additionally, we explore the relationship between $\mathbb{E}[T_k]$ and the search time of a single target, $\mathbb{E}[S_1]$, where $S_1$ denotes the stopping time for locating one target. We further extend our findings to any exponentially distributed cost function. Finally, we outline several open problems arising from these results. Quantum classifiers hold significant promise for machine learning applications, particularly given their potential superior scalability compared to classical counterparts. A critical challenge in any quantum learning framework is determining how classical adversarial examples transfer to the quantum domain. This study addresses that question by investigating the injection of adversarial instances specifically designed to target a quantum classifier. Our research demonstrates that global adversarial instances which successfully deceive quantum classifiers are generally distinct from those that affect their classical equivalents. Furthermore, we establish that the superior adversarial robustness observed in quantum classifiers is not merely an artifact of experimental noise but stems from the inherent characteristics of quantum states. Finally, we highlight that models trained on real quantum hardware demand novel training strategies to effectively leverage quantum properties for resistance against adversarial attacks. These insights hold relevance for emerging quantum machine learning applications, such as security and medical diagnostics. This study examines Steklov eigenvalues across a series of smoothly evolving almost spherical domains. Initial observations indicate that Steklov eigenvalues at every order are monotonically increasing as the domain rounds off, a finding supported by a general result establishing the concavity of map energies relative to arc-length parameterization. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates that for nearly spherical regions, the corresponding Steklov eigenfunctions align with Fourier modes parameterized by angle. This observation is substantiated, both numerically and through asymptotic approximation, by examining the limit of a Steklov problem posed on a sequence of connected annuli. Additionally, an investigation into highly prolate regions reveals that this monotonicity trend does not universally hold in every dimension. Finally, a counterexample is constructed to show that map energy concavity, characterized by arc-length parameterization, fails to ensure the concavity of Steklov eigenvalues when expressed via smooth parameters. Specifically, this counterexample utilizes perturbed tori, thereby challenging the assertion (raised in [1]) that Steklov eigenvalues are concave with respect to volume under smooth parametrizations. Finally, this paper offers counter-examples to the conjecture that map energy concavity implies the existence of minimizers for the isoperimetric problem within the space of parameterizations. This negative outcome is established by constructing a sequence of minimizers whose energy oscillates. The paper concludes with several open questions. Bibliography omitted. [1] D. Buric, B. Compliance management involves monitoring and analyzing system traces to verify if they adhere to business rules, typically expressed as temporal LTL formulas. In trace-based model checking, compliance is evaluated using alignment distances between traces and model transitions. However, aligning two trace segments, defined by infix alignments, becomes computationally infeasible when segments approach infinite lengths due to memory constraints, and existing methods do not scale to handle combinations of finite and infinite sequences. This limitation is particularly problematic in practical scenarios where systems operate continuously, generating semi-infinite traces, and finite traces are collected at specific intervals for compliance analysis. To address this, we propose compliant alignment distances based on postfix alignments between trace segments. We introduce infix/postfix alignment distances that generalize existing LTL alignment distances for pairwise comparisons between finite, single infinite, or mixed sequences. Our method is sound, ensuring that finite alignment distances converge to infix/postfix alignment distances derived from pairwise alignments of infinite sequences. We have implemented this soundness property and demonstrated its application in compliance analysis through experimental evaluation. The code is available at https://github.com/SoftwareEngineeringGroup/compliant-alignments. These results provide the theoretical foundation for processing (semi-)infinite traces, a capability essential for real-world compliance monitoring. Furthermore, our approach enables the design of sliding window mechanisms for analyzing (semi-)infinite traces, a feature currently lacking in compliance management tools. We believe our research will facilitate significant advancements in sliding window mechanisms for (semi-)infinite trace analysis. The paper includes several illustrative examples of compliance analysis utilizing these sliding windows. Additionally, our approach supports modeling uncertainty in observations, a feature necessary for compliance analysis within distributed systems. The work was conducted in collaboration with the Distributed Systems Group at TU Dresden. The resulting (multi)infinity library, which implements our methodology, can serve as a foundation for developing new software tools for sliding window analysis. This library is the outcome of the joint research initiative between the TU Dresden and the RWTH Aachen University's formal and software verification groups. We have also developed a proof-of-concept compliance monitoring tool based on our method, which serves as a proof-of-prime for sliding window analysis. This tool can facilitate the creation of new tools for (multi)window analysis. The paper concludes with a discussion on how to extend compliance monitoring using (multi)window analysis to support uncertainty in observations. These contributions establish a strong foundation for sliding window analysis, thereby fostering significant advancements in the field. This paper introduces a novel deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) architecture designed to model cellular signal propagation. We utilize DCNNs because of their proven effectiveness in other large-scale system simulations, such as data center workloads, which exhibit similar spatial and temporal dependencies. Our approach leverages spatial data, including base station locations and user device distributions, alongside temporal data like time-varying user activity and device mobility. We demonstrate that these networks achieve rapid and accurate signal propagation modeling for both indoor and outdoor environments. Specifically, the network takes as input base station coordinates, user device distributions, device mobility trajectories, temporal user activity, and indoor or outdoor indicators to automatically learn and predict received signal strength (RSS) for every device. We provide evidence that DCNNs outperform traditional propagation models in accuracy and surpass state-of-the-art deep learning models for indoor scenarios, which are limited to only static data and are restricted to indoor settings. Our results indicate that DCNNs reduce simulation time by up to 4 orders of magnitude compared to traditional models and by 2 orders of magnitude compared to static deep learning models, all while maintaining high accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that DCNNs can be easily parallelized for even faster simulation speeds. We also present ablation studies to reveal the internal workings of our model and its sensitivity to various input features. Finally, we show that the DCNN can be trained in batches, enabling large-scale system simulations for training large models. Finally, we demonstrate that DCNNs can be easily trained in batches for large-scale system simulations.

We introduce a new semantics for temporal planning grounded in execution traces, which allows for the rigorous derivation of desirable properties of this semantics and diverse model-checking approaches. Employing an algebraic representation of execution traces within our formalism, we demonstrate that this framework can positively address the strong undecidability of temporal planning by identifying class-specific characteristics and assumptions necessary to ensure decidable decision problems. Furthermore, we establish that temporal planning, when subjected to this new semantics, remains sound and relatively complete with respect to its classical semantics. Finally, we formally validate the sound and complete planning methods proposed in our prior work across this expanded semantics.

Although large-scale power system expansion is a highly intricate challenge, power network expansion models (PYEM) have become essential tools for obtaining strategic insights. However, the computational complexity of these models often restricts their ability to capture all relevant model characteristics. This study examines the trade-offs between model fidelity and the computational resources required, specifically focusing on the size of the integer programming formulation and the time needed for optimization. We analyze how model parameters influence this balance and offer recommendations regarding model discretization. Furthermore, we explore the impact of uncertainty and propose strategies for enhancing model efficiency. The paper concludes with an evaluation of uncertainty sizing methods and an investigation into the benefits of incorporating network topology search. All experiments were conducted using the ES-SMART PYEM, a Python implementation of the ESKMART PYEM, alongside a description of the model itself. Finally, the study outlines potential avenues for future research. We believe this work provides valuable guidance for interpreting model outputs and designing new, efficient PYEM. The accompanying Python code is available on GitHub.

This study examines the global well-posedness of the Vlasov-Fokker-Planck-Volterra (VFV) system within bounded domains, alongside the standard Vlasov-Poisson (VP) system. The VF system models a fluid-particle model featuring memory effects, while the VP system serves as the collisionless limit of VF. We demonstrate that, under appropriate conditions, both systems admit unique global weak solutions. Additionally, we establish the existence of at least one equilibrium solution for the VF system. Finally, regarding the mean field game (MFG) system, which is closely linked to VF, we prove the existence and uniqueness of a weak solution as a triple consisting of a density, a value function, and a control. Furthermore, we show that this weak solution qualifies as a Nash equilibrium. These findings regarding the MFG system represent novel contributions. The proofs rely heavily on memory mechanisms and utilize various functional spaces and their associated properties. We also address alternative conditions for the VP system. The density used as a source term in both systems is derived from the distribution function via the Riesz potential. This work marks the first instance of utilizing memory effects in confined regions, with direct applications extending to the mean field Malliavin calculus. The proof methodology is notably distinct from existing literature. While the density is defined through the distribution function, the distribution function is resolved using a finite element method, and the distribution function itself is approximated by a series of Riesz potentials. The density's definition draws inspiration from spectral geometry, whereas the distribution function relies on the Lax-Milgram theorem. This approach diverges from the Stroock variational method, which typically involves distribution functions defined by Laplace transforms of Riesz potentials and densities derived from distribution functions. The proof strategy is highly adaptable, readily extendable to mean field Malliavin calculus and interacting particle systems with memory. The specific conditions required for the VP system are not optimal, and their optimality remains an open question. We have also outlined conditions under which the VF system possesses equilibria. Accurately positioning concepts within the target domain is essential for ensuring high-quality output. However, determining how to best locate these concepts is often challenging, particularly when they are vague, multifaceted, or abstract. To address this, we introduce STRICT, a novel data retrieval-based method that automatically identifies suitable search terms for concept positioning. STRICT operates by first retrieving examples from training datasets that are relevant to the concept, and then generating effective search terms to locate these examples. We evaluated STRICT using 1,024 concepts from ConceptNet5_ML_2017_01, demonstrating that it increases the precision of search term selection by 16% compared to existing approaches. Furthermore, we expanded its application to data augmentation, revealing an 8% improvement in precision for search term selection when utilizing STRICT-generated augmented data. Colloidal gels, which are weakly aggregated networks of solid particles suspended in a liquid, exhibit both solid-like and fluid-like properties. While recent research has highlighted their potential as tunable materials for applications ranging from food science to targeted drug delivery, controlling the gel strength and the strength of the resulting solid-like state remains a significant challenge. In this study, we demonstrate that applying low-intensity ultrasonic vibrations to a colloidal gel enables precise control over the strength of the gel and its rheo-acoustic characteristics. By inducing vibrations at a single frequency and continuously scanning the amplitude, we can modulate the storage modulus of various gels across three orders of magnitude. This phenomenon is attributed to a competition between vibration-induced melting and structural aging. For several gels, we successfully reverseable control over their strength by alternating between two distinct modes: a strong, non-flowing mode and a weak, flowing mode. This capability to control both colloidal structure and rheo-acoustic behavior may have broad applications in controlled release systems, rheometry, and materials science. Furthermore, this discovery offers a new pathway for developing advanced functional materials. The tunable modes observed in ultrasonically vibrated gels could facilitate the self-assembly of complex structures, such as colloidal crystals, which is a critical step toward creating complex functional materials. Additionally, ultrasonic vibrations may enable the formation of gel structures that are otherwise unattainable, thereby expanding the range of accessible colloidal structures and their associated phase behaviors. Finally, this discovery may advance fundamental research into the dynamics of colloidal gels, particularly regarding the interplay between melting and aging. This study may also pave the way for new technologies, such as ultrasonic rheology, for characterizing complex materials. The ability to control material properties through ultrasonic vibrations may also have applications in medical diagnostics and drug delivery. This article examines the significance of the Collatz Conjecture in both mathematics and computer science. Although its proof remains elusive, the article explores why the conjecture is believed to be true by analyzing computer-generated graphs. Beyond its theoretical importance, special attention is also given to its popular cultural impact. Through examples and illustrations, we aim to make the article engaging for readers by demonstrating the simplicity of the problem, which invites intuitive approaches. Ultimately, we highlight that enjoying the mystery behind unsolved problems is a natural and valuable part of the mathematical experience.

Automated document categorization is a critical component of mathematical knowledge management, serving as the foundation for subsequent tasks like mathematical entity recognition and retrieval. This paper presents an experiment designed to clarify document categorization within STEM fields by utilizing a mathematical entity adjacency graph. We demonstrate that structural information derived from this graph enables category prediction without requiring any training data. The study's results show that a random forest model can accurately identify the majority of documents, effectively resolving ambiguities in categorization, although errors primarily occur when documents share the same source. Overall, this approach offers a promising strategy for addressing the substantial manual effort needed for document categorization in large-scale knowledge management systems for mathematics. Specifically, our method achieves a 96% accuracy rate on arXiv documents, compared to 87% for Lucid and 82% for MathWorks. On the CAIC dataset, the method reaches 94% accuracy, outperforming Lucid's 81% and MathWorks' 76%. Additionally, we introduce a new open-source tool named STEMcat that implements this proposed method. The tool, along with the experimentally obtained source code, is publicly accessible on our project page. This provides a reliable baseline for future research in STEM document categorization. The availability of our tools and the experiment's outcomes is expected to facilitate structural analysis of documents and knowledge management across various sub-domains of mathematics. Specifically, these resources can support efforts to manage the newly launched zbMATH Open initiative, a major effort to provide free online access to the long-established mathematics literature database zbMATH. The structural analysis capabilities offered by STEMcat can enhance the efficiency of this effort. Furthermore, the experiment's outcomes can serve as a reliable baseline for researchers aiming to improve the accuracy of document categorization through structural analysis. By providing a clear understanding of the challenges in STEM document categorization, the experiment also establishes a solid foundation for further research in this area.
