The success of modern research hinges on the ability to choose the most promising ideas, a challenge often referred to as "selectivity." However, the literature lacks comparative studies on the effectiveness of different heuristics used to identify the best candidates. This paper introduces the "Effective Pairing Problem" (EPP), which serves as a model for the selection process conducted during peer reviews of grant applications, paper submissions, and similar contexts. We demonstrate that efficiency improves when agents maintain expertise in multiple similar subdomains and leverage domain similarity to make better selections. Furthermore, we prove that the EPP is NP-hard and present an algorithm capable of finding near-optimal pairings. Additionally, we employ the price of stability to establish upper bounds on the cost incurred by sub-optimal matchings. Our findings indicate that even when only partial information regarding selection is available, the EPP remains solvable. Finally, we present computational results comparing various heuristics for choosing winning pairs. These results reveal that relying solely on local information significantly reduces efficiency, underscoring the necessity of considering the broader context. Ultimately, the EPP offers a robust framework for enhancing the quality of decision-making processes driven by selectivity. To our knowledge, this work represents the first formalization of the grant review process. Beyond its theoretical contributions, EPP solvers can assist researchers by clarifying the impact of the selection phenomenon on the overall system. Furthermore, our framework extends to other domains driven by selectivity, such as hiring, promotions, investments, and funding. We have made the EPP algorithm available on GitHub to facilitate its application in these various settings. By providing a clear understanding of how local and global selection strategies influence outcomes, we aim to foster more transparent and informed decision-making. We believe this approach will assist both individuals and institutions in achieving their goals. Finally, we acknowledge the potential ethical implications of our work, particularly given the sensitivity of the issues it addresses. We have addressed these concerns in our paper by proposing the use of the stability index as an ethical metric. This index quantifies the extent to which a given matching is stable, thereby offering a quantitative basis for ethical considerations in the pairing process. By utilizing such metrics, we can ensure that the algorithms we develop not only optimize for specific objectives but also align with ethical principles. In conclusion, we demonstrate that a combination of theoretical analysis, computational experimentation, and ethical consideration can lead to the development of effective and responsible algorithms for complex decision-making problems. Recent evaluations of automatic summarization metrics, such as Abstracting over Fine-tuned BERT (ABF) and TerB, have demonstrated that their performance is inferior to human judges. However, these methods, including SummEval, rely on traditional information-theoretic concepts like precision and recall. This paper introduces SummScore, a comprehensive scoring metric designed to evaluate summary quality. It shifts the focus from information overlap to summary excellence by assessing a summary's coherence and informativeness through a cross-encoder. SummScore demonstrates a stronger correlation with human ratings than SummEval, significantly improving SummEval's correlation on the CNN/DailyMail dataset while maintaining its correlation on the SAMSum dataset. Additionally, SummScore exhibits strong correlation on the PaperSummary dataset, where existing summary assessment methods fail to do so. The code is accessible at https://github.com/lyu123/SummScore. SummScore can be used for both internal and external summary evaluation. Experimental results indicate that it yields higher scores for human-written summaries and more accurately reflects human preferences. Furthermore, SummScore displays reduced bias toward system-generated summaries compared to SummEval. Finally, SummScore offers the computational efficiency of a test-set-only approach, requiring approximately 10 times less time than SummEval. The paper also details the challenges and limitations of SummScore. Code for calculating SummScore is available at https://github.com/lyu123/SummScore. This work introduces a robust and computationally efficient framework for restoring digital signals based on noisy quadratic measurements. Unlike the standard approach for noisy linear projections, which utilizes Orthogonal Matching Pursuit, our method employs Coherent Pursuit. We present a theory of noise robustness that offers theoretical guarantees for both the reconstruction algorithm and the underlying reconstruction problem. These guarantees are achieved through new inequalities that extend the concepts of restricted isometry and mutual coherence to quadratic data within the regime of low relative noise. Furthermore, our framework supports fast and accurate reconstruction even at high quadratic sparsity levels. Unlike previous methods that rely on non-convex regularizers or large linear sparsity to handle such settings, our solution employs a minimally modified convex regularizer. This work is grounded in a series of experiments designed to test the empirical performance of our theory. The code is accessible at https://github.com/rggarg/coherent-pursuit. In this study, we demonstrate that the dissipative region of compressible turbulence is significantly influenced by large-scale perturbations. Through a systematic turbulence simulation utilizing the pseudo-compressible model, we generate turbulence under various dissipation rates and reflect conditions where large-scale behavior impacts the dissipative range. Our results indicate that compressible turbulence within the dissipative range exhibits greater intensity and energy when amplified by high Weibel instability, and the influence of the instability is more pronounced in the inertial range. Furthermore, turbulence intensity in the dissipative range is more sensitive to initial conditions regarding the instability, while the Kolmogorov scaling index shows less dependence on initial conditions compared to the weibel range. Finally, we observe that large-scale perturbation amplifies the frequency of shock waves in the dissipative range, thereby increasing the intensity of thermal disturbances caused by shock wave oscillations. These findings suggest that the thermal instability mechanism in the dissipative range warrants further investigation. Additionally, we provide quantitative evidence regarding the impact of large-scale instability on dissipative-range turbulence, offering a foundation for exploring the connection between large-scale and small-scale phenomena. This research holds significant implications for understanding the compressible fluid dynamics of the interstellar medium. This study presents a numerical analysis of laser absorption and the spatio-temporal evolution of thermal profiles within liquid media. By addressing assumptions often overlooked, we demonstrate that liquid absorption dynamics are often non-trivial and significantly impact the final thermal distribution. Utilizing a simplified yet robust numerical model, we validate this by examining water absorption across various scenarios. These methodologies are subsequently applied to a definitive case study: a femtosecond laser experiment conducted in the same medium. The resulting time-dependent thermal profiles serve as the foundation for a rigorous explanation of the complex self-diffraction patterns manifesting in the spatio-temporal intensity profile observed at the focal region. This phenomenon offers valuable insights into liquid absorption during ultrafast laser interactions, a critical factor for numerous applications. Furthermore, the model employed is versatile and applicable to a broad spectrum of liquid and non-linear media. We conclude by outlining the potential for further investigations enabled by this approach. Keywords: laser absorption, liquid absorption, thermal profile, self-diffraction, ultrafast laser. Design processes typically involve collaborative dialogue between human designers and computational systems, forming a rich source of data for understanding design cognition. However, extracting design knowledge from this dialogue is challenging due to its unstructured nature and the presence of noise. This paper outlines our conclusions from the I-CAD'21 workshop on Design Process Computing, specifically addressing the challenge of matching design artifacts with dialogue mentions. We demonstrate that natural language-based mining of design dialogues is highly sensitive to data pre-processing choices, such as segmentation and POS tagging, which directly impacts system performance. Furthermore, we highlight the need for a standardized corpus of annotated dialogue data to serve as a common evaluation benchmark for future research in this field. The resources discussed in this paper can be accessed at https://github.com/linguistics-and-ai/nlp-mining-design-dialogues. Additional information regarding the raw data is available at https://github.com/lingoai/dp-cognition. Our code is released under the Apache 2.0 License, and the associated raw data is made available upon request. Our models require no retraining and perform effectively out-of-the-box. We believe that a corpus of annotated dialogue data holds significant value for the fields of natural language processing and design cognition. We look forward to collaborating with dialogue researchers to develop a corpus that accurately captures the unique linguistic characteristics of dialogue and to partnering with computational designers to annotate it. By enabling the creation of a design dialogue corpus, we aim to facilitate the construction of pre-trained models capable of generalizing across various datasets, thereby advancing the study of the cognitive processes underlying dialogue. This could lead to new research areas, such as designing dialogue agents that mimic the dialogical reasoning processes of humans. Our code is released under the Apache 2.0 License. Current state-of-the-art stream processing systems, including Apache Flink, Microsoft StreamSets, and Apache Spark, are primarily designed for bounded stream buffers rather than unbounded data streams. This limitation creates a significant challenge for analysts who require access to both running streams and their historical contexts. To address this, we present H-STREAM, a new system architecture that integrates high-throughput stream processing with cost-effective storage and query capabilities for unlimited data histories. H-STREAM achieves this by directly leveraging existing stream processing infrastructure and high-throughput data serving systems like Apache Parquet and Apache Iceberg. We outline the H-STREAM design and demonstrate its practical application using the H2O platform. Our evaluation indicates that this approach enables efficient processing of unbounded streams and economical storage and querying of multi-year data histories, all while utilizing current stream processing and data serving infrastructure. Additionally, we highlight how H-STREAM facilitates new data analytics workflows and offers a flexible foundation for developing user-facing analytical tools. We anticipate that H-STREAM will provide a foundational design for future analytical tools and data products. H-STREAM is available as an open-source project on GitHub. For more information, visit https://h2o.ai. The authors are members of the H2O Analytics Engineering team.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has become a leading method for translating natural language, yet translating knowledge base (KB) contents presents unique difficulties due to the presence of non-verbal entities like names, numbers, and dates, as well as the specific syntax and semantics required for knowledge base (KB) languages such as SPARQL. This study introduces a duplicate mechanism designed to enhance the translation of SPARQL KB contents by enabling a multi-input, single-output architecture. The mechanism operates in two phases: first, it generates duplicates for duplicated entities within the query content based on entity linkages; second, it constructs a rich KB graph using both the duplicated entities and original entities. We evaluated the approach using SPARQL KB translation tasks, showing that our duplicate mechanism outperforms state-of-the-art single-input models by 7.6 F07 scores. We introduce a straightforward approach to assess and compare scientific papers that bypasses traditional citation and venue-based metrics. This method relies on the co-authorship networks of the paper's authors and their subsequent publication records. Experimental results demonstrate that this technique outperforms conventional metrics in both predicting future citations and identifying field-specific excellence. Furthermore, the method is significantly easier to apply across different research domains. Given the ease of transfer, our approach may encourage scholars to assess their work independently of specific venues and outside the confines of impact factors. To our knowledge, this is the first effort to simultaneously substitute both bibliometric and venue-based metrics. Additionally, we release the Python package `python-absolute-impact` to facilitate the method's usage. The source code, including examples and documentation, can be accessed at https://github.com/marcelo-goncalves/python-absolute-impact. The `python-absolute-impact` package is also available on PyPI, with the license included in the package itself. The data utilized to generate the cited figures is provided in Supplementary Material 1. Our findings are also documented in a preprint available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03309v1. This study examines neural network (NN) validation and robustness against NN-specific uncertainties. We demonstrate that utilizing a polynomial gauge to quantify NN approximation error yields a robustness guarantee concerning a classification model's misclassification rate derived from these uncertainties. Furthermore, we derive a practical lower bound for this lower bound of the misclassification rate, which can be estimated through data augmentation. Our theoretical findings are validated through simulations and experiments within a neural force control context. These results are applied to a force-controlled robotic system engaging in a physical interaction with a soft, deformable object. We show that our robustness guarantee offers safety assurances by establishing limits on the robot's interaction forces and its deviation from a reference trajectory. Additionally, we evaluate existing NN validation techniques and propose two novel approaches. We provide a summary of these methods and demonstrate their validity through various examples. Ultimately, we illustrate that these methods support safe control applications by delivering practical safety guarantees. This involves employing validation tools to assess NN estimation errors, thereby facilitating the design of safety-critical control applications with provable safety guarantees. Specifically, we show that these tools can serve as valuable components in a safety-critical control loop, enhancing safety-critical applications and offering safety guarantees where none previously existed. This is achieved by utilizing validation tools to quantify NN approximation errors and incorporating these estimates into a safety-critical control loop. Grouping is a fundamental capability for computer vision systems, facilitating complex tasks like map generation, place recognition, and 3D reconstruction. While most state-of-the-art grouping techniques are limited to identifying disjoint associations, real-world scenarios often demand the modeling of overlapping relationships. This paper presents a place recognition pipeline that leverages functorial hierarchical grouping to simultaneously extract landmarks, features, and overlaps from images. By employing category theory to define the overall structure of data processing, this approach offers a novel perspective on the field. We demonstrate that category theory serves as an effective framework for analyzing image processing workflows and propose a specific functorial grouping method. Experimental results show that this method performs competitively with recent disjoint grouping algorithms and establishes a new state-of-the-art in place recognition when utilizing overlaps. Furthermore, we find that carefully selecting which overlaps to model can significantly enhance performance. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/SebastianSchaeffler/functorial-grouping. Additionally, we have released a dataset comprising 2 million images of urban scenes from 1,000 cities, featuring annotations for landmarks, features, and overlaps to support research in this area. The dataset can be downloaded from https://github.com/SebastianSchaeffler/LandmarkDataset. Its usage is further detailed in a companion paper, also available at the same repository. Ultimately, this work aims to advance the community's understanding of functorial hierarchical grouping with overlaps, highlighting its potential to generate valuable insights for place recognition research. The proposed methodology is expected to yield significant improvements in place recognition outcomes. The paper concludes by outlining several promising avenues for future research in this domain. Streaming tensor ring methods are increasingly utilized for real-time data processing, yet they struggle with data loss caused by transmission errors in low-bandwidth environments. This study focuses on visual information, demonstrating that streaming tensor ring encoders can still generate reasonable outputs despite local data loss, which allows for restoration. We introduce a patch monitoring-based streaming tensor ring restorer designed to identify regions in the generated data linked to lost encoder inputs and to implement corrective measures. Our approach leverages pattern matching and loss propagation analysis to locate erroneous output patches and input tensor ring elements, subsequently employing an interpolation strategy for restoration. Experimental evaluations on simple geometric shapes confirm the method's effectiveness. Furthermore, comparisons with other state-of-the-art streaming tensor ring restorers, including a patch splicing approach, show that our proposal delivers superior restoration performance. This paper introduces a novel issue, the Iterative Graph Standardization Problem, which presents a constructive approach to graph isomorphism. We demonstrate that if a polynomial-time solution exists for this problem within the linear graph isomorphism domain, then the graph isomorphism domain in general would also possess a polynomial-time solution, effectively resolving the long-standing graph isomorphism problem. Furthermore, we establish connections between this problem in the linear domain and the concept of maximum weight autonomous sets (MAS). Specifically, we derive the maximum weight autonomous set polynomialization (MASP) problem. We provide an algorithm with $O(n^3)$ complexity to determine the existence of MAS in the provided linear graphs. Additionally, we outline the relationship between MASP in two specific graph types and the chromatic number polynomial solution (CPSP). Consequently, we develop a maximum weight autonomous set existence (MASX) algorithm for bipartite graphs with $O(n^3)$ complexity and for perfect matchings in general graphs with $O(n^2)$ complexity. Finally, we prove that solving the MASP problem in the line graph domain in polynomial time would also enable the polynomial-time solution of the Chromatic Number Problem. This would further contribute to solving the P vs NP problem. The study concludes by presenting examples and counter-examples that elucidate the relationships among these domains. These results aim to offer new perspectives and insights into the Chromatic Number Problem and the broader issue of graph isomorphism. The proposed graph domains are characterized by the existence of polynomial-time solutions to specific problems, thereby establishing a new criterion for the P vs NP question. This study investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of a physical model for monolayer graphene, in which electrons experience electrostatic interactions with charge carriers and the substrate. The thermodynamic potentials of this system are calculated using canonical ensemble statistical mechanics. The electric field applied to the system via the transverse direction serves to modify the coupling constant of the electrically interlayer-biased graphene. The results indicate that the physical model exhibits the unique behavior of a fermion within two-dimensional space; however, this fermion demonstrates either bosonic or quantum degenerate characteristics depending on the magnitude of the electric field. Specifically, bosonic behavior is observed at high electric field strengths, whereas quantum degeneracy occurs at low to moderate levels. Furthermore, the thermodynamic potential shows sensitivity to variations in the electric field even at moderate strengths. These findings suggest that applying a transverse electric field offers an additional degree of freedom to tune the thermodynamic properties of electrically interlayer-biased graphene. Consequently, these outcomes may hold significant relevance for applications involving heat management in interlayer-biased graphene devices. Additionally, the electrical modulation of graphene's thermodynamic potential could facilitate new thermoelectric technologies for energy harvesting. Finally, the present model offers a theoretical foundation for interpreting the quantum phase transition observed in interlayer-biased few-layer graphene. To achieve this, further experimental and theoretical investigations into the thermodynamic properties of few-layer graphene are required. In such studies, an applied perpendicular electric field should be utilized to adjust the electric field across the charge layers responsible for electron-electron interactions between layers. Furthermore, heat flow through interlayer-biased few-layer graphene could be characterized by measuring heat flow through the intercalant. For this measurement, heat would be injected into the system through the substrate using localized heating. In both scenarios, the perpendicular application of the electric field would induce changes in the thermodynamic potential, thereby triggering an electric field-induced quantum phase transition in interlayer-biased graphene. To observe this transition, measurements of thermodynamic potential changes should be conducted across a range of applied electric fields. Finally, given the presence of charge-neutral and charge-neutral point layers on opposite sides of the electron-hole bifermion gas, the thermodynamic potential changes resulting from these transitions may exhibit distinct features. Specifically, the thermodynamic potential of the electron-hole bifermion gas is particularly sensitive to variations in the electric field, even at moderate strengths. This finding may facilitate the future control of the thermoelectric properties of interlayer-biased graphene through the application of perpendicular electric fields

We report on our low-frequency observations of the M dwarf system CR Draconis, consisting of two M6.5 stars in a 1.2-day orbit, conducted over 17 years using the LOFAR Low Frequency Array. Our data reveal a significant increase in radio emission from the cooler component (component A) spanning 2018 to 2020, characterized by a flux density of approximately 0.5 mJy at 20 MHz and a minimum in emission around 2021. These fluctuations occur on timescales of days to weeks, with no correlation to the orbital period. The emission is likely of electron-cyclotron maser (ECM) origin, evidenced by its linear polarization (up to 100%) and low degree of circular polarization (around 10%). We propose that CR Draconis serves as an ideal target for studying stellar magnetic fields and ECM emission, as its cool magnetic field regions remain stable over long periods, and its close binary nature allows for the investigation of magnetic field evolution. Furthermore, the strong radio emission from component A, combined with its M6.5 spectral type, suggests that stars with cooler spectral types may be more efficient at generating such emission than previously believed. Future observations of CR Draconis with LOFAR and the Low Frequency Array for Star Formation (LOFAR-LFAS) may uncover new emission events, potentially including the elusive radio emission from the cooler star associated with flares. Additionally, spectral analysis of ECM radiation could provide insights into cool magnetic regions, stellar magnetic fields, and flares. This study underscores the necessity of long-term monitoring of flare stars to capture rare radio events and to study their evolution. We conclude that follow-up observations of CR Draconis using LOFAR and the LFAS are crucial for understanding the magnetic fields and flares of M dwarfs. Neural Radiance Fields (NRFs) have become a premier method for novel view synthesis, capturing scenes from unrestricted camera angles with high fidelity. However, applying NRF-based voxelized virtual character models directly to virtual reality (VR) presents significant performance challenges, as real-time rendering of 360-degree videos is often unattainable on standard GPUs. This study introduces an efficient, real-time VR framework designed for both training and rendering 360 videos using NRFs. Our approach involves converting 360 video frames into spherical patches, which are then voxelized and rendered via voxelized NRFs. To address the high computational demands of rendering 360 videos, we implement a multi-GPU strategy utilizing both CPU and GPU resources. Furthermore, to accommodate dynamic human motion, we integrate an articulated neural body model alongside a hand model focused on specific tasks. The entire system is validated using the Human3.6M dataset for movement capture and the OSU-Hand Gesture Dataset for the hand model. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework generates 360 videos with superior quality, achieving competitive PSNR and SSIM scores compared to state-of-the-art methods while delivering real-time performance on a single GPU and VR-ready output utilizing multiple GPUs. We demonstrate that the link symbols associated with Chern-Simons theory form a representation of the Askey-Wilson algebra. This finding implies that the coefficients of the Chern-Simons link invariants for two specific links, $9_{46}$ and $11_{134}$, satisfy tri-linear relations defined by this algebra. Additionally, we compute the necessary link symbols.

Furthermore, we elucidate the connection between these link symbols and the $6j$-symbols of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ quantum groups. This relationship suggests that the Askey-Wilson algebra also represents the fusion algebra of any of its subalgebras. By leveraging this framework, we are able to derive the Chern-Simons invariants for the two-component links mentioned above.

Finally, we discuss several applications of this result within SU(k) TQFT. Specifically, we establish the linear independence of the set of invariants $\{W_{3k}(L)\}$ for knots $L$ of link type $3k$, and we calculate the values of $W_{9}(L)$ for all knots $L$ possessing $31$ crossings. Additionally, we present the first explicit computation of $W_{15}(L)$ for all knots $L$ with $151$ crossings. We also address the relationship between the link symbols and the Askey-Wilson algebra in both directions.

Finally, we show that the fusion coefficients of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ quantum groups can be expressed as the Wronskian of a set of special functions derived from the Askey-Wilson $4W$ identity. This expression serves as the quantum analogue to the Chern-Simons invariant of the unknot. Finally, we explore the application of this expression in determining the Chern-Simons link invariant for any given link. Specifically, we compute the Chern-Simons invariants for all knots with $14$ and $15$ crossings. This result extends and complements previous findings by D. Bouaziz, A. Belali, and M. B\'echir. We employ cluster Monte Carlo techniques to study the thermodynamics of two-dimensional frustrated trimer antiferromagnets, where three spins interact within a triangle. These methods are well-suited for systems exhibiting strong spatial correlations. Our analysis targets materials characterized by weak interactions between trimer units. The study is applied to relevant physical systems, including S = 1/2 networks of trimer triangles found in CaYb(VO$_4$)$_2$ and CaSc$_2$(PO$_4$)$_2$. Our findings demonstrate that the ratio of inter- to intra-triangular coupling strengths governing the transition from 2D to 3D ordering can be precisely determined from the temperature dependence of the specific heat. Furthermore, we show that these theoretical results align with the experimental observations in CaYb(VO$_4$)$_2$ and CaSc$_2$(PO$_4$)$_2$. Finally, we investigate the impact of strong anisotropic interactions between the triangular units. These interactions can generate a variety of complex phases, ranging from paramagnets to spin-liquid states, as well as multiple types of magnetically ordered states. The phase diagrams for these materials are derived from the calculated thermodynamic properties. Additionally, we examine the phase diagrams for the Hamiltonians that best represent CaYb(VO$_4$)$_2$ and CaSc$_2$(PO$_4$)$_2$. This enables us to estimate the relative positions of phase transitions in the temperature range where we can reliably calculate thermodynamic quantities, and to qualitatively describe the nature of their low-temperature phases. Finally, we discuss the potential to calculate other physical quantities that could provide deeper insights into the nature of the low-temperature phases and the mechanisms driving them. This could be achieved by analyzing the momentum dependence of the dynamic spin structure factor, which we have also begun to calculate. This approach could offer new insights into the origin of spin gaps and the mechanisms behind spin-ice behavior in these materials. Our ultimate goal is to identify the low-temperature phases and the mechanisms that govern them. To achieve this, we plan to conduct more detailed investigations that will go beyond the calculation of thermodynamic properties. This will involve analyzing the eigenstates of the Hamiltonian to determine whether the low-temperature state is a simple product of the trimer ground states or if it represents a more complex spin-liquid state. To accomplish this, we will extend cluster Monte Carlo calculations to the nuclearity limit, which will also allow us to calculate the eigenstates directly.

Although pre-trained language models have advanced significantly, they still fail to consistently match task-specific models in few-shot learning performance. This discrepancy is particularly pronounced among dataset collections that mimic real-world scenarios without requiring model fine-tuning. This study investigates whether meta-fine-tuning on dataset collections can enhance zero-shot performance. We contend that fine-tuning on a single dataset collection is suboptimal due to potential dataset biases. Instead, we demonstrate that a hierarchical approach—meta-fine-tuning on a dataset collection followed by evaluation on downstream zero-shot tasks—is more effective. Furthermore, we present a novel method that enables meta-fine-tuning on multiple dataset collections using a small batch size. Finally, we illustrate that combining model parameter updates with prompt text updates further improves zero-shot performance. Experiments across various NLU tasks confirm that our proposed methods surpass prior art and yield consistent improvements for state-of-the-art models. We introduce a novel technique designed to accurately determine the positions of (sub)millimeter source candidates within the redshifted cosmic microwave background "high-z Sudoku" experiment. This approach yields a root mean square (RMS) error of approximately 0.2 pixels, equivalent to 1.5 arcseconds, for (z;S_N) sources of roughly 10^-9 W m^-2 at 1.4 GHz. The core methodology involves precisely locating sources in a well-understood, low-redshift reference dataset prior to mapping the high-z Sudoku field. By applying this same location algorithm to the resulting maps, we can reliably identify the positions of high-redshift sources. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the technique's accuracy is unaffected by variations in source density, provided the source population adheres to a reasonable model. We also outline how to achieve the potential precision limits, which are dictated by instrumental noise levels. Given that source positions are now known, we show how to generate clean redshift estimates for these candidates and establish a minimum density threshold required to reliably identify robust position candidates. These findings suggest that the method is both robust and effective for identifying (sub)millimeter sources at high redshifts. The code is accessible at https://github.com/kevinmccreight/highz_sudoku. This research is based on work utilized by the Planck Collaboration.

We investigate a novel magnetic order in the 2D Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice, utilizing large-scale quantum Monte Carlo simulations on finite systems ranging from 1000 to 10,000 sites. Our study reveals a hidden ordered phase, which we designate as H-order, that emerges when third neighbors are coupled via either ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic interactions, despite this state representing only weak long-range order. The H-order corresponds to a first-order nematic phase, a category previously unobserved in Heisenberg models. We demonstrate that the magnetic susceptibility of the thermal NIM model exhibits a distinct kink at the transition temperature, a feature that serves as a dynamical indicator for detecting symmetry-breaking transitions within the h-order regime. Furthermore, we show that the dynamical spin structure factor, $S(k_{\pi},\omega)$, is capable of detecting ferromagnetic ferromagnetic (F-F) transitions, a finding that contrasts with static properties which indicate that F-F transitions are weak first-order transitions. Finally, we examine a recently proposed spin-liquid phase on the triangular lattice, demonstrating that the second moment of the dynamical spin structure factor, $\langle S^2 (k_{\pi},\omega) \rangle_{\omega}$, exhibits a pronounced peak at the h-order transition temperature, thereby distinguishing this phase from others. These findings underscore the critical role of dynamic signatures in elucidating the phase diagram of frustrated magnetic systems. We investigate a SU(3) gauge-Higgs theory restricted to a U(2) subgroup by analyzing the behavior of U(2)-even and U(2)-odd Wilson loops across temperature and coupling variations. This system exhibits a restriction-derestriction transition, where the system is either confined strictly to the U(2) subgroup (derestricted) or allowed to explore other gauge configurations (unrestricted). Unrestricted configurations are favored by higher temperatures and gauge couplings. Our findings indicate that this transition aligns with first-order phase transitions at all studied coupling values within the examined temperature range. Notably, specific critical points at higher temperatures demonstrate signs of signal overlap between the U(2) and unbroken SU(3) ensembles, which may impose constraints on the systems under investigation. Furthermore, we observe that U(2)-even and U(2)-odd Wilson loop correlations serve as an effective tool for studying this transition. Finally, we discuss the connection between this mechanism and the deconfinement transition in QCD. These results provide a foundational understanding of phase transitions in Higgs theories featuring extended gauge groups, a topic relevant to physics beyond the Standard Model. This serves as a preliminary step toward investigating U(1) even and odd observables in the Higgs sector of the SO(10) Grand Unified Theory, which supersedes the Standard Model. Such research is currently being pursued in collaboration with the group of C. David Carone at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. Carone has previously proposed that the U(1) deconfinement transition within the SO(10) Higgs sector is a first-order transition, contingent on the specific direction of the Higgs vacuum expectation value. This hypothesis is supported by our observed signal overlap at U(1) critical points, which we demonstrate in this study. Additionally, our findings regarding U(1) deconfinement are consistent with our earlier work. These results suggest that our methodology can be utilized to explore physics beyond the Standard Model. Specifically, we conclude that extended gauge groups, including the SO(10) Grand Unified theory, are viable candidates for future investigation. This is evidenced by the successful description of phase transitions in the Higgs sector of these extended models using only partial data from restricted Wilson loop observables. To fully characterize the phase transition in the SO(10) Higgs sector, our analysis will need to be expanded to include other relevant Wilson loop variables. Antiferromagnets are crucial for both fundamental research and technological applications, particularly in spintronics, where the interaction between spins and electric currents generates a voltage known as spin polarization. The magnitude of this voltage is directly linked to the temperature at which antiferromagnetic ordering begins, as indicated by specific heat anomalies. However, the relationship between this critical temperature and the magnitude of spin polarization remains unclear. In this study, we investigate the Cr$_2$Al compound, a recently discovered antiferromagnet with a transition temperature of approximately 200 K, using a combination of first-principles calculations and neutron diffraction experiments. Our results reveal an in-plane triangular antiferromagnetic structure characterized by strong exchange interactions between chromium atoms. The exchange interactions derived from our first-principles findings align well with the experimental data, while the agreement between simulated and observed neutron diffraction patterns confirms a first-order magnetic transition. These outcomes demonstrate that the network of exchange interactions, rather than just the transition temperature, plays a pivotal role in determining the properties of antiferromagnets. Furthermore, the strength of these interactions suggests a significant exchange coupling between spin currents and polarization in Cr$_2$Al. This study examines a kinetic equation formulated with a velocity-dependent collision frequency designed to mimic quantum kinetic models that include backscattering. For hard sphere potentials, the collision frequency scales with velocity as $v^{-\frac{2\alpha}{3}}$ (where $\alpha=1$ represents the quantum regime and $\alpha=0$ the classical one), a dependence that is "weak" near zero compared to velocity-independent models. We establish the uniqueness of weak solutions and derive entropy properties for these equations. Through the formal limit of zero Knudsen number, we demonstrate that the equilibrium state is no longer the Maxwellian but is instead governed by the collision frequency, representing a new generalized thermodynamic equilibrium. In the strong kinetic regime, the solution approaches the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, whereas in the slip regime, it yields a new generalized Stokes' equation dependent on the collision frequency. Finally, numerical simulations are conducted to validate the theoretical findings. The introduced velocity-dependent collision frequency enables the model to capture rarefied gas flow characteristics that go beyond the limitations of the velocity-independent Navier-Stokes-Fourier system. Furthermore, the existence and uniqueness of solutions are rigorously proven. To the best of our knowledge, this marks the first instance where a collision frequency lower than Maxwell's (proportional to $v^{-2/3}$) is rigorously applied to the Boltzmann equation. The $\alpha$ parameter in the collision frequency can be extended to other values, allowing the model to address more complex molecular interactions. Ultimately, the velocity-dependent collision frequency represents a valuable alternative to the traditional Maxwellian closure, which is often difficult to justify for general rarefied gas flows. Future research will focus on proving the convergence of the kinetic solutions toward the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. Additionally, this collision frequency model is applied to simulate various rarefied gas flows, including plane Poiseuille flow, channel flow, and flow around obstacles, with results compared against other collision frequency models and experimental data. These analyses confirm that the collision frequency model is highly effective for rarefied gas flows. The availability of an analytical solution in the slip regime further enables the examination of the relationship among slip coefficients, the collision frequency parameter, and the Knudsen number. Ultimately, the collision frequency model is shown to be an ideal approach for simulating rarefied gas flows. The findings regarding slip coefficients are also presented. Semantic Analyzers (SAs) are large-scale neural language models capable of extracting implicit semantic knowledge from extensive text databases. While SAs demonstrate strong performance in various downstream tasks—many of which do not require labeled data by leveraging implicit knowledge encoded during pre-training—they also pose significant challenges. First, their dependence on massive datasets for training results in prohibitively high computational costs. Second, their outputs often appear unintuitive to humans, which can hinder the development of effective downstream applications, particularly when researchers attempt to create labeling guidelines based solely on SA results. This study aims to address these challenges through targeted modifications to existing training protocols for SAs. Specifically, we propose (1) utilizing minimal training data to reduce the requirements for training set size, and (2) incorporating human-friendly examples to enhance interpretability for researchers. Extensive experiments conducted across eight datasets yield the following key findings: (a) the familiarized training framework for SAs is both feasible and effective, and (b) the approach is highly robust across diverse domains. The complete code is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/taehyunglee/FAMSA}. This work represents an initial step toward familiarizing Semantic Analyzers. Future investigations into advanced familiarization techniques will be necessary to further improve human researchers' ability to utilize these models. The forthcoming Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) aims to investigate the internal structure and dynamics of nucleons and nuclei, offering a comprehensive view of non-perturbive strong interaction physics. The proposed ELISe experiment will analyze the EIC's primary electron beam using a sophisticated spectrometer featuring novel silicon tracking sensors. These sensors are chosen for their superior spatial resolution and fast readout capabilities, allowing for precise vertexing of electron interactions with hadrons or nuclei. This selection underscores silicon as the optimal material for vertex detectors in particle physics. We outline the specific technical advancements required for the ELISe silicon tracking detectors, detailing the engineering challenges involved in producing them and the necessary solutions. Furthermore, we present simulation results regarding the performance of these advanced silicon sensors for ELISe and discuss their broader applicability to future high-energy physics initiatives. This work is based on a collaboration between the Institute of Nuclear Physics Polish Academy of Sciences (IFJ PAN), Helmholtz-Institut Niels Bohr Institutet (HINI), and Vienna University of Technology (TUW). IFJ PAN and HINI possess extensive experience in silicon detector R&D, manufacturing, and readout systems, having contributed to experiments at the LHC, ILC, PEP-II, and PEP-II. TUW has demonstrated world-class expertise in silicon sensor design, fabrication, and testing. Together, these institutions have a proven track record in developing and deploying advanced silicon tracking detectors for major particle physics experiments. In 2012, the optical light curves of the low-luminosity active galactic nucleus (AGN) NGC 4395 exhibited a significant fluctuation, with the source's brightness varying by approximately a factor of 2.5 over 100 days. This study employs a diffusion model, a standard framework for describing fluctuations in accreting systems, to analyze these variations. We demonstrate that the data can be accommodated by a single-model fit that aligns with established models for both oscillatory and outburst-like systems. Consequently, the physical origin of the observed fluctuation remains ambiguous. The primary objective of this work is to elucidate the underlying mechanism responsible for fluctuation in low-luminosity AGNs. Furthermore, the multi-day timescale of the variations suggests that the broad-line region (BLR) in NGC 4395 is relatively compact, implying that the AGN's black hole mass is likely below 10^7 solar masses. This finding corroborates the correlation between black hole mass and AGN fluctuations. Ultimately, the fluctuation in NGC 4395 serves as a valuable case study for investigating fluctuations in low-luminosity AGNs. Additionally, we briefly discuss potential future applications of the diffusion model. Given that the model's parameters are independent of the fluctuation type, future research could leverage the model's parameters to investigate the nature of fluctuations in AGNs. Such analysis could aid in elucidating the nature of BLRs and the fluctuations arising from the BLR. This study presents spectropolarimetric observations of HD 58260's magnetic field, conducted using high-resolution spectra of Fe I lines from a hydrogen-arc discharge. The magnetic field is characterized via the Zeeman effect analysis of the radiative transfer in these lines under non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) conditions. The results indicate that the magnetic field is primarily radial, with its magnitude decreasing as distance from the surface of HD 58260 increases. This trend is supported by the observed polarization spectra of the Fe I lines, which show that the magnetic field is stronger near the surface compared to the outer layers. These findings align with the star's classification as a rapidly rotating, low-luminosity magnetic star. The research involved a collaboration between the P. Curie University and the P. L. Kapitza Institute of Applied Physics. Additionally, the paper includes the full data analysis code for Zeeman analysis of radiative transfer in stellar atmospheres at non-local thermodynamic equilibrium. Keywords: magnetic fields, stars.

This paper establishes the inversion of the generalized Laplace operator, known as the Dunkl Laplacian, within one dimension. It derives formulas expressing the Laplace and Beltrami operators under the Bonsall metric on hyperbolic space as integral operators, utilizing the Dunkl intertwining operator. Furthermore, these results are applied to analyze certain integral transforms linked to the Hankel transform. The discussion also highlights specific integral identities involving Bessel functions and their generalizations. Additionally, certain integral transforms and functions related to the generalized error function are investigated, alongside an exploration of their potential significance in mathematical physics. The study presents self-duality properties of the Fourier-Dunkl transform relative to the Bonnal group, along with inversion theorems and various integral identities for the Dunkl transform. Finally, the authors address the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the generalized heat equation under the Bonsall metric through the application of the Dunkl transform and Hankel transforms of order $-1/2$. The analysis also covers the solution to the generalized wave equation relative to the same metric, specifically for point sources represented by Dirac measures, by employing the intertwining operator alongside the Bessel transform of order $1/2$. The analysis concludes with an investigation into two generalized fractional integrals, which are utilized to develop a generalized Riemann-Liouville integral paired with a generalized Hankel transform of order $\alpha > -1/2$. This specific case is further developed in a subsequent paper. The authors acknowledge Dr. Bonnal for providing the metric on $\mathbb{H}^n$ and Dr. Gordon for valuable discussions. Additionally, the interplay between Hankel transforms and the Riemann-Liouville integral is explored in a separate publication. Finally, the authors extend gratitude to Dr. Stein for his insightful comments regarding Hankel transforms and fractional integrals. This work was partially funded by a grant from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada. Some findings were presented at the conference "Harmonic Analysis and its Applications" held in Cluj-Napoca, Romania, in July 2004.

The galaxy NGC 5253 is renowned for its compact starburst nucleus, characterized by a low metallicity of approximately $Z \sim 0.2$~$Z_\odot$ and a compact star formation region roughly 100 pc in diameter. This study presents ALMA observations of the H30$\alpha$ recombination line, alongside 1.3 mm and 8.6 $\mu$m dust continuum data, which reveal a complex network of filamentary structures within the star-forming area. We conducted a detailed analysis of the H30$\alpha$ emission, deriving the total luminosity ($L_{H30\alpha}$) and rest-frame velocity dispersion ($\sigma_{H30\alpha}$) for the galaxy. By comparing these values with 1.3 mm dust continuum observations, we identified the spatial distribution of HII regions. Furthermore, we calculated the star formation rate (SFR) using both H30$\alpha$ and 8.6 $\mu$m data, comparing the results with the SFR derived from the total luminosity of the galaxy. Finally, we examined the relationship between the dust mass ($M_{dust}$) and the gas mass ($M_{H}$) within the star-forming region. Our findings indicate that the HII region distribution aligns with the compact star formation region seen in optical and H$\alpha$ images, confirming NGC 5253 as a compact starburst. Additionally, the SFRs derived from H30$\alpha$ and IR8.6$\mu$m are consistent with the SFR obtained from the H30$\alpha$-based measure, demonstrating that this recombination line serves as an effective tool for studying star formation in the galaxy. The $M_{dust}/M_{H}$ ratio in NGC 5253 is notably lower than in the Milky Way, suggesting that dust is not a primary component of the interstellar medium in this compact starburst. These results suggest that the star formation process in NGC 5253 differs from that in the Milky Way, where dust plays a significant role. Overall, this research underscores the necessity of incorporating recombination lines into future studies of star formation. More broadly, for any ergodic $\mathbb{Z}^n$-action $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu)$ where $n \ge 2$, the only continuous orbit equivalences are the trivial ones; consequently, no non-trivial continuous orbit equivalences exist between such actions. This paper presents a straightforward yet flexible framework for assessing Conditional Expectation Functions (CEFs) within both parametric and nonparametric contexts. By treating the CEF as a conditional mean of a dummy variable whose expected value shifts with the explanatory variable of interest under different regimes, we demonstrate that regressing this dummy on the explanatory variable yields an accurate estimate of the CEF's first derivative when properly weighted. This technique accommodates either a continuous or discrete regressive variable. For continuous variables, we show that a regression-discontinuity design utilizing this approach achieves a minimax pointwise convergence rate of $n^{-1/3}(\log n)^{1/3}$ under bandwidth weighting, assuming histogram kernel estimates for both the CEF and its derivative. For regression discontinuity designs involving a discontinuous CEF, we extend a recent method by Kline (2013) to estimate the CEF derivative via local regression and apply this to the CEF itself. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the estimator remains asymptotically normal and derive its asymptotic variance to enable hypothesis testing. Regarding continuous variables, we show that locally estimating the dummy variable's mean and variance—without requiring them to be independent of the explanatory variable—enhances estimation accuracy. Although the analysis focuses on dummy variables, we also briefly address estimators based on continuous variables. Finally, we apply this methodology to re-examine the impact of family size on child labor. Simulations indicate that our estimator outperforms both local polynomial and kernel estimators of the CEF. Additionally, a Monte Carlo study of the discontinuous design confirms that our proposed estimator achieves optimal pointwise convergence rates. To address bandwidth selection, we also introduce a straightforward cross-validation criterion. To achieve these findings, we developed new software, which is made available. Finally, we discuss extensions to multivariate settings and higher-dimensional CEFs. The epidemic trajectory of the coronavirus (COVID-19) represents a intricate and dynamic system. To manage this process effectively, one must analyze it based on specific components while anticipating future developments. This article presents a developed observer algorithm designed to model the dynamic elements of epidemic progression, similar to the models applied to the coronavirus. The core concept relies on an observer-based approach; its efficiency is demonstrated through two case studies: one applying the algorithm to a simple sinusoidal function and another regarding the coronavirus. These examples illustrate that the proposed observer framework can be utilized to assess dynamic system properties, specifically to predict the evolution of the coronavirus. Additionally, the study examines the stability and invariance of the observer under various conditions, noting that these factors are essential for the state estimator's practical implementation. The paper concludes with a discussion on these aspects.

Ultrashort pulse lasers are essential for numerous applications, and high-peak-power oscillators utilizing Kerr-lens mode-locking are widely regarded as the premier solution. However, the underlying principles of this technique are not always clearly understood. This work investigates the fundamental characteristics of Kerr-lens mode-locking by analyzing its geometric properties and examining key features through numerical simulations of propagation within the cavity. These findings provide a solid basis for developing fast optical simulations and for designing new ultrafast laser architectures. Additionally, by examining propagation with and without Kerr-lens mode-locking, we explore the transition from self-starting to non-self-starting mode-locking. This explanation clarifies why shorter pump pulses and higher absorption coefficients favor the self-starting regime, while longer pump pulses and lower absorption factors make it more challenging. Furthermore, the study investigates the impact of intracavity optical components on Kerr-lens mode-locking and examines how alterations to these elements affect stable pulse parameters and the transition to non-self-starting behavior. Finally, the influence of active Kerr-lens mode-locking is examined, and a method for actively initiating Kerr-lens mode-locking is presented. The rapid design of ultrafast oscillators based on these geometric properties is expected to become a standard approach in the field. Additionally, incorporating active Kerr-lens mode-locking is anticipated to enable higher peak power and superior stability. Ultimately, the principles of Kerr-lens mode-locking can be extended to other applications utilizing similar techniques. Specifically, understanding this phenomenon is highly beneficial for the design of ultrafast fiber lasers and high-peak-power amplifiers. Furthermore, as free-space optical communication increasingly relies on high-peak-power lasers, interpreting the geometric properties of these systems is expected to aid in the development of more efficient free-space communication technologies. Finally, examining the geometric properties of Kerr-lens mode-locking can enhance the understanding of other techniques that rely on similar mechanisms. For instance, fiber Bragg grating mode-locking exhibits behavior analogous to active Kerr-lens mode-locking, and the general properties of this technique can be elucidated by first understanding the geometric properties of Kerr-lens mode-locking. Additionally, the geometric properties of Kerr-lens mode-locking are highly relevant to the field of ultrafast chemistry, where this technique is considered one of the most promising tools for driving chemical reactions. The ultrafast time resolution and high peak power achievable through Kerr-lens mode-locking are expected to enable the study of chemical reactions with unprecedented detail. Online federated learning (FL) utilizes distributed devices to iteratively and sequentially train machine learning models, making it particularly suitable for resource-constrained environments where batch sizes are small and communication bandwidth is limited. This paper introduces a resource-conscious asynchronous online federated learning framework designed to train nonlinear regression models for time series data. The scheme handles time-series regression requests from distributed clients while accounting for device heterogeneity in terms of computation speed, battery capacity, and communication bandwidth. Clients collaboratively train a global nonlinear regression model by exchanging predictions with the server, a process that involves the server transmitting optimization signals to selected clients and updating the model based feedback. Clients may perform multiple local updates before communicating with the server, a strategy that can be adapted to individual resource constraints. We employ a weighted average for model aggregation, assigning weights proportional to the number of local updates, and prove the scheme's convergence under specific assumptions. Furthermore, we demonstrate through experiments that this approach outperforms both traditional online learning and naive online federated learning methods. The code is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/ashokkumar2000/Ra-FL}. Additionally, we provide a Python package implementing the proposed solution, which will be released on PyPI. We anticipate that this package will serve as a foundational resource for future research on resource-aware online federated learning. Interested researchers are encouraged to visit our project website at \url{https://v4000.github.io/Ra-FL/}. The system is also available on Google Play. Ultimately, we aim for resource-aware online federated learning to become a standard solution for resource-constrained distributed devices, thereby enhancing privacy, security, and efficiency in resource-limited settings. Our research group is actively seeking candidates with a background in machine learning, distributed systems, or online learning to join us. This study investigates thin silicon membranes as potential light absorbers for photovoltaic devices, employing a three-dimensional photonic band gap crystal served as a back reflector to enhance light absorption. The thickness of the silicon membrane was systematically varied from 1.5 micrometers down to that of a single atomic layer. The research details the fabrication processes for silicon membranes, 3D photonic band gap crystals, and the final composite structures. Reflectors were constructed using silicon membranes with thicknesses of 1.5, 0.75, 0.2, and one atomic layer. Reflectance measurements were conducted across the visible to near-infrared spectrum (400–1100 nm). The findings indicate that the single-atom-layer silicon membrane functions as an efficient reflector within its band gap. Furthermore, by incorporating a 3D photonic band gap crystal as a rear reflector, the absorption of a 1.5 micrometer silicon membrane reaches 100% across the entire visible to near-infrared range. Additionally, the single-atom-layer silicon membrane effectively reflects light within its photonic band gap, thereby boosting the overall reflectance of the 3D photonic band gap crystal. Recent developments in Riemannian geometry have yielded new examples of Ricci-flat graphs with a high Cheeger constant, a property where high expansion is typically incompatible with the absence of Ricci curvature. This paper introduces a family of graphs $G_{n, k}$ constructed through a cover-based approach, where we demonstrate the existence of a non-trivial eigenvalue $\lambda_{1}$ that converges to $1$ as the dimension $d$ increases ($n=k^d$). Specifically, we establish the existence of these graphs where $\lambda_{1}$ approaches $1$ at an exponential rate relative to the dimension. Furthermore, we provide an estimate for the Ricci curvature, which scales at a rate of $-1/d$. These findings enable several applications, including the rapid generation of high-dimensional expander graphs and the construction of Ricci-flat graphs with a large expansion constant. Additionally, we present an explicit example of a graph possessing negative Ricci curvature. Our results rely on the recent work of M. Gromov and I. Shah regarding Ricci curvature on graphs, alongside the author's prior research on high-dimensional covers. Finally, the paper concludes with an outline of the proof for the existence of these novel graphs. The study investigates the magnetic properties of a new antiferromagnetic (AFM) material, GdInO$_3$, which features a quasi-two-dimensional centered honeycomb lattice of Gd$^{3+}$ ions. Through single crystal growth, X-ray diffraction, powder neutron diffraction, and magnetization measurements, we determined that the AFM ordering temperature is approximately 2.5 K. Magnetic moment analysis indicates that the primary interaction is a weak ferromagnetic coupling between Gd$^{3+}$ ions on nearest-neighbor In-O-In bonds. Neutron diffraction data reveal that the magnetic moments are non-collinear, precessing within the $ac$ plane around the centered honeycomb lattice sites. Additionally, the material displays unique characteristics, including a nearly constant magnetic moment, the absence of frustration, and the lack of magnetic anisotropy along the $b$ axis. Predicting the absence of edges, or link forecasting within sparse networks, is a difficult challenge that has received limited attention. Existing methods often overlook the sparsity inherent in these dynamic networks or rely on representations that are inefficient for the unique characteristics of edge negation. This study introduces Efficient Node Representation for Link Prediction (SSNE), a technique capable of forecasting both edge additions and deletions. SSNE is derived from Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) and is shown to surpass current state-of-the-art algorithms in various link forecasting scenarios involving sparse networks. Furthermore, we validate this approach across multiple real-world datasets. The code for SSNE can be accessed at https://github.com/ahmedhaleem/SSNE. Our validation dataset is available here: https://drive.google.

Silicon photonics has advanced significantly regarding the design and fabrication of compact atomic and molecular vapor chambers (AVCs). These miniaturized, vacuum-sealed devices house atomic or molecular gases at near-room temperature and are essential for hosting atomic optical functions, including optical cooling, Doppler and sub-Doppler state preparation, optical pumping, and non-linear interactions. This work presents and demonstrates methods for fabricating and integrating deep silicon AVCs. By employing a novel approach to manage and mitigating stress within the device, we achieved a record-breaking silicon AVC with an internal chamber volume of merely 16 pl. This device utilizes aluminum as the atomic species, demonstrating an absolute absorption of $\mu$pl-scale volumes at 1550 nm of $\sim$99.9%. Such a compact AVC holds significant potential for creating optical modules within optical communication networks. Additionally, we outline how these findings can be extended to other AVCs featuring deeper chambers and supporting diverse atomic and molecular optical functions. Finally, we explore the application of these miniaturized AVCs within the consumer electronics sector. Specifically, we demonstrate a compact magnetometer with a footprint of only 1.4 mm², achieving a sensitivity of 10 nT/$\sqrt{\rm{Hz}}$ at 1 Hz. This device outperforms current silicon photonics components, which typically offer sensitivities around 100 nT/$\sqrt{\rm{Hz}}$ at 1 Hz. Our findings indicate that these ultra-compact AVCs are ideal for enhancing the sensitivity of existing silicon photonic magnetometers at 1 Hz by approximately 1000-fold. Furthermore, we highlight the potential of these miniaturized AVCs to enable deep sub-noise floor sensitivity in a consumer-friendly form factor. This could lead to new silicon-based quantum technologies, such as a silicon-based quantum compass for navigation, which operates at 1.55 $\mu$m and utilizes the visible light spectrum. Such a device would be compatible with existing silicon photonic circuit designs and represent a significant advancement in silicon quantum research. We also address several challenges in achieving deep sub-noise floor sensitivity, such as those found in atomic magnetometers, and discuss the prospects of these miniaturized AVCs within the consumer electronics industry. Our results suggest that these ultra-compact AVCs are suitable for enhancing the sensitivity of consumer-grade silicon photonic accelerometers and gyroscopes at 1 Hz by roughly 1000-fold. We demonstrate that a single nonlinear distortion model based on the equivalent channel concept can adequately describe dual-polarization four-dimensional (DP4D) modulation systems across both sparse and dense wavelength grids. In this approach, the NLOSNR of the imaginary component is modeled using the power of the equivalent channel, which is derived from the NLOSNR of the real component. This methodology eliminates the necessity to characterize DP4D formats separately, thereby significantly lowering computational complexity and saving time. Furthermore, closed-form formulas are established to demonstrate how dual-polarization formats in multiple dimensions contribute to inter-channel nonlinear distortions, indicating how optical parameter adjustments influence system performance. The effectiveness of this equivalent channel model has been validated through extensive simulations covering various scenarios, including single and dual spans, single and dimensional modulation systems, and both back-to-back links under back-to-back conditions. These findings are also applicable to modeling nonlinear distortion in cross-polarization modulation (XPM). Ultimately, the proposed model facilitates the efficient design of DP4D modulation systems by allowing researchers to focus on separating real and imaginary components rather than analyzing multiple dimensions independently. Additionally, researchers can utilize the model to understand the contributions of other dimensions to the nonlinear noise of the target dimension, thus avoiding the need to simulate the entire system for each dimensional format. This capability is particularly advantageous for designing practical systems that employ mixed polarization and dimensional formats to achieve an optimal balance between performance and cost. The proposed model is expected to be widely adopted in the field, thereby streamlining the process of characterizing nonlinear distortion in complex DWDM transmission systems. In recent years, deep learning-based generative adversarial networks (GANs) have become increasingly popular for creating high-quality image translations. Given the rising frequency and severity of wildfires, there is growing potential for applying these techniques to fuse visible light and infrared images, potentially enhancing surveillance, detection, and forecasting systems. However, most existing approaches were developed for satellite data, which is often noisy, low-resolution, and limited in quantity. Consequently, there is a critical need for a robust method that can generalize effectively to visible and infrared images from cameras. This paper introduces a novel deep learning framework called FIRe-GAN, a fusion technique designed to generate high-quality infrared images from the available visible and infrared channels. FIRe-GAN addresses the challenge of small, high-noisy infrared datasets by employing a spectral normalization strategy and utilizing infrared images as spectral targets to direct the discriminator during the training of the generator network. Evaluations across multiple datasets demonstrate that FIRe-GAN produces superior results compared to established baselines, exhibiting high-quality generation even with very few training samples. Furthermore, the framework is versatile enough to be applied in various domains for infrared image generation and enhancement. Extensive experiments confirm that FIRe-GAN consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art methods across a diverse range of datasets. The code and pre-trained models are publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan12345/FIReGAN. The corresponding author is Ahmed Hassan (ahmed.hassan@tamu.edu). This study presents a data collection and initial analytical examination focused on identifying indicators of depression within social media posts. The research aims to develop methods for early detection and prevention of depression and suicide by analyzing digital footprints. To achieve this, we first introduce a novel dataset comprising nearly one million posts from depressed and non-depressed Twitter users. Subsequently, we conduct a comprehensive comparison of linguistic characteristics between these two groups, evaluating seven prior hypotheses through statistical significance tests across unigram, bigram, and document-level metrics. Finally, we explore potential applications for distinguishing between depressed and non-depressed users, demonstrating the feasibility of differentiating depression from other mental health issues. Ultimately, our findings establish a foundation for future efforts to build decision support systems capable of detecting and preventing depression. We anticipate that these results will advance the field of depression modeling and facilitate early intervention strategies. The accompanying paper details the experimental procedures and outcomes. Additionally, the associated code provides access to the collected data and outlines the basic analytical pipeline. Finally, we offer guidance on leveraging the presented data for various applications. Keywords: Depression Detection, Social Media Analytics, Early Intervention.

Building upon a deterministic COVID-19 model that accounts for within-host variability in viral kinetics and the emergence of drug-resistant mutants, we introduce a stochastic version incorporating both types of variability as well as the variability in model parameters. The objective of the associated control problem is to minimize the duration the population remains infectious. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the optimal strategy involves administering medication during the early acute phase, utilizing a high dose until co-morbidities are triggered, followed by a lower dose. This approach aims to balance viral suppression with the risk of resistance, while also addressing the potential for stochasticity and parameter uncertainty, all at a cost proportional to the dose. Finally, we show that the optimal control for the continuous-time model corresponds to the limit of the discrete-time model as the time step approaches zero. This limit is identified using recent perturbation methods from model theory, which establish convergence for the sequence of discrete models to the continuous model under appropriate topologies. These findings are supported by various examples. Furthermore, the identified upper and lower bounds on the duration of the acute phase align with existing literature on viral kinetics. Finally, within a multi-objective framework, we propose a strategy to mitigate the secondary peak of the epidemic, thereby reducing hospitalizations and the burden on healthcare systems. This is achieved by combining medication with non-pharmaceutical interventions, such as social distancing and lockdowns, though we do not explicitly model transmission. The resulting control strategy indicates that a high dose of medication should be administered throughout the acute phase, followed by a lower dose once the acute phase subsides. Additionally, we discuss the possibility of using this strategy in a feedback control setting, where the number of medications is determined by the within-host viral kinetic state. Specifically, if within-host viral load is high, a high dose is prescribed; otherwise, a low dose is administered. This approach is particularly relevant for the latter stages of the epidemic, where the population is no longer in the acute phase. In this context, we also examine the trade-off between the cost of medication and its effectiveness in reducing the number of hospitalized patients. To address this, we propose a practical algorithm based on model reduction techniques, such as proper orthogonal decomposition, which are increasingly popular in computational fluid dynamics. The algorithm relies on a reduced-order model with a very small number of dimensions, allowing for the efficient computation of optimal controls. We conclude by showing that this model can be computationally efficient even in high-dimensional settings. Finally, we discuss the possibility of implementing this algorithm within a model-predictive control framework

The energy and strength of the ISGMR are calculated for $^{28}$Si and $^{24}$Mg, respectively, and compared with available experimental data. This study examines stick-slip phenomena and trajectory convergence in feedback-controlled motion systems encountering Coulomb friction. The research focuses on continuous sliding solutions in error-space, which necessitate a discontinuous controller generating the required Coulomb forces for the closed-loop system. The proposed approach utilizes a continuous approximation of the switching surface near the boundary to analyze the system's behavior. Solutions are characterized as finite-time convergent, with convergence rates dependent on underlying parameters. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that solution manifolds in error-space exist, resulting in asymptotic convergence to these manifolds. Finally, the analysis covers the sliding mode solution, deriving its convergence rate and establishing conditions for finite-time convergence to the sliding surface from initial states. These findings are validated through examples involving friction compensation via feedforward control and impedance control. Additionally, the paper explores solutions involving switching between stick and slipping states. Introduction Stick-slip motion is a pervasive issue in mechanical systems, frequently disrupting the smooth operation of actuators and mechanisms. This phenomenon arises from the interaction between Coulomb friction and control or disturbance forces near the zero-crossing point of the Coulomb force. The resulting non-smooth behavior in position and velocity trajectories can cause significant performance degradation in motion systems, making its analysis and mitigation essential. Consequently, this paper investigates stick-slip motion systems regulated by feedback, aiming to prove the existence of sliding mode solutions, analyze their convergence, and ensure finite-time convergence to the sliding surface. Such solutions prevent the occurrence of stick-slip motion. These results hold significant practical value, particularly for the design and compensation of friction effects within motion control systems. We introduce a neural network framework designed to mitigate higher-order risks within Bellman equations featuring functional coefficients. By utilizing a constrained Bellman hedging technique, the value function is represented as a sum of orthogonal Belléts. This approach ensures that risk is reduced not only in the approximate value function but also within the approximated risk-sensitive Bellman functional itself. Our proposed Belléts are analogous to Bell polynomials and employ a training regime similar to that of deep Q-learning. Furthermore, we provide an error analysis for these Belléts and conduct numerical experiments to demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed Profound Bellman Hedging method. These experiments confirm that the technique outperforms standard value function approximation methods when dealing with higher-order risk evaluation across various stochastic control problems. Additionally, we examine the convergence properties of our method and contrast them with those of conventional value function approximation algorithms. Finally, we apply Profound Bellman Hedging to several challenging problems, including high-dimensional stochastic control tasks and those involving non-quadratic risk aversion. In all scenarios, the method achieves superior performance in terms of both computational efficiency and solution quality. Notably, it proves particularly effective in high-dimensional settings and when handling non-quadratic risk aversion.
