Sequential recommender systems are designed to enhance user experience by supplying timely suggestions. However, they often fail to capture the true motivations behind a user's recent interactions, leading to irrelevant recommendations. To address this limitation, we introduce the concept of "Implicit Motivation" (IM), a hidden user drive reflected in the sequence of items they consume. We developed the Implicit Motivation Network (IMN), a deep learning model capable of learning and representing this implicit motivation from historical interactions. The IMN effectively filters spurious correlations between past items, capturing only those relevant to generating accurate suggestions. We validated the effectiveness of IMNs across two large-scale industrial datasets: a news recommendation system and a journey planning service. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating implicit motivations significantly improves both recommendation accuracy and coverage. Furthermore, we conducted ablation studies to verify the model's ability to identify motivations consistent with human intuition and explored how implicit motivations evolve over time. Finally, we applied this framework to model motivations within tweet retweet sequences. The source code is available at https://github.com/SeungWooLee94/Implicit-Motivation-Network. Our empirical analysis confirms that the implicit motivations captured by IMNs are non-trivial, complex, and dynamic. This work underscores the critical role of implicit motivations in sequential recommender systems and establishes a new modeling framework for determining a user's true intent. We anticipate that this approach will be valuable for building more human-centric industrial recommender systems. Additionally, the methodology can be extended to other domains, such as sequential purchase recommendation and journey planning. Dr. Infante and Dr. Gomez-Ferrero recently introduced practical methods for calculating turbulent shear flow drag, based on a specific class of special functions known as double confluent Heun functions. By extending this framework to broader scenarios, we demonstrate that the resulting transformed double conflufient Heun equation possesses a key symmetry: any solution can be generated from any other through a shift in the dependent variable followed by a subsequent shift in the independent variable. We refer to this as the transformable dHe equation. Furthermore, we show that all singularities of the transformable dHe equation are redundant, allowing it to be fully represented by a single regular singularity with an arbitrary location. This provides a general symmetric formulation of our previous unfolding theory, which connects to broader mathematical concepts. Additionally, our extension enhances the practical applicability of the unfolding theory, enabling the solution of previously unsolvable boundary value problems. Finally, we outline methodologies for broadening these results to the general dHe equation. However, as we will explain, this extension introduces a new challenge: a residual symmetry that complicates practical implementation. To address this, we introduce a restricted version of the transformable dHe equation, termed the shiftable dHe equation, which retains the driving symmetry of the transformable version while excluding the residual one. We name the result of this process shiftability. Our findings suggest that shiftability represents a fundamental property applicable to all instances of the dHe equation. Consequently, we utilize this insight to generalize our findings to practical applications involving Heun functions. We demonstrate this by extending the findings to the Nielsen $U$ function and Puiseux Heun equation, both of which exhibit shiftability. This results in a generalized practical application where arbitrary boundary conditions are resolved using a monotonically varying master solution derived via a shooting method. This approach is fully applicable to the shiftable dHe equation, the Nielsen $U$ function, and the Puiseux Heun equation. The findings are supported by numerical evidence. Overall, our approach offers a new perspective on the dHe equation and its applications, advancing both theoretical understanding and practical utility. Compressed sensing represents a widely adopted framework for reconstructing structured signals from sparse measurements, typically utilizing an orthogonal basis like the Fourier transform that aligns with the signal's support. Typically, signals are assumed to be drawn from a single distribution, with heterogeneity modeled as a random mixture across different constructions. This study focuses on rank-one matrix approximation for groupwise structured matrices, demonstrating that the essential limit is determined by the rank within each group rather than by sample size or mean squared error. Through both theoretical analysis and numerical experiments, we establish that for rank-one approximation, the essential limit exists for every group individually, even in scenarios with diverging sample sizes and heterogeneous distributions. Furthermore, we show that for groupwise Fourier data, this limit corresponds to rank 2, consistent with prior single-limit findings. The resulting limit is significantly lower than the rank necessary to achieve a fixed mean squared error, highlighting the critical role of groupwise heterogeneity. Additionally, we investigate the essential limit for rank-k matrix approximation under groupwise heterogeneity. Our results indicate that for $k \geq 2$, the limit is defined by the rank of the best approximation achievable within each group. We conclude that these limits are fundamental properties of the available data, independent of specific matrix constructions or error metrics. Finally, we explore how these limits influence matrix reconstruction and develop algorithms capable of achieving these essential bounds. By leveraging group-specific structures, our proposed algorithms can reach these optimal approximations, offering a more efficient alternative to current methods. This work provides a foundation for understanding optimal reconstruction strategies for structured matrices with groupwise heterogeneity, a prevalent scenario in real-world applications. This insight is particularly relevant for Fourier data, where groupwise heterogeneity arises from variations in signal-to-noise ratios, sampling patterns, and experimental conditions. Our approach enables the creation of reconstruction algorithms that adapt to groupwise structures, thereby enhancing reconstruction quality. We illustrate this with applications to MRI and fluorescence microscopy. Ultimately, our framework demonstrates that superior reconstructions can be achieved without requiring prior knowledge of which group a given sample belongs to, effectively circumventing the need for manual segmentation. This represents a significant advancement over existing methods, which often depend on manual segmentation to assign samples to specific groups. By exploiting groupwise structure, our methods can surpass current state-of-the-art techniques for Fourier data. The resulting algorithms are versatile and applicable to various reconstruction tasks involving groupwise heterogeneity, including Fourier data, low-rank tensor completion, sparse signal recovery, and compressed sensing. We provide an intrinsic framework for investigating the topological properties of the Haldane model without assuming the presence of on-site potential. Our approach demonstrates that while the presence of potential facilitates the determination of topological characteristics, the fundamental nature of the topological effect is inherently rooted in the system's geometry. Furthermore, we analyze the evolution of the system's topological attributes as this geometric parameter varies. We also extend our method to the generalized Kane-Mele model and apply it to the triangular lattices of Na$_3$Bi and Bi$_2$Te$_3$. Additionally, by introducing geometric terms into the experimental setup on a honeycomb lattice, we successfully observe a geometrically driven quantum phase transition. These findings underscore the significance of the inherent topological model in clarifying the origin of topological phenomena and advancing topological experimental research. Furthermore, our work establishes a framework for exploring the intrinsic topological features of material surface states. Finally, we conclude by discussing the broader implications of the inherent topological model for future investigations.

However, due to experimental uncertainties in these measurements, a more rigorous test of lepton flavor universality in $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transitions requires comparing the sum of branching ratios across multiple final states. We propose a new semi-inclusive observable, $\mathcal{R}_{e/\mu}^{\mathrm{S}} = \frac{\mathrm{BR}(b\to s\mathrm{X}e^+e^-)}{\mathrm{BR}(b\to s\mathrm{X}\mu^+\mu^-)}$, which in the mass-independent (MI) limit within the Standard Model approaches unity. We demonstrate that even in the absence of new physics, deviations from this MI limit arise from Standard Model effects, such as photon-pion interference in exclusive channels and MI logarithmic terms. These effects are calculable and can be used to estimate the scale of new physics, $\Lambda_{\mathrm{NP}}$, assuming no Standard Model deviation. Our analysis indicates that the LHCb measurement of $\mathcal{R}_{K^{(\ast)}}^{\mathrm{S}}$ is sensitive to a MI violation of approximately 10%. Additionally, we examine semi-inclusive observables for specific final states, including $K\pi$ and $KS\pi$, and their ability to constrain MI deviations. Finally, we address the issue of double counting when combining semi-inclusive and exclusive observables. We show that combining them only within the same kinematic bin leads to significant double counting, whereas combining them across different bins results in a more conservative (smaller) estimate of the MI violation. This suggests that the current tension in $\mathcal{R}_{K^{(\ast)}}^{\mathrm{S}}$ may be overstated, and we provide a corrected estimate of the MI violation. We also discuss potential new physics scenarios that could explain the observed deviations in $\mathcal{R}_{K^{(\ast)}}^{\mathrm{S}}$. Finally, we compare our findings with existing semi-inclusive and inclusive results, demonstrating that our method allows for a more accurate and consistent combination of these data. This study addresses the decentralized design of distributed Eulerian regulation gains for linear time-invariant systems with multiple inputs and outputs. The problem involves a network of agents, each utilizing dynamic state machines to estimate system matrices and compute regulation gains. Building on the distributed solution by De Donat and Sontag (2013), this paper extends the approach to multi-channel systems while maintaining access to only local relative relative degree information. Furthermore, the solution enables each agent to independently adjust its adaptation speed without disrupting other agents, thereby enhancing the architecture's robustness. Finally, a detailed performance analysis is conducted through specific examples and tractable numerical simulations. The second part of this work focuses on implementing the extended solution in a real-world experimental setting. A key challenge in this implementation is ensuring that each agent distributes its computational load evenly among its neighbors to avoid computational bottlenecks. This issue is resolved through a real-time distributed regulation gain optimization method inspired by recent research from our group. The implementation is demonstrated using a real-time wind tunnel for plasma actuation on a flexible wing model within our aeroelastic control laboratory. This example serves to illustrate a practical application of the proposed solution in a distributed network of dynamic systems. Notably, the extension to nonlinear systems is straightforward and follows the approach outlined by De Donat and Sontag (2013). Consequently, this approach offers a robust plug-and-play method for the distributed regulation of multi-channel systems. The primary limitation of this solution is its reliance on right coprime factorization, which restricts it to systems where the relative degree is defined. However, this constraint is not significant, as the distributed solution can be easily adapted to such cases by increasing the dynamic order of the agents' state machines. Other limitations include the necessity of persistent excitation for agent convergence and the inability to modify the distributed regulation gains online. Future research will focus on developing adaptive distributed solutions for online tuning of distributed plasma actuation. Specifically, this work serves as a proof of concept for implementing distributed plasma actuation, bringing the proposed solution closer to its potential application in real-world scenarios. We introduce Atlas, integrated into OpenStreetMap, as the inaugural Atlas layer. This system functions as both a data repository and a framework for diverse data operations, including point-in-set queries. The layer offers fine-grained, globally distributed data with high update frequency, accessible via various interfaces. These capabilities hold significant value for numerous data science and machine learning initiatives, such as real-time traffic monitoring and analysis, point pattern analysis at global and local scales, and the study of spatial and temporal dynamics. We outline the architecture and services of this fine-grained data operation framework and discuss its specific applications. The Atlassians community continues to expand, contributing additional layers like those for points of interest, road types, and land use, while also abstracting fine-grained information into coarse-grained sets and performing operations on these layers. At present, these layers collectively span 160 countries, 4,000 cities, and 60,000 towns. We invite researchers and developers to collaborate with us in building and expanding the Atlas layers community. Our goal is to provide fine-grained, real-time data operation services that facilitate efficient and scalable processing of OpenStreetMap data. Furthermore, we aim to enhance the open-source software ecosystem, which has historically lacked fundamental data operation services. The principles governing evolution remain constant, yet timescales vary significantly across different organisms and environments. Consequently, evolutionary dynamics must be examined in the context of timescales for the parameters under consideration. This review highlights two primary sources of timescale variation: the frequency with which evolution-impacting events occur, and the magnitude of those events when they do occur. Additionally, the impact of negative selection is addressed. Finally, the concepts of timescales and modifiers are applied to investigate the evolution of complexity and large phenotypic shifts. The article concludes by outlining unresolved questions regarding these topics. For instance, while modifiers are essential for large shifts, their presence does not guarantee the emergence of complexity. Furthermore, the mechanism driving the increase in modifier frequency remains an open issue, and the role of positive selection requires clarification. The review also explores the feasibility of constructing a comprehensive model that integrates multiple rates, modifiers, and selection effects. Finally, it examines the evolution of large phenotypic shifts and the molecular basis of complexity, emphasizing the intricate relationship between genes and phenotypes. Molecular complexity is noted as a prerequisite for large phenotypic shifts, yet the necessity of large phenotypic variability for complexity is deemed less certain. The text concludes by proposing several future research directions. Keywords: evolution, timescale, modifiers, complexity, large shifts, genes and phenotypes.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) has become a highly promising approach for building universal speech representations. However, the impact of hostile data contamination on speech SSL performance remains largely unexplored. Drawing inspiration from the Hostile Grammar Benchmark, this study introduces a comprehensive examination of speech representation performance under significant text-based linguistic contamination. We utilized Speech-to-Text (ST) and Speech-to-Speech (STS) hosted SSL models (MSP) trained and evaluated exclusively on speech data, where a subset of the training corpus was replaced with sentences extracted from various text corpora. Our research demonstrates that SST and MSTS models exhibit marked differences in performance regarding grammatical categories, with longer sentences posing particularly severe performance drops. Furthermore, we found that models trained on balanced corpora outpaced those trained on single corporora, and that the impact of the top 20 most frequent vocabularies can be observed even with minimal contamination levels. Finally, we propose a metric to quantify the susceptibility of speech SSL models to hostile data, which shows a strong correlation with observed performance degradation. These findings offer valuable insights for assessing the robustness of speech SSL models against large-scale text-based adversarial attacks. The code and datasets are accessible at: https://github.com/alexsanchez1996/Hostile-Speech-SSL. Decentralized marketplaces represent a transformative evolution from traditional centralized platforms. Historically, these latter systems have faced significant challenges, including the erosion of consumer trust and the exacerbation of information asymmetry. Over time, their operational models have become increasingly complex, leading to a steady decline in user base and market share. The primary obstacles to their sustainable operation stem from the difficulty of ensuring trustworthiness and fairness, which are critical for long-term success.

The core issue driving these difficulties lies in the inherent trilemma of decentralization, security, and scalability. Although the concept of decentralized marketplaces is not new, only recent technological advancements have made them viable. Specifically, advancements in cryptography, smart contracts, and other foundational technologies have finally enabled these markets to function reliably. This paper explores the practical implementation of decentralized marketplaces, analyzing how emerging technical solutions have effectively addressed the trust and fairness issues that have long plagued decentralized digital trading. Through this examination, we aim to offer valuable insights for researchers and practitioners endeavoring to build more efficient and practical decentralized marketplaces. Finally, we outline potential future research directions in this promising domain. We hope this study provides meaningful perspective for the continued development of decentralized marketplaces. Keywords: Blockchain, Decentralized Marketplaces, Trustworthy Markets, Smart Contracts, Cryptography.

The E-value, recently suggested by Angrist et al. (2019) and Anderson et al. (2021), serves as a metric to quantify the strength of unmeasured confounding in observational studies. We propose extending the E-value to missing data contexts and developing a corresponding estimation framework with an associated estimator that demonstrates asymptotic normality. This approach allows researchers to assess sensitivity concerning potential unmeasured confounding within missing data scenarios. Furthermore, we integrate this sensitivity examination with Bayesian hypothesis testing. A simulation study was conducted to evaluate the finite-sample performance of the proposed estimator, and the practical utility of the method is demonstrated through an application to a dataset from an observational study. The R code for the estimator is available at: https://github.com/taekyu-lee/E-value. Additionally, we have released R code for the Bayesian sensitivity examination under the same repository link. This work investigates the Laurent expansion of the quantum plane, denoted as $A_q = \text{exp}(\log(q)E_{12})\otimes \text{exp}(\log(q)E_{21})$. We demonstrate that this algebra possesses a comprehensive set of infinitesimal symmetries within the Lie algebra $q\mathfrak{sl}_3$. Furthermore, we characterize the structure of the maximal compact subalgebra of $q\mathfrak{sl}_3$, showing that it is also generated by infinitesimal symmetries of $A_q$. Notably, we present the first $q$-deformation of the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ W-algebra as the maximal compact subalgebra of $q\mathfrak{sl}_3$. Additionally, we construct the explicit action of $q\mathfrak{sl}_3$ on the space of Laurent series in two variables and elucidate the action of $q\mathfrak{w}_2$ on this series space. The structure of $q\mathfrak{sl}_3$ is closely linked to the action of the braid group $Br_3$ on the quantum plane, which presents a novel result. We observe that the braid group $Br_3$ acts faithfully on the space of formal power series in two variables, in contrast to its action on the space of formal power series in one variable. This finding resolves an open question, as it represents the second $G$-space (following the case for $Br_2$ in one variable) where the $Br_3$ action is faithful. Finally, we explore the relationship between the quantum plane and the Fock representation of the Virasoro algebra. Specifically, we show that the Virasoro algebra, equipped with the Shapovalov form, acts on the quantum plane $A_q$. This action is isomorphic to the action of $q\mathfrak{w}_2$ on a one-dimensional space of formal power series in two variables, where $\mathfrak{w}_2$ represents the Jordanian deformation of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$. This finding provides a direct link between the Virasoro algebra and the quantum plane. As a consequence, we establish that the action of the Virasoro algebra on the space of formal power series in one variable is faithful. This result serves as the final missing piece in a complete description of $G$

Recent advancements in wireless communication have enabled the emergence of the Internet of Vehicles (IoV), a technology that has significantly enhanced various applications including traffic management, smart driving, and autonomous applications. However, growing privacy and security concerns within IoV remain a critical challenge. To address these issues, Federated Learning (FL) has been proposed to enhance data privacy. Nevertheless, FL faces other limitations, such as insecure aggregation, that need to be resolved to ensure robust privacy and security in IoV. Consequently, researchers are increasingly exploring the integration of Blockchain (BC) with FL to strengthen privacy protection and security mechanisms. This paper surveys the literature on proposed solutions that combine BC and FL to secure IoV services. It begins by examining the challenges associated with standard FL and offers a detailed analysis of how BC can mitigate these issues. Subsequently, it provides an in-depth review of scholarly studies proposing a blockchain-federated learning framework for IoV. Finally, the paper identifies key research gaps in existing literature and offers suggestions for future directions. We believe this work will be valuable to researchers in the fields of IoV, Blockchain, and Federated Learning. Furthermore, the proposed blockchain-enabled federated learning framework is intended to serve as a foundation for subsequent studies in blockchain-supported FL research. Additionally, to support newcomers in the field, we have developed a research roadmap outlining future trends and suggested topics for investigation. This roadmap was created based on an analysis of the limitations of current solutions and the gaps in the literature. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 defines the scope and background, while Section 3 details the architecture of the proposed solution. Section 4 reviews related work, and Section 5 provides an in-depth analysis of the literature. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper and outlines our future research direction regarding blockchain-enabled federated learning frameworks for IoV. Given our background and research experience, we aim to contribute to the IoV domain by developing secure, privacy-preserving, and efficient machine learning frameworks for various IoV services, with a primary focus on intelligent transportation systems. Additionally, we intend to explore the synergies between emerging technologies, including Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Internet of Things (IoT), and IoV. Furthermore, we plan to investigate the integration of BC and its potential to address security and privacy challenges in IoV, with a specific focus on enhancing the security and privacy of blockchain-federated learning frameworks. Our research will also examine how BC enables trust, transparency, and data integrity within FL, and how these frameworks can optimize resource

The Large Hadron Collider's Run 2 data at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV were analyzed to measure the ratio of production cross-sections for the $B_s^0$ and $B^0$ mesons, $\mathcal{R}_{B_s/B^0} = \sigma(B_s^0) / \sigma(B^0)$. This ratio was determined by examining the production of final-state muons originating from the semi-leptonic decays of $B$ mesons. The analysis utilized both inclusive and tagger-based muon samples, applying corrections for background muons and potential double-counting effects. Additionally, the muon-tagged inclusive cross-sections for $B^0$ and $B^\pm$ mesons were derived. The results indicate that $\mathcal{R}_{B_s/B^0} = 0.972 \pm 0.046 \pm 0.045$, where the initial error represents statistical uncertainty and the secondary error represents systematic uncertainty. This finding aligns with previous measurements from LEP, RHIC, and Tevatron experiments, as well as ALICE studies conducted at $\sqrt{s}=2.76$ TeV and $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV. Furthermore, the analysis confirms a ratio of prompt to non-prompt $B_s^0$ and $B^0$ production of $(1.00 \pm 0.11)$. These outcomes demonstrate the effectiveness of muon tagging as a technique for $B$ meson measurements in heavy-ion collisions. The findings support the presence of a $B$ factory-like $b$-quark environment at the LHC during low-energy runs, alongside a notable increase in $b$-jet beauty fragmentation fractions toward the $B_s^0$ state. These capabilities highlight the experiment's potential for investigating $B$-physics processes, including CP violation, mixing, and rare decays. This study was conducted by the LHCb collaboration. The full results are published in Phys. Rev. D 101, 012004 (2020). The corresponding paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.07090. The dataset is available at https://cms-lbc-gw.cern.ch. For further information, visit the experiment's website at https://lhcb

The development of quantum computers demands cooling systems capable of reliably achieving and sustaining sub-kelvin temperatures. This paper introduces a novel cryogenic system at Fermilab designed for the temperature-controlled testing of emerging large-scale, multi-qubit processors. Utilizing a customized dilution refrigerator system, the facility can cool various cryogenic loads to temperatures as low as 0.5 mK. The setup features a turntable that allows for the simultaneous temperature measurement and alignment of up to eight samples, with the capacity for further expansion. The load plates are engineered to support various qubit technologies, accommodating a wide spectrum of qubit frequencies. The system's temperature stability, cooling curves, and characterization results are presented. This quantum computing test facility is currently open for user proposals. The setting enables the investigation of cryogenic materials' properties, the characterization of qubits and their associated electronics, and fundamental tests of qubit coherence and entanglement. This system is part of the International Laboratory for Collaborative Quantum Technologies (ILCQT), a new research infrastructure at the Fermilab National Laboratory. The ILCT project is a collaboration between Fermilab, the University of Chicago, Argonne National Laboratory, and the University of Notre Dame. The facility is scheduled to open for user testing in the summer of 2022. The ILCQT project is funded by the U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science, National Quantum Initiative (NSF), and University of Notre Dame. The ILCQT project is led by Dr. Michael Devoret (U of Chicago) and Dr. Michael Hofmann (FermiLab). Dr. Michael E. Schimtz (Argonne) presented the paper. The authors are: Michael E. Schmidt, Michael G. Ray, Michael L. Lauer, Michael E. Schimtz, Michael L. Lauer, Michael L. Roukes, and Michael E. Sargent. The publication date is 2022-07-11. Crypto and cryptography are frequently used interchangeably, but while crypto encompasses all technologies utilizing encryption, cryptography focuses specifically on the mathematical and logical methods used to create them. This latter discipline, which requires specialized knowledge, is often mistakenly assumed to be inherently secure. However, numerous studies reveal that even seasoned developers make errors when implementing crypto within crypto-agnostic applications. Such mistakes can introduce vulnerabilities, potentially compromising application security. Our investigation examines real-world instances of Python crypto misconfigurations and errors, identifying patterns in how cryptography is incorrectly implemented across various non-crypto-specific apps. We analyze both user-reported issues from public bug tracking systems and independently discovered vulnerabilities. Our findings highlight common pitfalls and anti-patterns, offering recommendations to prevent crypto-related issues and underscoring the necessity for effective communication between application and crypto developers. Furthermore, we explore potential solutions, such as automated verification tools, to facilitate proper implementation. Finally, we discuss how these tools can be adapted to assist developers in correctly configuring and using cryptographic systems. The Python Crypto Abuses in the Wild repository, which hosts our collected dataset, is also made available to the public. The complete paper and additional resources can be found at https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2475905922000807. Our insights are also available as a presentation at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=11444444444. Additionally, our work was featured in an episode of the Security Engineering Podcast, which synthesizes our paper and interviews its authors; the episode is accessible at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=11444444444. The podcast is also available on Apple Podcasts at https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/python-crypto-abuses-in-the-wild/id1513854901/episodes/python-crypto-abuses-in-the-wild. Recent years have seen a significant rise in the availability of high-resolution aerial imagery and video captured from UAVs and other aerial platforms, driven by an increasing capacity to collect data at extensive scales. However, current machine learning models for high-level tasks, such as semantic segmentation of urban areas, typically depend on manually labeled datasets for training. This limitation becomes particularly challenging when attempting to train and evaluate models across larger datasets. This paper introduces an automatic annotation framework named VALUE (Voting-based Automatic Annotation), which leverages the extensive scale of these datasets to enhance the reliability of label quality. VALUE utilizes an unsupervised, self-supervised approach to generate initial predictions through object detection and semantic segmentation models trained on unlabeled data. It then employs a voting-based mechanism to refine these predictions and improve the overall robustness of the labeling process. Experimental results using VALUE to annotate data from the xView-2 and Mapillary datasets demonstrate its effectiveness in producing high-quality annotations across these extensive datasets. The study confirms that VALUE achieves superior performance compared to the individual models contributing to the voting process. Furthermore, VALUE exhibits consistent results across both datasets, validating its ability to generalize reliably at scale. To support future research in large-scale automated annotation, the VALUE framework and associated methods have been made available at https://github.com/robertkoster/VALUE. This work aims to advance the field of high-level computer vision tasks by significantly reducing the manual effort required for data labeling. The code and data used in this study will be made publicly available. (Video demonstrations can be found at https://youtu.be/4214142114o and https://youtu.be/4214142114o). Additionally, the authors' contributions to the VALUE framework are listed as follows: Robert Koster - Conceptualization, Methodology, Software, Formal Analysis, Investigation, Visualization, Writing (original draft, review & editing); Jeroen Maassen - Conceptualization, Writing (review & editing); Floris Geerts - Writing (review & editing); Wouter Vanden-Bempt - Writing (review & editing); Geert Vanckacker - Writing (review & editing). Corresponding author: Robert Koster.

This paper introduces NuSPAN, a novel proximal mean network designed for challenging nonuniform sparse inverse problems. The development of NuSPAN stems from the observation that many such problems exhibit inherent self-similarity, a property that can be leveraged to enhance inverse problem solutions. The core mechanism of NuSPAN involves a proximal averaging operator capable of handling data inconsistencies and enforcing self-similarity priors. We provide a theoretical analysis of this operator, demonstrating that it generates a median-filter-like effect. Theoretically, we establish the nonexpansiveness of the fixed-point operator linked to NuSPAN, proving the convergence of the algorithm under mild conditions. To evaluate NuSPAN, we apply it to two primary scenarios: (i) seismic reflectivity reconstruction and (ii) image denoising involving nonuniform inhomogeneities. Numerical experiments confirm that NuSPAN outperforms competing algorithms in both scenarios. Furthermore, we demonstrate that NuSPAN is universal and can be adapted to various other problems characterized by self-similarity, including anisotropic total variation denoising, total variation deconvolution, and self-similarity promoted sparsity. Finally, we provide an open-source implementation of NuSPAN. Our findings suggest that NuSPAN is both effective and efficient for addressing self-similarity in seismic reflectivity reconstruction. Additionally, we anticipate that NuSPAN will be a versatile tool for addressing other universal sparse inverse problems where self-similarity is present or can be artificially induced. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of proximal mean networks to seismic reflectivity reconstruction.

Keywords: Nonuniform sparse problem, self-similarity, proximal mean network, median-filter-like effect, convergence analysis, anisotropic total variation denoising, total variation deconvolution, self-similarity promoted sparsity, seismic reflectivity reconstruction.

We introduce a technique for modeling operator spectra in two-dimensional quantum field theories by combining two existing approaches. The first approach utilizes wavefunction overlaps to represent operator insertions within path integrals. The second applies universal corrections to Haagerup net results, accounting for the finite number of sites on the Hugston-Haagerup manifold. By integrating these two methods, we achieve more precise and comprehensive operator spectra. Our findings demonstrate that this method accurately reproduces the central charges of free boson and Ising models, revealing distinctive features of their operator spectra, including operator merging. Additionally, we enhance the accuracy of the Haagerup model's operator spectrum, successfully identifying previously unresolved degeneracies. Finally, we explore potential extensions of our results to other Kauffman invariants. Our findings indicate that the universal corrections identified for the helicity net can be extended to the Temperley-Lieb net, thereby providing the first explicit construction of the operator spectrum for the Potts model. Furthermore, our results suggest that the universal corrections for the helicity net offer a framework for modeling operator spectra in the corresponding corresponding statistical model. This could potentially enable the explicit construction of operator spectra for various models, such as the classical Ising and free fermion models. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that universal corrections can significantly improve the accuracy of Kauffman invariant applications, offering a pathway to the explicit construction of operator spectra in diverse models. Furthermore, we anticipate that universal corrections will become an essential component of any quantum field theory framework derived from graph invariants. This is because such theories invariably require the explicit description of operator spectra. Consequently, our findings establish a foundation for explicitly constructing operator spectra in various models, including the classical Ising and free fermion models, and enhance the accuracy of the operator spectrum for the Haagerup model. Additionally, we propose that universal corrections will be an essential element of any quantum field theory derived from graph invariants, as these theories fundamentally rely on the explicit characterization of operator spectra. Our findings thus demonstrate that universal corrections can substantially enhance the precision of operator spectrum constructions in diverse models, such as the classical Ising and free fermion models, while also enabling a more explicit description of operator spectra in the Kauffman model. Ultimately, our findings indicate that universal corrections will play a crucial role in explicitly constructing operator spectra in various models, thereby significantly improving the accuracy of the resulting spectra. Furthermore, we suggest that the application of universal corrections to the helicity net offers a promising approach for explicitly constructing operator spectra in different models, thereby enhancing the accuracy of the resulting spectra

Historical linguistic corpora serve as essential resources for historical linguistics, providing structured semantic and syntactic insights through part-of-speech (POS) tagging. However, applying state-of-the-art tagging systems to older languages often fails because existing systems are typically built on annotations derived from a single grammar, whereas historical corpora usually reflect a fusion of multiple competing grammatical perspectives. Consequently, annotations from historical texts lack inter-annotator agreement, rendering them unsuitable for training and evaluating standard monodimensional tagging systems. To address this, we propose a new dependably tagged dataset comprising around 100,000 tokens from a 17th-century Dutch corpus. This approach utilizes state-of-the-art multilabel deep neural networks that process each token individually and predict a set of possible POS tags. We present a preprocessing algorithm that filters out unreliable tags to ensure dataset consistency. Additionally, we evaluate the dataset using standard classification metrics and demonstrate its utility by retraining and assessing various POS tagging systems. Ultimately, this method offers a scalable strategy for creating consistently tagged historical corpora that could facilitate the development of efficient morphosyntactic tagging systems for historically distant languages. Empirical results confirm the feasibility of the proposed approach. By generating dependably tagged corpora, we advance the reliability of historical corpora as resources for historical linguistics. Furthermore, we argue that the morphosyntactic information within these corpora is best represented as an ensemble of multiple interpretations rather than a single consensus. This work advances the concept of multivalued tagging, which we contend is the most robust linguistic representation for historical corpora. Finally, we detail the experimental procedures used to create the dependably tagged corpus and analyze the resulting corpora. The dataset is available at: https://osf.io/4q52b/. The source code can be found at: https://github.com/maartenwagemans/DependablyTaggedCorpus. Please cite our publication: Maarten S. Wagemans, Maarten van Erp, and Siebe Vanhove. 2021. Dependably part-of-speech labeling of historical corpora through set-valued prediction. In Proceedings of the 2021 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, EMNLP 2021, Online Proceedings, 5751–5761. Non-uniform integrability characterizes the passage to the limit under the integral sign for sequences or nets of integrable functions. This property is fundamentally linked to the weak topology applied to $L^1$ spaces or more generally to Banach function spaces. The primary objective of this book is to present a systematic, unified, and extended theory of non-uniform integrability by utilizing Banach function spaces, with a specific emphasis on Köthe--Maharam spaces. To achieve this goal, an extended theory of vector-measure decomposition is developed, building upon the foundational work of S. Choquet and J. L. DeWitt. Furthermore, the concepts and findings from this book represent a logical extension of the original theory regarding non-uniform integration. Key applications include deriving necessary and sufficient conditions for vector measures to possess the Radon--Nikodym property within Banach function spaces, addressing the problem of vector measures defined on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of a topological space to possess this property, and resolving the problem of vector measures to serve as densities for Radon measures on topological spaces. Additionally, the book explores the theory of non-uniform integration specifically concerning the topological space itself. Finally, the text presents an original application concerning the continuity of the center of gravity mapping for body parts. The development of these results was supported by scientific and educational cooperation between Czech Technical University in Prague and the University of Belgrade's Faculty of Electronic Engineering. This collaboration has produced a series of monographs and scientific papers that have enriched the theory of non-uniform integration and its applications, with this book serving as the culmination of that series. Formal specification has long been recognized as a potent method for elucidating and verifying the properties of software systems. Nevertheless, identifying suitable scenarios for its implementation remains challenging. This difficulty stems partly from human cognitive biases and partly from technical hurdles, including imprecise requirement definitions, an overemphasis on post-development cost-benefit analysis, and a lack of awareness regarding emerging tooling capabilities. To address these issues, we introduce a novel approach that integrates the formalization of requirements directly into the process of capturing user demands. Our method employs a smart assistant constructed as a specialized language processor, featuring an intuitive user interface and automated algorithms. This method significantly lowers the barriers to entry for formalization, thereby facilitating clearer requirement communication and enhancing the overall development workflow. We have implemented this approach in the form of a software product known as SmartSpec, which supports the formal specification of requirements using the CityRE model. Through this tool, designers can achieve faster development cycles, clearer requirement definitions, and automated generation of both formal specifications and prototypes. The primary advantages of our method are its tool-supported implementation, automated processing, and language flexibility. In this study, we present a detailed analysis of the method, illustrate its application using the CityRE model, and demonstrate its benefits through practical examples. The findings indicate that this approach effectively aids developers in producing formal specifications for requirement documents. Furthermore, our results suggest that SmartSpec can be utilized to formalize human requirements at any stage of the development lifecycle. By automating this process, we aim to mitigate post-development costs associated with systems created through traditional design methods. Ultimately, formalization of requirements represents a significant step toward fully automated development for software systems. We contend that this form of automation is essential for the successful creation of software. We demonstrate that SmartSpec achieves this by generating formal specifications for the CityRE model, thereby producing software that is both understandable and verifiable. This process introduces no significant overhead for developers, as they interact with a user-friendly interface and do not need to manually write low-level code. Furthermore, the resulting software is not only formal but also functional, as SmartSpec automatically produces a prototype. Consequently, our findings indicate that SmartSpec facilitates the formalization of human requirements at any phase of the development process. Our results confirm that SmartSpec enables the formalization of city requirements at any stage of the development lifecycle. The CityRE model is thus constructed, analyzed, and prototyped at every phase, from the initial idea generation to the final product realization. In the realm of superconducting quantum computing, operational errors and decoherence frequently disrupt quantum computations. To address this, the inverse-based concealed QEC (ICQEC) protocol is proposed to mitigate losses of quantum information and computational results by executing a concise set of operations on encoded qubits. This study introduces an ICQEC protocol designed to detect phase-flip (Z) errors, implemented on a state-of-the-art superconducting quantum processor featuring four transmon qubits coupled via flux-tunable couplers. Compared to standard QEC (CQEC) methods, the ICQEC approach reduces operational gates by 50% while achieving comparable performance. Experimental data confirms that for a single error event, ICQEC effectively identifies and corrects Z errors. Additionally, an optimized high-depth sequence of ICQEC operations is evaluated, demonstrating a significant enhancement in fidelity compared to the corresponding unoptimized sequences both with and without error correction. These findings validate the efficacy of the ICQEC protocol for QEC tasks, offering a promising strategy to minimize operational gates in near-term superconducting quantum apparatus. Furthermore, regarding computational tasks involving deep quantum circuits, utilizing the ICQEC protocol within the quantum circuit can serve as error detection to improve the fidelity of logical computations. Consequently, this work provides a viable solution for reducing gates in near-term superconducting quantum circuits, holding significant value for practical applications. The source data and source code are accessible at https://github.com/ICQEC-Group/SQEC2022. Additionally, detailed experimental results can be found in Data in Brief, Volume 42, 108306 (2022), and the corresponding source code is available on GitHub. Every preorder can be depicted as an equivalence relation between sets, provided there are sufficient colimits, specifically regular epimorphisms. This method, established by Bunge, is fundamentally associated with the Grothendieck topology of effective epimorphisms. Consequently, it is natural to inquire under what conditions on a regular category all preorder morphisms admit such a depiction. The answer to this question serves as the primary focus of this article. While one direction of the equivalence is straightforward, the other constitutes the main result. To establish it, we utilize two auxiliary results: the first extends Bunge's result to $\mathbb{S}$-complete categories, and the second demonstrates that if all preorder morphisms admit a depiction, then every equivalence relation is effective. Although not required for the main proof, the second auxiliary result may hold independent interest. Together, these findings provide sufficient conditions for a regular category to possess the ability to depict all preorders as equivalence relations, thereby extending the effective epimorphism (glueing) property beyond objects to preorders within any $\mathbb{S}$-complete category. Notably, this extension cannot be achieved through a weaker depiction where only preorder morphisms with surjective images are required to be depicted as equivalence relations. To our knowledge, this specific characterization of preorders in regular categories has not been previously noted in the literature. We illustrate this with an example involving the category of schemes, which is $\mathbb{S}$-complete but does not depict all preorders as equivalence relations; the nature of these preorders is explored in the section on this example. Additionally, we examine how the choice of Grothendieck topology influences the existence of these descriptions of preorders. Finally, we outline an open research line concerning the relationship between effective epimorphisms and symmetry of preorders, which may hold independent interest. This relationship is complex, particularly in the context of Grothendieck topoi, as evidenced by various instances and counterexamples. For instance, in any topos, the symmetry of a preorder is equivalent to the effective epimorphism property of its inclusion into its symmetrization. However, this equivalence does not necessarily extend to preorders within an arbitrary $\mathbb{S}$-complete category. To address this, we introduce a regular categorical property that ensures the equivalence holds for preorders in any $\mathbb{S}$-complete category, even without assuming a topos structure. The rising availability of satellite imagery has enhanced our capacity to monitor and forecast oceanic conditions, yet extreme events in these regions continue to pose significant risks. This study introduces a new class of models based on Copulas designed to predict joint extremes in spatially dependent time series across multiple dimensions. We outline the theoretical underpinnings of this approach and its relevance to oceanic settings. Furthermore, we develop a series of tests to assess symmetry in spatial and temporal dependence within extreme bounds. Our simulation results indicate that spatial and temporal tests detect asymmetry in conditional peaks for spatially dependent data, while both spatial and temporal tests identify asymmetry in conditional marginals for locally dependent data. Finally, we apply the proposed methods to simulate and analyze extreme phenomena in spatially dependent multivariate time series. Key findings include: (i) detecting an extreme wave event in the North Atlantic; (ii) observing that joint extremes in sea level pressure in the North Atlantic exhibit greater negative tail dependence than the upper dependence; and (iii) confirming that extreme events in significant wave height and crest factor demonstrate different dependence structures compared to those in wave direction. These results confirm that the proposed methods are effective for extreme environments like the ocean. The object-oriented R package `multico` is available at [https://multico.r-forge.r-project.org/](https://multico.r-forge.r-project.org/). The R code required to replicate the results is provided in our online supplementary material. The data used in this study can be accessed via the European Marine Data Centre at [http://emdc.data.europa.eu/](http://emdc.data.europa.eu/). Natural language descriptions of text data play a crucial role in image-text retrieval, yet learning to represent them is difficult due to significant distributional gaps between text and images. To tackle this challenge, we introduce VT-CLIP, a novel visual-assisted text representation learning method that offers two key advantages over current approaches: 1) learning visual-guided text representations through image-text alignment, and 2) enhancing text representations via a cross-modality contrastive learning strategy that leverages color and shape cues from images. On the text-image retrieval benchmark, VT-CLIP achieves new state-of-the-art results with accuracy scores of 76.1% for image-to-text retrieval and 74.5% for text-to-image retrieval. The code and experimental results are accessible at https://github.com/VT-CLIP/VT-CLIP. Additionally, our implementation supports customizable visual-assisted text datasets, including the new TextDescription-100K dataset featuring 100k image pairs with paired descriptions, as well as datasets derived from COCO, DUT, and MS-COCO. We have also released a C++ implementation of VT-CLIP to facilitate efficient training and deployment. Specifically, our C++ code incorporates a new high-performance feature extractor, TextDescription-Embedding Network (TDENet), which delivers state-of-the-art performance on text description datasets while maintaining low computational costs. We also provide a PyTorch implementation of TDENet to support research and development. The PyTorch implementation is available here: https://github.com/VT-CLIP/VT-CLIP-PYTORCH. We examine a framework where both the target operator and the initial approximation subject to noise are non-Hermitian matrices. This structure is particularly relevant for simulating non-unitary quantum evolutions, quantum operations, and quantum instruments. Our approach extends operator transitioning, a technique for rapidly estimating Hermitian matrix operators from a starting point. In this work, we generalize the method to handle non-Hermitian matrices, introducing a strategy to mitigate the significant noise amplification that typically occurs in this regime. To demonstrate the breadth of this methodology, we present three applications: a technique for rapidly estimating the density matrix, another for efficiently approximating the adjoint map, and a third for efficiently estimating quantum instruments. Collectively, these findings offer foundational elements for the emerging fields of quantum reverse engineering and quantum machine learning. Furthermore, we validate all theoretical results with numerical experiments. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/QuantumMachineLearningLab/QML_lab. Finally, we illustrate that these methods can enhance the performance of various quantum reverse engineering protocols in both noisy and noiseless quantum computing environments. Additionally, our techniques can boost the efficacy of multiple quantum machine learning approaches for quantum operator learning, as well as support other types of quantum operator learning. Our methods are implemented in QML_lab, a Python library designed for quantum operator learning. QML_lab supports applications in quantum reverse engineering and quantum machine learning, offering support for unitary and non-unitary operator learning, circuit learning, and neural network learning. These tools are accessible as open-source software. Our software is available at https://github.com/QuantumMachineLearningLab/QML_lab. Diagnostics in radiology and pathology frequently involve augmenting digital images with machine learning models, image segmentation, measurement data, and expert commentary. Standardized image formats like DICOM and TIFF typically lack the capacity to encode these supplementary information outputs. To address this limitation, we introduce Highdicom, a free, open-source Python framework that enables the creation of standardized representations for images and remark data. The framework offers pythonic and intuitive abstractions for modeling diagnostic findings and images through the lens of radiology and pathology, alongside tools for validating and visualizing data. Additionally, it provides tools for combining images and remarks with models and numerical data into queryable objects. Evaluation by pathologists and radiologists indicates that Highdicom facilitates a consistent data model and generates human- and machine-readable representations that align with medical image processing practices. By allowing applications to produce diagnostic results that can be easily visualized and integrated with well-defined image datasets, Highdicom facilitates applications such as expert consensus and medical image record management. This paper investigates a general class of electromagnetic configurations within Einstein-Maxwell theory that yield a surface term in the Noether charge associated with the Einstein-Hilbert action. We demonstrate that these configurations correspond precisely to vacuum solutions of Einstein-Maxwell theory that satisfy both dilaton and asymptotic equations. Furthermore, we apply this framework to Einstein-Maxwell theory in three-dimensional spacetime to derive the Virasoro algebra for charged black holes and to characterize the disorder of these same solutions. As a potential future extension, we aim to integrate this method into the program by Brown and Henneaux, which seeks to identify algebras formed by solutions that either preserve the asymptotic symmetry or generate it. This determination is essential for understanding the dual conformal field theory in the context of the AdS$_2$/CFT$_1$ holographic duality. Additionally, we intend to explore a more general scenario by incorporating gauge fields into the action that vanish on the boundary but are not necessarily electromagnetic in nature. This broader approach holds significant potential for characterizing a wider range of vacua, including those with chiral symmetry breaking. Ultimately, this methodology could help determine whether such vacua can be interpreted as critical points of a dual conformal field theory. These topics will be addressed in a forthcoming publication. In the current manuscript, we provide a comprehensive description of how to construct the relevant algebra using a general class of solutions. Specifically, we illustrate this with a class of linear dilaton backgrounds in three-dimensional spacetime that admit both left and right Virasoro charges, thereby generalizing the previously studied case of Einstein-Maxwell theory with no boundary vacuum. This class encompasses all vacua of Einstein-Maxwell-Dirac theory that possess both left and right fermion charges. By explicitly calculating the surface term of the Noether charge for these vacua, we show that they satisfy the same conditions required to form an Virasoro algebra as their electromagnetic counterparts. Finally, we demonstrate that these vacua can be viewed as critical points of a Dirac field defined on the same asymptotic solutions. The existence of these vacua is particularly significant in the context of chiral symmetry breaking within the AdS$_2$/CFT$_1$ duality. The results presented herein provide a detailed characterization of such a scenario.

Deep learning models have recently demonstrated significant potential for analyzing DNA sequences. Nevertheless, creating custom models often demands extensive manual feature engineering and domain-specific DNA data curation. This study investigates whether standard, off-the-shelf deep learning models utilizing one-hot encoded nucleotide sequences can effectively address common DNA sequence analysis challenges. We evaluate both sequence-agnostic approaches and those incorporating specific pre-training strategies for DNA to determine if they yield superior performance. Through an extensive comparison across multiple tasks and datasets, the research highlights the significant capabilities of general-purpose deep learning models when applied to DNA analysis without task-specific modifications. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the distinct advantages of these models in DNA sequence analysis stem from the encoding of higher-order DNA pattern information within Stacked Denoising Autoencoders and embedding techniques derived from DNA-specific pre-training. This line of research is anticipated to facilitate significant advancements in DNA analysis for bioinformatics and computational biology fields. The source code and datasets are accessible at https://github.com/taehyungkim1201/DNA-Representation-Learning. Additionally, an interactive web application for exploring one-hot DNA pattern representations has been developed and is available at https://dna-representation-learning.net. Building upon the group conservation analysis for viscous fluid dynamics presented in Part I, this study extends the research by investigating the conservation laws associated with high-speed compressible fluids, specifically within the context of compressible Navier-Stokes equations. The analysis explores solution invariance properties under a group of transformations that include space and time translations, the Lorentz transformation, rotation, the Galilei transformation, translation in the specific entropy, as well as transformations regarding density, enthalpy, and pressure. Notably, the Lorentz transformation indicates Freidman's conservation law, a principle recognized as the conservation of Euler's invariant. Furthermore, the study examines the relative entropy production rate derived from the compressible Navier-Stokes equations and its connection to the conservation law under entropy transformation, demonstrating an entropic conservation law for isentropic flow within the compressible Navier-Stokes framework. Ultimately, these findings contribute to an organized understanding of conservation principles in viscous fluid dynamics, as previously analyzed in Part I. These results also offer valuable insights for formulating conservation laws across various fields of fluid mechanics, including gas dynamics, viscous fluid mechanics, and hydrodynamics. Additionally, the research addresses the formulation of conservation laws for the conservation of mass, momentum, energy, and entropy in viscous fluid systems. Finally, the analysis identifies new conservation laws for compressible Navier-Stokes equations and establishes new invariant solutions for the Lorentz transformation. These contributions address several open problems previously identified in the literature. Specifically, the new conservation laws identified here provide a foundation for further research into conservation law formulation, while the invariant solutions offer a starting point for solving systems of nonlinear partial differential equations. Additionally, the invariance properties of the Lorentz transformation derived in this paper offer valuable insights for advancing the field of fluid mechanics. Keywords: Group analysis, conservation law, viscous fluid dynamics, compressible Navier-Stokes equations, Lorentz transformation.

This paper introduces a novel convolutional network architecture designed for image classification that incorporates orientation into the convolution operation. We propose a new convolutional kernel definition that convolves two matrices using their elements as complex numbers, enabling the preservation of orientation. Additionally, we incorporate a mechanism to reset the orientation of convolved matrices, ensuring the network can still solve orientation-sensitive tasks. Experiments conducted on two synthetic benchmarks and one natural image dataset demonstrate that our network effectively learns to utilize orientation for image classification. Notably, in certain cases, it surpasses a standard convolutional network that ignores orientation. The network is expected to be valuable for addressing other orientation-sensitive challenges. Tessellating irregular surfaces with regular quad meshes presents significant challenges. This cost-effective method for modeling irregular geometry involves partitioning the surface into an "inner" area covered by a regular coarse grid and a "boundary" zone represented by quads of varying orders. Higher orders are assigned to boundary quads based on the count of inner grid elements they adjoin; for instance, quads surrounding a single inner element are given first order, while those surrounding four inner elements receive fourth order. This paper introduces a novel approach employing Integer Linear Optimization to generate high-order coarse quad grids on CAD models, a critical step for optimizing the finite element analysis of CAD-based structures. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method yields quads with superior orders compared to standard CAD tools. Additionally, the feasibility of the method is confirmed through a finite element analysis case study. Ultimately, this paper outlines a practical and efficient strategy for high-order quad discretization, a requirement increasingly demanded by the advancements in finite element analysis and computational fluid dynamics. Specifically, this method is highly relevant to modern computational fluid dynamics, where the need for unstructured, high-order meshes is growing. Furthermore, the method is versatile and can be extended to other irregular geometries, such as irregular polyhedral meshes. Finally, the source code for the method is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan123/ILOQuads. The code is written in Julia and utilizes the IPOPT and Cbc solvers from the CPLEX CP modeler. Future work will explore parallelizing the method and developing user-friendly interfaces for CAD software like SolidWorks and CATIA. This paper derives analytical formulas for the expected values and variances of the sample correlation coefficient across all 72 distinct data arrangements for $n=4$. These formulas are extended to generalize expressions for all $k!$ possible arrangements of data for any sample size $n$. The study introduces novel analytical formulas for the $j$th moment of the $k!$ arrangements, where the first four moments yield the mean, variance, skewness, and kurtosis. Additionally, new formulas for the cross-moment between two arrangements are presented, with specific applications detailing the moments and variance of the $U$ statistic for all $2k$ arrangements of two datasets. This approach introduces a new moment-based test for the equality of two correlation populations, offering an alternative to Fisher's $z$-transformation method. Finally, Monte Carlo simulations are employed to validate the derived analytical results. The paper concludes by suggesting two alternative tests: a moment test for $n > 10$ and a Monte Carlo test suitable for $n < 10$. Furthermore, an R package named `CorrelationTest` is introduced, which implements both the Monte Carlo and analytical tests for arrangements of datasets. This resource includes an online calculator for arrangements up to $n=7$, allowing users to input datasets and obtain arrangements alongside their correlation coefficients, expected values, variance, and associated tests. The package also provides an arrangement test based on kurtosis. Ultimately, this work establishes a foundation for exploring analytical and Monte Carlo solutions regarding arrangements of datasets through datasets of increasing size. All formulas, calculations, and simulations were performed using R version 4.2.1. The accompanying R code is available at: https://github.com/rajan-kumar/CorrelationTest. Recently, researchers have explored generating post-hoc alternative explanations for recommendation models. LIME-RS is a prominent method in this category that creates local surrogate models to identify influential items and signal your system. However, we observe that LIME-RS' surrogates often lack commitment, meaning they fail to consistently determine the most impactful items, which undermines their reliability. Additionally, we demonstrate that LIME-RS' surrogates exhibit stability issues, as similar inputs can yield vastly different results within the method. To address these problems, we introduce the Graph Explainability with Learned Mask (GELM) framework, which builds upon LIME-RS. GELM constructs a bipartite graph connecting samples to items, where the edges represent the masks learned by LIME-RS. We then train and evaluate graph neural networks using these edges as input features to generate explanations. Experiments across three standard benchmark datasets show that GELM significantly outperforms LIME-RS in terms of stability and commitment. Furthermore, we demonstrate that GELM naturally generates counterfactual explanations, allowing us to assess its capacity to provide actionable feedback for users. Finally, we present a user study involving 20 participants to evaluate the method's effectiveness in a real-world setting. The results indicate that our approach generates high-quality explanations that users find more actionable. To our knowledge, this is the first framework to jointly address the commitment and stability challenges of LIME-RS within a single model. In the pursuit of efficient thermoelectric materials, a fundamental principle dictates that heterointerfaces must firmly pin the Fermi level within the host bandgap to prevent carrier generation through phonon-assisted thermal excitation from the conduction band into the valence band. This study investigates near-surface ultra-narrow gap InAs quantum wells doped with Ga and graded interfaces as strategies to anchor the Fermi level. Using *in situ* X-ray photoemission spectroscopy to track interface pinning across various growth temperatures, we observed that incorporating Ga into the quantum well lowers the quantum confined Stark effect, thereby raising the Fermi level relative to the conduction band edge. Furthermore, graded interfaces serve to pin the Fermi level within the bandgap, with this pinning effect becoming more pronounced as the growth temperature increases. These findings offer critical insights for the design of high-performance quantum well heterostructures intended for thermoelectric applications. Notably, our results align with previous observations in Gr/InAs quantum wells, where the narrow bandgap of graphene facilitates effective Fermi level pinning. Ultimately, the ultimate pinning of the Fermi level in near-surface quantum well heterostructures is governed by the interplay between quantum confinement, the specific material bandgap, and the nature of the quantum well capping layer. Finally, we introduce a novel dataset, ProDex, designed to assess the resilience-performance trade-off across varying resolutions. ProDex offers a unique feature by providing paired datasets with identical model capacities, enabling a direct comparison of regional versus global representations. We also examine how this choice affects training dynamics. The results and analysis are expected to guide future efforts in improving the resilience of visual models. The young AU Microscopii (AU Mic) system is frequently cited as evidence for the survivability of exoplanets around active M stars. This study examines the atmospheric stability of AU Mic b and c by correlating their transit times with stellar activity and UV variability. We analyzed 11 AU Mic transits from the GALEX archive, separating them into a dormant phase (2005–2014) and an eruptive phase (2015–2019). Our results show that the AU Dic transit (2017.461) occurred during a significant X-ray and UV eruptive event, while the AU Lib transit (2019.248) took place in a relatively quiet period. Using high-resolution far-UV spectroscopy from HST/STROBEs and IUE, we examined the AU Dic event to identify potential atmospheric escape signatures. We detected a single, highly ionized carbon line (C VI) at 50.4 Å, which we attribute to the highly active AU Mic star rather than planetary outflow. Additionally, a broad emission feature at 112.8 Å, linked to O II, was observed during this event. Our analysis indicates that the O II emission is also a stellar signature, likely arising from the hot coronal plasma typical of AU Mic. Finally, we compared the activity levels at the times of AU Lib and AU Dic with those of other transiting planets around M stars. We found that both exoplanets traversed relatively quiet regions, a trend consistent with other studies. However, we note that the AU Mic system lacks the robust data required to definitively confirm or refute the presence of a protective magnetic shield. Consequently, we conclude that the current evidence is inconclusive regarding the true resilience of exoplanets to stellar activity. Future observations of AU Mic transits are necessary to better understand the interaction between AU Mic and its exoplanets. This research is based on data from the GALEX, HST, and IUE archives. This study examines the radiation response drag force acting on a subrelativistic (low-velocity) charged macro-particle moving through a resistive continuous medium, such as air under standard conditions. The research establishes a local time-dependent framework for the dielectric response of this medium. Within the slowly varying regime, the dielectric function $\varepsilon(\omega)$ is approximated as $\varepsilon(\omega) \simeq 1 + \frac{\omega_{p}^{2}}{\omega (\omega - i\tau^{-1})}$ (with $\tau^{-1} \gg \omega_{p}^{2}$), where $\omega_{p}$ represents the plasma frequency and $\tau^{-1}$ denotes the relaxation frequency. These parameters are linked to the density and transport cross-section of the charged particles constituting the medium. Analytically, the radiation response drag coefficient is determined as $\kappa = \frac{\pi e^{2}}{3c} \omega_{p}^{2} \tau$, where $e$ is the elementary charge and $c$ is the speed of light. For low humidity, low-pressure air at standard temperature, $\kappa$ ranges from $10^{-17}$ to $10^{-19}$ CGSE units. Additionally, numerical simulations were conducted to calculate the complex complex refractive index $n(\omega) = \sqrt{\varepsilon(\omega)}$, the spectral energy loss rate $-\frac{dE}{dx}d\omega$, and the differential energy loss rate $\frac{dE}{dy}$. The results indicate that the substance's response becomes negligible at distances greater than $\tau v$ from the macro-particle, where $v$ is its velocity. Finally, the potential application of this resistive drag force in particle accelerators is explored. In classification tasks, the closest neighbor method is a widely used statistical technique for assigning labels to new data points. However, its effectiveness relies heavily on the assumption that training and testing datasets are evenly distributed; violations of this assumption can severely degrade performance. To address the challenge of distributional imbalance, this study introduces the Uneven data distribution (UED) metric to quantify the disparity in distribution patterns between two datasets. Subsequently, we propose the Closest Neighbor using Uneven data (CN-U) approach, which addresses distributional bias by selectively sampling from the larger dataset to construct a more representative training set. We evaluate the classification accuracy of CN-U against the standard Closest Neighbor and K-Means algorithms using a publicly available dataset. Furthermore, to ensure a fair comparison, we demonstrate how to generate paired datasets with uneven distributions via a simulation-based approach. The comprehensive analysis of these uneven pairs aims to establish a standardized benchmark for measuring classification accuracy in future studies. The associated software package, UEDdata, is available at https://github.com/robertol/ueddata. This framework is intended to serve as a foundational tool for developing statistical methods that can adapt to uneven distribution patterns. The findings are documented in the paper available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.07105. Additionally, the results regarding distributional unevenness were published in Scientific Reports (2021, 11: 5002), and the sampling techniques for handling uneven distributions have been submitted to Scientific Reports for consideration under the title "A sampling approach to handle uneven distributions in classification tasks." Utilizing the same sample selection and follow-up strategies as Paper I, we have confirmed 1,010 quasars, including 40 new detections at redshifts $z>2.5$. These findings are derived from spectroscopic observations using the 3.9-meter Anglo-Australian Telescope (16 quasars), William Herschel Telescope (13), and Liverpool Telescope (371), alongside optical spectroscopy from the William Herschel Maun Observatory (351) and the National Observatory of the University of Chile (247). Additionally, we report on 10 quasars previously known, which were re-observed to extend the wavelength range and confirm their high-redshift classification. We present an experimental investigation into charge tunneling between a quantum dot and a superconducting reservoir using radio-frequency gate sensing. This study examines how macroscopic quantum phenomena, specifically the proximity effect and charge parity, emerge within the dot as a function of the superconductor's induced gap. This process is influenced by variations in system parameters, such as the dot's level structure and tunnel coupling strength. By analyzing the dot's response to environmental gate-sensing perturbations, we uncover novel aspects of charge transfer to the superconductor, including the formation of Andreev bound states and charge poisoning effects. Furthermore, our findings highlight that the charge parity gap exhibits a weak temperature dependence and remains distinct from the Andreev gap. These insights into dot-superconductor systems can facilitate the development of novel qubits and quantum sensors capable of detecting sub-gap excitations. Additionally, we propose a theoretical framework to interpret the experimental data, offering a pathway to investigate the quantum nature of the charge in this system. Finally, our results suggest promising avenues for future research, such as investigating the impact of gate-sensing on the evolution of dot excitations and exploring the potential for quantum-sensing applications.
