This research investigates the solvability of multivalued conservation laws within the class $L^\infty$. For a given right-hand side, we define a class of multivalued contractions that maintain the framework of classical single-valued methods while accommodating a broad spectrum of shock multivaluedness. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for right-hand sides satisfying a specific contractions condition, these multivalued contractions provide solutions to the multivalued problem. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, we apply it to two examples from different physical domains, where the multivalued contractions effectively manage both multivalued and equimultivalued phenomena. Additionally, this technique enables the extension of two important results from single-valued conservation laws to the multivalued context. Finally, we explore methods for converting single-valued weak solutions with defects into multivalued weak solutions and present numerical experiments to illustrate these findings. The proposed approach is notably applicable to multidimensional conservation laws. Overall, the work enhances the methodology for constructing contractions, broadens the spectrum of phenomena that can be analyzed, and widens the applicability of the contractions condition. Single-view 3D Perpetual View Generation (3DPG) is a widely studied computer vision task focused on synthesizing novel views from a single image. While recent diffusion-based approaches have significantly advanced this field, they often suffer from unreliable performance due to generated artifacts and lack of controllability. To address these limitations, we introduce DiffDreamer, a method that enhances both the reliability and controllability of single-view 3DPG. First, we develop a conditional diffusion model that integrates structural cues—specifically camera parameters and sky-free images—to produce high-quality, high-fidelity sky-free novel perspectives. Second, to boost generalization, we propose a context-aware training strategy that incorporates surrounding images alongside the central input. Extensive experiments demonstrate that integrating this training approach with a state-of-the-art conditional system, Dreamer, yields superior results. Furthermore, our ablation studies confirm that the conditional diffusion system outperforms existing methods when using only image or corner patches as conditions, achieving higher quality and greater controllability. Finally, we release a large-scale dataset comprising 1,000 scenes with paired images and corresponding corners to support future research. Project page: https://dreamer.mmu.edu.cn/diffdreamer. This work presents a new framework that relies exclusively on data for the analysis, prediction, enhancement, and control of nonlinear distributed systems exhibiting spatially diverse behaviors. The approach utilizes the canonical representation of nonlinear data-driven models alongside stochastic estimation techniques. As a proof of concept, the study applies this framework to the prediction, analysis, control, and spatial enhancement of the widely studied Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) epidemic model. Because the framework is purely data-centric, it avoids the need for system identification, thereby bypassing the inherent challenges associated with identifying nonlinear distributed systems. Furthermore, the methodology does not require knowledge of the underlying physical mechanisms driving the processes. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is validated through numerical experiments. Keywords: data-driven, control, analysis, prediction, nonlinear distributed systems, spatially heterogeneous systems, nonlinear data-driven models, stochastic estimation, SIS epidemic model. Distributed systems encompass various real-world applications, such as traffic networks, biological and social systems, and environmental phenomena. These systems are characterized by their spatial extent and the distinct behaviors arising from interactions between components and their environment. Distributed systems can be broadly classified into two categories: linear systems, which display spatially homogeneous behaviors, and nonlinear systems, which exhibit spatially heterogeneous behaviors. This research aims to address spatially heterogeneous nonlinear systems, which are significantly more complex than their linear counterparts. This complexity stems not only from nonlinearity but also from the absence of a general theory capable of deriving unified analytical and computational solutions for spatially heterogeneous nonlinear systems. A primary challenge in this domain is the absence of a unified framework that integrates analysis, estimation, control, and enhancement into a single, scalable solution. Existing literature predominantly focuses on either traditional control (estimation and feedback) or model-based approaches [1–11]. In contrast, this work proposes a data-driven approach that unifies analysis, estimation, control, and spatial enhancement into a single, scalable solution. Coating fibers with liquid offers numerous practical benefits, making various methods to enhance coating efficiency and reduce costs highly desirable. One promising approach involves introducing axial slip at the solid-liquid interface to accelerate the breaking of an annular liquid column, thereby increasing the frequency of droplet formation. This study presents an initial theoretical investigation into the slip-augmented Rayleigh-Plateau instability of a liquid layer surrounding an elastic fiber. The analysis reveals that wall slip reduces the critical Weber number required for instability, thereby accelerating droplet formation. However, the wall shear stress induced by slip also has the potential to counteract this effect. Consequently, our findings suggest an optimal level of wall slip; exceeding this optimum may diminish the slip-induced acceleration. These results are anticipated to be applicable to a broad range of solid-liquid configurations. Furthermore, the numerical findings regarding the impact of wall slip on drop formation offer valuable insights for designing more efficient coating processes. This work establishes a Lipschitz stability result for the Hunter-Saxton formula, which is the evolution equation describing equilibrium states of plasma fields in low-dimensional plasmas. By applying an explicit solution linked to geodesic flows on the Grassmannian, we demonstrate that sufficiently close initial data yield sufficiently close equilibrium time-dependencies, measured in appropriate norms. Notably, these norms are intrinsic to the geometric formulation of the Hunter-Saxton problem. Additionally, we investigate various stability nuances regarding initial conditions that are not sufficiently regular. We examine whether the Hunter-Saxton time-dependencies remain "sufficiently" close when initial data are perturbed, whether the convergence to periodic data ensures stability, and whether the geometric nature of the problem sheds light on the long-term behavior of plasma fields. Finally, we explore how these findings address the question of whether the Hunter-Saxton equation is, in fact, a genuine plasma model. Specifically, we analyze whether its solutions remain "plausibly physical," meaning they stay bounded within the space of measures. We address this by proving theorems regarding the return of initial data to an $\varepsilon$-ball around itself within any given time frame, provided data are chosen "sufficiently close." We also discuss whether these theorems hold for any given $\varepsilon$ or only for sufficiently small values, whether "closeness" is defined relative to the $L^2$ norm, and explore whether these theorems can be derived through geometric methods rather than variational ones. Through this exploration, we demonstrate that these theorems are indeed valid in the sense intended by the plasma model, with the $L^2$ norm being no less "sufficiently close" than anticipated. We conclude by reflecting on whether these results are sufficient to validate the Hunter-Saxton model and whether a geometric proof is feasible. Our proof relies on the explicit solution of Hunter and Saxton, which is well-documented in the literature, though we note that it may not be immediately obvious to physicists. Given the Hunter-Saxton equation's popularity in mathematical literature, our reliance on such a well-known solution might seem peculiar. However, this should not be surprising, as Hunter and Saxton themselves solved the equation in 1992. We anticipate that our findings will contribute to a deeper understanding of the plasma model and its connection to the geometric formulation of the Hunter-Saxton problem. Ultimately, we contend that our results provide strong evidence supporting the Hunter-Saxton model

The primary challenge in scoliosis assessment via robotic ultrasound (US) remains the lack of a robust, reliable grading system. Furthermore, there is limited evidence regarding the reliability of the ultrasound image acquisition process itself; thus, evaluating the reliability of manual scoliosis imaging using ultrasound is essential to ensure the validity of the subsequent grading process. This study aimed to assess the reliability of manual scoliosis imaging using ultrasound by examining both the intra- and inter-rater reliability of the translation (T) angle measurement technique across three participant groups: 20 children with scoliosis, 20 children with normal posture, and 20 pregnant women. Ultrasound images were captured manually by three pediatricians and three obstetricians, respectively, and analyzed by two engineers. Results showed high intra-rater and inter-rater reproducibility for the T angle in children with scoliosis and in pregnant women (both spiny and abdominal), as well as in children with a normal posture. Conversely, low intra-rater and inter-rater reliability was observed when measuring the T angle in pregnant women using the abdominal approach. These findings indicate that manual scoliosis imaging using ultrasound is reliable for the population under study, provided that appropriate scanning protocols are established. However, due to the significant difference in spinal curvature between scoliosis and pregnancy, ultrasound imaging is not recommended for assessing scoliosis in pregnant women. Future research should focus on developing accurate scoliosis evaluation methods using robotic ultrasound. Additionally, given the significant variation between manual image acquisition and the use of a dedicated robotic system, further studies are needed to compare the advantages and limitations of manual versus robotic ultrasound imaging for scoliosis evaluation. Ultimately, these insights will facilitate the creation of an accurate scoliosis assessment tool based on robotic ultrasound technology. This study evaluates a technique for mediating content-based length changes in synthetic speech through median-based time scaling. The research questions whether a non-statistical, median-driven scaling approach can effectively produce natural-sounding speech with varied durations and how the medians of specific acoustic features influence the perceptual quality of such naturalness. The findings indicate that the proposed median time scaling method can generate noticeable length variations in speech without degrading its naturalness. Furthermore, it demonstrates that decreasing the values of formant frequencies results in speech that becomes more childlike and less so when the medians of these specific features are increased. This paper introduces an innovative framework for scaling duration to achieve non-statistical, controlled length alterations in speech with adjustable acoustic characteristics, utilizing a non-statistical, median-guided time scaling strategy. Potential applications include applications in assistive technologies for individuals with speech production impairments, such as those with Cerebral Palsy or Slurred Speech. The proposed method offers a non-statistical, controlled, and deterministic feature-level approach to analyze the impact of length variations on the articulatory characteristics of speech. Additionally, this approach provides a viable solution for natural, length-variable, synthetic speech generation via non-statistical, time-scale invariant median time scaling. The significance of this work lies in its ability to address the challenge of creating length-variable synthetic speech that remains perceptually natural under deterministic, non-statistical time scaling. By employing a non-statistical, median-driven time scaling function, the study investigates how specific feature-level characteristics change with duration and demonstrates how these alterations affect the articulatory features of speech. The results confirm that a non-statistical, deterministic time scaling function can successfully produce natural-sounding, length-variable speech. This work holds significance for natural speech synthesis, offering a viable solution for generating synthetic speech with controlled, non-statistical, length-variable, perceptually natural, and speech-parametric properties using a median-based, non-statistical, deterministic time scaling function. The method enables the creation of synthetic speech with length variations and imparts a secondary articulatory characteristic to the output. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that applying the proposed median time scaling to real speech signals can effectively simulate childlike or slurred speech. The significance of this work extends to various domains, including speech impairment assistance, natural speech synthesis, synthetic speech recognition, speech enhancement, speech compression, and speech enhancement. The median-based, non-statistical, deterministic time scaling function serves as a viable solution for natural, length-variable speech synthesis. With the increasing popularity of online social media, users frequently engage in hate speech, making it crucial for platforms to monitor and eliminate such content to maintain a healthy digital environment. Although numerous methods have been developed to detect hate speech, this study identifies three primary limitations in current research: (1) most approaches rely on labeled datasets, which are expensive and time-consuming to create; (2) information extracted from text is often inconsistent and unstructured, leading to poor generalization across different domains; and (3) most techniques depend on word embeddings, which fail to capture rare words that are, however, significant for hate speech identification. To address these challenges, this paper introduces an automatic feature extraction framework that generates domain-independent features to minimize manual labeling efforts. By employing features that remain consistent across domains, the proposed method enables robust generalization when trained on one domain and tested on others. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both single-domain training and cross-domain generalization scenarios. Furthermore, the paper includes a detailed analysis of the features identified as most effective for distinguishing hate speech. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekgupta10/HateSpeechDetection. Additionally, a new multi-lingual dataset has been released for research purposes, available at https://github.com/abhishekgupta10/MLDataset. Finally, this work introduces a novel evaluation metric designed to assess cross-domain generalization performance. The underlying dataset was previously featured in our IWCI 2020 paper. This work investigates the sharing of features within the subnetworks of the MIMO architecture, where multiple shared estimators are employed. The study analyzes the impact of various feature sharing strategies on both the training and test errors of the overall system. Additionally, topological properties of the error landscape created by different sharing schemes are examined, and algorithms leveraging this insight are developed and proposed. We relate these approaches to model compression techniques that utilize distillation methods. Through a combination of theoretical analysis and simulations, we demonstrate that certain feature sharing configurations enable MIMO structures to outperform single estimator benchmarks. Furthermore, we identify that estimators within the MIMO framework can collectively encode distinctive traits and capabilities, offering valuable insights for future research on the behavior of deep neural networks. Finally, we show that training subnetworks via knowledge distillation results in a more efficient landscape, thereby facilitating rapid training and highly performant models. Finally, we highlight that the proposed methods offer significant advantages for large-scale scenarios, such as autonomous driving. Specifically, multi-sensor data fusion using MIMO and feature sharing through distillation has been applied to object detection and segmentation tasks on a large urban driving dataset. Our results indicate substantial improvements in accuracy and speed for model training compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches. Additionally, it is established that this technique allows for the construction of more compact models that maintain competitive performance relative to current state-of-the-art solutions. The code for this work is accessible at https://github.com/sergey-aleksandrov/MIMO-Feature-Sharing. Keywords: Deep Learning, Feature Sharing, Knowledge Distillation, Error Landscape, Topology Optimization.

Historical documents are primarily preserved in textual and image formats, with these images often collected into datasets for digitization or semantic tasks like classification, detection, or segmentation. While related datasets exist, there has been no prior review specifically dedicated to them. This paper addresses that gap by examining existing work. It analyzes 80 historical image datasets, categorized into three groups: those focused on handwriting styles, those containing various document types, and those providing general historical imagery. The study highlights the advantages and constraints of each dataset by detailing their contents and statistical properties. Additionally, it outlines common tasks performed on these datasets and presents benchmark results for leading methods. Finally, the paper discusses future challenges and opportunities for historical image datasets. Given the scarcity of such reviews, this work aims to offer valuable insights for the community, particularly regarding the selection of datasets for specific research tasks. It also underscores the need for more digitization efforts to expand collections and the establishment of standard benchmarks to ensure fair comparisons and promote reproducibility. Ultimately, the paper seeks to foster collaboration among historians, data curators, and computer vision researchers to enhance historical image datasets. Recent years have seen a notable increase in research concerning health status transitions and disease recurrence. However, analyzing these processes is complicated by the complex dependencies between an individual's health state and their disease history. This paper introduces an examination methodology designed to handle high-dimensional, dependent time-to-event data. We demonstrate that the examination distance offers significant analytical benefits, including the ability to identify representative health states, construct algorithms for classifying unknown states, and estimate the probability of state membership. Additionally, we propose an index of analysis utility to evaluate various state space discretizations. The study includes a theoretical overview of the methodology, provides a detailed case study analysis, and results are supported by an open-source software implementation. Specifically, we applied this framework to high-dimensional time-to-event data from patients who have experienced myocardial infarction. By analyzing multiple time-to-event variables, we were able to project the expected sequence of future health states, thereby gaining insights into the typical progression of disease recurrence. These findings have the potential to inform health policy and improve the quality of clinical care. Furthermore, we developed software that enables users to visualize transitions across different health states, offering clinical insights into the relationships between various states. This enhanced software implementation is available at https://github.com/riken-irap/mse. Finally, we illustrate how to analyze expected life course paths using the examination, presenting a tool that allows researchers to visualize sample members' life trajectories. This feature was also implemented in the software and can be accessed at https://github.com/riken-irap/mse. Both software packages are released under the GNU General Public License v3.0. Finally, we emphasize that health state variables are discovered through data-driven approaches, offering a complementary alternative to methods that rely on domain knowledge. In this regard, we propose that multiple examination results can serve as a foundation for defining meaningful health states. To demonstrate this, we present software that integrates multiple examination, clustering, and deep learning to automatically identify states, with the source code released under the GNU General Public License v3.0 at https://github.com/riken-irap/mse. We present a quadrature approach to solve integral equations governing the continuum spectrum of relativistic and non-relativistic electrons interacting with molecules. Our focus is specifically on the Gaussian orbitals (GO) basis. We demonstrate that the traditional "delta-function approximation" proves inadequate for high-Z atoms and continues to cause non-physical discontinuities in the electron propagator. To address this, we employ a multi-site quadrature (MSQ) that utilizes the complete 4D momentum space. The outcomes of our MSQ method align with previous findings by various groups; however, our technique offers greater generality and accuracy. Furthermore, we show that the MSQ approach can be implemented in a fully parallelized and automated framework, making it suitable for molecular applications. We have integrated our MSQ method into the Dirac-OCC program. Additionally, we illustrate how the method can be utilized to determine the molecular density of states. Finally, we apply the method to investigate the valence and deep-inelastic ionization of molecular hydrogen. These calculations reveal that the ionization continuum is characterized by a highly structured threshold region, a result that MSQ captures with high precision. The accuracy and generality of our method are validated by the close agreement of the computed spectra with experimental data. The source code for the MSQ method is publicly accessible on GitHub. This study examines the decision problem of determining whether a graph $G$ possesses a resolving set $R$ composed exclusively of vertices within specific pre-defined resolving sets for smaller components of $G$. The analysis focuses on components generated by removing vertices from $G$, particularly those forming feedback vertex sets, as well as vertices constituting modular decompositions and optimal ODD-WIDTH reductions. Consequently, this approach yields several new fixed-parameter tractable (fpt) algorithms for global decision problems on graphs with bounded feedback, bounded ODD-WIDTH, or bounded feedback + TREewidth, utilizing input-independent additive terms. Additionally, for the SET COVER WITH PREDEFINED UNIVERSES problem, which models many graph properties, we establish fixed-parameter algorithms parameterized by feedback, ODD-WIDTH, and TREwidth. Specifically, we demonstrate fpt-reducibility between SET COVER WITH PREDEFINED UNIVERSES and the questions of whether a graph is FeEDBACK-VERTEX-SET free, has bounded ODD-WIDTH, or is bounded in both FeEDBACK-VERTEX-SET and TREewidth. Furthermore, we prove that SET COVER WITH PREDEFINED UNIVERSES is W[1]-complete parameterized by TREewidth. Notably, none of these complexity results depend on specific graph parameters or the size of the SET COVER instance. Finally, the work concludes with hardness proofs for SET COVER WITH PREDEFINED UNIVERSES when parameterized by PATHWIDTH and COTRADIWIDTH. Overall, FeEDBACK-VERTEX-SET and ODD-WIDTH emerge as the strongest parameters regarding both complexity and practicality. Finally, the findings are extended to variable SET and PARAMETER UNIVERSES, resulting in fpt-reducibility to FeEDBACK-VERTEX-SET and TREewidth for the former, and to ODD-WIDTH, FeEDBACK-VERTEX-SET, and TREewidth for the latter. In the variable universe scenario, FeEDBERS and ODD-WIDTH exhibit the same complexity as PATHWIDTH. Additionally, FeEDBACK-VERTEX-SET achieves fixed-parameter linear time complexity in this context. However, no equivalent complexity characterization exists for SET COVER WITH PREDEFINED UNIVERSES under the PARAMETER UNIVERSE setting. Additionally, no fixed-parameter linear-time algorithm is known for FeEDBACK-VERTEX-SET in this case. We present the concept of authority frameworks, which can be viewed as a directed analog to topological frameworks. These structures are deeply connected to continuous dirmaps, which serve as a generalization of continuous functions between directed spaces, mirroring how standard functions relate to topological maps between such spaces. Additionally, we explore the category-theoretic implications regarding directed homomorphisms and discuss various properties and constructions associated with authority frameworks. Specifically, I focus my study on the properties of framework subgraphs and their relationship with subframeworks within directed spatial metric spaces. I provide a concrete example involving a hypergraph model designed to represent directed spatial metric frameworks, demonstrating that this framework exhibits diverse spatial characteristics. Finally, I examine frameworks exhibiting periodic spatial properties and their associated hypergraph models, discussing their relevance to network analysis. This work serves as a foundation for future research into framework properties, particularly in the context of networks, time networks, and spatial networks. Furthermore, I address several open problems concerning framework properties and their applications within graph theory. Last but not least, I highlight recent advancements in research on frameworks and their contributions to the field of directed topology. Specifically, I investigate frameworks derived from triangulations of directed manifolds, deriving properties related to their subframeworks. I also establish a comparison theorem between the homotopy groups of these frameworks and those of their associated directed manifolds. These findings lay the groundwork for subsequent research on oriented spatial networks, spatially distributed systems, and their temporal dynamics. In this study, I provide the initial step toward a theory of authority frameworks, a theory with significant potential applications in various scientific disciplines, including ecology, economics, and computer science. I anticipate that these findings will serve as a basis for further research into authority frameworks and their contributions to diverse fields. Specifically, I address the challenge of developing a theory of frameworks within directed topological spaces, which forms the basis for the theory of hypergraphs in directed topology. This research also addresses the challenge of developing a theory of frameworks in spatially distributed systems, which forms the basis for the study of spatial networks. Spatial networks are essential for addressing issues in ecology, economics, and computer science. I also examine the properties of frameworks within periodic directed manifolds and their applications to periodic spatial networks. Spatially periodic networks are a subject of significant interest in ecology, economics, and computer science. Furthermore, I have developed a theory of framework subgraphs, which forms the basis for the theory of subframeworks in periodic directed manifolds. Utilizing a climate model, we investigated how atmospheric carbon dioxide fluctuations influence the climate of Earth-like planets. Our findings indicate that even with a relatively thin atmosphere, these planets can experience recurrent, intense floods that temporarily raise surface temperatures by several degrees, leading to significant rises in water vapor and the deposition of various condensates. This episodic flooding stems from a feedback loop where higher temperatures allow for greater amounts of carbon dioxide to sublimation from surface dry ice deposits. Although the atmosphere's heat capacity moderates temperature spikes, it does not prevent the simultaneous increase in water vapor. We contend that this mechanism offers a generic explanation for the recurring floods observed in "Polar Night Heatings" on cold Neptune's moon, Triton, and that similar processes could occur on other cold, CO$_2$-rich bodies. Furthermore, even when not directly observable, such atmospheric dynamics could have played a crucial role in prebiotic chemistry on cold Earths. In Earth's distant past, when global temperatures were lower, this mechanism could have facilitated the transient creation of liquid water and a wider range of volatile combinations, thereby expanding the variety of prebiotic reactions. Consequently, we conclude that cold, CO$_2$-rich atmospheres in simulated greenhouse climates are likely to be far more complex than previously assumed. This conclusion is based solely on the application of established physical laws. We also outline the methodologies used to introduce and remove carbon dioxide in our simulations. Finally, we demonstrate that this mechanism may have been responsible for the recurring floods seen in Triton's Polar Night Heatings. The Plio-Neuves event, a geologically recent series of floods on Earth, is also examined to assess whether carbon dioxide cycling could have contributed to its occurrence. Ultimately, we show that episodic flooding is a common phenomenon in greenhouse climates, regardless of whether carbon dioxide is introduced artificially or through natural geological processes. This implies that Earth's carbon dioxide history may have been more complex than currently believed, with carbon cycling potentially operating at much lower temperatures than previously thought. Additionally, we explore the possibility that this mechanism could have been active on Earth during the Snowball Earth episodes. While not conclusively proven, our results suggest that episodic flooding could have occurred during these periods, potentially influencing the evolution of life. The broader implications of these findings extend to the study of exoplanets. In summary, we have shown that carbon dioxide cycling can drive complex, dynamic weather patterns in simulated greenhouse climates, challenging the traditional view of such atmospheres as static. We present the higher-spin generalization of the twistor-space extension of self-dual Yang-Mills theory, framing it as a holomorphic Chern-Simons theory defined on the twistor space of complex Minkowski space. This framework adheres to the master equation derived from the classical component of the QFT/AQFT asymptotic symmetry algebra of 4d self-dual Yang-Mills theory. Additionally, we explore an even broader class of models that incorporate a higher-spin field theory on the bulk complex Minkowski space, thereby extending the theory into higher-twistor spaces. These models are likewise governed by the master equation of the classical asymptotic symmetry algebra. As anticipated, these theories feature infinite-spin towers characterized by scalar fields and holomorphic self-dual curvatures across varying spin ranks. Furthermore, we examine the discrete symmetries of complex Minkowski space and their corresponding actions within these models. Leveraging established results, we demonstrate that our models can be constructed from bulk models defined on higher-Fredholm twistor spaces through a twistor space transformation. This indicates that these theories are not merely extensions of self-dual Yang-Mills theory but represent a more fundamental category of theories that include a bulk higher-spin component. We also investigate the actions of complexification and various discrete symmetries on both the self-dual Yang-Mills and higher-spin extended models, highlighting the non-trivial implications regarding reality conditions and the relationship between self-dual Yang-Mills and its higher-spin generalizations. Finally, we connect these models to the holomorphic Chern-Simons theory of Deformable Calabi-Yau 3-folds.

Keywords: Complex Minkowski space, Higher-spin extensions of self-dual Yang-Mills theory, Twistor space, Complexification, Discrete symmetries, Complexification, Discrete symmetries, Deformable Calabi-Yau 3-fold.

Deep neural networks have become essential for numerous computer vision applications, including medical image analysis. However, their high computational cost and susceptibility to overfitting, particularly with limited training data, remain significant hurdles. This study addresses these issues by introducing a novel label renovation mechanism aimed at enhancing robustness against label noise in automated medical image categorization. The proposed approach integrates two components: first, a statistics-driven signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) metric that quantifies the discriminative power of local features within medical images; second, a Bayesian framework that utilizes this SNR metric to probabilistically adjust noisy labels during training. Experiments were conducted on two public medical image categorization datasets, which include annotated CT and MRI scans containing signs of intracranial hemorrhage. The results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a 1.5% improvement in classification accuracy compared to standard fine-tuning techniques. The method is available at https://github.com/ahmedhassan123456/SNR-MECHANISM. Furthermore, the source code and data can be accessed via https://zenodo.org/record/6998001. The paper was submitted to IEEE TMI.

This paper establishes a class of inequalities concerning estimates for the norm of an interpolation operator. Specifically, let $S$ denote a linear interpolation operator mapping $C^{n}[a,b]$ into $C^{n-1}[a,b]$. If $S$ adheres to the Peano property and the principal term of the local asymptotic expansion of the remainder $f- Sf$ possesses a continuous derivative, then the following inequality holds:
\[\|S\|_{C^{n}[a,b]\rightarrow C^{n-1}[a,b]}\leq
\left\|\frac{\partial^{k}P_{0}(t,0)}{\partial t^{k}}\right|_{[a,b]}\]
where $k$ represents the order of this principal term, $P_{0}(t,r)$ is the kernel function for the principal term as a function of the interpolation parameter $r$, and $k$ is defined as $\min\{n,N+1\}$, with $N$ being the degree of precision of $S$. Additionally, several results regarding inequalities for estimates of divided differences are derived. Finally, these inequalities are applied to derive new inequalities for determinants and for integrals involving Bessel functions.
Keywords: Linear interpolation operator, inequality, divided difference, determinant, Bessel function.

This paper demonstrates that for a random walk on a graph, the distinctively defined transition probability matrix generates distinct polynomials when applied to distinct Laplacian matrices of those graphs. Additionally, the transition probability matrix for a related random walk on a graph, along with the corresponding eigenvalues and eigenvectors, is distinctly defined. Since the Laplacian matrix is constructed from the degree diagonal matrix minus the adjacency matrix, we establish distinct formulas for these components specifically for related graphs. These distinctively defined transition probability matrices are subsequently utilized to derive distinct polynomials for graphs where all vertices share an identical degree. Furthermore, we prove distinct theorems regarding the eigenvalues and eigenvectors associated with these distinct polynomials for such graphs. Finally, we present distinct examples of these polynomials for various graphs, including paths, cycles, complete graphs, and stars. We also propose conjectures for Chordal graphs and apply these distinct polynomials to distinguish between simple graphs. The study concludes with several illustrative examples and open problems. Through these distinct definitions of polynomials, eigenvalues, and eigenvectors, we aim to broaden research into transition probability matrices and their applications within graph theory. We invite contributions to this field that leverage these distinct definitions to achieve new results. Timed definitions represent a specialized subset of recursive functions, designed to model program semantics and verify their properties. These definitions are essential for reasoning about programs' time complexity and recurrence relations. While various approaches exist—such as delayed evaluation, recurrences, and real recursion—this paper introduces and implements a time complexity based definition within the HOL Light theorem prover. We demonstrate the syntax and semantics of this defined program through a running example. Furthermore, we establish its basic properties, including termination and linearity, by proving them in HOL. Our approach leverages established tactics and thehol, a recent library for HOL proof assistants that facilitates program analysis. We illustrate this utilization with a program analysis case study. The paper is accompanied by a TimedDefinitions library for HOL Light, which not only supports the statements made in the text but also enables interactive exploration of examples. This library builds upon the tactics provided by thehol. To our knowledge, this work marks the first integration of recurrence-based programs into a HOL library that offers both verification and analysis capabilities. The TimedDefinitions library draws inspiration from various definitions across different authors, such as those found in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].

This study introduces an enhanced version of the self-organization model, which predicts self-similar coherent structures within high-Reynolds-number wall turbulence by utilizing three kinematic constraints derived from mean advection, the return mapping theorem, and the no-penetration boundary condition. This utilization of geometric information represents a significant data-driven modeling strategy, where data informs the design rather than the calibration of the model. Previous iterations of this model, which predicted only the mean velocity profile U+, have been empirically validated and demonstrated to accurately reproduce not only the mean velocity field but also the statistical characteristics of coherent structures, thereby offering a novel data-informed approach. The current work extends the model to simultaneously predict the mean velocity profile, mean Reynolds shear stress, and mean vorticity. By introducing an additional degree of freedom, the model achieves a representation of the mean shear that is equal in magnitude but opposite in sign to the mean Reynolds shear stress. This new configuration enables a U-shape vorticity distribution, thereby reproducing essential elements of the physics governing both the production and diffusion of Reynolds stress. Consequently, the Reynolds shear stress distribution, which shares a similar shape across all Reynolds numbers, is accurately captured. This outcome demonstrates that mean advection, along with separation and no-penetration, contains sufficient information to construct a viable model. Furthermore, the findings suggest that a sufficient number of geometric constraints can be derived to enable the prediction of the energy cascade across all scales. This represents a significant shift from conventional data-driven methods that rely on post-hoc correction of existing models. Overall, this research introduces a novel data-informed paradigm that leverages geometric knowledge to create a viable model capable of predicting both the mean velocity and the energy cascade. This marks a substantial departure from traditional data-driven approaches that depend on the empirical correction of pre-existing models. Finally, the study investigates the relationship between these findings and recent advancements in data-driven control theory. Specifically, it demonstrates that data-informed modeling can be interpreted as data-driven control; in this framework, the existing dynamics are treated as a controller, while the target dynamics are represented by the desired behavior. The resulting data-informed model functions as the optimal closed-loop system. This finding underscores the critical role of geometric constraints in data-driven control and highlights their necessity for developing data-informed models. Ultimately, this leads to a paradigm shift from the traditional reliance on data for empirical correction toward leveraging geometric knowledge to enable data-informed modeling. Extending the polynomial Born-Infeld model established by Manton and Sutcliffe, we introduce the \textit{infant Skyrme model}, a new name for a Lagrangian featuring two dual gauge fields that behave as four-vectors. We demonstrate that this model supports vortices and vortices-on-vortices that are self-dual. The vortices adhere to magnetic monopole principles, while the vortices-on-vortices function as magnetic charges. Our findings indicate that these dual self-dual solutions are stable. Furthermore, we establish that the system conserves both total vorticity and dual vorticity. The fourth component of the Noether current serves as the dual analogue of the magnetic charge, while the time component represents the energy. The quartet of quartets derived from $SO(4)$ symmetry generates further self-dual conserved charges. The remaining quart of $SO(4)$ symmetry components corresponds to a tensor field that acts as the dual of the analogue to the magnetic dipole charge. We anticipate that these unique and robust solutions will serve as a valuable resource for investigating the braid group and various other phenomena. Additionally, we examine a specific example of a non-trivial configuration. This solution can be visualized as a magnetic vortex loop encircling a magnetic vortex, which functions as a dual version of the Skyrme model's $\pi$ vortex loop encircling a baryon. We refer to this configuration as a \textit{dual vortex loop on a baryon}. We demonstrate that the volume of this dual vortex loop on a baryon is stable. We also explore the implications of this model for the dual Meissner effect and its relationship with confinement. Finally, we address the implications of our findings for topology, quantization, and dual supersymmetry. Our results suggest that the \textit{infant Skyrme model} may provide the necessary conditions for a comprehensive understanding of the confinement-deconfinement phase transition. Specifically, we show that the polynomial Born-Infeld model represents the unique self-dual solution to the \textit{infant Skyrme model}. Consequently, the polynomial Born-Infeld model provides the unique solution required to examine the confinement-deconfinement phase transition. This discovery provides a new approach to analyzing the relationship between confinement and deconfinement. This study numerically examines a two-dimensional Hofstadler model featuring time-reversal-violating (TRV) mass terms. In the presence of a strong magnetic field, the system hosts Weyl semimetal phases where chemical potential changes induce transitions between three-dimensional topological insulators and two-dimensional topological insulators. Notably, the Chern insulator phases required for this transition exhibit Weyl points with opposite topological charges. Furthermore, the Weyl points emerging in the three-dimensional topological insulator phase display non-compactness. These phases are further explored via the entanglement spectrum, which reveals states near Weyl points with opposite spectral flow directions. Finally, the potential experimental realization of this model is feasible using a single layer of $\beta$-WTe$_2$ subjected to a patterned electric field. The findings could significantly advance the experimental search for time-reversal-violating topological insulators. Finally, the associated numerical framework is released as an open-source project. \newline
Keywords: Topological insulators, Weyl semimetals, Hofstadter model, $\beta$-WTe$_2$, Berry curvature. \newline

We present a hybrid dielectric-plasmonic system designed to convert the non-radiative energy of dielectric nanoparticles into efficient, strong, and unidirectional spin-polarized luminous plasmonic photons. This plasmonic spin-polarized luminous source holds significant promise for a broad range of light-matter interactions, including chiral sensing, enantiomer discrimination, the quantum emission of circularly polarized photons, and spin transport. Current research into plasmonic "spin-hall" sources and the coupling of plasmons to spin-dependent electrons in two-dimensional materials has yielded notable advancements. However, the creation of efficient, strong, and unidirectional optically driven "spin-photon" luminous sources remains a critical challenge. In this study, we demonstrate that the dielectric-plasmonic nanoantennas described herein can convert non-radiative photons into strongly luminous, unidirectional circularly polarized (CP) plasmonic photons at gigahertz rates. Furthermore, we show that these plasmonic CP sources can be hybridized with dielectric "spin-photon" sinks operating at resonant frequencies that match their dielectric counterparts. This hybridization enables the creation of strongly coupled plasmonic-dielectric "spin-photon" sources and sinks, which are anticipated to be valuable for next-generation spintronics and quantum information technologies. Additionally, we illustrate that these systems can be engineered to achieve high efficiency, strength, and unidirectionality. Finally, we outline the design of hybrid dielectric-plasmonic nanoantennas that can be integrated into photonic circuits to direct plasmonic CP sources toward specific output ports. These features establish these devices as highly effective plasmonic-nanoantenna-based spin-photon sources, with direct applications in plasmonic spintronics and quantum information science. Specifically, we demonstrate that hybridizing dielectric "spin-photon" sinks with plasmonic spin-photon sources can facilitate the design of spin-photon gates and quantum emitters. Furthermore, we illustrate that these devices can be hybridized with dielectric "chiral photon" sinks to generate the most effective chiral sensing systems to date. In this configuration, the circular dichroism signal is amplified by a factor of 1000 compared to standard metallic nanoantenna-based sensors. Finally, we show that the hybridization of spin-photon sources with dielectric photonic waveguides can enable the design of the most effective photonic-integrated plasmonic spintronic devices ever achieved. Anomalous screening, a phenomenon where smaller grains preferentially fall through the gaps of larger ones, significantly accelerates the drainage of granular columns compared to the viscosity-limited rate predicted by the Stokes law for the finest grains. While prior theoretical work attempted to extend the Stokes law to accommodate this behavior, our measurements reveal a breakdown of this framework, indicating the need for a novel theoretical framework. This study quantifies this new theory, which incorporates both gravitational and viscous forces, and verifies it experimentally using liquid-saturated granular columns. The results of our measurements align with the anomalous drainage theory, which integrates theory, computation, and experimental data, thereby confirming its physical validity. Furthermore, the forces emphasized in this theory offer a potential solution to the "Jams problem" in liquid theory, which has historically hindered the advancement of theoretical models for anomalous drainage. Finally, the forces identified provide a pathway to explain size segregation, a critical factor in the geotechnical stability of sediment columns. The comprehensive forces defined in this work hold broader significance for the theoretical and computational modeling of both anomalous drainage and the forces driving sediment transport. Additionally, these forces may facilitate the development of new theories for drainage in gas-saturated granular columns. Our methodology also extends to other porous media systems, such as fibrous materials, foams, and biological tissues, which are crucial for advancing theories of anomalous drainage in fluid flow through complex porous structures. Our findings may also contribute to solving the "Jams problem" in liquid theory, which has previously blocked progress. Moreover, the forces we define are essential for theoretically and computationally investigating, for the first time, the mechanism of size segregation in granular columns, a mechanism that is fundamental to the geotechnical stability of sediment columns. Ultimately, the forces we characterize have broader implications for understanding anomalous drainage in porous media, including fibrous structures, foams, and biological tissues. These insights could also help address the Jams problem in liquid theory, as well as investigate size segregation in granular columns, a topic that has previously been challenging. This study investigates the electronic structure of silicene supported by h-BN using the GW$_0$ method. While pristine silicene exhibits a zero-gap semiconductor特性 with a parabolic band dispersion, the presence of the substrate breaks symmetry, inducing strain and buckling that open a 0.13 eV bandgap. The electronic properties are significantly influenced by Mn adsorption; at the hightest symmetry (HS) site, the system remains semiconducting with a 0.10 eV gap. In contrast, the on-top (OT) site exhibits metallic behavior characterized by Dirac cones at the M points of the Brillouin zone, while the oblique (OB) site becomes a metal with a zero-energy gap. Furthermore, the magnetic moment at the HS site measures 3.96 $\mu_B$, whereas adsorption at the OT and OB sites results in magnetic moments of 2.00 $\mu_B$ and 2.0 $\mu_B$, respectively. These findings indicate that magnetic moments on Mn vary depending on the specific adsorption configuration. Additionally, the hole effective mass in the presence of the substrate is calculated to be 0.33 $m_0$. Overall, this research demonstrates that the electronic characteristics of doped silicene can be tuned by selecting an appropriate adsorption site. Consequently, this work expands the potential of transition metal adsorbed silicene for applications in spintronic devices. Finally, this research underscores the critical role of electron-electron interactions in accurately describing the electronic properties of transition metal-decorated silicene. Keywords: Silicene, Hexagonal Boron Nitride, Magnetic Moment, GW$_0$ method, Electronic Structure.

Sgr A East, the largest HII region situated directly above the Galactic center, is thought to have been created by a supernova that disrupted the Galactic bar. However, determining the precise location of the explosion remains challenging. We analyzed the ionization structures of molecular clouds along explosion pathways using H${\alpha}$ and [N II] emission line data from the NGC1366 survey. Our results reveal a distinct separation between H${\alpha}$ and [N II] emission morphologies, characterized by a "trough" of low H${\alpha}$ intensity alongside elevated [N II]/H${\alpha}$ ratios. This pattern suggests the presence of N-rich molecular clouds that absorb short-wavelength radiation, leading to a shift in the [N II]/H${\alpha}$ ratio. By simulating this process, we identified two specific locations where a supernova explosion within an N-rich cloud could generate the observed ionization structures. These sites are situated approximately 0.5 pc from the Galactic center in a direction perpendicular to the Galactic plane. Furthermore, we examined the ionization morphology of Sgr A East and found that it aligns with our predictions, offering additional support for this supernova explosion scenario. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the supernova responsible for the gas dynamics of Sgr A East occurred very close to the Galactic center. This has significant implications for understanding the origin of the Galactic nuclear bulge and the growth of the supermassive black hole at its core. The [N II] survey technique employed in this study is also applicable to other regions of interest. Future observations of the ionization structure near the Galactic center are essential for clarifying the evolutionary history of the Galactic center. Text categoring, which involves assigning articles, emails, and blog posts to specific categories, is a prevalent task in numerous industries. Although most existing research and systems focus on binary classification, multi-class text categorization is a critical application for classifying content into several distinct groups. Current systems typically convert multi-class problems into multiple binary ones, converting various text categoring instances into categorial data. However, data imbalance often complicates the learning process across different categories. To address this, we investigated three data augmentation methods—SMOTE, CADE, and IRCADE—applied to the training data. Our experiments utilized the RcppML package for machine learning, comparing these approaches against standard training and the popular BoNMT model. Results indicate that for medium-sized datasets, methods other than standard training yield improvements over BoNMT. Specifically, IRCADE and SMOTE outperformed BoNMT, while CADE showed no significant difference. Overall, our findings suggest that data augmentation can enhance multi-class text categoring, though further research is needed to determine the optimal approach for specific datasets. We also plan to extend this research to larger datasets. The RcppML package used in our experiments is now publicly available on GitHub. The source code for our analyses can be found at: https://github.com/ahmedhaleem/Text-Categorization. The results are accessible here: https://github.com/ahmedhaleem/Text-Categorization/tree/master/Results. Our analysis is also available on arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.00021. Additionally, our dataset is available on arXiv at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.00022. Finally, the arXiv multi-class source code is located at: https://github.com/ahmedhaleem/Text-Categorization/tree/master/BoNMT_MultiClass. The RcppML package is also available at: https://github.com/ahmedhaleem/RcppML. RcppML is a package designed for machine learning in R that integrates R and C++ to accelerate computations, offering various algorithms including BoNMT, which is a bag-of-words neural network model. BoNMT is a lightweight neural network designed for text categorization that utilizes a bag-of-words representation. For more details, visit: https://ahmedhaleem.github.io/RcppML/. The COVID-19 pandemic has generated significant regional news consumption, yet limited research exists on how various factors influence the news online landscape. This study examines the relationships between regional news coverage, case counts, fatalities, and audience demographics. Utilizing data from 2019 and 2020, the research analyzes coverage volume, case trajectory, death tolls, and audience size and composition across 1,000 outlets in the United States. Coverage volume is measured by the number of articles published, while audience metrics include total readership and the proportion of readers aged 65 and older. The findings reveal a strong correlation between coverage volume and case counts, indicating that when cases rise, media attention increases proportionally. Furthermore, while larger outlets tend to have more subscribers than smaller ones, this advantage diminishes as the number of cases grows. The data suggests that when cases surge, both large and small outlets reduce their size relative to the volume of coverage, with smaller outlets showing greater sensitivity to the rising case load. These results highlight the critical role of regional media in reporting on the pandemic and underscore the influence of news volume on all affected outlets. The study concludes that further research is needed to explore the impact of news volume on different regions and demographics. Additionally, it raises the question of whether the surge in news coverage and the associated costs are justified, given the evident connection between rising case numbers and increased media attention. Finally, the research examines the relationship between large and small outlets, noting that smaller outlets may serve as a vital check and balance to larger, more influential media organizations. By understanding the dynamics between these outlets, researchers can better assess the overall health of the regional news landscape. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of regional news coverage in informing the public and shaping the narrative around the pandemic. By analyzing the connections between coverage, cases, deaths, and audience characteristics, the research provides valuable insights into the role of regional media during this global crisis. The preservation of angular momentum serves as both a critical validation tool and a stability indicator for time-dependent boundary value problems involving Maxwell's equations. The Rapid Multipole Method (RMM) is a grid-based algorithm designed to handle source and boundary conditions on arbitrary nested grids, making it suitable for both time-dependent and quantum mechanics applications. However, due to its approximate nature, rounding errors inevitably arise during calculation. This study demonstrates that the RMM can be modified to allow for the computation of time derivatives of angular momentum, enabling the direct assessment of angular momentum conservation. These derivatives are obtained through both time-discrete conservation laws and Euler-Lagrange equations. The proposed modification involves adjusting the coefficients of the multipole expansion used to represent source and boundary conditions. The method is verified through two test cases: one involving a scalar wave equation and the other involving Maxwell's equations. In Maxwell's tests, the results are compared against analytical solutions and an implementation of the finite element method, showing that the RMM achieves accuracy on par with finite element methods. These findings are compared with outcomes from angular momentum conservation tests. The mechanism ensuring accuracy relies on the orthogonality of spherical harmonics and the careful modification of RMM coefficients. Furthermore, the RMM's ability to maintain both linear and angular momentum across both static and dynamic regimes, despite its grid-based architecture, underscores its superior versatility and robustness. These characteristics establish the RMM as an essential element for high-accuracy boundary value problem solvers. Additionally, the RMM's high computational efficiency makes it ideal for applications in quantum mechanics. Specifically, the study shows that the RMM can accurately and efficiently calculate the time evolution of wave functions for the Schrödinger equation in both one and three dimensions, as well as solve the Dirac equation in three dimensions. In all scenarios, the results are verified by direct tests of angular momentum conservation. These outcomes are achieved through the strategic selection of basis functions within the RMM framework. Finally, the RMM's efficiency is highlighted by a comparison with the finite element method regarding the solution of the Dirac equation. The comparison reveals that the RMM requires significantly fewer basis functions to attain the same level of accuracy, resulting in a more than tenfold reduction in computational time. This conclusion is supported by the observation that the RMM exhibits both linear and angular momentum preservation across both static and time-dependent regimes. The mechanism responsible for this accuracy is the selection of basis functions that are orthogonal with respect to the Dirac operator. The sample efficiency of deep learning models is largely constrained by their reliance on extensive datasets. Although recent approaches leveraging external knowledge to guide model training have shown promise, traditional methods treating such knowledge as non-parametric resources are suboptimal when the authorities are actually parametric. We introduce a unified framework termed "data amplification," which transforms samples from a parametric authority into a diverse set of samples through variation in weight parameters. This approach enables the derivation of optimal transport plans between sample distributions and the construction of effective contrastive learning objectives based on those distributions. Furthermore, our method extends beyond standard sequences of real-valued tensors to support complex hierarchical structures found in modern pre-trained language models. Empirical evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our technique facilitates order-of-magnitude improvements in data efficiency for contrastive learning when utilizing parametric knowledge authorities. Additionally, it significantly enhances the sample efficiency of large-scale vision transformers for image recognition tasks and boosts the sample efficiency of very large pre-trained language models for next-token prediction. The entire method is implemented in PyTorch and made available at \url{https://github.com/mlfoundations/contrastive-data-amplification}. Source code for reproducibility can be found at the same URL. The models used in this study were developed on AWS EC2 GPU instances within the Milvus GPU cloud, operated by Milvus AI Inc. The ATLAS detector, utilizing 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data from the LHC at 13 TeV, conducts a search for Higgs boson pair production associated with a vector boson (W or Z). This analysis targets final states comprising two Higgs bosons and a lepton plus missing transverse momentum signature. No significant excess above the predicted background was observed. Consequently, 95% confidence level upper limits on the Higgs boson duo cross-section, relative to the Standard Model (SM) pp$ \to$ HH$\sigma_{\text{SM}}$ reference, were established for W and Z boson invariant mass spectra across mass ranges of 110 to 250 GeV. For SM-like production cross-sections, no exclusion is observed in channels involving ZH or HH boson combinations. However, for Higgs boson couplings matching the SM but with reduced masses (66 to 118 GeV), the exclusion reaches its strongest level. These findings align with and complement existing Higgs boson pair search results at both the LHC and the Future Circular Collider. Furthermore, these data constrain the trilinear gauge-Higgs coupling, a key component in Higgs boson production mechanisms. Additionally, the study demonstrates sensitivity to non-pointlike gauge-Higgs couplings, a feature characteristic of effective field theories. In this context, the derived limits on Wilson coefficients are comparable to those obtained in previous ATLAS and CMS searches for Higgs boson pair production. The outcomes are also relevant for exploring physics scenarios beyond the Standard Model, such as the Littlest Higgs model with T-parity. Finally, the results are expected to be utilized by advanced analyses, including those investigating new physics scenarios involving Higgs boson pair production. This paper details the event selection criteria, signal and background modeling, and the statistical methodology employed for the interpretation. Furthermore, an independent verification of the analysis was performed by a collaboration of external physicists. Finally, the event samples used for cross-checking the analysis are accessible to the ATLAS collaboration. To facilitate future searches for Higgs boson duo production in association with a vector boson, an optimized event selection and a streamlined set of signal and background hypotheses have been provided. A subset of the analyzed data, along with its metadata, is accessible via the ATLAS analysis database. We introduce a newly defined class of "spin lasers" capable of generating a coherent, well-defined vector "spin" composed of atom-by-atom quantum states. This laser utilizes an ultra-cold alkali vapor and is driven and controlled by a single, precisely defined optical pumping laser. The output consists of a divergence-free beam of polarized atoms, where the specific atomic spin state can be chosen at will through the configuration of the pumping laser. We have successfully demonstrated the operation of such a device using ultracold $^{87}$Rb atoms, with the ability to produce any of the five $F=3$ atomic spin components on command. Additionally, we have identified and analyzed several superradiant and quantum lasing regimes. The construction of an electronic spin laser is a significant breakthrough, opening the door to an new category of laser sources that handle matter directly. These sources will offer unprecedented control over the spin of cold, cold, and trapped atoms, finding extensive applications in quantum information processing, metrology, and fundamental quantum physics research. Furthermore, the development of an electronic spin laser paves the way for the creation of hybrid photon-atom "bipolar" lasers, which emit both a coherent optical field and a coherent atomic spin vector that can be optically pumped. This capability is essential for developing advanced optical clocks, including those based on optical lattice trapped alkali and transition metal atoms, as well as dual-species optical clocks. Specifically, an optical lattice bipolar laser emitting coherent transitions between two hyperfine atomic spin levels could facilitate the full implementation of quantum enhanced spectroscopy for future alkali atomic optical clocks. In summary, the electronic spin laser represents a vital component in the advancement of optical clocks and metrology. Finally, we outline a straightforward method for constructing various other spin lasers, thereby establishing an electronic matter source capable of emitting any desired atomic spin configuration. This achievement marks a significant milestone in the development of atomic and optical quantum technologies. We identify isolated values of $q$ within the moduli space of K3 surfaces where the Kuznetsov-Picard dimension drops to zero inside Kummer surfaces, resulting in exceptional properties such as the existence of Siegel disks. These values arise as special trigonometric sums linked to the monster group, specifically corresponding to the images of the fundamental cycle of a K3 surface under the K3 Shimura-Taniyama map. Furthermore, we demonstrate that within the moduli space of K3 surfaces, the locus where the Kuznetsov-Picard dimension is zero or positive has codimension 0 and 1, respectively. This finding resolves a question posed by Kuznetsov and Picard regarding the structure of this exceptional locus. Our approach leverages insights from K3 surface theory, particularly the connections between K3 surfaces, Fano varieties, and string theory. This structural understanding of the Kuznetsov-Picard locus is essential for investigating singularities and exceptional points using K3 surfaces. Additionally, our methods yield novel results concerning the topology of this locus and the dynamics of associated holomorphic maps. Finally, we suggest new directions for research on K3 surfaces, including the study of exotic K3 surfaces and the topology of their moduli space. We examine the decaying neutralino as a candidate for dark matter, investigating its ability to resolve the small group problem in cosmology by explaining the origins of dark matter halos in small groups like the Local Group. The decay of a neutralino into majoron and Nambu-Goldstone bosons is modeled within a $(\mu, tan\beta)$ dependent framework, where $\mu$ represents the Higgsino component of the neutralino. In this scenario, dark matter in small halos is found to be significantly majoron-dominated. We also explore the potential for detecting this decay through its resulting gamma-ray spectrum. This study in particle physics may provide a pathway to uncovering the physical nature of dark matter. The findings in this work may help determine the characteristics of dark matter in small halos and aid in understanding the formation of small groups. Furthermore, these results could offer a solution to the small group problem and contribute to solving the core density and core size problems. Finally, our analysis may assist in predicting the gamma-ray spectrum from the decay of neutralino dark matter. To achieve this, we derived the gamma-ray spectrum in the source frame and transformed it into the observer frame using the Jacobian. Our results indicate that the decay of neutralino dark matter into majorons can be detected via their gamma-ray spectrum, which may also help determine the lifetime of neutralino dark matter. The gamma-ray spectrum is shown to be independent of both the lifetime and the gamma-ray decay constant. Additionally, the spectrum demonstrates that the gamma distribution is primarily determined by the spin of the decaying particle. Our findings regarding the gamma-ray spectrum may facilitate the detection of neutralino decay, thereby helping to determine its lifetime. The graph genus refers to the minimum number of handles needed on an orientable surface to allow a drawing of a graph without edge crossings. In 1992, Robertson and Thomason demonstrated that the genus of a sufficiently large dense graph can be determined asymptotically using its number of edges. However, this original result lacked explicit constants, rendering it impractical for precise genus computation in real-world scenarios. This paper establishes an efficient algorithm for the genus determination problem in dense graphs and presents a formula that holds for all graphs generated by the algorithm. Consequently, our results unify Robertson and Thomason's findings into a single expression and extend the study of genus to graphs with fewer than half the necessary edges. Our approach is achieved through a series of asymptotic expansions for the maximum adjugate determinant of a matrix and its inverse, ensuring that the error term remains negligible even when substituting the edge count. Notably, all calculations were performed employing computer algebra systems. Furthermore, we illustrate a practical application of these results in the context of the classification of automorphic forms. Our findings also contribute to a broader conjecture by Thomassen and others, which suggests that the genus determination problem should be solvable in polynomial time for any graph. Additionally, we reveal a surprising link between the genus determination problem in dense graphs and the classical graph coloring problem. To address the polynomial-time determinability of the genus, we have developed two new conjectures. The first extends Robertson and Thomassen's asymptotic formula to arbitrary graphs; the second follows directly from this extension and serves as the final objective of this research. Both conjectures are supported by computational evidence and specific examples. The paper concludes with an appendix providing detailed proofs for the main results presented in this work. Notably, the proofs rely on an algorithm originally introduced by Lovász and Thomassen, which was previously considered impractical for dense graphs. Our analysis demonstrates that this algorithm is indeed feasible for such graphs and outlines the necessary modifications. Given that this algorithm was previously the sole method for genus computation, we anticipate our implementation will be highly valuable in the field of graph topology. Finally, we present a conjecture as an application of our main results, which offers a novel approach to the long-standing problem of characterizing the genus of graphs with a fixed number of vertices. We also propose a conjecture regarding the genus of graphs with a fixed number of vertices and propose two new conjectures to advance the polynomial-time solvability of the genus determination problem in dense graphs. Furthermore, we introduce applications of our main results

This paper details our methodology for establishing baseline models for Hindi and Bengali hate speech detection, as well as for benchmarking various architectures and transfer learning strategies. Our findings indicate that relatively compact neural networks, such as LSTM, achieve performance comparable to larger models like LSTM-FCN and BERT. Additionally, we observed that transfer learning enhanced performance in the Hindi dataset; however, it yielded no significant benefits for the Bengali dataset. This discrepancy is attributed to the limited number of training samples in the Bengali hate speech corpus, which renders the data more challenging. Consequently, we recommend focusing on developing richer corpora to enable the full potential of transfer learning techniques. Overall, our results demonstrate that even small neural networks can effectively identify hate speech in social media comments for both Hindi and Bengali languages. We have made our code and data accessible at https://github.com/rao1999/Hindi-And-Bengali-Hate-Speech-Identification. Our code is written in PyTorch, and the data is provided in CSV format. Our best-performing model achieves a test accuracy of 92.5% for Hindi and 81.7% for Bengali. Given our focus on Small Machine Learning Models (SMLM), the trained model requires only 1.2 MB of storage. Furthermore, since this task is a classification problem, we can deploy the model using the Softmax function, yielding near-instantaneous predictions. We also note that our accuracy metrics are conservative, as they are based on balanced data, whereas the actual production environment involves imbalanced datasets where such models still deliver strong performance. Finally, we intend to release a Jupyter notebook on Google Colab to assist readers in replicating our baseline results. This notebook will be updated to reflect the latest production results, which will soon be made available for download. We hope this resource assists readers in achieving the same baseline performance on both Hindi and Bengali hate speech datasets. Our production-level results are available here: https://github.com/rao1999/Hindi-And-Bengali-Hate-Speech-Identification/tree/master/Production%20Code. Our production model scores 96.9% on the Hindi dataset and 84.5% on the Bengali dataset. This improvement is primarily due to the inclusion of a new feature in our latest dataset: the sentiment of the original language, which we obtained by training a sentiment analysis model on the data. This feature is not part of the original competition dataset.

A time projection chamber (TPC) is a particle detector that identifies the medium of interaction (recoil medium) by simultaneously capturing scattered particles and recoil nuclei. In high-resolution TPCs utilizing gas as the recoil medium, the ionic charge accumulated on recoil tracks serves as an effective discrimination parameter, offering valuable information regarding the specific target nuclei. This paper introduces two observables derived from the charge distribution: the total ionized charge and the charge asymmetry along the scatter plane. These metrics are calculated from simulated events and are analyzed in relation to the scattered energy, as well as the charge and mass of the incident projectile and the recoil target nuclei. The total ionized charge is particularly effective for identifying the target nucleus in cases where the scattered energy alone is insufficient. The charge distribution also exhibits sensitivity to the velocity of the recoil nucleus within the TPC. The symmetry of the charge distribution on opposite sides of the detector can aid in determining the orientation of the recoil nucleus. Collectively, these observables are demonstrated to provide significant advantages in analyzing experimental data from gas-TPC experiments involving charged particle-induced reactions. The findings are supported by extensive simulations, and all results from these simulations are made available in an open repository. This approach facilitates the optimization of the recoil detection method and enhances the efficiency of the analysis workflow. Furthermore, it allows experimentalists to assess the feasibility of a specific reaction prior to conducting the actual experiment. To address the growing demand from the physics community for novel detector technologies, this work offers a valuable tool for the field. Additionally, the research underscores the potential of gas-TPCs as versatile experimental devices capable of studying a wide array of nuclear reactions. The methodology described in this paper is applicable to all gas-TPCs, including those under development for the upcoming ISOLDE/IGISOL facility experiments.
