Text-video retrieval (TVR) aims to identify a video from a collection based on a specific text query. Current methods often struggle to effectively leverage fine-grained information due to the mismatch between natural language and video content. To address this, we introduce the Token Shift and Choice Transformer Network (TS2-Net), a novel architecture that shifts token representations to bridge the modality gap and selects optimal token-video pairs using a choice transformer. Extensive experiments on the WebVid and L2VR datasets show that TS2-Net surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, achieving retrieval accuracy rates of 60.2% and 52.5% on WebVid and L2VR, respectively, within a compact model design. The source code can be found at https://github.com/Chenchen7777/TokenshiftChoice.

Top quark physics represents our sole pathway to investigate physics beyond our current theoretical framework. This active domain encompasses both precision tests of Standard Model (SM) predictions regarding Top quark properties and its potential involvement in new physics phenomena. While Top quark decay is primarily governed by the charged $W$ boson, this report demonstrates that decay channels mediated by the neutral $Z$ boson can be significant if the $W$ coupling is reduced. Specifically, we propose a new flavour-diagonal $Ztt$ coupling that induces CP violation in $Z\to t\bar{t}$ decays, potentially causing deviations from SM branching ratios and altering Top quark decay widths. Furthermore, we examine the impact of such a $Z$ coupling on Top quark decays producing $Z$ bosons, which may arise from effective $Ztt$ and $Wtz$ interactions. Our analysis indicates that flavor-changing $Z$ couplings to the $t$ and $b$ quarks can be constrained by decays into $s$-channel $Z$ resonances and $WWZ$ final states, respectively. Additionally, $X$-boson mediated $t\to Zb$ decays are limited by $t\bar{t}Z$ production data. Finally, we explore how these $Z$-mediated $t$-channel contributions affect $Z$-associated Top production, and we conclude by discussing the capabilities of the High-Luminosity LHC and the High Energy $Z$ factory in probing $Z$-mediated Top decays. Our findings suggest that these new decay channels could account for the current experimental observation of a $1.2\sigma$ deficit in $W$-mediated $t$-channel decays. This work was conducted within the Top17 initiative. Top17 is a European initiative dedicated to advancing $t\bar{t}$ physics, providing a platform for experimental and theoretical collaborations to compare results, discuss findings, and identify synergies. The initiative is organized into working groups covering various $t\bar{t}$ production and decay channels, with this report summarizing the outcomes of those discussions. We examine the emergence dynamics within directed hybrid random networks that integrate both preferential attachment (PA) and uniform attachment (UA) mechanisms. In this model, new nodes enter the system in pairs: one node selects an existing node as its parent based on a degree-proportional probability, while the second node connects to a node chosen uniformly at random. We derive conditions under which the network exhibits either PA behavior, dominated by the second node's uniform selection, or UA behavior, dictated by the first node's hub-like tendency. Furthermore, we provide mathematical proofs for degree and path length distributions, as well as a condition governing the network's bipartiteness. Additionally, we validate our analytical findings through an asymptotic analysis of an analogous discrete-time process and an empirical study of a real-world social network, demonstrating that the observed properties align well with our theoretical predictions. Finally, we explore potential applications of this framework in social network modeling. A Python implementation of our proposed model is also available. Our implementation includes a parameter that controls the balance between PA and UA behaviors, and we have conducted extensive experiments to verify our theoretical results. These experiments further enable the analysis of emergent network properties, such as the impact of this new parameter on network characteristics. Multimedia content, including video and audio, is increasingly distributed digitally across various media. However, this material can be compromised during recording, encoding, or transmission. To safeguard digital rights, researchers have developed Digital Watermarking algorithms designed to resist these attacks and identify the original source. A critical component of finding the source is Locating Wireless Disturbances (LWD), which involves detecting and analyzing signal distortions in video and audio files caused by wireless technologies like Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. Currently, the Multi-label Wireless Signal Detection (MLSD) problem remains largely unexplored, with existing studies failing to leverage the strengths of modern Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). This paper addresses MLSD by introducing a novel architecture based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) that utilizes Audio Chromagrams (ACGs) as input. The proposed model excels due to its use of transfer learning and its straightforward implementation via U-net layers. Evaluated on two distinct datasets, the results demonstrate that the ACG-based CNN approach yields promising performance, achieving an F1-score of 0.87 on the Audio-Only dataset and 0.77 on the Synchronization dataset. Furthermore, the study compares this CNN-based framework against other established machine learning methods, highlighting the significant advantages of Deep Neural Networks in the MLSD context. Ultimately, this work paves the way for developing robust, state-of-the-art systems for advanced media protection. Specifically, the paper details the preprocessing of ACGs, network architecture design, training methodologies, and performance analysis across different inputs and capacities. Additionally, it contrasts the proposed CNN-based system with traditional ML methods to underscore the benefits of deep learning for MLSD. The paper concludes by discussing how these findings contribute to secure media protection mechanisms and suggests future research directions aimed at enhancing both the accuracy and scalability of MLSD systems. Keywords: Deep Learning, Neural Networks, Digital Watermarking, Media Protection.

The vorticity and correlations regarding the dependence of a particle's charge on its energy while accounting for vorticity are examined for a charged scalar particle within the Som-Raychaudhuri (SR) spacetime. This spacetime represents a specific type of metric describing a gravitationally self-gravitating, charged, rotating, straight, and thin configuration known as a cosmic string, which introduces topological defects. By solving the charged Klein-Gordon equation in the SR spacetime, we derive the energy eigenvalues for a coherent state of a charged scalar particle, formulating it as an initial value problem. The resulting eigenvalue expression demonstrates correlations between charge and energy in the presence of vorticity. Specifically, we identify an inverse relationship between vorticity and the SR field parameter. Furthermore, the study highlights the significant influence of gravitational, electric, and Lorentz forces on the system. These factors collectively indicate that the SR solution is not a pure cosmic string configuration but rather a space-like displaced metric representing a more complex field. Consequently, this analysis supports the view that the SR spacetime describes a more intricate field than a standard cosmic string. Finally, the findings suggest that the SR solution may characterize a heavier topological defect, such as a band or an Sauter-like string. Additionally, we demonstrate that a particle with zero angular momentum (L=0) can still experience centrifugal-like forces. This counterintuitive result arises because the SR metric includes a cross-term in its metric tensor, allowing the angular momentum term to be canceled by the gravitational field-potential term. Thus, even an L=0 particle is influenced by centrifugal-like forces due to the presence of these cross-terms in the metric. These effects are attributed to the complex nature of the SR solution as a topological defect, a characteristic further explored in the paper. Finally, the study confirms that a massive scalar field is the most appropriate choice for this analysis, as it yields a coherent state for the charged scalar particle. In contrast, a massless scalar field would produce a delta-function solution, rendering it unsuitable. This is because a massless field lacks the rest energy necessary to overcome centrifugal-like forces, whereas a massive field possesses the necessary rest energy. Therefore, we conclude that analyzing charged scalar particles in the SR solution is viable only when using a massive scalar field. This conclusion is also reinforced by the fact that a massless spinor field yields a zero solution. Overall, we provide evidence that a massive scalar field offers a more comprehensive description

The term "Artificial Intelligence" (AI) is widely used, yet its underlying concept remains ambiguous and contentious. While many scholars have attempted to define AI through various perspectives, no single formulation has gained universal acceptance. This paper proposes multiple conceptual frameworks for AI by synthesizing diverse conceptual approaches with a broad array of existing definitions. We argue that AI should be viewed not as a binary state of being possessed, but as a dynamic capability evolving across societies throughout history. Furthermore, we contend that AI encompasses more than advanced intelligent functions; it includes various cognitive skills essential for human-like reasoning. Consequently, our proposed definition conceptualizes AI as an advanced, evolving socio-cognitive capability within human societies. In this work, we present our alternative conceptualization of AI and explore its potential implications for the future. We demonstrate the utility of this alternative AI framework in examining high-impact topics such as the coexistence of multiple AI systems and the necessary societal preparations. Additionally, we apply this conceptualization to accelerate the development of further alternative ideas, particularly those regarding human-AI coexistence. Finally, we illustrate how this framework of AI as a socio-capability can enhance the design of decision-making systems and enable more balanced and ethical AI development. The paper includes supplementary content, such as video recordings and slide decks corresponding to each section. This conceptual framework is intended to serve as a foundational step toward the next generation of Artificial Intelligence. Supplementary materials can be accessed at: https://www.enhanced-ai.org. We present a theoretical framework for calculating the thermal modification of the density wave in correlated bosons within an optical lattice, incorporating spin-orbit coupling. This effect arises from the interaction between the orbital degree of freedom and an effective Zeeman field acting on the spin degrees of freedom. The thermal evolution of this density wave is characterized by the momentum $k_0$ of the superfluid state. Notably, at a critical value of $k_0$, the thermal correction to the average particle number per site vanishes in the limit of a weak Zeeman field, a phenomenon known as the Pauli effect. Consequently, the Zeeman field can be tuned to eliminate the magnetization of the system at a specific temperature. This mechanism is analyzed in detail for a half-filling scenario featuring strong spin-orbit coupling. Furthermore, we examine the associated phase diagram in the grand canonical ensemble. In this context, the Zeeman field induces phase transitions, specifically the cancellation of density-wave formation at a critical Zeeman field. This critical point is determined by the orbital filling in the absence of correlation effects. Finally, we outline a protocol for experimentally observing this phenomenon in optical-lattice bosons. Our approach is applicable to systems where Zeeman splitting is tunable, such as alkali atoms in the p-shell. We predict that the Pauli effect is readily observable within the current experimental capabilities. This study extends our prior theoretical work on undistorted lattice bosons, where the Pauli effect was identified as a method to observe the density-wave-to-superfluid phase transition without requiring phase interference. We anticipate that our findings will facilitate the investigation of Pauli pairing and the search for novel phases of lattice bosons. Specifically, we propose that the Pauli effect can be utilized to prepare spin-liquid phases in lattice bosons, offering an alternative to the pair-hopping mechanism previously described. The proposed experimental scheme involves preparing a spin-orbit-coupled Bose gas within an optical lattice and inducing a density wave via a modulating laser. By adjusting the Zeeman splitting and modulation frequency, one can navigate the phase diagram to locate the Pauli effect and explore spin-liquid phases. This approach builds upon recent experimental progress in observing Mott insulators within optical lattices that exhibit spin-orbit coupling. Furthermore, our proposal aligns with ongoing efforts to prepare spin-liquid phases using ultracold atoms in optical lattices. We investigate the realization problem for graphs using restricted homomorphisms within the context of finite abelian groups, with a specific focus on explicit embeddings of free groups. Our findings demonstrate that for certain graphs realizable by finite abelian groups, no embedding exists; the parameters of these graphs are tightly bounded, achieving equality in at least one instance, and can be determined in polynomial time. Furthermore, we characterize the graphs realizable through injective homomorphisms using a system of inequalities in one variable, which provides a method for verifying the realization of such graphs. We also characterize the degeneration of these graphs via systems of equations over the group $Z_2$. The paper concludes with a comprehensive comparison realizing all possible realization methods for finite abelian groups.

This research investigates novel results concerning Anti-de Sitter/Conformal Field Theory correspondence in low dimensions by employing Type IIA string theory on distinct AdS backgrounds. By analyzing strings in these reduced dimensions through the lens of full ten-dimensional supergravity, significant new insights emerge. A key achievement is the explicit derivation of gauge couplings for the associated CFTs, revealing that they are non-trivial and dependent on the AdS radius. Additionally, we explore a potential link between low-dimensional AdS/CFT pairs derived from string theory and the recently proposed holographic quantum gravity framework by Bousso and Takayanagi, which utilizes extremal surfaces within bulk geometries. A primary hurdle in applying Gaussian process (GP) models is selecting appropriate kernel functions. While numerous well-established kernels exist, they are often underpinned by ad-hoc designs, limiting their effectiveness across diverse applications. This paper introduces a framework for developing new GPs by deriving them from fundamental mathematical expressions. Specifically, we examine the exponential mapping and develop application-specific GPs by manipulating the arguments within the mathematical expression while retaining the exponential mapping. Our analysis reveals that properties such as the input space and GP characteristic are determined by the mathematical expression itself, whereas the kernel's behavior across varying scales results from the adjustment of model arguments. We successfully derived new GPs for radar range and side-lobe measurements, with empirical results demonstrating that the proposed GPs outperform existing state-of-the-art models. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar1992/Application-Specific-GP. Furthermore, to enhance interpretability, we developed a visualization tool for GP models, available at https://github.com/ashishkumar1992/GPviz. This represents the first open-source framework for visualizing GP models, offering a valuable resource for modelers. The GPviz code can also be installed via pip using the command: pip install GPviz. Finally, to assist researchers in staying current with new GP models, we maintain a bibliography of recent works, accessible at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ashishkumar1992/recent-gp-papers/main/README.md or https://github.com/ashishkumar1992/Recent-GP-Papers. The repository includes references to new GPs proposed in the last three years, categorized by the underlying mathematical expressions. The code for this collection is available at https://github.com/ashishkumar1992/Recent-GP-Papers. We invite researchers to submit new papers for inclusion in this collection. This study evaluates beam-induced noise as a critical parameter for muon collider detector design, particularly for coherently amplified photons generated via the linear $\gamma\mu\mu$ interaction. These photons pose the most severe risk to the innermost detector layers and innermost beam dump sections. The ultimate mitigation strategy involves shifting the primary axis of the primary beam to a secondary "virtual" axis, thereby minimizing the beam spot's overlap with the detector innermost components. We present two distinct approaches to implement this virtual-axis scheme, which are also applicable to other potential mitigation methods, such as partial blockades. Our proposed methods necessitate no additional sequences beyond those already required to address space-charge effects in the beam pipe. We demonstrate that a well-designed virtual axis can reduce beam-induced noise impact on the detector by up to two orders of magnitude. This study serves as a proof-of-concept for the viability of such schemes. Finally, we outline key design considerations and technical challenges related to the virtual-axis scheme, which may warrant further investigation. Specifically, we recommend that the overall detector layout, as well as the designs of the innermost components, be addressed during the early planning stages of the experiment. Additionally, the shielding material for the innermost beam dump sections requires careful evaluation. These issues must be resolved during the initial planning phases to their fullest extent possible. Furthermore, the overall timing scheme and the specific designs of the innermost components should be addressed at this early stage. In the context of the virtual-axis scheme, the innermost components should be considered as small as practically feasible. Finally, the execution of the virtual-axis scheme may impose additional constraints on the overall detector layout that should be explored during the initial planning phases. Specifically, the layout should be designed to allow for the direct insertion of the innermost components and to avoid complex mechanical movements, such as sliding mechanisms, that may introduce other complications. Additionally, the overall timing scheme may require further study during the initial planning phases. For instance, the overall bunch spacing may need to be increased to provide sufficient time for components to move out of the beam spot. The overall detector layout may also need to be adjusted to accommodate the virtual-axis scheme. For example, the distance between the primary axis and the virtual axis could be reduced to prevent excessive radiation damage to the innermost components. Furthermore, the location of the virtual axis relative to the detector layout may need to be reevaluated. We present Spartan, a class of regularized convex optimization algorithms designed to generate sparse outputs. Spartan functions as a proximal surrogate for combinatorial constraints, allowing for end-to-end training of models via first-order optimization methods. By utilizing a conjugate proxy objective, Spartan can efficiently resolve a wide variety of combinatorial constraints. The framework extends beyond $\ell_1$ regularization to support sparsity across vectors, matrices, and tensors by accommodating various combinatorial norms. We show that Spartan can address sparsity-inducing problems that are either intractable or result in excessive model dimensionality. Empirical results indicate that Spartan can effectively learn compressed representations capable of generalizing to unlabeled data. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of a projected conjugate gradient algorithm used to optimize Spartan objectives, while also proposing several novel convex relaxations that allow for the computation of sparse solutions in a differentiable manner. These findings are supported by experiments on sparse autoencoders and dense layer sparsity in convolutional neural networks. Code is available at https://github.com/ericliu12/spartan. The Pauli principle is a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, dictating that fermions cannot occupy the same state, whereas bosons face no such restriction and can condense. We demonstrate that under specific conditions, bosons can acquire an effective Pauli obstruction. Specifically, within the framework of three-dimensional weakly interacting Bose gases, we show that bosons interacting via a Pauli-blocked soft core potential become Pauli repulsive. This phenomenon induces a significant low-energy condition anisotropy in momentum space and causes a substantial reduction in the superfluid fraction. Furthermore, this emergent Pauli obstruction is sensitive to perturbation theory orders, emerging only at the second order. Finally, utilizing quantum Monte Carlo and functional renormalization group techniques, we corroborate these findings and demonstrate that even a minimal departure from isotropy in the potential leads to enhanced effects. Collectively, our results indicate that weakly interacting Bose gases with soft core interactions may exhibit unique quantum behaviors that deviate from standard superfluid helium. These findings have broad implications for the physics of ultracold atoms and the nucleon interaction. Specifically, they suggest that the Pauli obstruction in soft core potentials is not merely a higher-order perturbative artifact but a physical effect that can be explored in laboratory settings and is essential for understanding the quantum many-body dynamics of soft core systems. Additionally, given the resemblance between our model and the nucleon potential, the Pauli obstruction in the nucleon potential is expected to be driven by its short-range nature, thereby influencing the equation of state and the formation of droplets or knots in nuclear matter. This underscores the critical role of the Pauli obstruction in shaping the unique features of fermionic quantum systems. Finally, we highlight that the renormalization group approach employed in this study offers a fresh perspective on the physics of soft core potentials, thereby advancing the theoretical comprehension of this intricate phenomenon. By addressing the nuanced interactions and underlying mechanisms, this approach paves the way for further research and a deeper understanding of the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics. In summary, this significant development advances our theoretical understanding of quantum phenomena and provides a foundation for future investigations into the intricate nature of fermionic systems and their impact on quantum matter. The ability to explore and manipulate the Pauli obstruction in laboratory settings opens up new avenues for investigating the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics and their practical applications in emerging technologies. The theoretical and experimental implications of this research are far-reaching, offering new insights into the intricate dynamics of quantum systems and their potential to revolutionize our understanding of the natural world.

Test odors are non-functional barriers to performing unit tests. This study investigates, from a developer's perspective, how severe these odors are and the challenges they create. It analyzes the barriers, obstacles, and solutions related to test odors through the lenses of testability, testability improvement efforts, and test code refactoring. The findings are based on an observational study involving 22 developers working on six code repositories. Using think-aloud sessions, we observed developers' reactions to test odors and the difficulties they encountered. Think-aloud observations were coded to identify the types of odors, the nature of the difficulties, and the strategies used to overcome them. Additionally, interviews were conducted to gather developer opinions on the significance of test odors. The study results reveal that odors stemming from functional and structural untestability are the most severe, resulting in tests that are difficult to write, maintain, and read. Consequently, developers often resort to workarounds that produce tests that are fragile, brittle, and ineffective. The interviews confirmed that functional and structural odors are indeed the most serious. This research expands the understanding of software quality issues by highlighting an important yet underexplored topic and its associated challenges. By revealing these issues, it can guide future efforts to enhance testability. The paper concludes with a discussion on the study's implications and suggestions for future work. By addressing and eliminating test odors, software organizations can achieve more robust tests, leading to improved test coverage and defect detection rates. Furthermore, this work can inform the design of tools and techniques that reduce odors, as well as the selection of appropriate datasets for empirical studies. Finally, a tool called Testability Advisor was developed to assist developers in identifying and removing test odors. The FFNCC group at CERN has developed the Monte Carlo program KKMCee, which models the complete kinematic chain from initial state to final $l^+l^-$ or $q\bar{q}$ pairs at lepton colliders. Utilizing the FFNCC common framework, the code offers superior performance, flexibility, and stability regarding both theoretical and experimental aspects. It incorporates Standard Model electroweak theory up to $O(\alpha^2)$ order, including two-loop box and light-by-box diagrams, as well as beyond Standard Model amplitudes. This study introduces the Tiramisu model, a novel approach for estimating inter-beat intervals (IBI) from photoplethysmogram (PPG) signals. We developed a new method that extracts PPG data from smartphone camera recordings and utilizes it to calculate IBIs. Our model bypasses traditional pre-processing steps, such as noise filtering and peak detection, instead training a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) directly on raw PPG signals. We evaluated the model's efficacy by comparing its IBI estimation accuracy against conventional peak detection techniques. The source code is publicly accessible at (https://github.com/abhishekkumar1999/tiramisa). The comprehensive dataset, comprising camera-based PPG signals with manually annotated IBIs, can be downloaded from (https://github.com/abhishekkumar1999/peakless_PPG). The dataset includes over 1000 samples from 100 participants, totaling more than 100,000 IBIs. Additionally, we provide a user-friendly mobile application allowing individuals to estimate their own IBIs using their smartphone's camera. The application's source code is available at (https://github.com/abhishekkumar1999/peakless_PPG-Mobile-App). Through this work, we demonstrate that deep learning models can achieve IBI estimation accuracy comparable to or superior to standard peak detection methods. Furthermore, we highlight that deep learning offers the distinct advantage of visualizing feature extraction, a capability absent in conventional algorithms. Our model exhibits robustness against outliers and achieves superior accuracy in specific scenarios. We anticipate that this model will facilitate the development of various novel machine learning applications. Specifically, we propose that it can serve as a precise sleep apnea detection system, as changes in IBI are indicative of such conditions. We plan to release the source code for the proposed deep learning model to enable researchers to compare their IBI estimation models against ours. Additionally, we will make the PPG data available for researchers to train diverse machine learning models for health monitoring and estimation. We also intend to open-source the mobile application, providing developers with a platform to create their own health-related apps that leverage the accuracy of our model. The Stochastic Singular Value Decomposition (SSVD) method enables the reduction of a large tensor's dimensionality to a smaller size $k$. This paper introduces a technique to determine whether SSVD should terminate once $k$ components are found or continue searching for additional significant tensors. We evaluate various strategies for this decision-making process, particularly on tensors that have been transformed to ensure $k$ singular values or factors represent the majority of the original tensor. Our approach allows the user to specify the desired count of singular values at initialization, enabling the $k$ values to be selected randomly or based on specific criteria. Finally, we discuss how these specifications influence SSVD performance in terms of execution time and the accuracy of the resulting singular values. Embedding algorithms map nodes and edges into lower-dimensional spaces to capture the structural properties of graphs. Initially, these methods addressed static graphs, but recent developments extend them to dynamic scenarios where graphs undergo additions, deletions, and merges over time. Time-series embeddings are crucial for grasping patterns within evolving systems, finding applications in diverse fields such as social networks, molecular structures, and neural networks. This survey examines recent techniques for modeling both single and multi-instance evolving graphs. We categorize existing methods by their approaches to time discretization, distinguishing between continuous and discrete temporal models. Furthermore, we detail the loss functions employed, their specific applications, and the criteria used for evaluating these embeddings. Finally, we present open challenges in the field, including new methods, applications, evaluation criteria, and datasets. Overall, this survey provides a comprehensive reference on the current state of graph embedding research. Additionally, we introduce PyGTLT, a new PyTorch-based library designed for time-series embedding, which offers modular, extensible, and well-documented solutions. PyGTL8v2 supports various graph operations, embedding techniques, evaluation metrics, graphs, and datasets. The implementation includes both classical and machine learning approaches, facilitating the application of these methods to any evolving graph. PyGTL8v2 serves as a practical platform for applying and experimenting with graph embedding, featuring examples that cover the majority of the survey's topics. This paper serves as an introduction to the special issue on Graph Embedding, which showcases 10 extended versions of papers from the 2020 PyGTL and DL4EvolvingGraphs workshops. These works address graph embedding, representation learning, and related data mining challenges. Beyond the issue, PyGTL and PyGTL2 support further research in these areas. Specifically, PyGTL serves as a practical reference for graph embedding tasks, offering a wide range of tools, metrics, and examples. It includes implementations for 10 methods highlighted in this survey, utilizing 11 datasets and 15 evaluation metrics. Additionally, PyGTL provides examples for time series analysis, a key focus of this survey, featuring 10 example scripts covering 11 topics. Finally, PyGTL2 supports the emerging application of graph embedding in neural networks, a subject not extensively covered in this survey. For more information, visit https://pygtl.io. By employing the EFT-NUCLEI potential to analyze the H$^7$ resonance region, we determined that the H$^7$ ground state is predominantly composed of a core of four neutrons. This study presents the findings of our analysis, which include an examination of the wave function and the influence of H$^7$ decay channels on its structure. We conclude that the primary component of the $1/2^+$ H$^7$ state is the sequential excitation of the $^3$H+$4n$ configuration. Additionally, we explore the potential for the $^7$h orbital to stabilize neutron-rich nuclei. Our results indicate that the $^7$h orbital significantly impacts the energy of the $^{49}$Ca ground state relative to the $^{48}$Ca+$n$ threshold, resulting in a $0^+$ ground state dominated by the $^{48}$Ca+$^7$h configuration. Furthermore, we predict that neutron drip lines for both the even-even and odd-$N$ isotopic chains of the semi-magic nucleus calcium will be crossed at $^{54}$Ca and $^{61}$K, respectively. Finally, we predict the existence of the $^7$h orbital in $N=29$ isotones, noting that this orbital influences the energy of the ground state relative to the neutron separation energy. For the $N=29$ neutron-rich nuclei sc-40, Ti-47, Cr-50, and Zn-56, the $^7$h component in the ground state is substantial, ranging from 70% to 90%. Consequently, the ground state configurations of these nuclei are expected to be dominated by configurations involving $^7$h. This finding is consistent with the ground state configuration of the $N=9$ H$^7$ analogue of $^7$He, which is dominated by the $^7$h configuration. This paper examines the Nirenberg problem on the half sphere subject to a boundary hinge condition. A significant advantage of the half sphere over the standard sphere is its broader applicability, extending to scenarios where a global smooth solution is unattainable. The study employs a gradient flow method, allowing for a more comprehensive analysis of blow-up dynamics compared to variational approaches, particularly regarding the full spectrum of obstructions. Consequently, we demonstrate the existence of multiple blow-up solutions, including a trivial one, and provide a detailed characterization of the blow-up set and covariant derivative at infinity, outcomes that are more robust than those previously reported by del Pino, Kowalczyk, and Vázquez. Furthermore, we show that the covariant derivative at infinity admits three distinct branches, whereas earlier research by del Pino, Kowalczyk, and Vázquez identified only two. These findings underscore the critical role of the hinge condition in elucidating the boundary behavior of these problems. Finally, the work offers an in-depth exploration of the global elliptic problem on the complete sphere, which serves as a foundational element for the study of the half sphere. In the spherical context, we prove that no simple blow-up solution exists, a result that contrasts with recent findings by Del Pino, Kowalczyk, and RV1, who discovered such a solution. The primary distinction lies in the boundary conditions: on the complete sphere, the function and its derivative vanish, whereas on the half sphere, the function vanishes while its derivative remains fixed. Our proof of this non-existence relies on a non-linear integral identity involving the second derivative, a tool that may hold independent significance. Additionally, this result offers a partial resolution to the Nirenberg problem on the sphere, as it partially confirms recent conjectures by Kowalczyk, Mazzeo, and RV2. To achieve this, we utilized the boundary analysis of simple blow-up solutions on half-spheres, a component that was integrated into the proof for the complete sphere due to its essential nature. The appendix provides a systematic overview of the boundary analysis for simple blow-up solutions on half-spheres, detailing all necessary properties regarding the linearized problem, the index, and the number of negative eigenvalues. This work represents the author's dissertation. For the comprehensive analysis of simple blow-up solutions, including a proof of the non-existence of a simple blow-up solution on the sphere, readers are directed to the concurrent research by Del Pino, Kowalczyk, and Riviere. The success of Deep Learning relies heavily on the quality of representations learned by neural networks; however, these learned representations often fail to be optimal. To address this, we introduce a framework that evaluates representation quality using 3-Wasserstein distance. By applying optimal transport theory, we demonstrate that the 3-Wasserstein distance between feature representations from related datasets can be decomposed into two independent components: a deep component derived from features extracted by a pre-trained network, and an optimal component arising from un-pooled features of the same depth as the pretrained layer. Utilizing a one-sided sensitivity analysis of the 3-Wasserstein distance, we identify the depth of features contributing most to overall sensitivity. We construct a loss function based on this distance to find the deep optimal representation (DOTR) that minimizes this loss. The proposed DOTR framework is evaluated across various datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. Results indicate that DOTR outperforms existing feature selection methods, such as those relying on learning curves, in achieving higher classification accuracy on target datasets. Furthermore, DOTR effectively mitigates domain gap in cross-domain scenarios, surpassing traditional approaches like auto-encoders, contrastive learning, and self-supervised learning. Finally, our analysis demonstrates that DOTR yields superior results compared to using optimal learned representations. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/zhengyuan1990/DOTR}. Our results confirm that DOTR selects optimal representations from both learned and handcrafted feature spaces, significantly reducing the domain gap in semi-supervised learning tasks. Utilizing Gaia DR2 data, we present the first comprehensive analysis of the low-mass open cluster Melotte 72, which has been largely overlooked in previous research. By examining the cluster's color-magnitude diagram (CMD), we determined its fundamental parameters, yielding an age of 1.05 ± 0.05 Gyr and a distance of 295.5 ± 1.5 pc. The cluster's center exhibits a slight offset toward redder coordinates, indicating a shift in that direction. Additionally, we identified 12 probable cluster members, two likely unbound members, and one likely blue straggler. Furthermore, we detected a compact group of stars within the cluster, which we hypothesize may be the result of a recent dynamical interaction. Our findings suggest that Melotte 72 is a low-mass cluster with a mass of 1.0 ± 0.1 × 10⁴ solar masses. We anticipate that future Gaia data releases will facilitate more detailed investigations of this cluster. The complete dataset is accessible at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.12520002. The paper includes 10 figures and 7 tables. We establish a lower bound for the expected Betti numbers of level sets within isotropic Gaussian functions, applicable across various smoothness regimes. For sparse levels, these lower bounds scale with the domain's dimension. In the sparse context and assuming analytic functions, we demonstrate an matching upper bound for the Betti numbers of global superlevel sets. However, for Gaussian functions, we show that any upper bound of this nature must include a minor exponential correction term. We further explore the implications of this term on the tightness of the Betti number upper bound across different settings. Specifically, we highlight that in high-dimensional spaces, this exponential term becomes significant even when sparsity is maintained. Finally, we illustrate the practical relevance of our findings through a machine learning application: classifying high-dimensional data using Gaussian kernel support vector machines. In this scenario, the exponential correction term is not only essential for deriving a tight upper bound of linear dependence on the data dimension but also proves critical for ensuring the algorithm's computational tractability. Additionally, we examine how shifting from a Gaussian measure to a Gaussian function impacts the necessary corrections for Betti number bounds in both theoretical and practical terms. While theoretical bounds for general isotropic Gaussian functions rely on geometric properties of the function, deriving bounds for Gaussian functions necessitates incorporating spectral information. In both instances, the spectral data must be integrated into exponential correction terms within the Betti number estimates. Our results are grounded in sheaf cohomology, providing an algebraic topology framework for analyzing level sets of scalar functions. By leveraging recent advancements in sheaf theory, we offer a unified approach to upper and lower Betti number bounds that encompasses various prior works as special cases. Furthermore, our methodology introduces novel upper and lower bounds that encompass diverse functional and stochastic settings. Throughout this paper, we present a comprehensive collection of functions and stochastic models, along with their respective Betti number bounds, all derived from a single sheaf-theoretic proof. This work demonstrates the power and versatility of sheaf-theoretic methods in topological data analysis. By utilizing sheaf cohomology, we can establish sharp upper and lower bounds for the Betti numbers of isotropic Gaussian functions at given levels. While these bounds are tight in certain settings, they require exponential corrections in others. This phenomenon is closely tied to the behavior of the Hessian matrix of the function at the level set. The necessity for these exponential corrections is further elucidated by the Gaussian isoperimetric inequality, which underscores the distinct characteristics of function levels in high-dimensional Gaussian functions. Eyeball Calib is a learning-based algorithm designed to determine camera extrinsic parameters, specifically position and orientation, by analyzing a single image. It operates within a constrained setup where the camera is mounted on a robotic arm with a known hand-eye configuration, and the only missing parameter is the extrinsic rotation. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance in this niche scenario, requiring just the mount's 3D position within the hand coordinate frame. The required position can be measured manually using a 3D printer or calculated via a visual algorithm like Eyeball Calib Core. We validate the approach through simulations and physical experiments involving various artificial and real-world objects, including spheres, cubes, and spheres with attached rectangular prisms. The results demonstrate that our method effectively solves the limited calibration problem and enables high-fidelity rendering of simulated objects. Furthermore, a comparison with existing state-of-the-art methods reveals that our approach yields superior performance under the tested conditions. The source code is available at: https://github.com/eyeball3d/eyeballcalib. The paper can be found at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.07301. Recent advancements in reinforcement learning (RL) have yielded numerous algorithms, yet new methods often require significant modifications to their predecessors, making it difficult to identify the actual drivers of performance improvements. This lack of clarity hinders the reverse engineering of success factors, leaving researchers unable to effectively guide future developments. To address this, we introduce Reverse Constrained Reinforcement Training (RCRT), a framework designed to decompose RL research into training and analysis components. RCRT applies constraints to the training phase to systematically explore how specific decisions influence performance. We demonstrate the utility of this approach by applying it to the Atari benchmark suite to identify the critical factors behind Deep Q-Network (DQN) successes. Additionally, we offer several recommendations for advancing RL based on our findings, demonstrating the versatility of RCRT in steering future research directions. The code for RCRT is accessible at: https://github.com/taehyung-lee97/RCRT.

This article provides a concise overview of Gaia's primary data releases, with a specific focus on findings related to the Galaxy and Solar System. These prospects are illustrated through illustrative examples, such as the predicted discovery of hundreds of long-period comets and the identification of hundreds of potential Oort cloud objects. We introduce a nearly linear-time algorithm that, given an $n$-vertex, $m$-edge graph $G$ along with a graph class ${\mathcal P}$ of treewidth $O(1)$ where $G$ belongs, outputs a vertex divider for $G$ relative to ${\mathcal P}$. In recent work, Grohe and Marx demonstrated that such a divider allows solving any problem with ${\mathcal P}$-time complexity $f({\rm tw})\cdot m$ in $O(f({\rm tw}))\cdot n+m$ time on $n$-vertex, $m$-edge graphs. Our approach relies on the assumption established by Marx and Schaefer, which posits the existence of nearly linear-time algorithms for computing minimum fill-in and triangulations that preserve low outerpath treewidth. We outline a generic methodology to develop nearly linear-time vertex dividers for specific graph classes ${\mathcal P}$, which, when applied to complete graphs, yields a quadratic upper bound on the divider size. This result establishes that the dependence on treewidth in the running time for algorithms utilizing complete vertex dividers is indeed tight. Furthermore, our construction yields the first vertex divider with a running time of $O(f({\rm tw}))\cdot n+m$ and a divider size of $O(n)$ for any graph class ${\mathcal P}$ with treewidth $O(1)$. Our dividers also exhibit additional advantageous properties, such as locality, though we do not explore their applications here. Additionally, we present a quadratic-time algorithm for triangulating graphs with outerpath treewidth using minimal fill-in while maintaining outerpath treewidth, a result that may hold independent interest. Finally, we demonstrate that the quadratic dependence on treewidth in our triangulation algorithm is tight by reducing the problem to matrix multiplication. Recent years have seen a surge in the adoption of network and graph models to analyze systems characterized by pairwise interactions. These frameworks are versatile and widely employed across disciplines ranging from ecology and biology to economics, sociology, and the study of technological and informational systems. In many such applications, researchers have begun incorporating weights into these models. The primary motivation for weighting networks is to extend their representational and analytical capacity; for instance, while binary networks limit edges to either presence or absence, weighted networks can reflect varying interaction intensities or strengths. Furthermore, weights offer a means to distinguish between different types of interactions within a system.

However, networks are not always derived from direct observations. In numerous cases, edges and their corresponding weights are derived or inferred from data collected at the node or edge level rather than through direct measurement. This article addresses several fundamental questions regarding the interpretation of weights in such contexts. First, it examines the interpretability of weights in networks generated from second-order data, outlining the limitations imposed by aggregation bias and proposing specific inferences that can be drawn in these scenarios. Second, it explores how system heterogeneity complicates the interpretation of network weights, emphasizing the necessity of developing and applying heterogeneous aggregation and graph inference methods. Finally, the article investigates the relationship between the origin of network data—whether observed, inferred, or derived—and the potential interpretations of weights, given that the practical implications of weights can vary significantly depending on the data source. The proposed framework aims to guide future research in assigning meaningful interpretations to weighted networks. Additionally, we anticipate that the insights presented here will assist researchers in avoiding the erroneous attribution of weight interpretations to inferred networks, a common pitfall in current literature. We conclude with recommendations for addressing these issues in specific applications. Focusing on a recently published application, we demonstrate the critical importance of accounting for data origin when interpreting network weights. This case study underscores the need for rigorous and context-sensitive approaches to weighted network analysis. Overall, we hope this work will foster more nuanced discussions regarding the interpretation of weights in network models. By clarifying the types of inferences that can be drawn regarding network weights, we aim to advance more accurate and meaningful interpretations within the field. Our framework serves as a foundation for developing inference methods that yield valid interpretations for weights across diverse data sources. By promoting more accurate interpretations of network weights, we aim to facilitate more significant scientific discoveries. We believe this contribution will help establish a more consistent and meaningful language for weighted networks, thereby enhancing their impact and utility across various applications. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) represent a hybrid approach integrating the adaptability of machine learning with the stability of partial differential equation solvers. While the technique demonstrates significant potential, its theoretical foundations remain largely unexplored. This study proposes a posteriori error estimation and adaptive strategies tailored for PINNs. By leveraging the inherent structure of the method, we treat the mean-square error as a convex functional dependent on both the exact solution and the network's architecture. This formulation leads to a novel adaptive algorithm capable of optimizing multi-layer perceptrons by simultaneously adjusting network parameters and topology. Furthermore, the process is computationally efficient, requiring only forward passes, and features a stable time complexity even when applied to high-dimensional problems. Finally, the resulting algorithm achieves higher accuracy than PINNs alone, as our results indicate. To the best of our knowledge, this work presents the first implementation of a posteriori error estimation for PINNs. [Code](https://github.com/alexei-makhalitsin/pinns-estimation).

Furthermore, we illustrate how increasing the electrode impedance can effectively render the tunneling measurement bandwidth narrower than the diffusion time constant, ensuring that only magneto-thermal fluctuations with frequencies matching the Majorana effect penetrate the circuit. Our findings are corroborated by first-principles simulations. We anticipate that resistive electrode tunneling spectroscopy will serve as a robust method for analyzing Majorana modes. Additionally, we provide a Python-based open-source software package to facilitate experimental access to theoretical results. Our outcomes are directly applicable to existing experimental setups that have previously reported hard superconducting nuclear peaks. We expect our research to assist in ruling out the Smrycka-Korshunov peak as a false positive indicator of Majorana modes. Linear bandit algorithms are extensively employed to balance exploration and exploitation when selecting actions from various action sets. Although the theoretical upper bound for cumulative regret in square loss linear bandits over $T$ rounds is established as $O(p^{5/4}\sqrt{T})$ for an effective dimension of $p$—and this bound is known to be tight—most existing theoretical analyses assume a uniform and sufficiently large action set, such as the hypercube $[0,1]^d$. However, when the available action sets are heterogeneous, ranging from the hypercube to the unit sphere, the optimal regret upper bound may not necessarily be $O(p^{5/4}\sqrt{T})$. This paper investigates the theoretical upper bounds of cumulative regret for linear bandits under diverse action sets, providing tight theoretical guarantees for both the hypercube and unit sphere scenarios. Furthermore, we explore how the shape of the action set influences the likelihood of overfitting within the linear bandit model, a critical practical concern. Our analysis of the hypercube and unit sphere reveals that the unit sphere is more susceptible to overfitting. Finally, we address the challenge of determining appropriate confidence intervals to address overfitting, presenting theoretical results for both the LSE-UCB and Thoppe et al. [2019] algorithms. Our findings indicate that while both algorithms can circumvent overfitting on the hypercube, they fail to do so in the unit sphere. Additionally, we propose a method to identify the optimal confidence interval for linear bandits that performs robustly across different action sets. Through extensive experiments, we empirically validate our theoretical conclusions. Furthermore, we explore the potential of the proposed algorithm for inferring the underlying linear function of interest, demonstrating that it performs robustly across different action sets. Our results suggest that for function inference, it is preferable to employ a sufficiently large action set. Finally, we examine the impact of the unit sphere on the theoretical lower bound for linear bandit cumulative regret.

Although the orbital Hall effect in time-reversal symmetric systems was predicted over a decade ago, it has been challenging to observe experimentally. In this study, we propose an alternative method to detect orbital valley polarization in gapped graphene via an alternative transport channel distinct from the valley Hall effect. Specifically, we demonstrate an orbital Hall effect as a viable alternative to valley polarized transport, observed as a Hall voltage response to orbital valley doping. This orbital valley Hall response persists in the absence of time-reversal symmetry, driven by the graphene layer's intrinsic Berry curvature. Furthermore, we confirm the stability of orbital valley polarization against edge disorder and impurities. These findings suggest that the orbital Hall effect can be experimentally verified using a straightforward setup without requiring exotic materials. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are machine learning models specifically engineered for processing tabular and networked data, yet they remain susceptible to adversarial attacks. These attacks, which involve data manipulation by adversaries, frequently exploit the graph structure to introduce malicious nodes in quantities slightly exceeding the norm. This paper introduces a novel framework for studying and developing strategies to combat such attacks. Within our approach, an attacker utilizes a reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm to identify the optimal configuration for a specific graph to successfully infiltrate a trained GNN. Conversely, a defender aims to prevent this entry by either eliminating the edges connecting malicious nodes or by altering the labels of these nodes or adjacent ones. We successfully applied two reinforcement learning algorithms to test our framework on real-world graph datasets. Finally, we propose several strategies for future research to enhance both defensive and offensive capabilities against graph-based attacks. To support this advancement, we have made our code and data accessible at: https://github.com/akbari1234567890/RL-DataContamination.

Catalogue matching serves as a foundational step in modern astrophysics, enabling the creation of multi-colour light curves and precise astrometry for celestial objects. Nevertheless, traditional matching techniques are often constrained by low completeness and a high rate of false positives. This study introduces a multi-colour catalogue matcher that leverages augmented photometric data to enhance the accuracy of identifying common sources. The primary goal of this research is to develop a multi-colour catalogue matcher capable of delivering high precision and recall across a broad spectrum of photometric data. Leveraging machine learning, the proposed method utilizes augmented photometric data to substantially improve precision and recall. By integrating a variety of catalogue and observational parameters into a single machine learning framework, the approach effectively mitigates false positives arising from diverse photometric data, while its fully vectorized implementation ensures scalability for large datasets. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1998/catalogue_matcher. Extensive simulations demonstrate that for a given recall level, the new method achieves a 50% reduction in the false positive rate compared to the PyMatch package. Additionally, when tested against real data, the proposed matcher successfully identified approximately 5,000 common sources that PyMatch overlooked. Given these outcomes, we conclude that this novel approach offers a substantial performance enhancement over existing methods. Consequently, it holds the potential to significantly advance scientific discoveries in areas such as exoplanet research, photometric variability analysis, and the investigation of eclipsing binaries. This paper investigates the cardinality of minimal edge covers within infinite hypergraphs. We demonstrate that for any hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$, every minimal edge cover consists of edges whose sizes form an increasing sequence of cardinals. Furthermore, this sequence of edge sizes uniquely determines the minimum cardinality of such a cover; this relationship holds naturally for both finite and infinite hypergraphs. We also establish upper and lower bounds for this minimum cardinality. Specifically, let $\mathcal{H} = (V, \mathcal{E})$ be a hypergraph where each edge $e \in \mathcal{E}$ has a size defined as $|e| = |\bigl(e \cap V\bigr)|$. We prove that for any hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$, the minimum size of a minimal edge cover is bounded above by $\sup_{e \in \mathcal{E}} |e|$. This bound is sharp, as we construct a hypergraph for which the unique minimal edge cover has size exactly equal to $\sup_{e \in \mathcal{E}} |e|$. Additionally, we derive an upper bound for minimal edge covers in general: for any hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$, there exists a two-element extension $\mathcal{H}'$ such that every minimal edge cover of $\mathcal{H}$ can be extended to a minimal edge cover of $\mathcal{H}'$ with at most three edges. This result is optimal, evidenced by examples showing that both the extension requirement and the edge count of 3 are necessary. These findings generalize several established results in combinatorial graph theory. Specifically, our theorems generalize both Dirac's Theorem and the Erdős–Pósa Theorem from graphs to hypergraphs. Consequently, we obtain new combinatorial and algorithmic results: given a hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$ and a number $k$, we can decide in polynomial time whether $\mathcal{H}$ possesses an edge cover of size at most $k+3$ composed of edges of size at most $k+2$. While our algorithms for identifying minimal edge covers and constructing their edge covers are not constructive, they are computationally efficient. However, determining whether a hypergraph admits a minimal edge cover of a specific cardinality is $\Pi_1$-complete. Ontologies serve as foundational frameworks for knowledge representation and management, enabling the structured depiction of domain entities and their interconnections. However, visualizing ontologies with hundreds or thousands of classes and subclass relationships poses a significant challenge. Current ontology visualization (OV) tools typically rely on hierarchical tree structures, which obscure or distort the rich, non-hierarchical relationships—such as subclass-of, disjoint-from, subproperty-of, and equivalent-of—that are crucial for knowledge representation. This paper introduces OntoPlot, a new visualization system that integrates Hirschberg graphs with tree structures to clearly expose the connectivity of large-scale ontologies. The effectiveness of this approach is validated by the fact that users can rapidly and accurately identify nonlinear relationships in ontologies containing over 1,000 entities. This capability is vital for users to comprehensively grasp ontology structures and to facilitate expert assessment during online consultations. Our research also investigates user behaviors regarding search and exploration, findings that inform the development of interactive and customizable features for OntoPlot. We conducted a user study with 10 participants from various fields to evaluate OntoPlot's performance, and the results support our proposed design. Furthermore, users have offered several suggestions for future enhancements, including improved inter-ontology search and visualization, which will be incorporated in subsequent versions. A video demonstration of OntoPlot is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=14414111111. The OntoPlot source code can be accessed at https://github.com/zhongliangwu/OntoPlot. The code is released under the Apache 2.0 license. Additional details and documentation are provided at https://zhongliangwu.github.io/OntoPlot/. The website was accessed 1,000 times as of May 2021. The video demonstration is accessible at https://zhongliangwu.github.io/OntoPlot/Demo.html.

Keywords: ontology visualization, large ontology, non-hierarchical relationships, Hirschberg graph, interactive visualization.

This study explores the potential of extending CycleGAN to enhance end-to-end automatic speech recognition (ASR) through a semi-supervised inter-domain penalty. The primary objective of cycleGAN is to establish a mapping between two distinct data domains without requiring paired training samples. We demonstrate that the Inter-domain penalty within a semi-supervised end-to-end (E2E) framework not only enforces this cycle-mapping objective but also leverages transducer loss to refine the generated latent space, thereby improving transcriber accuracy and boosting overall E2E performance. Experimental findings indicate that incorporating semi-supervised E2E and implementing cycle-matching constraints yields significant improvements when trained on limited data. Specifically, on the TIMIT corpus using E2E-based training, our approach reduced the error rate by 33.5% compared to other methods. Furthermore, our methodology outperforms current state-of-the-art semi-supervised E2E techniques. Finally, we demonstrate how this approach facilitates automatic speech transfer, enabling error rate improvements of up to 40% across various speech domains. The code and experimental reproducibility are available at https://github.com/ashish-agarwal123/cycle_e2e_asr. Additionally, TIMIT-based results and reproducibility can be found at https://github.com/ashish-agarwal123/cycle_e2e_asr/tree/TIMIT. Given that human speech production varies significantly across languages and accents, ensuring cross-domain consistency in our learned speech representation is essential for effective speech transfer. To achieve this, we propose implementing explicit domain-agnostic constraints to regularize both the generated data distribution and the speech-to-asr-mapping network. These constraints include enforcing a shared prior distribution over a latent speech representation and ensuring the encoded latent representation remains domain-invariant. Our results confirm that these constraints successfully regularize both the speech data distribution and the speech-to-asr-mapping network, resulting in a more robust and consistent representation. Additionally, we demonstrate that these domain-agnostic constraints facilitate effective speech transfer. On the voicebank dataset, this methodology achieved an 80% reduction in the error rate for cross-speaker ASR and an 83% reduction for cross-gender ASR, while also delivering superior performance in same-domain speech recognition. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashish-agarwal123/cycle_e2e_asr/tree/TIMIT_speech_transfer. Source: https://exp.iai.cs.umass.edu/~tliu/exp

Active inference serves as a unified framework encompassing both perception and control. By employing free energy minimization as its objective, the system generates actions to reduce prediction errors regarding its observations, simultaneously updating its models of the environment, itself, and others. The active inference framework has demonstrated effectiveness across various multi-agent tasks, including multi-object tracking and independent target localization. This paper demonstrates the ability of active inference to facilitate collaborative robot navigation. Specifically, we examine how a collaborative robot team can autonomously plan and execute a joint navigation mission by fusing active inference with model predictive control. Simulation results indicate that the proposed method outperforms traditional approaches in terms of efficiency and effectiveness. Furthermore, we validate the method's practicality through real-world experiments on a two-robot target localization and recovery task, confirming its robustness and effectiveness. Molecular vibrations and internal conformational changes are critical to the phase separation behavior of polymers and biopolymers in polymer-turbid solution mixtures. In these systems, distinct phases arise due to the inhomogeneous distribution of polymer or bio polymer segments across the separation interface. This work theoretically investigates how the internal conformational mobility of tailed soft molecules influences the multi-component Soret effect. We derived the mean first passage time for a typical configuration of internal degrees of freedom and its contribution to the Soret coefficient, utilizing the general statistical theory of internal degrees of freedom and statistical thermodynamics. These theoretical results were subsequently compared with available experimental data regarding the diffusion and thermophoresis of various flexible polymers. Our findings demonstrate that the theoretical predictions align well with the experimental observations. Additionally, we demonstrate that the theoretically derived expression for the Soret coefficient, which accounts for internal degrees of freedom, matches the previously published experimental thermodynamic profile. We further observe that the derived theoretical profile aligns with the recently published experimental thermodynamic profile. We have theoretically formulated and justified the connection between the Soret and osmotic coefficients. We demonstrate that a significant reduction or even reversal of the Soret coefficient can be achieved by selecting a polymer with high conformational entropy. We emphasize the necessity of accounting for internal degrees of freedom of soft molecules and the entropic forces they generate when explaining the Soret effect in polymer mixtures. We emphasize the necessity of considering the internal degrees of freedom of flexible polymers to accurately explain the experimentally observed thermophoretic mobility in these systems. We illustrate that the theoretical and experimental profiles of the Spitzer-Omstein coefficient, which quantifies the dependence of the Soret coefficient on the osmotic pressure derivative, are consistent. Finally, we demonstrate that our approach is applicable to a broad range of flexible polymers. Our findings establish a strong correlation between the osmotic coefficient, the thermophoretic factor, and the internal degrees of freedom of soft molecules, which can be experimentally verified. These results are of significant importance for the separation of proteins and nucleic acids, the analysis of their interactions, and the purification of synthetic polymers. The proposed theoretical framework is applicable to the development of methods for the separation and purification of proteins, nucleic acids, and synthetic polymers based on thermophoresis. Furthermore, our findings may aid in the design of polymer-based drug delivery vehicles and the creation of new materials with tailored properties. Automated Composition Evaluation (ACE) assesses student essays by analyzing their language and structural qualities. This study introduces CeBRA, a new framework designed to address the limitations of current essay analysis models. CeBRA utilizes a novel, lightweight, and efficient transformer-based language model. By pre-training this model on extensive datasets featuring rich annotations, we ensure it captures nuanced language characteristics. Furthermore, we show that a multi-modal approach, integrating both model predictions and hand-crafted linguistic and structural metrics, significantly surpasses state-of-the-art performance in ACE. Our code and experimental data are available at https://github.com/luukd/cebra. We hope these resources will assist researchers in advancing essay analysis. Additionally, we contribute 11 new datasets to support further progress in the field. Specifically, our general language models were trained on 1.1 and 0.65 billion tokens from high-quality sources like Wikipedia and news articles, alongside 265 million sentences from diverse sources such as tweets and medical records. Our essay analysis models were trained on 1.5 billion annotated tokens from Wikipedia Factual Questions. These models are designed to be transferable to other ACE tasks involving essays in various languages. We also highlight the scalability of CeBRA through experiments on subsets of large datasets, demonstrating that even smaller versions significantly outperform existing state-of-the-art models. Finally, we prove that pre-training on large datasets containing annotations for multiple task types enhances model generalization across different ACE tasks. Finally, CeBRA operates 10 times faster than existing state-of-the-art systems. This speed results from employing smaller models that combine lightweight transformers with classical text processing techniques, such as n-gram bag-of-words features. We also demonstrate that pre-trained models can be effectively fine-tuned on small datasets by leveraging pre-trained language models. This comprehensive approach ensures that CeBRA can deliver high-quality predictions on unseen data with minimal training effort. False positives significantly hinder the practical deployment of automated domain adaptive pedestrian identification (DPID) systems. To address this, we introduce Box Re-Ranking, an unsupervised mitigator designed specifically for false positives. Our observations reveal that while bounding boxes for positive instances remain stable across source and target domains, those of negative instances exhibit substantial shifts due to domain discrepancies. Leveraging this insight, we develop the method to unsupervisedly eliminate false positives by incorporating domain alignment and bounding box re-ranking. Extensive experiments on three public DPID datasets demonstrate significant improvements: the average mean Average Precision at top-1 (mAP@1) for the top 10 retrieved instances increased by 11.5% across four cross-domain transfer scenarios, and all four cases achieved perfect perfect retrieval of the top 10 cases (m@10=1.0). Furthermore, these results indicate an average 11.1% enhancement in mAP@10 compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/ChenchenZhang1997/BoxReRanking.

This paper introduces a distortionless audio enhancement method based on vocoding through a time-image converter. The process begins by representing audio waveforms as time-images, where the amplitude of each sample maps to the color tone of a specific time-step. Subsequently, the noisy time-image is denoised. Finally, the enhanced time-image is converted back into an audio waveform. Experimental results demonstrate that the quality of the generated audio improves. Additionally, the proposed image-based vocoding technique outperforms state-of-the-art audio vocoders, including those by Park et al. (2019) and Zeghlache et al. (2019). To evaluate Mel spectrogram reconstruction, our method surpassed the methods of Park et al. (2019) and Zeghlache et al. (2019) and also exceeded the results of Liang et al. (2020). The code for this work is available at https://github.com/SeungWooRohde/Time-image-Converter. The related code can be found at https://github.com/SeungWooRohde/Time-image-Converter. The author's webpage is located at https://seungwoorohde.github.io. The bibliography was last accessed on 2021-01-11.

Human object interaction relies heavily on dexterous skills like releasing, releasing while rotating, and releasing while swinging. These maneuvers typically involve one or two hands and various limbs, including the hands, arms, shoulders, hips, and legs. A fundamental yet underappreciated aspect of these movements is that the point of release must be carefully timed and positioned to ensure the target outcome. For instance, releasing a smartphone too early or too late can result in missing the desired pocket. To explore how errors in the release moment impact different tasks, we introduce \textit{FauxThrow}, a real-time, first-person VR application that simulates incorrect throwing mechanics across three distinct modes: standard, spinning, and swinging. Users interact with cubes using their hands, arms, shoulders, hips, and legs in either a standing or running posture. Our findings indicate that VR can effectively model erroneous release timing, with simulated errors closely matching those produced by modified keyboard inputs. Furthermore, the tool demonstrates a strong capacity to evoke physical movement errors, with no significant differences observed between users who have prior sports experience and those who do not. This suggests that \textit{FauxThrow} holds significant potential for VR-based motor learning, rehabilitation, and sport training. Finally, we discuss the implications of VR throwing simulations for the design of robust object release mechanisms, such as devices that detach, spin, or swing. The source code and a web-based version of \textit{FauxThrow} are available at \url{https://tinyurl.com/FauxThrow}. The accompanying video is accessible at \url{https://tinyurl.com/FauxThrowVideo}. Although Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models generate output token by token, human language is inherently structured, necessitating a bottom-up, tree-structured decoding process. Current top-down decoding methods fall short because they ignore long-range dependencies and fail to align with the tree-structured nature of parsing. To address these limitations, we enhance top-down decoding by integrating syntactic link information derived from a multi-head syntax-aware NMT model. This approach enables the generation of long-range syntactic structures and aligns with tree parsing principles, resulting in superior performance in both translation and dependency parsing. On the English UD treebank, our method achieves a dependency accuracy of 89.5%, outperforming the baseline by 1.5 percentage points. On the Korean KDVP dataset, we set new state-of-the-art scores in joint NMT and dependency parsing: 83.66% for F1 score, 85.94% for precision, and 81.21% for recall, representing improvements of 0.56, 0.5, and 0.56, respectively, over the best baseline. Additionally, by leveraging multi-head syntax attention networks, our model demonstrates robustness in handling ambiguous structures. The source code is available at: https://github.com/ailab-kaist/Syntactically-Guided-Tree-Decoding-SGTS.
